question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance in light of Drogheda Rural’s success in delivering the highest number of new-build homes per capita and already achieving his 83,000 housing target per person, with the Housing Infrastructure Services Company (HISCo) a key contributor, to provide, in tabular form, details of planned HISCo investment, including ISIF-supported investment, for each year from 2026 to 2030, broken down by local authority and, where available, by rural areas and villages, towns and cities; and to identify the number of homes each investment is expected to facilitate.
reply:
In response to the Deputy's question I am informed as follows.
The Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) invests on a commercial basis to support economic activity and employment in Ireland. As part of its housing investment strategy, ISIF invests across the capital structure to support the delivery of new homes across a range of dwelling type and tenure, including through the provision of development finance, equity capital and investment in enabling infrastructure. To date, ISIF has committed over €2.5 billion to housing-related investments.
ISIF has committed €61.5 million to HISCo, a 50:50 joint venture with Cork County Council to provide infrastructure to enable residential development, as part of its broader housing investment programme. ISIF's housing investments are made on a commercial basis and are assessed on their individual merits and their potential to support increased housing delivery. ISIF will continue to consider investment opportunities which are consistent with its statutory mandate and investment strategy and are complementary to other State initiatives in the housing sector.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will urgently review the exclusion of HGV driving schools from the diesel rebate scheme in view of the substantial fuel costs incurred by these businesses, the essential service they provide in training HGV and bus drivers, and the potential impact on driver supply to the transport industry.
reply:
The Diesel Rebate Scheme (DRS) is a State aid that operates under Article 7(2) of Council Directive 2003/96/EC (Energy Tax Directive/ETD).
Article 7(2) explicitly allows EU Member States to apply a differentiated rate of excise duty to gas oil (auto diesel) used for commercial purposes, provided that the EU minimum levels of taxation are respected.
The ETD limits the scope of "commercial gas oil" to auto diesel used by specific segments of road transport. In line with this, the scope of Ireland’s DRS is defined by reference to road transport licensing criteria and includes licensed road haulage (goods transport) and passenger transport operators (such as bus and coach services).

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he is aware that some homeowners and tenants in areas classed as at risk of flooding report being unable to obtain any home or contents insurance, including cover for fire and theft, and not only flood cover; and whether his department or the Central Bank holds data on the number of such refusals.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 404 and 405 together.
The Government is taking a comprehensive and proactive approach to improving the affordability and availability of flood insurance in the Irish insurance market with the implementation of refoms under the Action Plan for Insurance Reform 2025-2029.
The decision on whether to offer home insurance, level of premiums charged, and the policy terms applied are matters for individual insurers based on an actuarial assessment of the risks they are willing to accept. The Solvency II Directive restricts Member States in terms of intervening in insurers’ pricing or underwriting decisions. Insurers rely on their own claims’ histories, risk assessments, and cost projections when deciding whether to provide cover. Factors such as inflation in building materials and labour are also influencing premium levels across the sector.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare. Neither my Department nor the Central Bank of Ireland hold data on the refusal of home insurance or flood insurance.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether an insurer is required to tell a customer the basis on which their property has been classified as at risk of flooding; whether any process exists for a homeowner with no recorded flood history to have that classification reviewed; and, if not, whether he will consider requiring one.
reply:
The Government remains committed to protecting Ireland’s present and future generations by investing in climate adaptation measures to manage the impacts of extreme weather. Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.
In terms of assessing flood risk, insurers use a variety of different flood data models (both internally developed models and flood models procured from third party vendors). Insurers will generally utilise (i) flood risk maps licenced from a third-party consultancy; (ii) bespoke flood maps based on individual historical claims experience/risk surveys undertaken of locations, and (iii) other information such as the flood defence benefit area data provided to Insurance Ireland by the OPW under the terms of the MOU, if applicable.
Insurance undertakings are bound by the provisions of the Central Bank’s Consumer Protection Code (the Code) in their dealings with consumers for the provision of financial services.

question: Deputy Ann Graves asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he acknowledges that further price increases on e-liquid products in budget 2027 could result in consumers switching to cheaper illicit vaping products or returning to smoking.
reply:
The E-liquid products tax was legislated for in Finance Act 2024, and it came into effect on 1 November 2025. The tax applies to both nicotine-containing and non-nicotine containing e-liquid products.
The primary purpose of EPT is to address public health concerns and to account for the negative externalities created by the consumption of such products. We are still learning about the long-term risks of vaping, over time these risks may cause diseases such as heart disease, lung disease and cancer. Ireland is committed to protecting our children and young people from the harms caused by nicotine use. Ireland’s specific tax per millilitre is in line with the taxation approach adopted in several other EU Member States.
As with all taxes, Revenue's approach to EPT is to support compliant businesses and taxpayers, while using intelligence-led interventions and enforcement measures to detect, disrupt and pursue illicit activity in the vaping market. Revenue is undertaking the appropriate compliance work to ensure that businesses are properly registered for supply of e-liquid products. EPT is collected on a self-assessment basis and compliance with the law is enforced using the full range of compliance interventions and enforcement provisions for self-assessed taxes. Revenue compliance interventions are undertaken on a risk-assessed basis and EPT may be examined as part of cross tax head checks.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed Poland's decision to apply an 8% VAT rate to petrol and diesel from 3 October 2026; whether such a measure is compatible with the EU VAT Directive; whether he has sought greater flexibility on fuel VAT at EU level; and the estimated cost to the Exchequer of each one percentage point reduction in VAT on petrol and diesel.
reply:
The EU VAT Directive which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply, generally holds that all goods and service are liable for VAT at the standard rate which Member States must set at a minimum of 15%. Ireland currently charges a standard rate of 23%.
If a good or service is included in a list of goods and services under Annex III of the Directive, a reduced rate of VAT or exemption may be applied. Member States are permitted to apply up to two reduced rates at a minimum of 5%. Ireland currently has two reduced rates of VAT of 13.5% and 9%. Member States may also avail of a derogation under the terms of the Directive that allows for a reduced rate of VAT be applied to specific goods and services that have historically been charged below the standard rate and not included under Annex III. Reduced rates applied because of a derogation cannot be moved lower than 12%.
As auto fuels are not included under Annex III there is no legal basis to apply a VAT rate below 15%. As such the standard rate of VAT, currently 23%, applies to auto fuels. This rate can be reduced as low as 15% but would require all goods and services at 23% to be moved to 15%. The estimated cost of a 1% reduction in the standard rate of VAT is €707m. The full year cost of the standard rate of VAT being reduced from 23% to 15% is estimated to be €5.7 billion.
It should be noted that any VAT reduction may not be passed to consumers.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the extent to which the limitation of help-to-buy relief to income tax and DIRT paid in the State in the four years preceding the year of application reduces or removes eligibility for former residents who have recently returned to the State after a period of employment abroad; whether any data is held on the number of help-to-buy claimants who were not tax resident in the State for part of that four year period; whether any alternative support for such returning former residents has been considered.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 395 and 396 together.
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
It is a principle of taxation that those who benefit from an Income Tax or a DIRT refund must have paid the Income Tax or DIRT in the first place. HTB aligns with Revenue’s standard operational four-year look-back period. question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for electricity was set at 0%, in each of the years 2020 to date; the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for gas was set at 0%, in each of the years 2020 to date; the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for electricity was set at 0% for domestic customers only, in each of the years 2020 to date; and the estimated revenue foregone if the VAT rate for gas was set at 0% for domestic customers only, in each of the years 2020 to date, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 367 to 372, inclusive, together.
I am advised by Revenue that traders are not required to provide a breakdown of their supplies by product type or customer category on either their VAT returns, their electricity tax returns, or their natural gas carbon tax returns. It is therefore not possible from Revenue's tax returns to identify the VAT generated on supplies of gas or electricity by fuel type, by customer type, or on a monthly basis as requested.
The Deputy should note that VAT-registered businesses, which include the majority of large energy users and non-domestic consumers, are entitled to reclaim VAT incurred on their energy costs as an input credit. As such, the net Exchequer yield from VAT on energy relates primarily to non-VAT-registered consumers.
I am further advised by Revenue that the VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within Annex III of the Directive, in which case lower VAT rates may apply subject to certain rules. On this basis, Ireland applies the second reduced rate, 9%, to the supply of gas for domestic or industrial heating or lighting and electricity since 1 May 2022 and this is currently due to run until 31 December 2030. Prior to 1 May 2022, the second reduced rate of 13.5% applied to these supplies. It is not possible, under the Directive, to apply the zero rate of VAT to the supply of gas or electricity.
I am advised by Reve

I am advised by Revenue that traders are not required to provide a breakdown of their supplies by product type or customer category on either their VAT returns, their electricity tax returns, or their natural gas carbon tax returns. It is therefore not possible from Revenue's tax returns to identify the VAT generated on supplies of gas or electricity by fuel type, by customer type, or on a monthly basis as requested.
The Deputy should note that VAT-registered businesses, which include the majority of large energy users and non-domestic consumers, are entitled to reclaim VAT incurred on their energy costs as an input credit. As such, the net Exchequer yield from VAT on energy relates primarily to non-VAT-registered consumers.
I am further advised by Revenue that the VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within Annex III of the Directive, in which case lower VAT rates may apply subject to certain rules. On this basis, Ireland applies the second reduced rate, 9%, to the supply of gas for domestic or industrial heating or lighting and electricity since 1 May 2022 and this is currently due to run until 31 December 2030. Prior to 1 May 2022, the second reduced rate of 13.5% applied to these supplies. It is not possible, under the Directive, to apply the zero rate of VAT to the supply of gas or electricity.
I am advised by Reve

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether, in the context of the carbon tax measures announced in Budget 2027, consideration was given to extending to liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the treatment applied to natural gas and kerosene; and whether representations have been received regarding the tax treatment of LPG users.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 357 and 366 together.
As per the most recent CSO Energy Use Survey (2024), around three in every five households use home natural gas or heating oil (kerosene) as their main home heating fuel. Around 1 per cent of households identified as using Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) as their main heating fuel according to this survey.
The Natural Gas Carbon Tax and the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax on kerosene used other than as a propellant has been reduced to €48.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted.
These reductions were targeted to provide a cost reduction on the two predominate home heating fuels in the country, taking into account the extraordinary, market driven, price increases to kerosene since March and an anticipated increase in natural gas price inflation arising from recent increases in unit rates by major suppliers. Reductions were not extended across all fuels.
LPG used other than as a propellant does not attract the non-carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax. Only the carbon component of Mineral Oil Tax (i.e. carbon tax) applies.
The carbon tax on LPG used other than as a propellant is currently paused at €63.50 per tonne of CO2 emitted. This is the same rate that has applied since 1 May 2025.
Finally, LPG used other than as a propellant also attracts a 9 per cent VAT rate.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will review the eligibility criteria for the help-to-buy incentive scheme to accommodate returning Irish citizens who do not meet the full four-year tax look-back window; and if he will consider expanding the window to account for a broader historical Irish tax record or, alternatively, factoring in verified future Irish income tax commitments.
reply:

The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, is whichever is the lesser of:
• €35,000 (from 07 October 2026); or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
In relation to the Deputies' proposals, the design of the scheme aligns with Revenue’s standard operational four-year look-back period. reply:

There was a total of 112 certificates issued in 2025 for all Section 481 projects (including the 22 Scéal projects). To date in 2026, 98 Section 481 certificates (including the 23 Scéal projects) have been issued.

As the regional uplift was an approved State aid, any restoration of the uplift would require approval from the European Commission. While the uplift was not a Regional Aid measure, it operated by reference to the regional aid map in force at the time it was introduced. A new regional aid map, covering a significantly smaller geographic area, came into effect in April 2021.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there is a standard, predictable approach to calculating VRT for vehicles taken in from the North of Ireland; the criteria that apply; and if this approach is consistent between makes, models and engine types and sizes.
reply:
Vehicles used in the State are generally required to be registered here, and Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT) is assessed and paid at the time of registration. The calculation of VRT is governed by Section 132 of the Finance Act 1992, as amended.
Under the law, the method for calculating VRT on a vehicle is based on the Category of vehicle involved. Within a Category, the calculation method is consistent across all makes, models, engine types and sizes. Furthermore, the VRT calculation method does not differ according to whether a vehicle is new or used at the time of registration, nor does it depend on where the vehicle has come from. Accordingly, the fact that a vehicle has come into the State from Northern Ireland does not impact on how its VRT is calculated.
VRT on Category A vehicles (passenger cars and certain light commercial vehicles) is calculated based on the vehicle’s value and its emissions level, with the level of the tax increasing in line with both factors. There are two components of the VRT charge for Category A vehicles, relating to their carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrogen oxide (NOX) emissions.
The CO2 component of the VRT charge is calculated by multiplying the value of the vehicle (its Open Market Selling Price - OMSP) by a percentage from a 20-band table, with the vehicle’s CO2 emissions level determining which band applies. question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the current value of the Future Ireland Fund; and the current value of the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) and the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF), were established in 2024 following the commencement of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act 2024 (‘the Act’).
Transfers to each of the funds are governed by the Act. Subject to an annual fiscal and economic assessment process, €2bn will transfer to the ICNF each year from 2025 – 2030, while 0.8% of GDP shall transfer to the FIF in each year from 2024 – 2035. In addition, each fund received an initial transfer from the National Reserve Fund (NRF) in 2024.
Management and investment of the FIF and ICNF rests with the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA), who invest each fund in accordance with their respective long-term investment strategies.
The financial accounts of the FIF and ICNF are published in the NTMA’s annual report each year, which are available on the NTMA’s website. A detailed schedule of investments held by the funds as at 31 December 2025, is published in the NTMA’s 2025 Annual Report.
I am advised by the NTMA that the value of the FIF as at 31 December 2025 was €12.7bn, and that the value of the ICNF on the same date was €4.1bn.
Transfers of €4.5bn to the FIF and €2bn to the ICNF occurred in 2026.

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Transport the extent to which he and or his officials have engaged with the Department of Infrastructure in Northern Ireland in respect of a reciprocal arrangement for smaller passenger vans (details supplied) and so on, to operate in each other's jurisdictions; if he has consulted with Tourism Ireland in respect of same; and if he has engaged with the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment regarding same.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. Under section 6(2) of this Act, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the granting of SPSV driver licences. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
Under the provisions of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, operators are required to hold an SPSV licence and an SPSV driver licence to carry persons for hire or reward in the State. The 2013 Act and its requirements only apply to services provided in the State - it does not provide for services across a border. The legislative position in Northern Ireland is similar. Thus, under current legislation, a taxi operator wishing to operate cross-border services, would have to apply for and obtain SPSV licences on each side of the border. Unlike other areas of transport - such as bus and road haulage operations - taxi services are not subject to EU harmonisation, so arrangements for regulating taxi services remain a matter for the relevant authorities in each EU Member State, in respect of services that operate in their jurisdiction.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the progress made towards giving effect to the changes agreed between CIÉ and the Trade Union Group representing staff with regards to CIÉ pension schemes; and a timeline for final implementation.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.
Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department is progressing the agreement of bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including review of the relevant draft Statutory Instruments, and the matter of increases to pension payments.
Under the Transport Act, 1950, a Statutory Consultation process is required regarding amendments to CIÉ Pension Schemes, which took place over the early summer, and representations from interested parties required review.
This process has now been completed and the S.I. text has been approved. My Department is progressing with the printing of the S.I.s and I expect to sign the orders imminently.

reply:

Given the NTA's responsibility in this area, I have referred your question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you have not received a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Ann Graves asked the Minister for Transport in light of the new Road Safety Authority, RSA, leaner permit regulations, his views on the need for a transitional exemption or extension process for long-term permit holders who are actively trying to finish their lessons, rather than a complete financial and administrative reset.
reply:
My Department is committed, under Action 7B of the Road Safety Strategy Phase 2 Action Plan, to addressing the issue of learner drivers holding multiple successive learner permits, particularly those who have never undertaken a practical driving test.
The Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2025 (SI 527/2025), which come into effect on 1 November 2026, introduce measures to address this issue. Under the new arrangements, learner permit holders who have held a permit for four years or more must provide evidence of having undertaken a practical driving test before they can renew their permit. Where this requirement is not met, they must start the learner permit application process again in order to continue learning to drive.
After seven years of holding a learner permit, any renewal application will be treated as a first application. The applicant will therefore be required to recommence the learning to drive process. For category B (car) applicants, this involves completing a driver theory test, obtaining a learner permit, undertaking 12 Essential Driver Training lessons and passing a practical driving test.
The learning to drive process is designed to ensure that learners acquire the knowledge, skills and competencies required to drive safely and that they progress to fully qualified drivers. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding progress in legislation to enable the National Transport Authority to apply for planning permission for delivery of the BusConnects programme of sustainable transport corridors in Cork; his Department’s view on Cork City Council bringing forward the necessary planning permissions directly if this legislation is further delayed.
reply:
The General Scheme of the Dublin Transport Authority (Amendment) Bill was originally given approval by Government on 17 September 2025. The Bill passed second stage in the Dail on 26 May 2026 and Committee Stage on 24 June 2026. I anticipate a date to be set for Report Stage in the Dail shortly.
The purpose of the Bill is to provide a clear legislative framework to extend the National Transport Authority’s (NTA) remit under section 44 of the Dublin Transport Authority Act 2008 (Act of 2008), to enable the NTA to undertake the construction of public transport infrastructure projects, such as BusConnects, in the State, as it currently does in the Greater Dublin Area (GDA).
For large scale projects it is important to have a National Authority who can provide public transport infrastructure outside of the Greater Dublin Area. The NTA has the capacity and experience in progressing megaprojects, having successfully secured planning consents for all 12 of its Core Bus Corridor schemes in Dublin as of 2025.
The provisions of the Bill will ensure Government’s ambition in megaproject delivery is complemented by a robust and appropriate legislative framework and will allow the NTA to submit planning applications to An Coimisiún Pleanála in respect of the infrastructure elements of BusConnects Cork.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 93 of 13 October 2026, the details of the re-examination of policy; the process envisaged as part of engagement with the National Transport Authority and Dublin City Council in coming weeks to determine the most appropriate next steps; the intended steps to be proposed by his Department; if those steps include legislation; the powers An Garda Síochána possesses to act against motorised rickshaws carrying passengers for reward; and the adequacy of same.
reply:
Further to Parliamentary Question No. 93 of 13 October 2026, I have written to both the National Transport Authority (NTA) and Dublin City Council outlining that I intend to hold a meeting with them in the coming weeks to discuss how regulation for rickshaws is best achieved.
The drivers of all vehicles used on public roads, including rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner, paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána. If a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is essentially considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles, i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with road traffic regulations.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the position Ireland intends to adopt on the joint proposal from the Governments of Germany and France to reduce the EU's mandatory CO emissions cut for new cars by 2035 from 100% to 80%, compared with 2021 levels at the EU Council meeting on 15 of October 2026.
reply:
The European Commission's December 2025 Automotive Package proposal moved away from the existing 100% tailpipe emissions reduction requirement for new cars from 2035 by proposing a 90% CO2 reduction target, with the remaining 10% addressed through a system of credits linked to low-carbon fuels and materials.
As of 16 October 2026, it is understood that France and Germany have reached political agreement on a common position on the Automotive Package. One element of their position is a 90% CO2 reduction target from 2035 without an offset requirement to be compensated by manufacturers through the use of low carbon steel or fuel credits.
The position put forward by France and Germany will need to be considered carefully by Member States through the normal Council legislative process. No agreement has yet been reached at Council level on this matter.
In its role as Presidency of the Council of the European Union, Ireland will continue to act as an honest broker, facilitating discussions among Member States and seeking progress on the file while ensuring that all views are fully reflected in the negotiations.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Transport the reasons for the ongoing delays in obtaining a category B driving test at Tallaght Driving Test Centre, where the estimated waiting time is 23 weeks as of 12 October 2026, compared with the Road Safety Authority's 10-week service-level target; the measures are being taken to reduce the waiting time; and the expected timeframe for bringing it in line with the target.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for all aspects of the National Driver Testing Service. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Authority for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.
Pending this response, I am assured by the RSA that work is continuing to reduce the waiting time for an invitation to book a driving test at all test centres in line with the target 10-week service level agreement. reply:

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Transport the action being undertaken by his Department for the provision of a specific electric vehicle (EV) charging point app which would include all EV charging providers, in order to provide a more streamlined and user-friendly service, in view that at present each provider has their own individual downloadable app.
reply:
The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), which has applied directly across the European Union since 13 April 2024, aims to improve the user experience for electric vehicle drivers by ensuring that publicly accessible charge points can be used without the need for a subscription or a specific mobile application.
Under AFIR, operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure are required to provide ad hoc charging and payment options, allowing EV drivers to charge their vehicles without entering into a contract with a particular charge point operator. This is intended to reduce reliance on multiple operator-specific applications and make public charging more convenient and accessible for consumers.
The Regulation also includes requirements for operators of publicly accessible charging infrastructure (who require payment for the recharging service) to set up an Application Programme Interface (API) that provides free and unrestricted access to both static and dynamic charging data, in order for the data to be made accessible on an open and non-discriminatory basis to all data users through national access points (in accordance with the relevant provisions related to such data). This will support the development of consumer applications that can provide information across multiple charging networks. A number of third-party apps are currently available and providing this data to the public that are not limited to any one charging operator.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Transport if he supports the transfer of responsibility for alcohol and psychoactive substance testing of aviation personnel from State authorities to individual airlines or other private entities; if the constitutional, employment-law, licensing, criminal-law, privacy, data-protection and fair-procedure implications of such a transfer have been fully examined; and whether consideration has been given to retaining testing as an independent State function while providing the IAA and/or An Garda Síochána with the resources necessary to operate an effective testing regime.
reply:
On 29 September the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) commenced a public consultation on the future regulatory approach to drug and alcohol testing in the Irish aviation sector. The consultation seeks the views of aviation stakeholders, employees, industry representative bodies, public authorities and members of the public on the most appropriate means of introducing a comprehensive framework to manage the safety risks associated with impairment arising from alcohol and other psychoactive substances. The deadline for submissions is 31 October 2026.
While the IAA is seeking views on a proposed Employer-Led Testing Framework with IAA Oversight, no decision has been taken yet on state policy in this area. The purpose of the consultation is to gather evidence, perspectives and views of all relevant stakeholders to inform future policy development.
My department will be engaging with the IAA following completion of the consultation process.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade which of the 23 commitments in Ireland's Diaspora Strategy 2026 to 2030 relate to access to housing for Irish citizens returning to the State; if the Department or the Minister of State for international development and the diaspora has engaged with the Department of Finance or the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on a housing or tax support for returning emigrants; if so, the outcome of any such engagement.
reply:
Ireland’s Diaspora Strategy 2026-2030 sets out 23 commitments across five interconnected threads: wellbeing and advocacy; identity and culture; connection and contribution; departure and return; and sharing our experience. The drafting of the strategy followed a year-long consultation of the Irish abroad, with 27 meetings in 17 countries, which were complemented by the first ever online survey of our diaspora, the Global Irish Survey, which received almost 10,000 responses.
The Strategy recognises that many returning emigrants can face practical challenges on their return to the State and, in line with the Programme for Government, commits to facilitating their return including through addressing administrative challenges and improving access to information and supports.
I am conscious that issues relating to housing can impact on someone's decision to return to Ireland. In responding to those who raised this with me directly during the consultations, I noted that housing, among other matters, are not just of concern to the diaspora but also affect people living in Ireland. Addressing them is a key priority for the Government and this work will go on outside of the diaspora strategy. This approach is reflected in the Diaspora Strategy (on page 6 and page 12).
I have not had any discussion with the Department of Finance or the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage on a housing or tax support for returning emigrants.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on the interstate case against the British Government regarding the Legacy and Reconciliation Act.
reply:

Last year’s Joint Framework was a momentous step forward, and what is needed now is full and faithful implementation of what was agreed.

I had further constructive engagements with the Secretary of State in Belfast in recent weeks as his team worked to progressing the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill’s progress to Committee Stage at Westminster.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding the total number of Irish passport cards issued since their launch in 2015, broken down by year.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 186, 187 and 192 together.
The passport card was launched in October 2015 and offers Irish citizens the convenience of travel, with a credit card sized travel document, to all EU Member States, the members of the EEA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), Switzerland and the United Kingdom. The Passport Card is fully compliant with International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) regulations concerning requirements for passports in card format.
In June 2026, I launched a next-generation passport book and card featuring world-first security technologies. In conjunction with the launch of the new book and card, the Passport Service engaged with national government border control and immigration authorities worldwide to advise them of the updates to Ireland's secure travel documents.
Each individual national government border control and immigration authorities are responsible for machine-readable zone (MRZ) scanners and automated e-gates at their airports. Government agencies maintain border sovereignty, deploy the scanning hardware, and run the security database checks. It is up to each country to ensure it keeps up with the advancement in passport design and enhancements. It was ensured, via the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, that all e-gates at Dublin airport received this update prior to the launch of the new passport book and card.
The Passport Service engages directly with over half a million citizens annually through it

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cé mhéad go sonrach atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na nOileán agus cé mhéad atá le baint ó bhuiséad caipitil na Gaeltachta sa chiorrú atá leagtha amach sa Bhuiséad ar airgead caipitil na Gaeltachta agus na nOileán ó €55,362,000 in 2026 go €50,362,000 in 2027.
reply:
Tá leithdháileadh iomlán de €628 milliún faighte ag mo Roinn i gCáinaisnéis 2027, lena n-áirítear leithdháileadh caiptil de €273 milliún. Foilseofar leithdháileadh mionsonraithe de réir fomhír san Imleabhar Meastachán Athbhreithnithe (REV) roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tá pleananna fíor-uaillmhianacha ag mo Roinn d'fhorbairtí caipitil chun tacú le pobail Ghaeltachta, pobal na Gaeilge agus pobail na n-oileán araon. Maoinítear na forbairtí seo as Clár C de bhuiséad na Roinne - An Ghaeltacht, an Ghaeilge agus na hOileáin. Is fiú a mheabhrú gur tháinig ardú ar an mbuiséad caipitil do Chlár C ó €30 milliún in 2025 go beagnach €55 milliún in 2026. Bhain cuid mhaith den ardú sin le trí phríomhthionscadal infreastruchtúir:
• Cé Inis Oírr,
• An tIonad Gaeilge agus Cultúir ar Shráid Fhearchair, agus
• athfhorbairt shuíomh Choláiste Lurgan in Indreabhán mar Ionad Oideachais agus Óige do Ghaeltacht Chonamara.
Rinneadh gealltanas i leith na dtionscadal seo sa Phlean Forbartha Náisiúnta, agus is cúis áthais dom an maoiniú a fháil chun iad a thabhairt i gcrích anois. Táim den tuairim mheáite go mbeidh an t-allúntas caipitil atá faighte ag mo Roinn leordhóthanach le freastal ar riachtanais chlár na Gaeltachta, na Gaeilge agus na nOileán i 2027 agus sna blianta ina dhiaidh sin.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will bring forward approvals for the current CCIF program for emergency cases.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality community facilities that are available to community groups in both urban and rural communities. Through the CCIF, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
I launched the latest round of funding under CCIF 2026 on the 26th March for enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres. The fund will be delivered across 2 categories with maximum funding levels of €25,000 and €100,000 respectively. The closing date for the CCIF 2026 has now passed.
I am committed to ensuring the applications received are processed quickly. Applications are currently being assessed and I expect to announce the successful projects under category 1 which provides funding of up to €25,000 in the coming weeks with approvals under category 2 providing funding of up to €100,000 being announced before year-end.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when the next round of the Local Enhancement Programme will be announced; and the level of funding that will be available for community groups.
reply:
The Local Enhancement Programme (LEP) is targeted towards supporting communities that are impacted by disadvantage, as identified in the Local Economic and Community Plan (LECP) of the relevant local authority. It generally provides small capital grants to community and voluntary groups for the improvement/refurbishment of their facilities and/or the purchase of equipment. The fund is administered locally on behalf of the Department by Local Community Development Committees (LCDCs) across the country, with support from their local authority.
The Local Enhancement Programme (LEP) for 2026 provided €7 million in capital supports. Each LCDC decided the projects that were funded under LEP 2026. The closing date for community groups to submit applications for LEP 2026 was 27 February 2026 and the list of successful projects was announced on 2 July 2026. Therefore, the 2026 programme is now closed.
I was delighted to secure current funding of €2 million for the LEP in Budget 2027 to assist community organisations in easing the pressure of rising operating costs. This is in addition to €5 million in capital funding that is available for LEP 2027. My Department is currently considering the detailed design of the LEP for 2027 and I hope to announce the new programme before the end of this year.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the level of funding remaining under the LEADER Programme 2023-2027; and the measures being taken to ensure that funding is fully utilised.
reply:
The LEADER Programme is co-funded by the European Union and is delivered through Local Action Groups (LAGs) across rural Ireland. A feature of the LEADER programme is that it is based on a community-led, bottom-up approach to rural development.
The 2023-2027 LEADER programme has total funding of €180 million, with 75% or €135 million available to support projects being completed by rural groups and businesses.
The funding is allocated in advance to LAGs to provide them with greater flexibility to manage their budgets over the programming period. Funding is then paid out by my Department as costs are incurred and claims for payment are submitted.
Using this allocation, LEADER LAGs have approved funding of over €76.8 million for some 1,537 LEADER projects countrywide. This means that c. 57% of the overall project allocation is committed, with some €58 million or 43% remaining. Of these, 551 projects have been completed to date, with the remainder due to be completed over the coming months and years. There are an additional 172 projects progressing through the approval stages across all sub-regional areas.
The €180 million also includes €45 million (or 25%) which is available to support the administration and animation costs of the LAGs involved in running the programme. Of this, €20.1 million has been drawn down to date, with some €24.9 million remaining. question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the funding allocated to the Social Inclusion and Community Action Programme (SICAP) for 2027.
reply: The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland's primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities across the country. The programme works with individuals and local community groups to address barriers to participation and strengthen community capacity. I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country. It should be noted that the final estimated allocations for each area will be confirmed in the Revised Estimates Volume which will be published in December, and considered by the relevant select committees. A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. This represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable, long-term basis. This provides greater certainty for those planning and delivering services and helps sustain integration supports in communities. My Department remains committed to supporting this important work and ensuring that SICAP continues to respond to the needs of disadvantage

• €74 million for social inclusion, including almost €65 million for the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP), which supports disadvantaged individuals and communities to participate more fully in local life.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the steps his Department is taking to assist students following the unexpected and immediate closure of a language college in Cork (details supplied) given that the abrupt closure of the college has left students who rely on it for their immigration status in a uncertain and distressing situation.
reply:
My Department is aware of the closure of the English language education provider in question.
As a private provider, it does not come under the remit of my Department. Nor does my Department have a role in issues arising from a private contract between a student and a provider.
However, such a closure creates uncertainty which has a significant impact on the learners, prospective students, and staff of that provider.
For a provider to be eligible to recruit students from non-EEA countries, the provider’s courses must be included on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP). The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with my Department. The provider in question was an ILEP listed provider.
ILEP listed providers are required to have arrangements in place for the protection of enrolled learners. These arrangements are to protect learners in the event that a provider fails, closes or is unable to deliver an ILEP-listed programme. In this case, the provider has had arrangements in place via an insurance product with Arachas.
The provider has been in contact with Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI) and advised that arrangements are being made to place learners with other providers in Cork and Dublin to enable them to complete their studies. Learners will be contacted by the provider directly.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to give a breakdown of how the €150m unlocked from the NTF in the Budget will be spent over the next three years.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for a multiannual investment of €150 million from the National Training Fund over the next three years, with €50 million to be provided in 2027.
The investment is intended to strengthen Ireland's capacity to anticipate and respond to emerging skills needs arising from technological, economic and labour market change, including the impact of artificial intelligence and the transition to a low-carbon economy.
The package responds directly to recommendations of the National Skills Council and will strengthen Ireland’s capacity to anticipate and respond to these changes. Funding will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and expanded opportunities for upskilling, reskilling and lifelong learning.
It will also build on www.aiready.ie, the national gateway for AI skills. Following the launch of Phase 1 earlier this year, the offering will be expanded to enable more people to access training and develop the skills required in a changing workplace.
Meeting future skills needs is essential to ensuring people can access quality employment, and businesses can continue to innovate and grow. This investment package will strengthen Ireland’s skills infrastructure, support labour market participation, help address skills shortages, and enhance productivity and competitiveness.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide further detail on the way in which employers will be able to access the National Training Fund funding announced as part of Budget 2027; the eligibility criteria that will apply; the expected timeline for the introduction of the application process.
reply:
In Budget 2027, I secured a €150 million package over three years from the NTF to strengthen Ireland's capacity to anticipate and respond to technological, economic and labour market change in the age of AI. This package will support curriculum renewal, educator capability, specialist and emerging skills needs, technology adoption, and lifelong learning opportunities across the economy. My officials are currently working through the details of the package.
This additional NTF funding will be delivered through existing NTF-supported programmes and mechanisms. It is important to note that the NTF is not a direct grant mechanism for businesses. This means that businesses do not apply directly to the NTF for grants in the way they might access enterprise supports through Enterprise Ireland. Rather, the NTF primarily funds education and training provision delivered primarily through the publicly funded education and training system, as well as employer-focused training programmes delivered through Skillnet Ireland's contracted training model. Therefore, as the funding will be delivered through established NTF-supported channels, employers will generally access supports through existing programmes operated through agencies such as SOLAS, the Higher Education Authority and Skillnet Ireland. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if a person (details supplied) in County Kildare can resume a chosen career given the previous issues that forced them to withdraw from the apprenticeship that they had commenced.
reply:
The apprenticeship system supports individuals in developing the skills, knowledge and qualifications required to build a successful career in their chosen field.
Where a registered apprentice has previously withdrawn from an apprenticeship due to personal or other circumstances, this does not necessarily prevent them from resuming their apprenticeship or pursuing a career in that occupation.
In general, a person who has withdrawn from an apprenticeship may be able to resume their apprenticeship, subject to meeting the relevant requirements, including securing an approved employer.
The options available will depend on the individual's specific circumstances, including the stage they had reached in their apprenticeship and the time elapsed since withdrawal.
The person concerned may wish to contact their Training Advisor to discuss their circumstances and the pathways available to re-engage with apprenticeship training. My Department and SOLAS are committed to supporting participation in apprenticeship and ensuring that individuals have access to appropriate information and guidance on available options.
The Apprenticeship Code of Practice for Employers and Apprentices sets out the rights and responsibilities of apprentices, employers and training providers, including arrangements relating to training, mentoring, progression and supports. The Code provides a framework for addressing issues and supporting engagement with the apprenticeship system.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide a detailed breakdown of the additional funding provided for in Budget 2027 in relation to the cost of maintaining existing levels of service, demographic growth and inflation; and separately, funding for new services, expanded services and reform.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides an additional €1.6 billion in current funding for health services. Of this increase, €155 million additional pay funding is being provided for workforce growth, equivalent to approximately 2.2% growth in staffing over the course of 2027, while €94 million additional non-pay funding is being allocated to support new and expanded services, reform initiatives and other Ministerial priorities.
The remaining €1.351 billion is being provided primarily to maintain existing levels of service and to meet underlying demand and cost pressures, including demographic growth, inflation, the full-year cost of existing commitments and pay-related costs.
The impact of demographic growth and inflation varies across different service areas. For example, demographic pressures are generally higher in areas such as Older Persons Services, reflecting population growth and ageing.
Similarly, inflationary pressures vary across care groups depending on the particular mix of non-pay expenditure. Funding requirements are therefore assessed on a service-by-service basis, taking account of the particular cost and demand drivers affecting each care group, rather than applying a single demographic or inflation assumption across the health system.
Detailed allocations by Health Region and care group will be set out in the Department's Letter of Determination and the HSE National Service Plan for 2027.

question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Health when a comprehensive endometriosis national service and strategy will be established.
reply:
Last October I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country. Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain.
The Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.
In conjunction with the publication of the National Endometriosis Framework, I also mandated an immediate action plan to accelerate development of our endometriosis services.

• In circumstances where an applicant is still over the income limit for a medical card, they are then assessed for a GP visit card, which entitles the applicant to GP visits without charge.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Health the reason reimbursement applications under the HSE Cross Border Directive dating back to November 2025 remain outstanding (details supplied); the number of applicants waiting six months or longer for reimbursement; whether sufficient funding has been allocated to clear the current backlog; the reason applicants are receiving conflicting information regarding the status of their claims; the urgent measures being implemented to support patients experiencing financial hardship as a result of prolonged delays; and if sufficient funding has been secured for future reimbursement demand.
reply:
The Cross Border Directive (CBD) allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the Cross Border Directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently processing applications received in early April 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the number of inspections, market surveillance checks and product sampling exercises carried out by the Health Products Regulatory Authority on cosmetic products used in nail salons and nail bars, including acrylic monomer liquids and gel nail products, in each of the years 2023 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the number of products found to contain substances prohibited or restricted under the EU Cosmetics Regulation; the enforcement action taken in each case.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) is the competent authority in Ireland for the regulation of medicines, medical devices, and other health products such as cosmetic products. The HPRA’s role includes helping ensure cosmetic products on the Irish market are safe for consumers and meet the requirements of the primary cosmetics legislation, as amended (‘the Cosmetics Regulation’). Each cosmetic product placed on the European market must have a designated responsible person (RP) established in the European Economic Area (EEA) or Northern Ireland.
Article 22 of the Cosmetics Regulation requires the HPRA to monitor compliance with the Regulation through in-market controls. The HPRA carries out market surveillance in collaboration with the National Environmental Health Service (NEHS), which is a part of the Health Service Executive (HSE). The NEHS’ role involves the sampling of products at retail/salon level as a part of the annual market surveillance plan.
Increased surveillance activity in late 2025 and 2026 was undertaken following the prohibition of trimethylbenzoyl diphenylphosphine oxide (TPO) in cosmetic products from 01 September 2025 under amended cosmetics legislation. This resulted in an increased number of non-compliant nail products being identified during targeted market surveillance activities.

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health to provide further details regarding her plans for the €7 million allocation for general practice reform in Budget 2027; and if the Strategic Review of General Practice will conclude by year end.
reply:
The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish the Strategic Review of General Practice, and bring forward a new, modern GP contract.
The review is a comprehensive examination of issues affecting general practice, focusing on GP training, GP capacity, Out of Hours services reform, the eHealth Agenda, and the financial support model for general practice. Significant progress has been made under the review, and the review is to be completed this year.
The review will identify the arrangements necessary to improve the current system of GP care as part of a primary care-focused health service and when completed will make recommendations for a more sustainable general practice into the future.
Budget 2027 provides for €7 million for the reform of GP services, ensuring funding is available for appropriate recommendations to be progressed early after the review is completed. It is expected the focus of the funding will be the reform of GP out of hours services, for better and more equality of access for patients.
The implementation of the recommendations from the review will build on the progress already made under the 2019 and 2023 GP Agreements in improving and better supporting our GP services, as well the progress in increasing GP training places in recent years and in recruitment of GPs from abroad, to improve GP capacity and access to GP services.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will commit to expanding the local improvement scheme, given the benefits to rural Ireland.
reply:
The Local Improvement Scheme (LIS) funds the upgrade of non-public rural roads and laneways, which are not usually maintained by local authorities. My department reinstated the Scheme in 2017, and it is a central element of the overall Rural Development Investment Programme. Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
Eligible road projects include works on non-public roads which provide access:
• to parcels of land, of which, two or more are owned/occupied by different persons, one of which must be for agricultural purposes, or
• for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for two or more persons, or
• to at least one parcel of land owned/occupied by a person engaged in agricultural activities and which separately provides access for harvesting purposes (including turf/seaweed) for at least one other person
In addition, works can be carried out on amenity roads, which are non-public roads leading to important community amenities such as graveyards, beaches and piers.
The scheme’s provision were last expanded in 2024, when the requirement for 2 landowners/occupiers to be involved in separate agricultural activities was reduced to one, and has resulted in an increase in applicants applying for works under the scheme.

question: Deputy George Lawlor asked the Minister for Health when publicly funded donor assisted reproduction services, including donor sperm IUI and IVF will be made available to same sex female couples or others who require donor gametes, if the Government has a specific timeline for the provision of this service including programmes of donor assisted treatment including sperm donation and if funding for this service have been provided for in the 2027 Estimates for her Department.
reply:
The Model of Care for Fertility was developed by the Department of Health in conjunction with the Health Service Executive (HSE) National Women and Infants Health Programme to ensure that fertility-related issues are addressed through the public health system at the lowest level of clinical intervention necessary.
The Model of Care comprises three stages of care. These begin in primary care (GPs), progress to secondary care through the six HSE-run Regional Fertility Hubs located across the country, and, where clinically indicated, advance to tertiary care.
Referrals for publicly-funded, privately-provided assisted human reproduction (AHR) treatment – including IVF (in-vitro fertilisation), ICSI (intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection) and IUI (intrauterine insemination) – commenced in September 2023, subject to patients meeting the criteria agreed by my Department and the HSE. The access criteria were developed by a multidisciplinary group, with reproductive medicine expertise and followed consultation with experts in the field along with a review of the international evidence. These criteria are in keeping with those applied in other jurisdictions.
The terms of the publicly-funded AHR treatment initiative are underpinned by the primary policy principle of supporting couples experiencing fertility issues and, most specifically, those who have been trying unsuccessfully to conceive naturally at the time in question.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health further to Parliamentary Question No. 70619/26, whether her Department or the Health Service Executive holds data on the number of claims managed by the State Claims Agency arising from alleged delay in ambulance response or allocation in each of the years 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the total amount paid in respect of such claims, in view of the reply from the Minister for Finance to Parliamentary Question No. 70619/26 stating that this matter falls under the remit of the Minister for Health; if so, to provide the figures; and if the Minister will make a statement on the matter.
reply:
The State Claims Agency (SCA) does not record information in respect of these claims in a manner which allows a response to the question, in a readily extractable format.
The SCA has been notified of 78 claims involving Members of the Public or Service Users relating to the National Ambulance Service between 01/01/2022 & 01/10/2026, as recorded on the National Incident Management System (NIMS). These claims are recorded under a variety of hazard categories on NIMS, including Crash/Collision (motor), Clinical Care, Exposure to Physical Hazards, Exposure to Psychological Hazards, and Exposure to Biological Hazards.
Of the 78 claims, 31 are finalised and 47 remain active as at 01/10/2026. A total of €1.775m has been paid out on the 31 finalised claims in the period.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he or his Department has any plans in place to address the long waiting times for the local improvement schemes; and if he will make funding available to local authorities as soon as possible for 2027.
reply:

Since 2017, over €201 million has been allocated to local authorities, resulting in the improvement of over 5,500 roads.
The 2026 scheme was launched in February with subhead funding of €17 million. While the Department provides LIS funding, local authorities administer the scheme and are responsible for managing waiting lists, selecting and prioritising roads and managing works undertaken. I note, however, that many factors affect the ability of local authorities to meet increasing demand, not just available funding. Factors such as weather conditions, costs and availability of contractors and labour are also relevant.

Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is central to building a sustainable health workforce and supporting the delivery of high-quality patient care. The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Of these, approximately 834 are expected to commence employment before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to commence from January onwards.
To be clear, there is no recruitment embargo in the HSE and recruitment has not ceased. Enhanced controls are currently in place in four Health Regions to ensure appointments are affordable, appropriately prioritised and aligned with areas of greatest patient and service need. Essential posts continue to be filled.
An important element of this approach is the recruitment of permanent staff to fill vacancies currently met through agency staffing. This can provide additional opportunities for graduates, support a more stable workforce, strengthen continuity of care and deliver better value for the taxpayer.

reply: In response to the meeting that took place with the Taoiseach, INMO and the Department of Health, the HSE issued a Circular to all Managers on the 1st of May 2026 instructing them to look favourably at applications for CIP. The HSE have established a Working Group to assist affected staff in their recovery and, where possible, their return to work, including through appropriate workplace measures and phased returns. Its work includes monitoring decisions on Critical Illness Protocol applications and following up on cases where applications have been refused. The group met all HSE Regions between 28 and 31 July to reinforce the need to assist affected staff appropriately and ensure that eligible staff receive support under the Protocol. The Department will continue to engage with the HSE Working Group.

My department supports successful applicants through phased payments and ongoing engagement through the project delivery period. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Health the actions are being taken to compensate the children who were affected by the delays in surgery for scoliosis and spina bifida; and if a public inquiry into the matter is being considered.
reply:
I published the independent report of the Children's Health Ireland Inquiry into Spina Bifida and Complex Scoliosis Scoping Exercise on 28 September following engagement with patients and families. Mr Farrell, the independent facilitator of the scoping exercise, recommended a Commission of Investigation covering four defined modules; waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the cohort of children who were not transferred to Temple Street post 2008.
Government has accepted the report's recommendations in full and have agreed to the initiation of drafting the Terms of Reference (ToR) for the proposed Commission of Investigation. Officials in my Department will work in close consultation with the Office of the Attorney General on drafting the Terms of Reference. There will be a call for input from advocacy groups on the ToR.
The final ToR will be submitted to Government for approval.

question: Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the reason no additional funding has been allocated to SICAP in Budget 2027, despite rising demand for its services; and the assessment that has been made of the impact on community organisations and the people they support.
reply:
The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) is Ireland’s primary social inclusion programme, which aims to reduce poverty and promote social inclusion and equality by supporting disadvantaged individuals and communities.
SICAP is a national programme delivered in both rural and urban areas by Local Development Companies (LDCs), providing targeted supports to those experiencing poverty, disadvantage and social exclusion.
I am pleased to have secured almost €74 million for SICAP and other social inclusion supports in Budget 2027. Just under €65 million of that allocation is for SICAP providing greater long-term funding stability for the programme and enabling the continuation of important work across the country. It should be noted that the final estimated allocations for each area will be confirmed in the Revised Estimates Volume which will be published in December, and considered by the relevant select committees.
A particularly welcome development is the provision of long-term funding certainty, with previously temporary funding for new arrivals made a permanent part of the core SICAP allocation. While this does not increase the overall SICAP allocation for 2027, it represents an important step towards ensuring that community integration supports can be delivered on a more sustainable basis. question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on the development of a new rural development policy.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 62, 73 and 83 together.
Since its launch in 2021, Our Rural Future has delivered vital investment and supports, strengthened local economies, and improved quality of life across rural Ireland.
Significant achievements include improvements in digital connectivity through delivery of the National Broadband Plan, the development of a national network of over 400 remote working hubs and improvements in essential services such as the delivery of 185 new or enhanced public transport services through the Connecting Ireland Rural Mobility Plan.
Other achievements include a significant focus on the regeneration and revitalisation of town and village centres and the enhancement of community facilities and public amenities, such as community centres, walking trails, libraries, playgrounds, and public realm works.
The next iteration of Our Rural Future, for the period to 2031, will be published by the Government later this month. It will build on the considerable progress and investment to date and provide a framework for the next phase of rural development.
Development of the new policy has been informed by an extensive public and stakeholder consultation process which took place throughout 2025 and gathered the views of well over 2,000 participants.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cárb as a dtiocfaidh an laghdú ar bhuiséad caipitil na Gaeltachta i mBuiséad 2027, agus cad é an buiséad caipitil go sonrach a bheidh ag Údarás na Gaeltachta in 2027 i gcomparáid le 2026; agus an ndéanfaidh sé ráiteas ina thaobh.
reply:
Tá leithdháileadh iomlán de €628 milliún faighte ag mo Roinn i gCáinaisnéis 2027, lena n-áirítear leithdháileadh caiptil de €273 milliún. Foilseofar leithdháileadh mionsonraithe de réir fomhír san Imleabhar Meastachán Athbhreithnithe (REV) roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tá pleananna fíor-uaillmhianacha ag mo Roinn d'fhorbairtí caipitil chun tacú le pobail Ghaeltachta, pobal na Gaeilge agus pobail na n-oileán araon. Maoinítear na forbairtí seo as Clár C de bhuiséad na Roinne - An Ghaeltacht, an Ghaeilge agus na hOileáin. Is fiú a mheabhrú gur tháinig ardú ar an mbuiséad caipitil do Chlár C ó €30 milliún in 2025 go beagnach €55 milliún in 2026. Bhain cuid mhaith den ardú sin le trí phríomhthionscadal infreastruchtúir:
• Cé Inis Oírr,
• An tIonad Gaeilge agus Cultúir ar Shráid Fhearchair, agus
• athfhorbairt shuíomh Choláiste Lurgan in Indreabhán mar Ionad Oideachais agus Óige do Ghaeltacht Chonamara.
Rinneadh gealltanas i leith na dtionscadal seo sa Phlean Forbartha Náisiúnta, agus is cúis áthais dom an maoiniú a fháil chun iad a thabhairt i gcrích anois. Táim den tuairim mheáite go mbeidh an t-allúntas caipitil atá faighte ag mo Roinn leordhóthanach le freastal ar riachtanais chlár na Gaeltachta, na Gaeilge agus na nOileán, lena n-áirítear Údarás na Gaeltachta, i 2027 agus sna blianta ina dhiaidh sin.
