question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the changes being made to the town and village renewal scheme to include urban villages.
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme (TVRS) is part of a range of measures under my Department’s Rural Development Investment Programme to support the revitalisation of rural Ireland. The Scheme is administered on behalf of the Department by local authorities across Ireland. Since the introduction of the Scheme in 2016, over €217 million has been approved for almost 2,000 projects across the country.
The 2026 Call for Proposals was launched in September 2026 with two funding streams available; the Main Scheme where grant funding for projects will range from €50,000 to €500,000, and the Project Development Measure with funding of up to €50,000 available per project. The closing date for the submission of applications is 22 January 2027. Details of the scheme’s parameters has now been issued to all local authorities.
The 2026 TVRS is designed to support the revitalisation of rural Ireland by focusing on stimulating town centre economic and social regeneration. This will be achieved through projects which support sustainable employment creation, town centre resilience and regeneration, enhancing our streetscapes, and bringing vacant and derelict buildings and lands back into use as community multi-purpose spaces through refurbishment and renovation. Whilst the focus will remain on rural towns and villages, this 2026 Scheme will operate a new pilot urban town initiative. question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health the number of newly qualified nurses and midwives who have been offered jobs in hospitals on completion of their studies in 2026; the number of newly qualified nurses and midwives who have not been offered roles due to the HSE hiring freeze; if there are vacancies in hospitals not being filled due to the hiring freeze; and her plans to ensure that these newly qualified medical professionals are offered jobs in Irish hospitals.
reply:
Attracting and retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives is vital to building a sustainable workforce and supporting high-quality patient care.
I have been clear that the HSE must make every effort to offer employment opportunities to nursing and midwifery graduates and support their transition into the public health service.
Since the beginning of 2021, the number of nurses and midwives employed in the health service has increased by 9,924, an increase of almost 25%.
At the same time, the HSE must manage recruitment within available funding and ensure that new appointments are properly prioritised. Strengthened controls have been introduced, but these do not amount to a blanket recruitment embargo. Essential and patient-facing posts continue to be filled, taking account of clinical need, patient safety, patient benefit and available funding.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates that 974 graduate nurses and midwives have confirmed start dates. Of these, approximately 834 are expected to commence before the end of this year, with a further 140 due to commence from January onwards.
The HSE continues to make offers where vacancies exist, including in areas with workforce pressures and high agency usage. Retaining newly qualified nurses and midwives within the public health service remains a priority for Government.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the position regarding any engagement she is having with childcare centres that have withdrawn from the core funding scheme; if any further engagement is proposed following the budget announcement related to the €550 cap on childcare fees.
reply:
I am aware that a small number of providers are regrettably considering withdrawing from the Core Funding scheme.
If a Partner Services wishes to withdraw from the Core Funding Programme, they must provide 3 months’ notice to the Scheme Administrator. This must be done by submitting a Service Request on the Early Years Early Years Hive outlining the withdrawal date and the reason for the withdrawal.
However, if an existing Partner Service decides not to enter a contract for the new programme year starting on 1 September, they, as private businesses, would no longer be subject to the provisions of the Core Funding Agreement and, by extension, the required minimum notice period to parents. They are also not required to provide a reason for choosing not to reapply for Core Funding to the Scheme Administrator.
Services may choose to leave the scheme mid-year with reasons stated as being denied a fee increase, temporary closures, financial difficulties, administrative requirements and personal reasons such as retirement.
The Department, through the local Childcare Committees, engages directly with any such service to highlight the benefits of staying in Core Funding, not only for their services but also for the families who avail of them. I am hopeful that the providers may reconsider their decision.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will report on his engagements regarding the LEADER programme under the next EU budgetary cycle.
reply:
The LEADER Programme is funded as an intervention under the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). Therefore, the development of the EU regulations relating to the post 2027 CAP and the new National and Regional Partnership Plan is of significant importance to my department.
To facilitate the on-going negotiation process for the post 2027 period, the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine established a CAP Consultative Committee, which includes representation from my department and other rural stakeholders.
I acknowledge that the proposed consolidation of the main EU funding programmes within a single National and Regional Partnership Plan for each Member State, financed through one overarching fund, is leading to uncertainty. However it is important to note that the draft regulations include the continuation of the LEADER programme as a mandatory measure.
Furthermore, the current draft regulations also proposed a 10% rural target in recognition of the valuable support provided to rural communities. I will continue to work to ensure that this provision can serve to provide adequate funding for LEADER in the next programming period.
My department continues to input into these draft EU regulations, to ensure continued prioritisation of LEADER in Ireland, and has consistently emphasised the importance of a ringfenced allocation for LEADER, to ensure the post-2027 programme can continue its vital role.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 697, 698, 699 and 700 together.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the actions she is taking to address the cost of childcare, specifically for families that use childcare centres that are not part of the core funding scheme.
reply:
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to ELC and SAC providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.
A key condition of receiving the significant State funding that is available through the Scheme requires that a Partner Service adhere to the Core Funding fee management system, which includes a freeze on fees at 2021 levels and fee caps. This is to ensure that the State’s significant investment through the Scheme is not absorbed by unnecessary fee increases.
These fee management conditions of the Core Funding Scheme apply exclusively to Partner Services who have signed a Core Funding Agreement. These regulations are not applied to services which remain outside of the Core Funding scheme.
It is a matter for providers to decide whether they wish to sign up to Core Funding and benefit from the significant financial supports it offers to providers and the certainty it gives to parents through the associated fee management measures. It should be noted that services that provide the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme and/or the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) are not required to take part in Core Funding, reducing the impact of the NCS as some families are not benefiting from the fee-control measures (fee-freeze and fee caps) or additional funding for quality provision that is provided by Core Funding. question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the national policy statement on outdoor learning and play in ELC.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality, mission is to enhance the lives of children, young people, adults, families and communities, recognising diversity and promoting equality of opportunity.
The key strategy delivering this mission in early learning and care is the First 5: Whole-of-Government Strategy for Babies, Young Children and their Families 2019-2028. This strategy recognises the importance of outdoor learning and play in young children’s lives.
Outdoor play is a core component of Aistear: the Early Childhood Curriculum Framework, recently updated by the NCCA, and the Síolta, the National Quality Framework for Early Childhood Education in Ireland.
'When the Roof is the Sky', is Tusla, Early Years Inspectorate’s guidance for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare services operating fully or mostly outdoors, promoting safe, enriching outdoor play and learning for children. This guidance published in 2023, encourages all services to reflect on how they use their outdoor space, and to take measures to ensure children have increased opportunities to spend time outdoors.
A policy statement on Outdoor Play and Learning in Early Learning and Care and School Age Childcare, including Childminding Settings, in Ireland, is currently under development. Once finalised later this year, it will be published in draft form, welcoming consultation from the sector.

It includes officials from the Department; the Department of Housing, Local Government, and Heritage; and the Department of Education and Youth.
Members of the Group have also met with local authority planning officials, nominated by the County and City Management Association Planning and Land Use Committee to identify important considerations for the review. question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the measures being taken to increase childcare capacity in the Kilshanroe, Johnstownbridge, Carbury and Enfield areas of county Kildare; and whether an assessment has been carried out of childcare demand and available capacity in these rapidly growing communities.
reply:

Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year.
The most recent published capacity data for the 2024/25 programme year estimated that there were 12,087 children enrolled in ELC and SAC services in County Kildare. This data also indicated that 43% of service providers in County Kildare had at least one vacant place and 52% had a waiting list.
However, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, particularly for younger children.
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality is supporting the development of early learning and childcare capacity nationally through Core Funding which was introduced in 2022.
This provides stability to services, and reduces the risk associated with opening a new service or expanding an already existing service.
The Government is also supporting the expansion of capacity through capital funding. question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the public consultation on the development of an induction process, as committed to under Nurturing Skills.
reply:
The Department continues to roll out ‘Nurturing Skills: The Workforce Plan for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare, 2022-2028’. It aims to strengthen the ongoing process of professionalisation for those working in the sector. It contains a range of commitments to raise the profile of careers in the sector and to support recruitment, retention and diversity in the workforce.
Nurturing Skills recognises the importance of an induction process for new entrants beginning their first job in the profession, to help them adjust to their new professional role with the support of experienced colleagues. The need for an induction process reflects on the responsibilities that are open to a student on a practice placement.
Nurturing Skills states that work will begin during the lifetime of the plan (2022-2028) on developing and incrementally introducing an induction process, through research, consultation, piloting and review, along with actions to develop services’ capacity and external supports for induction. This process will support movement towards a future requirement for all entrants into the profession (other than childminders) at all qualification levels to complete a supported induction period.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he will provide an update on plans to expand Líonra Gaeilge scheme to new towns.
reply:
Irish Language Networks may be recognised under the Gaeltacht Act 2012 provided that language plans have been agreed with the communities in the various networks in accordance with prescribed language planning criteria. Foras na Gaeilge is responsible under the Gaeltacht Act, 2012 for supporting organisations in the preparation and implementation of language plans in Irish Language Networks.
Three Irish Language Networks have been approved to date under the Gaeltacht Act: Inis, Baile Locha Riach and Cluain Dolcáin. In addition, two further networks in the north – Carn Tóchair and Iarthar Bhéal Feirste – have been approved under a non-statutory process administered by Foras na Gaeilge.
In 2020, Foras na Gaeilge reviewed the organisation's Irish Language Community Scheme and, as a successor, the Irish Language Network Development Scheme was launched. Among the aims of this scheme is that current grantees place a particular emphasis on working towards recognition as an Irish Language Network. Through the scheme, groups are being empowered to come forward and enter the next round of both the statutory application process in operation in the southern jurisdiction and the non-statutory process in the north.
Officials from my Department are currently engaging with their counterparts in Foras na Gaeilge regarding the potential expansion of the number of Networks. An announcement in this regard will be made in due course.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the process of the mapping exercise commenced in March 2026 to establish a comprehensive overview of current Continuing Professional Development opportunities and to identify any gaps between workforce skills requirements and available training provision.
reply:

The national Continuing Professional Development Mapping exercise included an extensive engagement with educators, practitioners, childminders, Continuing Professional Development providers, and key stakeholders through an online survey, 10 focus groups and 4 interviews session with strategic stakeholders.
The findings of the Continuing Professional Development Mapping exercise is currently being drafted by Crowe Ireland and will be presented to the Continuing Professional Development Oversight Group in Q4 2026. Furthermore, this report will provide a robust and evidenced-base overview of the current Continuing Professional Development landscape that will inform the next phase of development and implementation of the national Continuing Professional Development system.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the mid-point review of Nurturing Skills, which was due out by 2025, given that the mid-point review and revised implementation plan are scheduled to be completed in early Q2 2026.
reply:
The Department continues to implement Nurturing Skills: The Workforce Plan for Early Learning and Care and School-Age Childcare 2022-2028, which sets out a long-term plan to support a well-qualified, skilled, diverse and valued professional workforce that is centred on children’s rights, needs and potential and that provides quality experiences for children in partnership with families, and which continues to advance its professional development within a coherent and competent system.
The midpoint review, originally due in 2025, was postponed to allow key evidence to inform the review process, including findings from the OECD TALIS Starting Strong Survey, the CSO Early Learning and Care Graduate Outcomes report, and the publication of Shaping the Future: Early Years Action Plan.
The review has now been completed and draws on a comprehensive evidence base, including national and international research, administrative and sectoral data, and extensive stakeholder engagement. Consultation undertaken as part of the review included stakeholder engagement sessions, focus groups with early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners, and survey responses from the workforce.
The review assesses progress made across all five pillars of Nurturing Skills and includes a revised implementation plan covering the period 2026-2028. It identifies key achievements to date, considers ongoing challenges, and sets out priority actions for the remainder of the plan's lifetime.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide details of the proposed extension to the deadline for registration of childminders with Tusla as required under the National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028.
reply:
The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 (NAPC) committed to a review of the initial implementation of the regulations before 2028. Acting on feedback received from childminders and childminding representative organisations, I have brought the review forward, to ensure there is sufficient time to implement any changes arising from the review, before the end of the transition period.
The review which is being managed by an external research company commenced on the 19 June. Preliminary findings were delivered at the end of September, with the final report due at the end of October. As indicated in my Budget 2027 speech, these preliminary findings from the consultation suggest childminders want more time before mandatory registration. I will be making an announcement on this in the near future, looking to ensure childminders have the time and space they need. Following conclusion of this review and receipt of the final report, I will give consideration to the appropriate next steps.

question: Deputy Mark Wall asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide an update on the progress of the work being undertaken by an organisation (details supplied) for her Department in developing a searchable price comparability website for parents, as provided for under the partnership for the public good.
reply:
The Expert Group’s Partnership for the Public Good report, which was accepted by all of Government in December 2021, outlines recommendations geared toward promoting quality, accessibility and affordability in the early learning and care and school-age childcare sector.
Core Funding, the supply-side scheme, which was launched in September 2022, on foot of the Expert Group’s recommendations, has made significant progress in advancing the standardisation and transparency of fees in recent years. This includes the building of a universal fee table which incorporates fee information from all schemes; data validations on the fee table to conform to a standard format; a common fee structure which supports the implementation of maximum fee thresholds; and a phased introduction of manual fee table checks coordinated by local City/County Childcare Committees to ensure quality and accuracy of information.
This work forms part of a broader, phased strategy geared toward the standardisation of fees across the country, in line with the recommendations of the Partnership for the Public Good report.
Historical fees lists since 2022/23 and fees lists for the current programme year are available on the Childcare Search section of the NCS Website for every early learning and childcare service. The fees list tables include which schemes the service has contracted to and whether the service is a Partner service under Core Funding or not. question: Deputy Maurice Quinlivan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the status of plans to provide a community centre-community facility in the Garryowen area of Limerick.
reply:
The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible community spaces that are available to communities in both rural and urban areas. Since 2022, some €112 million has been allocated for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing facilities and the construction of new centres where such a need has been identified.
Earlier this year, I launched the latest round of CCIF for enhancement and refurbishment of existing centres. The closing date has now passed and I look forward to announcing successful projects before year-end.
I understand from Limerick City & County Council that they are working with relevant stakeholders for the development of a community centre for the Garryowen area, albeit that discussions are at an early stage.
I am committed to delivering further iterations of the CCIF in the coming years in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government for this to become a permanent rolling fund. I have indicated previously that the 2027 scheme will focus on new build centres and the eligibility criteria and funding limits that will apply will be announced when that scheme is launched next year. In the meantime, communities planning to develop a new community centre should be engaging with their local authority to advance the preparatory work required to be in a position to apply for funding.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if funding is available for the maintenance or repair of damage to playgrounds in disadvantaged rural towns following damage due to anti-social behaviour or wear and tear.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality provides funding to local authorities through the annual Capital Grant Scheme for Play and Recreation, which supports the development of new play and recreation facilities as well as the refurbishment and upgrading of existing facilities. The scheme can support improvements to playgrounds, including the replacement or upgrading of equipment that has deteriorated through normal wear and tear.
The Capital Grant Scheme for Play and Recreation has operated annually since 2013 and continues to support local authorities in improving the quality, accessibility and inclusivity of play facilities for children and young people throughout the country, including in rural communities.
Under the scheme, local authorities may apply for funding for projects aimed at refurbishing existing play and recreation facilities or developing new facilities. In 2026, funding of up to €22,000 per project was available, with each local authority required to provide matching funding of at least 25% of the grant awarded.
Responsibility for the day-to-day management, maintenance and repair of public playgrounds rests primarily with the relevant local authority. As such, there is no dedicated scheme within the Department specifically for repairing damage arising from anti-social behaviour.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if her Department will encourage and support more registered childminders in rural and growing communities to meet growing demand for childcare.
reply:
Childminders are a hugely important part of early learning and care and school-age childcare provision, and they continue to be the option of choice for many families.
All paid, non-relative childminders who work in their own homes can now register with Tusla and access the National Childcare Scheme.
The National Action Plan for Childminding 2021-2028 set out a pathway for the extension of regulation to childminders. A key objective of the National Action Plan for Childminding is to enable parents who use childminders to also benefit from State subsidies through the National Childcare Scheme. The Childcare Support Act 2018, which provides a statutory basis for the National Childcare Scheme, specifies that only Tusla-registered childminders are eligible to participate in the Scheme. The limitation of public funding schemes to Tusla-registered childcare providers helps to ensure that public funding is provided where there is assurance of the quality of provision.
As a result of the commencement of the relevant parts of the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Childminding Services Regulations, which came into effect on 30 September 2024, childminders are now able to apply to register with Tusla. The 2024 Act, under which the timeframes are established, provides for a transition period, in which childminders are being encouraged and supported to register, but registration is not yet mandatory. This phased approach aims to facilitate the largest possible number of childminders

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans for increasing capacity and funding for additional early childhood care and education spaces in Kildare.
reply:
Improving access to quality and affordable early learning and childcare is a key priority of Government.
Early learning and childcare capacity is increasing. Data from the Annual Early Years Sector Profile 2024/25 shows that the estimated number of enrolments increased by approximately 25% from the 2021/22 programme year.
However, it appears that demand for early learning and childcare remains higher than available supply in certain parts of the country, particularly for younger children.
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality is supporting the development of early learning and childcare capacity nationally through Core Funding which was introduced in 2022.
This provides stability to services, and reduces the risk associated with opening a new service or expanding an already existing service.
The Government is also supporting the expansion of capacity through capital funding. The Building Blocks Extension Grant Scheme, which is currently operating, is designed to increase capacity in the 1–3-year-old, pre–Early Childhood Care and Education, age range for full day care. Core Funding Partner Services could apply for capital funding to physically extend their premises or to construct or purchase new premises. Two services from Kildare are working closely with the Department to deliver quality, affordable places.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the steps being taken to encourage and incentivise childcare providers that have previously left the core funding scheme to rejoin.
reply:
I am aware that a small number of providers are regrettably considering withdrawing from the Core Funding scheme.
The Department, through the local Childcare Committees, engages directly with any such service to highlight the benefits of staying in Core Funding, not only for their services but also for the families who avail of them. I am hopeful that the providers may reconsider their decision.
As Core Funding is an optional scheme, service providers have the autonomy and business freedom to withdraw from or choose not to participate in Core Funding, even though this will result in the loss of the significant financial support it offers them and the substantial benefits and certainty it brings to families.
While the State cannot mandate providers to participate in the scheme, Core Funding has been designed with maximum participation of providers in mind as reflected in the year-on-year growth of investment in the Scheme (rising from €259 million in year 1 to over €482 million in year 5). This represents an increase of 86% in Core Funding in four years.
I was delighted to announce further investment in Core Funding in Budget 2027. The additional funding being made available in 2027 will see the projected allocation for Core Funding in the next programme year, which begins in September 2027, increase to over €650 million. Such an increase would represent an additional €170 million on the current allocation, or a 35% increase.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason for the delay in developing a national policy statement on the use of digital technologies and digital learning in Early Learning and Care, building on OECD (2023) Empowering Young Children in the Digital Age; and the status of this work.
reply:
The Department of Children, Disability and Equality, mission is to enhance the lives of children, young people, adults, families and communities, recognising diversity and promoting equality of opportunity.
As identified in ‘Ireland’s Literacy, Numeracy and Digital Literacy Strategy 2024-2033: Every Learner from Birth to Young Adulthood’, the meaning of digital literacy and the use of digital technologies are complex, particularly in the birth to three age cohort. Parents, early years educators and childminders are often presented with conflicting information. Given the need for greater clarity in this area, a commitment was made by the department to develop a policy statement on the use of digital technologies in ELC.
While Aistear, the early childhood curriculum framework does not set specific expectations for digital literacy, it does suggest possible opportunities for parents, early years educators and childminders to integrate digital technologies into children’s learning experiences. Through active, playful and enquiry led engagement, young children are supported to acquire the foundations for digital learning that are deepened and refined as they move through the education system.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason the consultation process on terminology relating to the ELC and SAC sector, committed to under First Five, has been put under review.
reply:
First 5 is a whole-of-government strategy to improve the lives of babies, young children and their families. It is a ten-year plan to help make sure all children have positive early experiences and get a great start in life. Under action D.1.A.8. there is a commitment to undertake a consultation process on terminology relating to the Early Learning and Care (ELC) and School Age Childcare (SAC) sector.
In this context, in 2024 the Department of Children, Disability, and Equality (DCDE) completed a review and frequency analysis of the terminology currently in use across a range of relevant sources. This work examined terminology as it appears in registered service names, media content, and approved academic qualification titles, and also involved engagement with international colleagues, with a view to establishing current prevalence of terms used across the sector nationally and internationally.
Timelines for a wider consultation process on terminology are currently under review while the Department focuses its engagement with the sector on the development of Shaping the Future, the Early Years Action Plan, and the National Conversation on Education. As part of the National Conversation on Education: the First 5 years and School-Age Childcare, DCDE undertook a public consultation process on the future of ELC and SAC including childminding. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason for the delay in a real-time finder of regulated ELC and SAC settings, which has been pushed to phase 3 of the First Five Implementation Plan.
reply:
First 5 is a whole-of-government strategy to improve the lives of babies, young children and their families. It is a ten-year plan to help make sure all children have positive early experiences and get a great start in life.
Under action C.8.2.9, First 5 commits to explore the potential to develop a real-time finder of regulated early learning and childcare places with links to inspection reports and other relevant information.
This action needs to be considered within the context of the current prioritisation of work under way to replace the platform for early learning and childcare schemes and programmes. A multiphase programme of work was tendered for in late 2025 to:
a) review options for a long-term digital system for early learning and childcare, including the option of modernising the existing system or developing a new system and
b) carry out a detailed analysis of the proposed long-term-digital system identified to include functional and non-functional specifications.
Following conclusion of this procurement, Deloitte were appointed in late March 2026. They will also carry out detailed requirements gathering and provide the necessary technical documentation to enable a call for tender for the design and build and implementation of such a system. This work will conclude in the coming weeks.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will clarify a matter (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 652, 653, 654, 655 and 656 together.
The Deputy has asked a number of related questions about the Assessment of Need process and the possibility of duplication of effort within the process. The process is briefly outlined below including certain key aspects which should address those questions.
Under the Disability Act 2005, an Assessment of Need is a specific assessment process carried out by the HSE to determine whether a child or young person has a disability as defined within the Act, and if they do, to identify the health and education needs (if any) arising from that disability.
A person may apply for an Assessment of Need if they think they or their child has a disability as defined under the Disability Act. The definition of disability is very specific in the Act. It is defined as a substantial restriction in the person’s capacity i.e. that a person has a significant difficulty with communication, learning, mobility or significantly disordered cognitive processes. In addition, this restriction should be permanent or likely to be permanent and require the continued provision of services to meet the person’s needs.
An application for an assessment is need is made by the applicant, if they are an adult born on or after 1 June 2002, or on behalf of the applicant where they are a child or are not in a position to apply on their own behalf.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of hectares of land currently under afforestation in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 650 and 651 together.
There are over 800,000 hectares of forests in Ireland. This represents just under 12% of the total area of the State. Ireland is a success story, as going from 1% forest cover to 12% today, we have reversed centuries of deforestation.
There are 84,013 hectares of afforested lands currently eligible to receive premia payments.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht when a decision will be made on RRDF applications.
reply:
The Rural Regeneration and Development Fund (RRDF) is a major capital investment programme, which seeks to support large-scale, ambitious projects that can achieve sustainable economic and social development in rural areas. The focus of the RRDF is on rural towns and villages with a population of less than 10,000 people.
To date, the RRDF has awarded over €611 million for 271 projects across Ireland. The assessment process for the RRDF applications received under this 6th Call for Proposals, which is undertaken on a competitive basis, is ongoing. Following the assessment of applications, it is anticipated an announcement of successful projects will be made before the end of this year.
I am committed to ensuring that the RRDF can continue to support high quality and transformational projects across rural Ireland in line with the objectives of Our Rural Future and the Town Centre First policy.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for a breakdown on where the recent cases of bluetongue have been found; if they were found on farms or in meat processing plants / factories; and to clarify if they were ovine or bovine.
reply:
As of 10 October 2026, 28 confirmed bluetongue herd cases have been recorded during the current reporting period. These comprise of 26 bovine herd cases and 2 ovine cases.
The bovine herd cases were recorded in Cork(2), Dublin(1), Kildare(5), Longford(1), Louth(1), Monaghan(1), Roscommon(1) Waterford(2), Westmeath(1), Wexford(9) and Wicklow(2). The two ovine cases were recorded in Kildare and Wexford.
None of the recent confirmed cases were detected in meat processing plants. The cases were identified though clinical investigations, targeted screening or private sampling undertaken for other purposes such as trade.
Bluetongue is a notifiable disease in Ireland. Where a veterinary practitioner suspects the Bluetongue virus disease, the regional veterinary office should be contacted so that the case may be investigated. If the disease cannot be ruled out on clinical examination, Departmental Veterinary Inspectors will take samples for laboratory testing.
Additional information, including a regularly updated case-table can be found on the Government website at: www.gov.ie/bluetongue.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his Department has formulated any contingency measures to support Irish farmers in the event of a highly reduced EU CAP budget.
reply:
Negotiations on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028–2034, which will determine the overall EU budget available for the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), are ongoing, alongside negotiations on the future CAP regulations.
Once these negotiations have concluded at European Council level, Ireland’s overall CAP allocation and the national co-financing rates required under the agreed regulations will be clear.
My Department will then work on designing the CAP chapter of the new National and Regional Partnership Plan, taking account of the specific needs and circumstances of Irish farmers and the wider agricultural sector. The objective will be to develop a CAP chapter that supports viable farm incomes, food production and food security, environmental sustainability and the vitality of rural communities, while ensuring that the measures are practical and workable for farmers and the implementing authorities.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reasons his Department rejected an offer of the planting of a forest in Adare, County Limerick to offset the carbon footprint for the hosting of a sporting event (details supplied); the reason they refused to meet with and engaged with the project promoters; and the measures being put in place to support carbon offsetting for this event.
reply:
I very much welcome and support progress being made by those seeking to establish new forests to help offset the carbon footprint associated with the hosting of an event in Adare. My Department has met with anyone who sought a meeting in this regard.
My Department provides a range of supports for the establishment of new forests. The establishment of new forests can provide a lasting environmental legacy beyond the event itself, delivering long-term benefits including carbon sequestration, biodiversity enhancement and an increase in Ireland’s overall forest cover.
My Department engaged in a Pre-Application Discussion (PAD) relating to seven potential planting areas at Adare in January 2026 and four of the areas were considered potentially capable of progressing subject the relevant licensing and environmental assessment processes. For archaeological reasons, three were deemed to be unsuitable at pre application discussion stage. My Department has not yet received any formal application related to any of the potential planting areas referred to above.
Two afforestation applications, not associated with the seven sites above, have been submitted to my Department in respect of lands owned by a public authority. These applications relate to carbon offsetting for the event.
My Department remains available to provide information and guidance on the forestry supports available and to assist those seeking to progress applications.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to consider purchasing a ship to be used by his Department to transport cattle from Ireland to international markets.
reply:
The intra community trade and export of live animals to third countries from Ireland is a private commercial activity which is regulated by my Department in accordance with EU and National Regulations. As such my Department is not considering the purchase of a ship to be used to transport cattle to international markets.
In order for Roll on Roll off vessel (RoRo/Ferry ) to be allowed carry vehicles containing livestock out of Ireland it must be approved by my Department in accordance with the provisions of Statutory Instrument (S.I.) No. 580/2007 - Diseases of Animals (Animal Transport) (Roll-on Roll-off Vessels) Order 2007.
In order for a dedicated livestock vessel to be allowed load and transport livestock out of Ireland it must be approved by my Department under the provisions of Statutory Instrument (S.I.) . No. 356/2016 - Carriage of Livestock by Sea Regulations 2016.
While this trade is a private commercial activity my Department is available to assess and approve vessels under the above Regulations to facilitate the transport of livestock out of Ireland.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he is considering the introduction of a dedicated farm succession scheme to support the transfer of farms to younger generations.
reply:
Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector.

However, farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to provide an update on the new Animal Welfare Strategy.
reply:
The term of Ireland’s first ever Animal Welfare Strategy 2021-2025 - Working Together for Animal Welfare reached a conclusion at the end of 2025.
In 2025, a process was initiated to develop a new animal welfare strategy, which will act as a framework for engagement and collaboration to direct future activities with the aim of benefiting both animals and Irish society.
Development of the strategy is almost complete following a broad stakeholder engagement including a non-statutory public consultation that was launched on 19th November 2025 and ran to 2nd January 2026. In excess of 1750 individual submissions were received as part of that process.
The new strategy will continue to adopt a ‘One Health, One Welfare’ approach, acknowledging and valuing the inter-dependencies between human, animal and environmental health, and taking an evidence-led approach to policy making, target-setting, monitoring and evaluation.
I anticipate that the new strategy will be published shortly.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. 70318/26, which stated that comparing Ireland's proposed ring fenced allocation of €8.162 billion under the Common Agricultural Policy for 2028 to 2034 with the approximately €10.7 billion for 2021 to 2027 is not a like for like comparison, to provide a like for like comparison of the two allocations, in tabular form, setting out which interventions are included in each figure; and if the he will make a statement on the matter.
reply:
The European Commission's proposals for the 2028-2034 period represent a significant structural change to the current model of CAP delivery, as it is proposed that the CAP will form part of a broader National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP), which consolidates several EU funding streams under a single framework.
Under the proposals, Ireland’s indicative ring-fenced CAP allocation is €8.162 billion, within a total NRPP allocation of €11.4 billion. In addition, the proposed framework is intended to allow Member States the possibility to supplement CAP interventions from the wider NRPP allocation, thereby offering flexibility to address national priorities.
As noted, comparing the proposed allocation for Ireland’s CAP for the 2028-2034 period with the current CAP period is not a like-for-like comparison, and the figures should be viewed in this context. Different interventions or schemes are included in the €8.162 billion ringfenced amount (as set out in the proposed NRPP Regulation), compared to the €10.7 billion figure for 2021-2027 (Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 schemes).
Under the current programme cooperation measures such as LEADER, EIP, territorial development & local cooperation, schools schemes, and measures related to knowledge sharing are funded from the 2021-2027 €10.7bn figure. These measures however are not included within the ringfenced amount for CAP income supports for the period 2028-2034 and will need to be funded from the general NRPP allocation.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will provide an update on the application for port listing of Killybegs in line with new regulations published over two years ago for the listing of port across the EU; that as a consequence of inaction the entire pelagic sector both catching and processing, is severely disadvantaged as Denmark and Latvia obtained port listing status within three months of publication of the regulations.
reply:
The “port listing” referred to by the Deputy relates to listing ports in order to avail of a derogation under EU regulation from the “Margin of Tolerance” requirement.
As provided for in the Control Regulation, the "Margin of Tolerance" is the difference between the estimated quantity of species recorded by the master in the fishing logbook and the actual weight of the catch once weighed and converted to live weight. The Margin of Tolerance for most species is 10%. Therefore, the live weight equivalent must be within 10% of the estimated live weight of each such species for the logbook to be compliant.
Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1474 sets out the requirements which must be met in order for a port to qualify for a derogation from the Margin of Tolerance. In order to apply to the European Commission for a port to obtain such a derogation, all of the following weighing systems, equipment, and control tools must be in place to ensure the accuracy of catch reporting and the necessary control thereof:
(a) a remote electronic monitoring system with closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras allowing the competent authorities of the coastal Member State to monitor the landing, transhipment, and weighing of all catches of relevant fisheries etc,
(b) a weighbridge or a crane weighing system to be used for the weighing of all catches of such fisheries,
(c) one or more water separators to enable dewatering of catches at landing prior to their weighing for these fisheries;

reply:

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the changes, if any, that will be made to the financial eligibility thresholds for the civil legal aid scheme arising from Budget 2027; whether the disposable income and disposable capital limits will be revised and when any such changes will take effect; and the estimated number of additional persons who will become eligible for civil legal aid as a result.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 621 and 622 together.
The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. Eligibility for the Civil Legal Aid Scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. Civil legal aid and advice is provided primarily through a network of law centres by solicitors employed by the Board. question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of private residential properties that are now owned by his Department or are managed by his Department to provide accommodation for former residents of IPAS centres.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 618 and 619 together.
The International Protection Accommodation Service is currently accommodating nearly 32,000 residents in 295 international protection accommodation centres around the country.
The Department provides accommodation to people who are applying for international protection. Some residents have reached the end of their application process and have been granted status that means they can remain in Ireland; they are provided with supports to transition out of IPAS accommodation.
The Department does not provide accommodation for people who have transitioned out of IPAS accommodation.
The great majority of IPAS accommodation capacity, whether contracted or State-owned, is located in group settings in larger properties, like former hotels, guesthouses, commercial and institutional buildings. A small proportion of more vulnerable applicants may be accommodated in smaller scale properties.
The property referred to in the Deputy's question was one of a number of smaller-scale properties purchased by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth for the accommodation of more vulnerable international protection applicants, for whom group accommodation would not be suitable. In relation to future plans for this property, correspondence has been received from Meath County Council regarding the property, and my officials are engaging with the Council in this regard.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a full up to date progress of an application for Irish citizenship (details supplied).
reply:
The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department.
This application is based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency.
Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family.
Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the work being undertaken to ensure employed or self-employed residents in IPAS housing make a financial contribution toward their reception costs.
reply:
In line with a Programme for Government commitment, a scheme for working international protection applicants to contribute to the cost of IPAS accommodation is in development.
IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all international protection applicants are entitled to material reception conditions.
The regulations further provide that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services.
The contribution rates are set out in a schedule to the regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn, as set out below.
Implementation of the contribution to cost scheme is underway and includes the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments.
The implementation process includes procurement of an appropriate third-party provider service, and will involve further detailed analysis as the scheme comes into operation including determining the implementation cost.
The project to implement a contribution model is still ongoing.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason the provisions of the Criminal Justice (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024 providing for the revised National Referral Mechanism for victims of human trafficking have not yet been commenced; the date by which he intends to commence those provisions; the interim arrangements in place for identifying and supporting victims pending commencement.
reply:
The Government is committed to a revised National Referral Mechanism (NRM) for victims of human trafficking, building on the existing multi-agency approach and expanding the range of authorities involved in the formal identification of victims. Under the current NRM, a range of Government Departments, State bodies and relevant organisations are involved in the referral of potential victims and in providing supports to these individuals, while An Garda Síochána currently has responsibility for the formal identification of victims of human trafficking.
The Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024 provides a framework for extending formal identification responsibilities to additional designated authorities. However, the revised NRM will be progressed through a phased administrative approach in order to allow for each body to prepare appropriately, as the role of competent authority brings significant governance and data-processing responsibilities, rather than commencing Part 3 of the 2024 Act. The priority continues to be expansion of the range of competent authorities involved in identifying victims and to ensure that the necessary operational arrangements are fully in place.
The focus of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, as National Anti-Trafficking Coordinator, remains focused on delivering a strengthened NRM that provides an effective and coordinated response for victims of human trafficking.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the implementation of his recent changes to the criminal legal aid scheme and his assessment of their impact on the operation of the court system.
reply:
Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts.
Under the Courts Service Act 1998, the management and administration of the courts is a matter for the Courts Service, while the allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and the management of court lists are matters for the Judiciary, in particular the Presidents of the Courts.
Since the commencement of the regulations on 1 July 2026 and as of 9 October 2026, almost 2,978 certificates (invoices for payment) for criminal legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.5 million in the District Court.
My department continues to keep the operation of the new criminal legal aid arrangements in the District Court under review following their introduction.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the way in which Budget 2027 will support urban areas with the highest concentration of disadvantage.
reply:
The SÍOL programme was launched on 8 July 2026, in line with the Programme for Government commitment to deliver funding for projects and initiatives in urban areas with the highest concentration of disadvantage. The programme targets small areas of disadvantage in our towns and cities, providing funding for infrastructure to improve the areas and the lives of the communities. Priority is being given to those Small Areas with the highest population of extreme disadvantage, and the scheme is designed to provide similar supports to these areas that is given to rural areas through schemes such as CLÁR.
The programme is focussed initially on 15 areas that have been designated as SÍOL areas. The programme takes into consideration the areas in Ireland already covered by the CLÁR programme, to ensure geographical complementarity. The SÍOL programme will be kept under regular review by my department with a view to potentially adding additional areas on an annual basis.
My Department has secured funding of €628 million in Budget 2027 and this will ensure that both rural and urban communities across the country will continue to benefit from a wide range of supports. The Community Development area was a particular focus of Government in Budget 2027, and as a result, funding for the SÍOL programme will increase from €5m to €6m next year. Capital funding of €31.5 million has been secured up to 2030 in the National Development Plan to support SÍOL.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on the merits of creating a standalone law that would make adults permitting underage drinking in their household or other setting illegal.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 555 and 571 together.
In relation to the issues raised by the Deputy, section 31 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988 (as amended) provides for a prohibition on the purchase, provision, or consumption of intoxicating liquor by a person under the age of 18. A breach of these provisions is a criminal offence, and licensees will be criminally liable for a fine of €3,000 for a first offence, and €5,000 for a second or subsequent offence. A conviction can also be used to ground an objection to the renewal of a licence by An Garda Síochána, or other objectors, and therefore, could ultimately cost the licensee their livelihood.
There are robust statutory provisions in place regarding the consumption of intoxicating liquor by persons under the age of 18. Under section 33 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988, as amended, it is illegal for a person under 18 to buy intoxicating liquor or to consume it in any place outside their home, or in another person's home where they are present by right or with permission.
The Intoxicating Liquor Act 2008 provides the Gardaí with significant powers to address the problem of alcohol sales to persons under the age of 18. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 70972/26, which stated that 29 individuals subject to valid deportation orders were released from custody in 2025, the status of the nine individuals not accounted for in that reply; whether each of these persons remains in the State.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 568, 569 and 570 together.
It is a central priority for me that Ireland's immigration system is robust and rules based. Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.
The removal of individuals involved in criminality, and those who pose a danger to society, is a priority for me as Minister. My Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure that high-risk individuals are prioritised for removal from Ireland.
The process of arranging enforced deportations and removals is often complex and can take time to complete. It frequently involves legal challenges, difficulties in obtaining travel documents, and the arrangement of flights and the necessary permissions for accompanying escorts.
As previously advised to the Deputy, in 2025, 29 individuals who were subject to valid deportation orders were released from custody at the end of their custodial sentences. A deportation order is valid unless revoked under section 3(11) of the Immigration Act 1999, as amended.
Fifteen of these individuals were subsequently removed from the State after being detained under Section 5 of the Immigration Act 1999 for the purpose of effecting their deportation. The median length of detention prior to deportation was 38 days. Of the fifteen individuals,

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí currently covering the Thomastown area of County Kilkenny.
reply:
The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act.
An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. The latest data on the allocation of Gardaí, including in the Thomastown area, can be found here:
https://www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/
It is important to emphasise that An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis. Gardaí see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement area, supported by all Divisional resources and units.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any review has been initiated following the European Parliament's adoption of Resolution B10-0424 by 381 votes to 167 to identify organisations, associations, charities, student bodies or other entities operating in Ireland that have links to, receive support from, or promote the ideology of an organisation (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 563, 564 and 565 together.
The Resolution referred to by the Deputy on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network was adopted by the European Parliament on 8th October.
While non-binding in nature, the Resolution addresses a wide range of issues linked to concerns about radicalisation and Islamist extremism in the European Union. It is addressed primarily to the Commission, and also to the Council and Member States.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will address delays in processing visa appeals for Palestinian students who have secured places at Irish universities and are at risk of missing the start of their courses as a result.
reply:
I am conscious of the exceptionally difficult circumstances facing people in Gaza and the wider region and my officials from my Department continue to engage closely with colleagues across Government in responding to those challenges.
As judicial review proceedings are currently before the Courts in relation to Palestinian study visa applicants, it would not be appropriate for me to comment on those matters in detail.
I can advise the Deputy that there has been no change in policy in relation to visa applications from Palestinian nationals. Applications from Palestinian students are assessed against the same criteria that apply to all visa-required nationals seeking to study in Ireland. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to the individual circumstances of the applicant and the information provided in support of the application.
It is important to recognise that visa decisions are based on the facts of each individual case. Refusal decisions may arise for a variety of reasons, including where applicants are unable to satisfy established immigration requirements relating to identity and documentation, financial resources, English language requirements, or other matters relevant to the assessment of the application. The reasons for refusal are communicated directly to applicants and may vary significantly from case to case.
All visa applicants are advised that it is their responsibility to provide as much supporting information as they consider neces

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he plans to bring forward legislation to combat nitrous oxide misuse in Ireland.
reply:
The classification of substances under the Misuse of Drugs Acts is a matter for my colleague, the Minister for Health. Nitrous oxide has a number of legitimate uses, particularly in the medical and catering industries, and I am informed that it is for this reason that it is not listed under the Misuse of Drugs Acts, nor is it the intention to classify it as a substance under those Acts.
However, the challenge, as with any substance open to misuse, is to regulate its supply chain effectively without unduly penalising legitimate enterprise.
The Minister of State with responsibility for the National Drugs Strategy, Jennifer Murnane O'Connor TD, has established a Working Group to address the availability and use of synthetic and semi-synthetic cannabinoids, nitrous oxide and other emerging psychoactive substances that may pose risks to public health and community safety.
The Deputy may be interested to note that I am advised by my colleague Minister Burke at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment that from February 2027, nitrous oxide will be subject to EU classification harmonisation and will be designated as a substance that is potentially harmful to human reproductive health and the nervous system. This reclassification is not merely a technical change; it is the trigger for further regulatory action. question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which a person (details supplied) who is a Thai national, married to an Irish citizen, living in the North of Ireland on a temporary EU pre-settlement scheme visa, land in Dublin airport and travel north within the law.
reply:
I can advise the Deputy that Thai nationals are visa required and will require an Irish visa to enter through Dublin Airport irrespective of their final destination.
Ireland and the United Kingdom have a shared responsibility and a shared interest in protecting the Common Travel Area (CTA). The CTA facilitates Irish and British citizens to move and reside freely across Ireland and the UK while maintaining access for citizens to a range of reciprocal rights and privileges central to everyday life. The CTA arrangements apply only to Irish and British citizens. All other nationalities remain subject to the immigration requirements in each jurisdiction, including individual visa requirements.
Any passenger landing at Dublin Airport and intending to travel onwards to the UK must meet the relevant UK immigration requirements, including holding any necessary visa, residence permission, or travel document required for entry to the UK.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Aindrias Moynihan den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta cén dul chun cinn atá déanta ó ceapadh an cheanneagraíocht atá freagrach as plean teanga bhaile seirbhíse Gaeltachta Mhaigh Chromtha; agus an ndéanfadh sé ráiteas ina thaobh.
reply:
Mar a cuireadh in iúl roimhe seo, tá Comhairle Contae Chorcaí ag obair le Foras na Gaeilge maidir leis na chéad céimeanna eile a bhaineann le plean teanga a dhréachtú do Mhaaigh Chromtha. Tuigtear go bhfuil comhaontú sínithe le Comhairle Contae Chorcaí mar cheanneagraíocht ar an bpróiseas pleanála teanga don bhaile agus an chéad sciar den allúntas atá ceadaithe agam ina leith íoctha leo, rud a chuireann ar a gcumas taighdeoir/éascaitheoir a earcú le tabhairt faoi na chéad chéimeanna comhairliúcháin le pobal an bhaile.
Leithdháiltear buiséad suas le €30,000 ar Bhailte Seirbhíse Gaeltachta chun pleananna a ullmhú agus cuirtear buiséad bliantúil €96,000 thar seacht mbliana ar fáil chun tacú lena gcur i bhfeidhm.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the mental health crisis de-escalation team in operation in Limerick; and if similar teams will be rolled out in other parts of the State.
reply:
A key recommendation of the High Level Task Force on mental health and addiction was the establishment of a Community Access Support Team (CAST) to divert those experiencing situational trauma or a mental health crisis away from the criminal justice system and towards the healthcare system. CAST is a partnership project between An Garda Síochána and the Mental Health Services of HSE Mid-West Community Healthcare in the Limerick Garda Division.
CAST enhances diversionary practices for those experiencing crisis and situational trauma leading to mental health difficulties, with the shared goal of providing a compassionate and effective response to people in distress. The pilot became operational in January 2025 and is of great benefit to vulnerable people in Limerick.
As part of the original workplan, an evaluation of CAST was undertaken by the University of Limerick.
Under a number of key pillars, the evaluation provides an evidence base that will help inform next steps, including any further rollout of this model of care, as appropriate. The recommendations from the evaluation are being considered by my Department and the Department of Health alongside key stakeholders.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps being taken to ensure our institutions and public IT systems are protected from cyberattacks (details supplied); and that any such cyberattack from a company with a presence in Ireland can be properly investigated and prosecuted.
reply:
My Department continuously evaluates and adapts its strategies to deal with the evolving cyber security threat landscape. Frontier AI models are creating unprecedented opportunities for cyber security; conversely however, they have the capabilities to create novel and heightened security risks. The National Cyber Risk Assessment, which I published in December 2025, highlighted how AI drives systemic risk by increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of cyberattacks.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), is an operational arm of my Department and holds the lead role in the management of major cyber security incidents across government. The NCSC also specifically monitors developments in AI-enabled cyber capabilities on a continuous basis and collaborates with our international partners in the EU and more broadly on this issue.
On the 7th of October 2026, I launched the National Cyber Security Strategy 2030 (NCSS) which contains measures aimed at building resilience against AI-enabled threats by tasking the NCSC to develop AI readiness across government, small businesses, and critical national infrastructure (CNI). It commits to leveraging AI to enhance national cyber defence capabilities, which the NCSC will progress through the development of an AI readiness plan.
The investigation of criminal acts rests with An Garda Síochána. Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the detection and investigation of any form of criminal activity, including onlin

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, under the temporary protection transition scheme, an applicant who was in continuous PAYE employment for the six months prior to 30 September 2026 may combine that employment income with self-employment income earned in the same period in order to meet the minimum income threshold of €29,432; and the way in which such an applicant should complete the online application form, which permits only one employment type to be selected.

Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on whether existing laws are sufficient to discourages instances of underage drinking.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 555 and 571 together.
In relation to the issues raised by the Deputy, section 31 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988 (as amended) provides for a prohibition on the purchase, provision, or consumption of intoxicating liquor by a person under the age of 18. A breach of these provisions is a criminal offence, and licensees will be criminally liable for a fine of €3,000 for a first offence, and €5,000 for a second or subsequent offence. A conviction can also be used to ground an objection to the renewal of a licence by An Garda Síochána, or other objectors, and therefore, could ultimately cost the licensee their livelihood.
There are robust statutory provisions in place regarding the consumption of intoxicating liquor by persons under the age of 18. Under section 33 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988, as amended, it is illegal for a person under 18 to buy intoxicating liquor or to consume it in any place outside their home, or in another person's home where they are present by right or with permission.
The Intoxicating Liquor Act 2008 provides the Gardaí with significant powers to address the problem of alcohol sales to persons under the age of 18. Section 14 contains provisions that allow a Garda who has reasonable grounds for believing that a person is under 18, and that he or she, or anyone accompanying that person, is in possession of intoxicating liquor for the purpose of consuming it in a place other than a private dwelling, to seek an expl
