question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the work of the AI in Schools External Advisory Taskforce; to list its membership; the number of meetings to date; and to indicate when it expects to report.
reply:
The AI in Education External Advisory Taskforce has been established to support the Department in developing a coherent national approach to the safe, responsible and effective use of AI across the school system at primary and post-primary level. Two AI Taskforce meetings have been held to date, 14 May and 21 September. The list of members will be published on gov.ie in the coming weeks.
Meetings are attended by teacher unions, management bodies and other stakeholders such as teachers, parents and students representative groups and research bodies and other relevant agencies. Its membership ensures a broad range of perspectives and expertise are brought to the discussion.
To support its work the Taskforce has established two working groups. The first is focused on assessment, including both summative and State-certified assessment, with the second Working Group focusing on teaching, learning and formative assessment.
The current phase of the taskforce is expected to operate over an initial 18-24 month period with outputs delivered on a rolling basis. Quarterly reports will be published on gov.ie in due course. These publications will provide greater transparency regarding the Taskforce's work programme and priorities.
The taskforce will help ensure that the department’s response is informed by practical experience, ongoing work across the education system, and emerging national and international developments.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of children in Ireland who are home-educated; and the measures in place to assess the quality of that education.
reply:
The Constitution of Ireland acknowledges the family as the primary and natural educator of the child and sets out the rights and duties of the State in the matter of education. The Constitution makes explicit that the State does not oblige parents to send their children to any particular type of school. Parents are free to provide education in their homes, in private schools, or in schools recognised or established by the State.
Tusla’s Alternative Education Assessment and Registration Service (AEARS) is under the remit of my department. AEARS is responsible for the regulation of provision for education in places other than recognised schools, including children who are home schooled or who are enrolled in a non-recognised independent school.
Parents who wish to educate their child in a place other than a recognised school are required to make an application to AEARS to have their child included on the Section 14 Statutory Register. AEARS will then carry out an assessment of the educational provision to determine if the child is eligible to be placed on the register. Assessments are carried out by an authorised person in line with the ‘Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places other than a recognised School’, issued by my department and which is available to view at the following link: Guidelines on the Assessment of Education in Places Other Than Recognised Schools (File Format PDF 1.3MB). www.tusla.ie/uploads/content/Guidelines_on_Assessment_of_Education.pdf

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy David Cullinane den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta an mbeidh an méadú €1 milliún ar mhaoiniú Fhoras na Gaeilge i mBuiséad 2027 leordhóthanach chun coinneáil suas le boilsciú agus le hardú ar chostais reatha; agus cén tionchar a bheidh aige seo ar chumas an Fhorais tacú le heagraíochtaí agus tionscnaimh Ghaeilge ar fud an oileáin.
reply:
Is í an Chomhairle Aireachta Thuaidh-Theas a cheadaíonn buiséid bhliantúla na gComhlachtaí Forfheidhmithe Thuaidh Theas, an Foras Teanga san áireamh. Cuireann Rialtas na hÉireann 75% de bhuiséad Fhoras na Gaeilge ar fáil agus tagann an 25% eile ó Fheidhmeannas Thuaisceart Éireann, de réir an chóimheas maoinithe a aontaíodh nuair a bunaíodh an Foras Teanga.
Cuireadh maoiniú comhaontaithe de €20 milliún ar fáil d'Fhoras na Gaeilge agus do Ghníomhaireacht na hUltaise i mbliana. Ardaíodh maoiniú Chlár na Leabhar Gaeilge go €2 milliún in 2026, an leibhéal is airde riamh. Chomh maith leis sin, chuir mo Roinn maoiniú breise os cionn €2 milliún ar fáil do chláir agus do ghníomhaíochtaí eile Fhoras na Gaeilge in 2026.
Fógraíodh maoiniú breise de €1 mhilliún i mBuiséad 2027 an tseachtain seo caite, chun tacú le hobair an Fhorais Teanga. Tá na pleananna gnó agus buiséid an Fhorais Teanga do 2027 fós á bplé ag na Ranna sa dá dhlínse agus beidh siad á gcur faoi bhráid na Comhairle Aireachta Thuaidh Theas roimh dheireadh na bliana.
Tabharfaidh an maoiniú breise seo cinnteacht don bhForas Teanga agus do na heagraíochta agus grúpaí pobail ar fud an oileáin a bhaineann tairbhe as na scéimeanna tacaíochta agus maoinithe a chuirtear ar fáil.

It provided families with a single online application process for first year places and introduced synchronised and streamlined timelines for schools to manage admissions and issue offers. question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Education and Youth the process for applying for a new Gaelcholáiste; to outline such a process; and if applications for new Gaelcholáistí will be considered other than if it this is the outcome of the public voting process which has been in place in various locations in recent years.
reply:
New schools are established in areas of demographic growth, as the resources available for school infrastructure have to be prioritised to ensure that every child has a school place.
Demographic requirements in an area determine the need or otherwise for establishing new schools and while there are no Irish medium or English medium schools planned currently (other than new special schools) this position is kept under constant review by my department.
The Programme for Government 2025, Securing Ireland’s Future, includes a commitment to establish Gaelscoileanna and Gaelcholáistí where there is demand and support parents choosing Irish-medium education for their children.
In November 2025 my department published a ‘Policy for Irish-medium Education outside of the Gaeltacht’ and established a Taskforce on Models of Provision for Irish-medium Education.
The role of the taskforce is to provide a platform for collaboration between my department and key stakeholders to develop a pathway to increase provision of Irish-medium education nationally. The taskforce's work is expected to be completed by the end of the year. It will make recommendations to my department on areas such as the criteria for Irish-medium education provision, how to support schools transitioning to Irish-medium and mechanisms to facilitate expansion of provision.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will review the criteria governing the recognition of overseas teaching service for incremental credit and pensionable service purposes; the number of years of overseas teaching service that may currently be recognised; and whether consideration is being given to recognising all teaching service completed abroad where it can be verified.
reply:
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education & Youth’s Circulars 10/2001, for primary teachers, and 29/2007 and 29/2010, for post-primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU.
There is no separate scheme in the Department to recognise overseas teaching service for pensionable service purposes alone and under the Department Pension schemes, service given in countries outside Ireland does not constitute pensionable service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland by a qualified teacher in a school or college must be deemed to be equivalent to teaching service given in a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland. This includes teaching service given in a public or private primary or secondary school abroad.
Criteria such as whether the school is subject to state funding, which can be of relevance when examining claims relating to private teaching schools, and the length of time the school has been in existence, must be satisfied for service at that school to be recognised for incremental credit. Where a school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.

reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
My department takes child protection very seriously and considers that the protection and welfare of children is a fundamental responsibility of all involved in the care and education of children.
Under the Education Act 1998, every school is managed by its board of management on behalf of the patron. The board employs the school’s teachers and other staff, except in Education and Training Board schools, where the ETB is the employer. Decisions on employing or engaging staff are therefore a matter for the school authority as employer, and my department has no role in employer–employee matters.

Vetting is carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau. Tusla – the Child and Family Agency has statutory responsibility for assessing child welfare and protection concerns and determines whether an allegation of abuse is founded or unfounded. question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on CLÁR applications for Carlow and Kilkenny.
reply:
The CLÁR programme provides funding under several measures for small-scale infrastructure projects in designated rural areas. Last year, I approved over €14 million for 238 projects covering community facilities and amenities, community vehicles, and specific support for island communities. Since 2020 almost €68 million has been allocated to over 1,500 projects including over €800,000 for 22 projects in Carlow and over €1.4 million for 35 projects in Kilkenny.
The 2026 CLÁR programme was launched on 10th March with the following measures:
Measure 1: Developing Community Facilities & Amenities
Measure 2: Mobility, Cancer Care, First Responder and Meals on Wheels Transport
Measure 3: Our Living Islands
The closing date for applications under all measures has now passed. Earlier this month I was delighted to announce over €2.5 million for 44 projects under measure 2 of the CLÁR programme. My officials are currently evaluating applications under measures 1 and 3 of the 2026 programme, including those from Carlow and Kilkenny under measure 1. I expect to announce the successful projects before the end of the year.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if post-primary schools are required to consider reasonable accommodation for students with dyslexia who experience significant difficulties learning a modern foreign language; the guidance issued by her Department on the application of reasonable accommodation to subject selection and participation in language classes; whether such consideration should include alternative subjects or other arrangements where appropriate.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 438 and 439 together.
Under the Education Act 1998, the School Board of Management (BOM), appointed by the school’s patron, is the body charged with the direct governance of a school and the principal manages the school on a day-to-day basis. Each school has the autonomy to design its own timetables and decide which subjects and programmes to offer based on the educational needs and interests of its students as well as considerations such as classroom space, staffing, time limitations etc.
The study of Modern Foreign Languages is optional at Junior and Senior Cycle. However, it should be noted that schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language and higher educational institutions may require a foreign language to be studied for matriculation purposes.
The Deputy may wish to note that Languages Connect, Ireland’s Strategy for Foreign Languages in Education 2017 – 2026 aims to increase and diversify the teaching and learning of foreign languages at all levels. A key action of the policy is to promote the importance of foreign language learning and to provide supports to schools and teachers in this regard.
A significant development under the Strategy is that, under the new Primary Curriculum Framework, Modern Foreign Languages (MFL) are being introduced on a phased basis from September 2026, Learning outcomes will focus on Language Awareness in 3rd and 4th class and Language Competence at 5th and 6th class. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department has issued guidance to post-primary schools on the position of students with dyslexia who hold an exemption from Irish and experience significant difficulty learning a modern foreign language; if not, if she will issue guidance clarifying that, while an Irish exemption does not automatically extend to a foreign language, such students should have their individual educational needs considered and should be informed of available alternative arrangements.
reply:
While individual schools may have their own rules in relation to the study of a foreign language, the Department of Education and Youth does not require students to study these subjects and therefore no exemption system exists.
Where an exemption from the study of Irish is granted, it should not be interpreted as an exemption from the study of other languages.
Any decision not to study a language should be made carefully and following detailed discussion with the student, their teachers and school principal. A student may commence the study of a language (including the study of Irish) at an appropriate level after the granting of an exemption from the study of Irish. The reasons for this will vary from student to student and may include having a background in language, that the subject is being studied at an ab initio level and/or that they have experienced an improvement in their ability to engage in language learning.
When making a decision it is important to remember that the study of foreign languages is a common entry requirement for many 3rd level courses and students/parents are advised to contact the school’s guidance teacher and seek advice on how best to proceed. 3rd level institutions may set their own rules for the entry requirements for the courses they offer, therefore a language exemption at 3rd level is a matter for the individual University. reply:

reply:
The Convention on Education was established to deliver on a Programme for Government commitment to hold a Convention on Education, bringing together all stakeholders in Education. The Convention on Education is the largest exercise in deliberative democracy in the state to date, with 150 people taking part. The 150 person membership comprises 30 parents and guardians, 30 school employees and early years educators, 60 education stakeholders and for the first time ever, 30 children and young people between the ages of 8 and 24 will be full members.
To ensure that all citizens had an opportunity to add their voice and perspectives to this important exercise in deliberative democracy, I launched a National Conversation in January 2026, in which over 42,000 people participated. The themes raised in the National Conversation, informed the agenda of the Convention on Education, which was approved by Government in April. Three meetings of the Convention on Education have taken place to date with the Convention due to meet again in November to continue its deliberations. I expect to receive the final report from the Convention in early 2027.
While Citizens’ Assemblies are a mechanism used by the Oireachtas to involve members of the general public in helping it respond to important constitutional, legal or policy questions, the Convention on Education has been designed by the Government to provide a deliberative perspective on the future of the Irish school system.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to consider allowing supports for the development and protection of beaches under the town and village renewal funds, which would specifically help coastal towns and villages.
reply:
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme was introduced in 2016 and is one of a number of measures designed to rejuvenate rural towns and villages throughout Ireland. Since the launch of the scheme over €217 million has been allocated to almost 2,000 projects across the country.
TVRS places particular emphasis on projects which support sustainable employment creation, town centre resilience and regeneration, streetscape enhancement, and bringing derelict and vacant buildings and sites back into use as multipurpose community spaces. The Scheme also supports the development of public realm works, recreational amenities, and town and village centre plazas with funding ranging from €50,000 to €500,000.
The priorities of TVRS are reviewed at the end of each scheme year to ensure that funding continues to be targeted effectively towards supporting vibrant and attractive communities, while responding to changing needs and opportunities.
While I recognise the important role that beaches can play in supporting the vitality of coastal towns and villages, the primary focus of TVRS is on the regeneration of the town or village itself.
However, through the Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme, my department does provide support for the development of beaches and coastal areas generally for wider recreational use. This includes funding for walking trails, tidal pools and other amenities for water-based activities.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to fund more youth workers serving the young people of the South West Inner City.
reply:

The department does not employ or fund individual youth worker posts directly. Rather, it provides funding to youth services and organisations, which are responsible for determining their staffing requirements and deploying resources to meet the needs of young people in their communities.
Core current funding of €90.1 million is available in 2026, representing 5% increase on the 2025 allocation. In 2026, more than €20 million in funding was allocated through City of Dublin ETB, including approximately €17.8 million under the UBU Your Place Your Space scheme, supporting the delivery of a wide range of youth services and programmes for young people across Dublin, including services operating in the South West Inner City area.
Building on the progress achieved in 2026, in line with the commitments in the Programme for Government relating to youth services, the 2027 budget is increasing the level of funding being made by an additional €7 million in current funding and another €4 million of NDP capital funding in 2027. This builds on the previous budget and reflects the Government’s continued commitment to strengthening the youth sector, including those living in the South West Inner City.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 425 and 426 together.

Schools that were included in the most recent expansion of the programme in 2022 were those with the highest levels of concentrated disadvantage as identified through the refined DEIS identification model. Schools were not required to apply for inclusion in the DEIS programme, and the model was applied fairly and equally to all schools. A detailed paper on the refined DEIS identification model is available on gov.ie.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department has conducted or commissioned any assessment of the impact of employment permits on housing demand in the State, including the additional housing requirement arising from permit holders and their dependent family members; if so, the findings of any such assessment; and if not, whether he intends to undertake or commission such an assessment.
reply:

This engagement is focused on evaluating that demand and the availability in the domestic labour force, while identifying alternative pathways aimed at contributing domestically to addressing shortages of skilled candidates in key sectors.
In considering changes to the occupation lists, my Department assesses not only labour market evidence but also wider whole-of-Government factors. These include the potential impact of inward migration on housing demand, transport capacity, healthcare, and other public services.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his attention has been drawn to the concerns of an organisation (details supplied) in relation to the requirement for their industry to have least half of their workforce to be EEA, UK, or Swiss nationals; and if any flexibility or derogation can be considered.
reply:
The Employment Permits Act 2024 requires that, in order for an employment permit to be granted, at least 50% of the employees of an employer are Irish/EEA/UK/Swiss nationals. This policy fulfils Ireland's obligations under the Union Preference principles of membership of the EU. The mandatory application of the 50:50 rule underpins the Government's employment creation strategy by requiring employers in the State to hire in a balanced manner from domestic and EEA labour markets.
Under this rule, an employment permit will not issue unless, at the time of application, at least 50% of the employees of the employer are EEA, UK or Swiss nationals. The Employment Permits Act does provide waivers to the application of the 50:50 rule : where the employer applying for the employment permit has been registered with Revenue Commissioners within the last two years and the application is supported by either Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland; or where the employer has no employees and the foreign national concerned will be the sole employee of the employer.
Officials of my Department recently concluded a review of Ireland's use of the 50:50 rule, the outcome of which recommended amending the Employment Permits Act 2024 to address critical recruitment difficulties in the health and social care sector through the creation of new sector-specific and sector-wide regulation-making powers.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if his previous commitment to make a decision to abolish subminimum pay rates for young workers in 2029 still stands.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, the National Minimum Wage Acts allow for lower, or sub-minimum rates of the minimum wage for those employees aged under 20 years of age. Those aged less than 18 years can be paid 70 per cent of the full minimum wage rate, while those aged 18 years and 19 years can be paid 80 and 90 per cent of the full rate, respectively.
Since the current system of youth rates is based on a percentage of the full minimum wage; when the minimum wage increases, these sub-minimum youth rates also increase, with young people in receipt of these rates seeing a commensurate increase in their wages.
As part of Budget 2027 Government agreed to accept the recommendation of the independent Low Pay Commission to increase the National Minimum Wage by 79 cent, or 5.6%, from 1st January 2027.
Sub-minimum youth rates will also increase by 5.6% on that date.
If we include the planned 2027 increase, the National Minimum Wage has increased by 46% since 2021 - well ahead of consumer price inflation.
In April 2025, as part of measures designed to bolster business resilience and support competitiveness, the Government agreed to defer a decision on the future use of sub-minimum youth rates until 2029.
This decision should be considered in the context of the significant increases in the minimum wage and wider improvements in statutory employment measures.
The Government will continue to closely monitor the use of subminimum youth rates to ensure they do not undermine fair pay or progression

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the methodology and criteria used to determine the number of employment permits made available under occupational quotas; the basis on which the numerical quota for each occupation currently subject to a quota was calculated; the labour shortages identified in each such occupation; and the number of permits sought by relevant sectoral representatives during the most recent review compared with the quota ultimately approved.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 404 and 408 together.
Ireland's employment permits system is designed to support employers in addressing identified labour and skills shortages while maintaining a clear policy preference for recruitment from within Ireland and the wider EEA.
Ireland's economic migration framework focuses on addressing skills and labour shortages, particularly in sectors of strategic economic importance, while facilitating the recruitment of non-EEA nationals where labour needs cannot be met from within Ireland or the EEA.
A number of policy areas, including employment, migration and education, intersect in addressing skills and labour shortages. In recent years, my Department has used the employment permits system to support an integrated response to these challenges and to help establish a sustainable domestic pipeline of labour for future vacancies. This has included the use of employment permit quotas together with additional conditions such as training and upskilling measures, where lower-skilled occupations have been removed from the Ineligible Occupations List.
To ensure the appropriate use of the employment permits system in respect of lower-skilled occupations, an occupation may be removed from the Ineligible Occupations List subject to a quota restriction on the number of General Employment Permits that may be granted, alongside initiatives designed to develop a domestic supply of labour.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether regulations have been made pursuant to section 47(12)(a) of the Employment Permits Act 2024 specifying accommodation to be provided to a foreign national as a condition of the grant of a general employment permit or seasonal employment permit; if so, to set out the employments and categories of employment to which such regulations apply; and if not, whether consideration is being given to making such regulations, particularly in respect of occupations subject to employment permit quotas.
reply:
The overarching objective for the State’s national economic migration and employment permit system is that the State’s employment permit system should help meet, in the short to medium term, the demand for skills and labour in the Irish economy without disrupting the Irish labour market.
The 2024 Employment Permits Act provides for a regulation making power under section 47(12) that allows the Minister to specify conditions for the grant of a General Employment Permit or a Seasonal Employment Permit in particular roles.
The Act allows that conditions may be set around accommodation, training, or expenses provided to the employment permit holder in question. These conditions may also cover measures taken by the employer to increase the skills knowledge, qualifications or experience within the sector, including employing trainees or apprentices. It also covers measures taken by the employer to reduce their reliance on the permit system, including through technical changes to work processes.
The Department is committed to keeping pace with rapid labour market changes and to proactively support sectors and addressing shortages as they arise. Active policy consideration is being given to the development of new regulations under these powers, in line with the national economic migration, and general migration policy.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide an update on his Department's work on the transposition of the Platform Work Directive.
reply:
The Improving Working Conditions in Platform Work Directive entered into force on 1 December 2024 and EU Member States have until 2 December 2026 to transpose the Directive into national law.
The Directive is significant, technically complex and wide-ranging, legislating for numerous areas. It seeks to ensure that people working through digital labour platforms have the correct legal employment status that corresponds to their actual working arrangements, enabling them to benefit from the employment rights to which they are entitled.
The Directive also aims to regulate the use of algorithms by digital labour platforms. It will make the use of algorithms in human resources management in platform work more transparent, ensuring that automated systems are monitored by qualified staff, and that workers have the right to contest automated decisions. The Directive also imposes substantial limitations on the processing of personal data by these systems.
My Department has undertaken extensive consultation with relevant Government Departments, agencies and stakeholders, and has also undertaken a public consultation process to inform the transposition of the Directive. Officials have also engaged with the European Commission's work on implementation of the Directive. The views received through these engagements have informed the development of the legislative measures required for transposition. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his Departments definition of "data sovereignty" and its policy approach to current geopolitical discussions on data sovereignty, residency and localisation.
reply:
My Department does not currently apply a single statutory definition of “data sovereignty”. Ireland is a signatory, along with all EU Member States, to the Declaration for European Digital Sovereignty, which describes digital sovereignty as the ability of the EU and its Member States to make their own choices about digital technologies and services while remaining open to cooperation with international partners. The Declaration also recognises data sovereignty as an important element of this broader objective and highlights the need to ensure appropriate protection for sensitive European data.
Our approach is also guided by and aligned with the EU framework governing data protection, data sharing, cybersecurity and digital resilience, including the GDPR and the wider Digital Decade agenda. The Government supports the secure and trusted flow of data across borders and an open, rules-based digital economy, while maintaining high standards of privacy, security and resilience.
In line with the Declaration, Ireland views digital and data sovereignty not as a basis for protectionism or broad data localisation requirements, but as a means of strengthening Europe’s ability to act independently where necessary, reducing strategic dependencies, and protecting its interests, values and security in the digital sphere.

reply:
My Department considered the resourcing requirements associated with Ireland's EU Presidency and identified and redeployed several civil servants to support Presidency-related work in the Digital and AI policy areas. Given the exceptional workload associated with the Presidency, including the advancement of key policy priorities and the delivery of major events such as the AI Summit, the Department also sought to supplement internal capacity through temporary secondments from external organisations.
Specific criteria were established for these opportunities. The Department sought experienced professionals with strong analytical, research and communication skills, and expertise relevant to digital, AI, technical, legal and policy issues, including familiarity with EU legislative and policy processes where appropriate.
These temporary secondments are designed to provide additional specialist capacity during the Presidency period and to complement the work of existing civil servants. All secondees complete the Department's onboarding and security requirements and they are subject to the Civil Service Code of Standards and Behaviour, as well as strict ethics, confidentiality, security and conflict of interest requirements., including declarations under the Official Secrets Act. Secondees serve as temporary members of staff under the direction and management of the Department.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the safeguards being put in place regarding the use of AI helpdesks and AI-tools to screen queries and complaints from the public within his Department and within bodies under its aegis.
reply:
There are currently no use cases, either deployed or in development, in which generative AI-based automation is embedded in processing or decision-making (including systems to manage helpdesks and/or complaints from the public).
My Department first issued a policy document on the use of Generative AI to all staff in July 2023. That policy highlighted some of the potential areas where Generative AI can deliver efficiencies, but it also set out the risks of using such technologies and the mitigations that staff in the Department must adopt to avoid those risks. This was based on contemporaneous guidance received from the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
The Department's original Generative AI Policy was reviewed again and updated in 2025. The revised policy position encourages and fosters greater use of Generative AI while also emphasising governance and accountability where AI tools have been used. General use cases include conducting research, creating initial drafts or layouts for documents, and supporting decision-making.
Department staff have been advised that they must make their own value judgements and be transparent and vigilant about any significant use of Generative AI. Staff remain 100% responsible for all outputs, and they must ensure that these are fit for use and factually correct. reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 391 and 392 together.
Where an employer does not engage in collective bargaining, a trade union may use the voluntary dispute-resolution procedures provided through the Workplace Relations Commission. The Code of Practice on Voluntary Dispute Resolution provides for the appointment of an Advisory Officer to assist the parties, with defined timeframes for engagement. Where the process does not resolve the dispute, the matter may, subject to the relevant statutory conditions, be referred to the Labour Court under the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Acts 2001 to 2015.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to outline any plans that he may introduce for compulsory safety reporting and monitoring of frontier artificial intelligence.
reply:
Frontier AI refers to some of the most advanced AI models currently in development. These models are increasingly being applied to scientific research, including areas such as healthcare, life sciences and materials science.
The rapid pace of technological progress has intensified international discussion regarding the governance of frontier AI, particularly in relation to model evaluation, safety testing, risk management, cybersecurity, access to computing infrastructure, and the development of common technical standards.
The EU AI Act provides what is often referred to as the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. While the term "frontier AI" is not specifically defined in the Act, the most advanced AI models are addressed through the Act's framework for general-purpose AI models, including those designated as posing systemic risk. These models are subject to enhanced requirements relating to risk management, model evaluation, incident reporting and cybersecurity. The European Commission AI Office has primary responsibility for the supervision of these obligations and plays a central role in the governance of advanced AI models within the European Union. In addition to its supervisory functions, it supports coordination among Member States and contributes to wider discussions on AI governance and safety.
The broader European approach combines regulation, technical standards, codes of practice, market oversight and international cooperation

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether his Department has assessed the position where the minimum annual remuneration for healthcare assistants and home carers, equivalent to €16.12 an hour on a 39 hour week, exceeds the national minimum wage of €14.15 an hour, such that Irish and EEA workers in the same roles may legally be paid less than permit holders.
reply:
National Minimum Wage (NMW) sets the out the minimum pay terms permitted to employ someone in Ireland. Minimum annual remuneration (MAR) thresholds set the minimum salary to recruit someone, from anywhere in the world, to work in Ireland and therefore regulates access to the labour market, shaping the composition of economic migration.
The Government's objective in establishing MAR thresholds within the employment permits system is to support fair remuneration, facilitate the attraction and retention of essential skills, ensure that employment permit holders have access to quality employment opportunities, can contribute positively to the Irish economy and have the financial capacity to support a reasonable standard of living for themselves and, where applicable, their families, without undue recourse to State supports.
In addition, aligning employment permit remuneration thresholds with broader earnings growth helps to mitigate the risk of disruption or displacement within the domestic labour market, including potential wage suppression. It also supports the objective of ensuring that the employment permit system complements, rather than substitutes for, investment in workforce development, innovation, productivity improvements, and skills enhancement. Maintaining appropriate remuneration thresholds helps to ensure that Ireland's employment permits framework remains balanced, sustainable and responsive to the needs of both workers and employers.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in relation to the general employment permit application, if websites (details supplied) are acceptable online platforms for the second job advertisement required for the Labour Market Needs Test.
reply:
The employment permits system is grounded in legislation that sets clear and objective criteria applied to the grant of an employment permit including minimum salary thresholds, availability of skills in the domestic labour market, and the eligibility of occupations. These criteria ensure that permits are issued only where there is a demonstrable shortage and that the system remains fair, transparent, and responsive to Ireland’s labour market needs.
The labour market needs test (LMNT) is a core safeguard within the system. It ensures that job vacancies are first made available to Irish and EEA nationals before an employer may recruit a non EEA national.
Where an LMNT is required, including for General Employment Permit applications, employers must advertise the vacancy through the Department of Social Protection’s JobsIreland and EURES online employment services, and on at least one additional online platform jointly for at least 28 days (continuously and unaltered). Suitable platforms for the additional advertisements should be accessible to the general public, the principal purpose of which is to publish offers of employment including for example online newspaper publications and employment websites.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to address a pension related matter (details supplied).
reply:
I am advised that the National Shared Services Office (NSSO) has examined the case referred to by the Deputy.
The person concerned served in the former Department of Posts and Telegraphs between 1969 and 1975. However, a distinction must be made between total period of employment and reckonable service for superannuation purposes.
Records indicate that the period from 14 July 1969 to 3 June 1973 was served in a non-pensionable capacity and, the service, therefore is not reckonable for pension purposes. The individual's pensionable service ran from 4 June 1973 to 12 May 1975 and amounted to 1 year and 344 days of reckonable service.
Under the superannuation arrangements applicable at the time, an officer was required to have a minimum of five years' qualifying pensionable service in order to be entitled to preserved pension benefits on leaving the public service. While the individual's overall period of employment exceeded five years, only reckonable pensionable service may be counted in determining entitlement to superannuation benefits. As the individual had less than five years' qualifying pensionable service, the individual concerned did not meet this statutory qualifying requirement and therefore there is no entitlement to a preserved pension under the terms of the applicable scheme.
The NSSO has reviewed the case and confirmed that the position is consistent with the relevant superannuation provisions. Pension benefits can only be awarded where the conditions prescribed

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to provide the necessary funding to address tidal flooding where family homes have been flooded at Cromane Lower, Killorglin, County Kerry.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 376 and 377 together.
Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme.
Localised flooding issues are a matter, in the first instance, for each Local Authority to investigate and address, and a Local Authority may carry out flood mitigation works using its own resources. Local Authorities may apply to the OPW for funding for flood mitigation and coastal protection works under the OPW Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme. Since its introduction in 2009, some €70 million has been approved under the Scheme for 930 local authority led projects that are delivering flood mitigation and coastal protection for some 8,000 properties.
In May this year, I was pleased to announce that the revised criteria for the Minor Flood Mitigation Works and Coastal Protection Scheme (Minor Works Scheme) are available and greatly increase the scope of the Scheme and provides local authorities with a greater opportunity to address localised flooding and coastal erosion risk within their administrative areas. The revisions include an increase in the upper threshold in funding for projects from €750,000 to €2 million and an increase in the OPW contribution from 90% to 95% for approved funding above €300,000. I have also expanded the Scheme to include interim flood mitigation measures for communities where a major flood relief scheme is planned, but not complete. Further revisions include the relaxing of some economic criteria.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to consider decentralising Government departments to Iveragh and south Kerry to boost economic growth in these areas.
reply:
Decentralisation was announced in 2003 to support the relocation of jobs and organisational functions across the Civil Service from Dublin to towns and cities throughout Ireland. From 2003 to 2011, the economic development programme for rural towns was supported through a number of interlinked policies and funding streams, including a programme of decentralisation in line with commitments in the National Spatial Strategy (2002 - 2020) to balance regional growth in Ireland.
On 17th November 2011, the Government announced the cancellation of the programme in light of substantial changes in the national budgetary and workforce environment. This decision was also influenced by the need to focus on programmes and projects that would best support economic recovery and identify significant expenditure savings and efficiencies. There are currently no plans to reintroduce this programme.
The Civil Service Mobility Scheme was introduced in 2018 to facilitate the structured movement of Civil Servants between Departments and locations across Ireland. The Scheme supports skills development, career progression and increased workforce flexibility and also allows civil servants to avail of transfers to posts located nationwide, including outside the Dublin area.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the estimated capital and current expenditure associated with implementing the European Digital Identity Wallet; the projected annual operating cost; and the source of funding for same.
reply:
Since 2024, my Department has invested a total of €4,628,866 in capital funding in the national Government digital wallet initiative. This initiative is being delivered on a phased basis, with funding provided over multiple years to support its design, development, testing, and rollout.
The implementation leverages a suite of technical building blocks and digital public infrastructure components to ensure the efficient and effective use of public investment. This approach supports the development of Ireland's national digital wallet, providing the foundation for Ireland's EU-compliant digital wallet under the European Digital Identity Framework Regulation.
As the solution remains under development and has not yet entered full operational service, separate estimates of ongoing annual operating costs have not yet been finalised. Operational requirements, including hosting, support, maintenance, certification and service management arrangements, will continue to be assessed as implementation progresses and the operating model is finalised.
Funding for this initiative to date has been provided through the Department's Digital Transformation Fund (DTF). Future operational costs associated with the national digital wallet will be met from Exchequer resources through the annual estimates process, in line with funding arrangements that apply to other national digital public services.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to provide further detail on the scope and intended focus of the enterprise tax review announced as part of Budget 2027; the specific areas of tax that will be considered as part of the review; the expected timeline for its initiation.
reply:
As announced in Budget 2027, a holistic assessment of Ireland’s enterprise support regime including grant schemes and tax incentives available to businesses will be undertaken. Further detail on this review will be announced in due course.
I expect that the assessment will examine the full range of enterprise supports, including grant schemes, tax incentives and business development programmes currently available.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of businesses that registered and submitted returns for each of the two accounting periods 1 May - 30 June and 1 July – 31 August for the e-liquid products tax (EPT); the volumes and values of e-liquid products subject to EPT in that period; the total tax collected; the available breakdown by geography, size and type of business making the return.
reply:

Businesses who engage in the first supply of e-liquid products in the State are obliged to register, and to account for the tax for each two-month accounting period.

question: Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the safeguards in place to ensure that Revenue enforcement and sheriff procedures adequately provide for exceptional circumstances when dealing with small, family operated businesses; and whether additional discretion should be available in cases where hardship, bereavement or serious family illness can be clearly evidenced.
reply:
I am advised that Revenue only refers outstanding tax liabilities to its enforcement agents, including sheriffs, as a last resort. Revenue’s strong preference is to engage constructively with taxpayers who are experiencing temporary cash-flow difficulties, and, where possible, to agree mutually acceptable payment solutions, including Phased Payment Arrangements (PPA) where appropriate, rather than resorting to debt collection or enforcement measures.
I am further advised that Revenue’s debt collection and enforcement framework incorporates a range of safeguards including constructive engagement with taxpayers in difficulty, a graduated series of contacts before any enforcement is initiated, and case by case discretion to take account of hardship and exceptional circumstances.
As part of Revenue’s standard debt collection procedure, where taxes become overdue in accordance with the statutory due date, a request for payment will issue with details of the tax(es) due, requesting payment within a set timeframe. This request outlines the consequences of continued non-payment and affords the taxpayer up to 10 days to engage. In the absence of payment or meaningful engagement, a final demand issues allowing a further 7 days for the customer to engage. It is only where there is continued lack of engagement from the customer in response to these notices that the case is escalated for enforcement action, which may include referral to the Sheriff.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the number of communities in Galway east that became newly eligible for CLÁR funding, following the recent review of the scheme; and if he will consider further expanding eligibility to rural communities experiencing population growth but which continue to face significant deficits in community infrastructure and services.
reply:
The CLÁR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in rural areas that were designated based on having experienced significant levels of depopulation over a defined period.
The 2025 Programme for Government made a commitment to carry out a comprehensive review of the eligible CLÁR areas. This review has now been completed, and an additional 110 electoral divisions (EDs) have been designated as eligible under the CLÁR programme.
The review was completed by the All-Island Research Observatory in Maynooth University utilising two nationally recognised datasets, based on the results from Census 2022. The Pobal HP Deprivation Index was used to identify areas experiencing socio-economic disadvantage. In parallel, the Central Statistics Office's Urban and Rural Life in Ireland classification was applied to distinguish areas based on their degree of remoteness and relative exposure to urban influence, with particular emphasis on geographical areas identified as being 'highly rural and remote'. Areas were required to meet the criteria under both datasets in order to be considered for inclusion.
As a result of the review, the ED of Crumpaun was newly designated in Galway and almost 70% of Galway is now designated for CLÁR.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group has met yet; if so, the matters discussed; the frequency with which it is due to meet; the schedule of options it will discuss; the manner in which its recommendations will be published and considered; and a timeline for same.
reply:
The Government remains committed to protecting Ireland’s present and future generations by investing in climate adaptation measures to manage the impacts of extreme weather. Accordingly, €1.3 billion has been committed to the delivery of flood relief schemes over the lifetime of the National Development Plan (NDP) to 2030. This will protect approximately 23,000 properties across various communities from river and coastal flood risk.
In terms of flood insurance, the Central Bank of Ireland has undertaken extensive research into the nature and scale of the flood insurance protection gap in Ireland. They found that 1 in 20 buildings (approximately 5%) have limited access to flood insurance; and that 54% of this gap is concentrated in Dublin, Cork, Louth, Clare, and Kildare.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether a person who has received the help to buy grant at the rate of €30,000 but has not yet drawn down their mortgage is eligible for the additional €5,000.
reply:
The Help to Buy (HTB) incentive, is a tax-based scheme to assist first-time purchasers with the deposit they need to buy or build a new house or apartment. It also aims to encourage additional supply of new houses by supporting demand.
HTB provides a refund of Income Tax and Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) paid in Ireland over the previous four years, subject to limits outlined in the legislation.
Based on the latest available data (30 September 2026), the scheme has supported over 70,000 individuals or couples to buy or build their own home.
For a property to qualify for the HTB scheme, it must be new or converted for use as a dwelling, having not previously been used as a dwelling. Additionally, the purchase value/approved valuation of the property must not exceed €500,000.The level of support available to first time buyers under the HTB scheme, was, until 6 October 2026, whichever is the lesser of:
• €30,000; or
• 10 per cent of the purchase price of the new property; or
• the amount of Income Tax and DIRT paid in the four years before application for the relief.
As announced as part of Budget 2027 the maximum amount of the relief, which can be claimed by a first time purchaser or self builder, increased by €5,000, to €35,000. The change was implemented by way of a Budget night Financial Resolution which took effect from 7 October 2026.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline the CPI projections that underpin the Budget 2027 rather than the HICP.
reply:
Under Regulation (EU) No 473/2013, my Department is required to send the macroeconomic and fiscal forecasts produced for Budget 2027 to the European Commission in the Draft Budgetary Plan (DBP) by October 15th. In line with guidelines from the Commission, my Department uses the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) as the measure of inflation used in its forecasts.
As the Deputy will be aware, my Department’s forecasts are independently endorsed by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council. A memorandum of understanding (MOU) between my Department and the Fiscal Council details the key elements of the endorsement process including the variables the Department is required to provide to the Fiscal Council. This MOU specifies that my Department forecast inflation on a HICP basis. As such, my Department projects inflation, as measured by the HICP rather than on the basis of the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position regarding any review of the requirement under the Irish Collective Asset-management Vehicles (ICAV) Act 2015 for the central bank to maintain a publicly accessible database of company directors that includes their name, date of birth, personal residential address and a copy of their signature; and if he is concerned about the implications on their privacy as a result of this requirement.
reply:
As you may be aware, the Department recently published a refreshed Ireland for Finance Strategy, ‘Vision 2030 - Renewed and Refocussed for a Digital Age’.
In the Strategy, the Department also highlights its intention to review the Irish Collective Asset-Management Vehicles Act 2015 (ICAV Act) and has identified this as a key policy action.
Section 11 of the ICAV Act 2015 requires the Central Bank to maintain an ICAV’s register of directors and secretaries, and Section 65(2) specifies the information that must be included in an ICAV's register of directors including certain personal data relating to directors. The requirement reflects long-standing corporate governance provisions that also apply under the Companies Act 2014.
The purpose of these requirements is to support transparency, accountability and effective regulatory oversight of ICAVs and their directors. In the context of investment funds, such information assists the Central Bank of Ireland in the discharge of its statutory supervisory functions and helps ensure appropriate governance standards are maintained.
Your concerns raised regarding the privacy concerns of directors is duly noted.
The Department will consider them for further analysis and review in the context of the wider review of this legislation.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has conducted a costing of the proposal to align the substantial shareholding exemption with the dividend participation exemption; and, if so, to outline the costs involved.
reply:
The Participation Exemption for Foreign Dividends regime was introduced in Finance Act 2024. The exemption, which applies simplifies the double tax relief system and enhances Ireland’s attractiveness for multinational businesses. The exemption is available, subject to conditions, in respect of distributions received from qualifying subsidiaries in EEA and treaty partner jurisdictions and jurisdictions that have imposed a non-refundable withholding tax on the distribution.
Section 626B TCA 1997, Substantial Shareholding Exemption, introduced in 2004, provides for an exemption from capital gains tax on certain disposals of subsidiary shareholdings, subject to conditions including shareholding, residence and trading requirements.
In relation to the costing of the proposal to align the aspects of Substantial Shareholding Exemption regime with the Dividend Participation Exemption, I am advised by Revenue that the data required to provide an estimated cost is not available on its statistical records.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider expanding or adjusting the Small Benefit Exemption framework to explicitly incentivise and favour locally administered town or chamber gift card schemes; if he will assess the way in which such a mechanism can prevent economic leakage and sustain local retail sectors in rural border towns.
reply:
Section 112B Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 (TCA) provides that an employer may give non-cash rewards (such as a voucher) to an employee without giving rise to a charge to tax where certain conditions are met. This is referred to as the Small-Benefit-Exemption (SBE).
The principle of the SBE has existed for over 20 years. When BIK was broadly introduced, in 2004, an issue arose as the provision of vouchers, gifts etc., from employers to employees in recognition of life events, or performance, became taxable events. In acknowledgement of this, Revenue applied an administrative concession to the provision of one benefit/gift, to the maximum value of €100. This concession was subsequently increased to €250.
Section 11 of the Finance Act 2015 introduced it to the Statute Books, providing for a tax-free threshold of €500, which could apply to the provision of one benefit/gift. In 2022, this increased to a tax-free threshold of €1,000, which could be provided via no more than two benefits/gifts. On 1 January 2025 this increased to a tax-free threshold of €1,500, to be provided via no more than five benefits/gifts.
The policy objective is to allow employers provide some form of recognition to employees that is not subject to tax in a manner that is straightforward and easy to implement. The provision is broad – a benefit is defined as ‘a tangible asset other than cash’. As such, it is not restricted to the issuance of vouchers. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the regulatory protections available to investors where an investment vehicle has entered liquidation and the regulated intermediary that advised on or serviced that investment has also entered liquidation (details supplied); the responsibilities that a regulated intermediary retains for advice provided prior to liquidation.
reply:

The law lists the various types of regulated investment services and investment. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has engaged with the Central Bank and an organisation (details supplied) on the credit risk posed by uninsured flood-exposed homes; and if he has considered the proposal by another organisation in August 2026 for mortgage top-up lending to fund property-level flood resilience works.
reply:
The availability of flood protection insurance is an important factor in protecting the financial resilience of property owners and in turn credit risk of properties in flood risk areas.
My Department and the Central Bank of Ireland are members of the Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group. This group will progress long term sustainable solutions to the protection gap, as set out in the Action Plan for Insurance Reform. Proposals, such as that outlined by the Deputy, may be considered by this group as part of their work.
There are channels in which flood risk and flood events can impact on credit risk in Ireland. A flood event damages buildings, fixtures, fittings and contents, and the lack of flood insurance could worsen the borrower's financial position, with potential consequences for probability of default. There is also a potential collateral channel, as buildings with higher flood risk, all else being equal, would be worth less.
Central Bank analytics have advanced significantly to support understanding how flood risk interact with the financial sector. Published research available on the Central Bank website includes:
• Flood Protection Gap Report: www.centralbank.ie/news/article/press-release-central-bank-publishes-flood-protection-gap-report-14-oct-2024.
• Flood Exposure in Business Lending: www.centralbank.ie/statistics/statistical-publications/behind-the-data/measuring-flood-risk-in-business-lending.
• Flood Exposure and Credit Conditions: www.centralbank.ie/

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to provide an update on his plans to support regeneration in towns and villages across Galway East.
reply:

They are a key link between local authorities and their communities. They work closely across multi-disciplinary town regeneration teams, including dedicated Capital Delivery Teams made up of technical and administrative staff, also funded by my department.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if his Department has assessed the potential financial and economic implications for Ireland of the European Commission’s proposed new own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment, including the potential cost to the Exchequer and impacts on businesses and consumers.
reply:
The European Commission published its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), to cover the years 2028-2034, in July and September 2025, including a package of amended and new own resources - i.e. revenue sources for the EU budget. The nine existing, amended and new own resources under the Commission's proposal include, for example, customs duties, contributions based on the Emissions Trading System, and an own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment (e-waste).
Member States' contributions to the EU budget are composed of the different own resources, and a Member State's share of each own resource will vary according to the nature of that own resource. If during negotiations an own resource is removed from the package, Member States would contribute that level of revenue according to the GNI-based own resource instead. For Ireland, the Department's analysis suggests our EU budget contribution would be marginally lower under the e-waste own resource compared to GNI.
With regard to potential impacts on businesses and consumers, the Commission's proposal stated that while Member States would contribute to the EU budget an amount proportional to €2 per kilogram of non-collected e-waste, it should be left to the discretion of the Member States as to whether to take any related domestic policy actions, in line with the principle of subsidiarity.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has considered reviewing the income thresholds that apply for the purposes of the Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) exemption for persons aged 65 years and over; his views on whether the current thresholds continue to reflect increases in the State Pension and other income supports in recent years; whether his Department has undertaken any analysis of the number of older persons who may no longer qualify for the exemption as a result of such increases.
reply:
The Deputy will be aware that Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) is a withholding tax that is deducted by Irish financial institutions on deposit interest paid or credited on the deposits of Irish residents.
Since 1 January 2020, the DIRT rate is 33%. DIRT is a final liability tax. This means that an individual has no further tax liability in respect of the deposit interest earned.
Deposit interest is specifically excluded from the Universal Social Charge. Individuals may however have a liability to Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) in certain circumstances.
Interest may be received without paying DIRT in certain circumstances. Where an individual, or their spouse/civil partner, is aged over 65 and their total income, including gross deposit interest does not exceed the annual exemption limit, as provided for in section 188 Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997, their deposit interest earnings are exempt from DIRT.
As the Deputy is aware, the current exemption limit is €18,000 in the case of a single person and €36,000 in the case of a married couple or civil partners. The relevant income thresholds may be increased further if the individual has a qualifying child. Additionally, marginal relief may be available where the individual’s or couple’s income exceeds the relevant exemption limit but is less than twice that amount. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance for and updated timeline for the completion of a review (details supplied).
reply:
The Central Bank of Ireland has provided me with the following information on the matter.
The Central Bank has commissioned an independent review of its enforcement activities.
The review is not focused on a specific case rather will evaluate the effectiveness of the Central Bank's enforcement activities and the role of enforcement within the wider supervisory framework. It will examine structures and processes for enforcement activity and decision-making; case-selection criteria and processes; timeliness; and transparency for the public, firms and individuals who may be impacted. It will have regard to best practice by regulators performing similar functions domestically and internationally and applicable international standards and principles.
The review is underway and as per the Terms of Reference (www.centralbank.ie/docs/default-source/news-and-media/press-releases/terms-of-reference---july-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=eb8711a_1) a report will be provided to the Governor by 31 January 2027 and published in due course.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he has considered introducing income tax relief on overtime earnings, particularly for workers maintaining essential public services and infrastructure; whether any such relief could be restricted to overtime verified through employer records or other auditable systems; and the estimated annual Exchequer cost of exempting the first €2,500, €5,000 and €10,000 of overtime earnings per worker.
reply:
It is a general principle of taxation that, as far as possible, income from all sources should be subject to taxation.
Ireland has a progressive income tax system which is structured such that the more income you earn, the more tax you pay. As a person’s income increases, they move up through the various rates and bands and, as a result, while the levels of take-home pay increase overall, the amount of tax they pay also increases.
The ‘Programme for Government 2025: Securing Ireland’s Future’, contains specific undertakings with regard to personal taxation, it commits to “implementing progressive changes in taxation if the economy remains strong, including indexing credits and bands to prevent an increase in the real burden of Income Tax while in the event of an economic downturn and unexpected deterioration in the public finances we would postpone changes to Income Tax credits or bands, as we did in Budget 2021”.
In Budget 2027 I introduced a significant personal income tax package with an estimated full year cost of €1.5 billion. This personal income tax package has been carefully designed to support workers.
The entry point to the higher rate of income tax for all earners is being increased by €2,500 for the 2027 tax year and subsequent years of assessment. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider extending the 9% VAT rate to qualifying beauty, aesthetic and nail-care services, which already applies to hairdressing services as part of the Finance Bill 2027 (details supplied). whether he acknowledges that extending the 9% rate would provide a fairer and more consistent VAT framework for the wider personal-care sector.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the VAT rating of goods and services is subject to the requirements of the EU VAT Directive with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.
Beauticians are not included in the categories of goods and services on which the EU Directive allows a lower rate of VAT, and therefore they would fall to be taxed by Member States at their standard rate of VAT – which in Ireland is currently 23%. However, the Directive allows that a Member State may retain certain long-standing VAT arrangements that they had in place, subject to strict conditions including that the terms of the historic arrangement cannot be extended.
On this basis, Ireland is permitted to retain its long-standing application of its reduced VAT rate – which is currently 13.5% – to services related to the care of the human body, which includes beautician services. In accordance with the Directive this arrangement is treated as a ‘parked’ rate, which means that it cannot be reduced below 12%. If Ireland were to cease the application of the parked rate to these supplies, then under the terms of the Directive these services would have to be subject to the standard rate of VAT

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht for an update on the forthcoming review of the CLÁR programme; the timeframe for its commencement and completion; and if the eligibility of footpath construction in rural towns and villages forms part of the review.
reply:
The CLÁR programme provides funding under a number of different measures for small-scale infrastructural projects in designated rural areas. Last year over €14 million was approved for 238 projects under the programme, with funding being provided for community facilities and amenities, community vehicles and specific support for island communities. The 2026 CLÁR programme was launched on March 10th.
In line with a commitment in the Programme for Government, a comprehensive review of eligible CLÁR areas was completed in advance of launching the 2026 programme. On completion of the review, an additional 110 electoral divisions (EDs) were included as newly eligible areas, including one additional area in County Galway.
In addition to this review, I consider the measures to be funded in advance of the launch of the CLÁR programme each year, including the eligibility criteria to be applied. I will again examine the measures being funded in advance of the launch of the 2027 programme. I have no specific plans to fund footpaths at this time given the focus on community facilities and amenities, and community vehicles and the existence of other funding streams across Government. However, I will keep the position under consideration.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Transport the status of plans to re-open the Mullingar to Athlone rail line; and if this is a priority for public transport in the region.
reply:
The reopening of the former rail alignment between Mullingar and Athlone was included as a recommendation of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review, published in 2024.
The Rail Project Prioritisation Strategy, published by the Department in December 2025 outlines how to best sequence and optimise the recommendations of the All-Island Strategic Rail Review.
The Strategy specifies short-term rail infrastructure investments, referred to as Early Interventions, to be delivered in the coming years, including a series of new track passing loops and platforms to boost the rail network’s resilience and capacity.

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport the extent of bilateral agreements currently in place between the Road Safety Authority (RSA) / National Driver Licence Service (NDLS) and non-EU jurisdictions for the reciprocal recognition and exchange of driving licences; the specific criteria, technical assessments, and verification processes, used to evaluate foreign driving standards prior to entering into such agreements; whether these assessments evaluate driver comprehension of Irish road signs and traffic legislation.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 341 to 346, inclusive, together.
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all Member States must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. As all Member States test drivers to the same standards, there can be mutual recognition of driving licences.
Ireland and other member states may also have bilateral driving licence exchange agreements with other jurisdictions. The main purpose of licence exchange agreements with non-EU jurisdictions is to ensure that anyone from those jurisdictions who obtains an Irish driving licence by exchange has been tested at an equivalent standard to drivers who passed a test in Ireland.
Reaching an agreement is not a matter of political will. The core principle is to ensure the continued safety of Irish road users in alignment with government and EU commitments to reduce road deaths and injuries by 2050 (Vision Zero). The RSA is responsible for undertaking a technical and independent review, to ascertain that the other licensing and testing regime is comparable with that in Ireland.
An agreement also allows for the verification of licences produced for exchange, to confirm whether the licence is valid and that the applicant is the licence holder. These processes are essential to protect the safety of Irish road users and the integrity of the Irish licensing system, and a bilateral ag

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport his plans to reduce toll costs in Meath.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). Moreover, the contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
Noting the above position, I have referred the question regarding tolls to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the initiatives being developed to combat social isolation in rural communities, particularly among older people and those living alone; and whether additional investment in community meeting places and local voluntary organisations is planned.
reply:
Loneliness and social isolation are complex issues that can arise from a range of social, economic, and demographic factors and, therefore, relate to policy areas across many departments. Issues such as access to transport, economic disadvantage or social exclusion can all contribute to isolation in rural areas. My department works closely with colleagues across Government to ensure that rural communities in particular are not left behind in the provision of public services.
With regard to my own department, ‘Our Rural Future’ recognises the importance of addressing loneliness and isolation, particularly for older people and those living alone. The next iteration of the policy, which is due to be published later this month will continue to focus on this important issue which impacts both rural and urban communities.
One of the values underpinning the new five-year government strategy in support of the community and voluntary sector, ‘Ar Scath a Cheile’, which was launched earlier this week, is a commitment to social inclusion, prioritising the needs of communities experiencing social or economic exclusion.
There are schemes and programmes operated by my department which directly help to address this issue. Of particular importance with regard to capital funding are the Community Centre Investment Fund, LEADER, CLÁR and the Local Enhancement Programme.
