question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the amount of the reduction in non-core funding for the social inclusion and community activation programme referred to in the Budget 2027 expenditure report; whether this relates to the €13 million provided in 2026 to support new arrivals and the communities where they settle; and the effect on SICAP programme implementers.
reply:

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether he plans to review the vehicle price ceiling under the SEAI electric vehicle purchase grant scheme; whether a tapered reduction in grant assistance above the ceiling has been assessed as an alternative to the immediate loss of eligibility.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting the transition to zero-emission and the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030.
Regarding the EV Purchase Grant, the maximum eligible vehicle price threshold for the grant will now be €50,000, rather than €60,000. This change has been made to target funding for EV transition towards lower price bracket cars and enables a greater proportion of the funding available within the National Development Plan to support the roll-out of charging infrastructure. The amended price threshold came into place for new applications received after 31 July 2026, and will be kept under review in 2027.
The EV grant system is continually reviewed to optimise EV purchasing with a view to replacing older, polluting vehicles. It should be noted that decisions on financial incentives, including EV grants, must be taken in the context of overall financial sustainability.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the provision of a borrowing framework for the technological universities.
reply:
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035 recognises the important role that higher education institutions, including Technological Universities, can play in increasing student accommodation capacity.
Building on the Programme for Government commitment, my Department is working with the Higher Education Authority and the sector to examine the financing arrangements required to support future student accommodation projects.
As Minister, I am committed to ensuring that Technological Universities have the tools to support strategic investment and expand accommodation provision. One model which is widely used internationally is a nomination agreement. These provide institutions with guaranteed beds for their students while giving developers the occupancy certainty needed to secure finance and deliver new accommodation.
At present, Technological Universities do not have approval to enter into nomination agreements. My Department is working with the Departments of Finance, Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, and the Higher Education Authority, to develop an appropriate mechanism, with the necessary safeguards and controls, to allow Technological Universities to enter into such agreements on a strictly limited basis. As part of this work, NewERA has agreed to undertake a financial assessment.
I will continue to advance this work to support the delivery of student accommodation while protecting institutional and Exchequer finances

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if there has been consideration given to enhancing graduate entry medicine tuition support or a state-backed finance scheme; and the future plans for same.
reply:
I am committed to ensuring that financial circumstances do not present an undue barrier to participation in higher education and tertiary education. This is particularly important in disciplines where Ireland faces significant skills shortages, including healthcare professions.
In Budget 2027, the Government further strengthened these supports through a €34 million student support package, including increases in SUSI maintenance grants, enhanced student contribution grant supports for families with multiple students in tertiary education, expanded eligibility for certain supports, and measures to assist students with the cost of attending college.
The question of introducing an interest-free student loan scheme has been considered in a variety of policy contexts over the years. Any proposal of this nature would require careful consideration of its affordability, overall cost to the Exchequer, administrative arrangements, repayment mechanisms, impact on student participation and interaction with the existing student support framework. It would also need to be assessed in the context of wider Government priorities and value-for-money considerations.
There may, however, be circumstances where alternative financing models could assist students who face significant education costs but who are not eligible for existing grant supports. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if annual targets have been established for each county or region for 2026 to 2030 regarding the Government target of 12,500 apprenticeship registrations annually by 2030, in tabular form; and, if not, the way in which the geographic distribution of the additional apprenticeship places required to meet the national target is being planned.
reply:
The information requested by the Deputy is not available as the national target of 12,500 apprenticeship registrations is not disaggregated by year, county or region.
Apprenticeships are national programmes delivered through a network of Education and Training Boards, higher education institutions and other training providers across the country. Many apprenticeship programmes, such as the electrical apprenticeship, are delivered in multiple locations. Programmes with lower demand may be delivered in a more limited number of locations.
Decisions on the local provision and capacity of individual programmes are matters for the relevant ETB, higher education institution or training provider. These decisions are made having regard to local and regional skills needs, employer demand, learner demand and workforce requirements, and in collaboration with SOLAS and the Higher Education Authority.
My priority as Minister is to ensure that apprenticeship continues to provide quality and accessible options for learners across the country, while responding effectively to the skills needs of employers and the wider economy.
Minister Harkin and I intend to publish the successor to the current Action Plan for Apprenticeship later this year. question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the appeal process available for third level students in relation to free fee's for Irish students in circumstances (details supplied).
reply:
The State pays tuition fees, under the Free Fees Initiative, exclusive of the student contribution, on behalf of eligible students attending approved full-time undergraduate courses. To qualify for funding under the Department's Free Fees Initiative, students must meet the criteria of the scheme including the residency requirements in their own right.
To meet the residency criteria a student must have been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK state for at least three of the five years preceding their entry to an approved third level course.
All students are required to meet the residency criteria of the scheme preceding their entry to an approved third level course. Under EU law, nationals of other EU jurisdictions are entitled to access education on the same basis as Irish citizens. Therefore, it would not be feasible to provide an exemption for persons of Irish nationality only.
The three out of five-year rule takes cognisance of students who wish to take time out to travel or work abroad. Such students can still meet the residency requirement if they have not been outside the countries referenced above for more than two of the previous five years. Similar, and in some cases more restrictive residency criteria apply in other countries. For example, in the UK, a student must be resident for the three years immediately preceding his/her commencement in college.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if there are plans to appoint a talent and innovation attache in South Korea during 2027.
reply:
I remain strongly committed to deepening international collaboration in research and innovation, positioning Ireland as a trusted and attractive global partner, and ensuring that our research ecosystem continues to attract and retain exceptional talent from around the world.
With Attaché officials having taken up duty in the Consulate Generals of Ireland in Boston and San Francisco in 2025, there has already been a clear value case made for their deployment. They have made significant inroads into the areas of their responsibility establishing strong networks with researchers active in the US and building up contacts with institutions well-placed to partner with Irish Universities.
Building on the success of our international engagement efforts and to further strengthen collaborative research and innovation partnerships, I will be appointing five additional Talent and Innovation Attachés. question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether his Department has assessed the extent to which existing electric vehicle incentives meet the practical needs of larger families and households requiring greater range, passenger capacity, boot space or towing capability; whether this assessment will inform future changes to the scheme.
reply:
The Government is fully committed to supporting the transition to zero-emission and the ambitious target to have 30% of private car fleet switched to electric by 2030.
In 2026, €170m has been allocated to support Ireland’s continued transition to Electric Vehicles (EV’s) including funding for EV purchase grants and home charger grants, and development of publicly available EV charging infrastructure.
Current incentives provided by the Department of Transport to support drivers' transition to electric include:
• a €3,500 purchase grant for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) up to €50,000 in value
• a pilot scrappage scheme, ICE2EV
• a home charging grant scheme
• an apartment charging scheme
• benefit-in-kind tax relief for BEVs
• VRT relief of up to €5,000 for BEVs and
• a low rate of annual motor tax.
It should also be noted that the cost of EVs in all market segments is beginning to reduce as the market matures and manufacturers expand their offerings. In addition, EVs can offer significantly lower running costs than conventional petrol or diesel vehicles.
The EV grant system is continually reviewed to optimise EV purchasing with a view to replacing older, polluting vehicles. It should be noted that decisions on financial incentives, including EV grants, must be taken in the context of overall financial sustainability.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on foreign birth registry applications for two persons (details supplied).
reply:
Foreign Birth Registration (FBR) applications are currently being processed within the turnaround time of 12 months from receipt of supporting documents. Applications that require further supporting documents will take longer to process.
By its nature, FBR is a detailed and complex process, often involving official documentation relating to three generations and issued by several jurisdictions. Such documents take considerable time to validate.
With regard to the specific applications about which the Deputy has enquired, the application forms and supporting documents were received by the FBR office on 03/06/2026 and 14/08/2026 respectively. Therefore, the applications are within the normal turnaround time. The Passport Service will contact the applicants directly if any further documents are required.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the projected increase of student enrolments over the next five years; and the anticipated additional funding that will be required to meet this demand.
reply:
In June, my Department published “Projections of Demand for Higher Education 2025–2045”, highlighting strong expected growth in demand for full-time higher education places over the coming years.
The report shows that overall student numbers are projected to rise significantly over the next five years, increasing by up to 18% from current levels, from 211,540 in the 2024/25 academic year to between 243,750 and 250,260 in the 2031/32 academic year, depending on the scenario considered.
The main drivers of this growth are a projected increase in undergraduate enrolment demand from Irish school leavers (demographic increase) and growth in postgraduate enrolment demand, with continued growth in non-EU postgraduate enrolment
Ireland experienced high annual births of over 70,000 between 2007 and 2012 (provisional number of births in 2025 was 54,125) – these individuals, who have been going through primary and secondary education, are now reaching higher education age. These trends have potential implications for funding for the higher education sector and will inform policy development and investment planning over the coming decade.
I am committed to supporting the higher education sector to meet this increasing demographic demand. The total allocation to higher education in Budget 2027 is €2.85 billion.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the reasons ICOT have been removed from the Interim List of Eligible Programs.
reply:
The Department does not comment on individual cases.
Inclusion on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) is necessary for a Higher Education or English language education provider to be eligible to recruit learners from non-EEA countries on Stamp 2 immigration permissions. The ILEP is administered by the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in conjunction with the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.
To have its programmes listed for this purpose, a provider must meet the relevant ILEP criteria on an ongoing basis. Where issues of non-compliance are identified and brought to the attention of the ILEP, these issues are reviewed and considered by a Committee comprised of officials from both Departments. Subject to its deliberations, this Committee may decide that the provider and its programmes are to be removed from the ILEP given the nature of non-compliance with established criteria. When such a decision is made and communicated, the provider may appeal within five working days and this shall be considered by the ILEP appeals committee.
It should be noted that the ILEP is in the process of being superseded by the TrustEd Ireland statutory quality mark. This new mark is currently being introduced by Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI). question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding a university student who has been refused progression to fourth year.
reply:
I am sorry to learn of the difficulties experienced by the student concerned.
Higher education institutions are statutorily independent and autonomous bodies with responsibility for the management of their own academic and administrative affairs. Decisions concerning a student’s academic progression are therefore matters for the institution concerned, and neither I nor my Department has a role in reviewing or intervening in individual cases.
A student who wishes to challenge such a decision should, in the first instance, engage with the institution and avail of any relevant internal review, appeal or complaints procedures. Information on these procedures should be available directly from the institution.
Publicly funded higher education institutions come within the remit of the Office of the Ombudsman. Where a student has exhausted the institution’s internal procedures and remains dissatisfied, it is open to them to contact the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman may examine complaints concerning administrative actions or procedures, including alleged unfair treatment, a failure to provide clear reasons for a decision, undue delay or a failure to deal properly with a complaint. However, the Ombudsman cannot examine matters involving academic judgement.
Further information on making a complaint is available at www.ombudsman.ie or by contacting the Office of the Ombudsman at 6 Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, D02 W773, or on 01 636 5600.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health if there has been a provision in Budget 2027 for medical cards to be issued to lung fibrosis patients as a matter of routine care.
reply:
Medical card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn per week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
People under 70 are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after deduction of tax, PRSI and Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/. People aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/.
The issue of granting medical cards on the basis of illness or a disability was previously examined in 2014 by the HSE Expert Panel on Medical Need and Medical Card Eligibility. The Group concluded that it was not feasible, desirable, nor ethically justifiable to list medical conditions in priority order for medical card eligibility. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Transport if he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the driver testing system, including matters relating to testing standards, consistency and the appeals process.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for the National Driver Testing Service, including all operational matters. The RSA conducts the driving test to a standard that complies with the EU Driving Licence Directive. Given the RSA's responsibility in this matter, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Authority for direct response. Please contact my office if a reply is not received within ten days.
Pending this response, the RSA provides an appeals process whereby, if an applicant is unhappy with how a driving test was conducted or they believe they were unfairly treated, they can appeal the decision or raise a complaint.
Under section 33(6)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1961, a person aggrieved by a test decision may also appeal to the District Court. The court will then examine whether or not the test was conducted properly. If the court determines that the tester did not conduct the test in accordance with procedures, a further test would be offered to the applicant free of charge.

MetroLink is Ireland's largest public transport infrastructure project and a key National Development Plan priority, delivering long-term benefits for economic growth, housing competitiveness and climate action. MetroLink will provide a high-capacity, fully automated metro connection Dublin airport with key destinations across the city, including a reliable 25-minute journey to the city centre.
Government consented to "Approval Gate 2" for MetroLink on 16th September, marking a significant milestone. With Government's approval, MetroLink will now be able to proceed to the procurement phase for the key contracts, with the main tender packs expected to issue to market in the first half of 2027 and heavy construction works anticipated to commence in 2028.
A programme of advance and enabling works will begin ahead of the main construction phase. question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Transport if he has examined correspondence received by the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht regarding speed signage in Gaeltacht areas that continue to display speed limits in English only; and the steps he will take to overturn the rules laid out by his Department on the matter.
reply:
My Department received correspondence from the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht on the 16 February 2026. I issued a reply to the Minister on 25 May 2026.
The Official Languages Act 2003 at (Section 9) Regulations 2008 (SI 391/2008) at Section 3.3 exempts road signage from the requirement under the Act. However, the Traffic Signs Manual at Section 1.1.52 states:
It is a statutory requirement that place names on information signs be in both Irish and English, except:
For names of destinations in Gaeltacht areas where there is a direction by statute that only the Irish language version of the placename shall be used; and where the spelling of a place name is similar in both languages, in which case only the Irish form of the name should be shown.
I wish to assure you that at all times, especially within Gaeltacht areas, roads authorities are aware of their obligations under the provisions of the Traffic Signs Manual. It must be noted that a significant amount of traffic signage has the same display in both Irish and English. In addition, speed limit signs in the Republic of Ireland are language independent; hence no Irish or English text is used with them. They display a number along with the abbreviation km/h. Abbreviations such as ‘m’, ‘km’ and ‘km/h’ are Système International units and, as such, are not in any particular language. The abbreviation km/h is used because on the Island of Ireland the speed limits in the Republic are set in kilometres

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Health for an update with regard to the regulation of vapes; and if she plans to restrict retail vaping outlets.
reply:
The focus of policy and legislation regarding nicotine inhaling products is on reducing youth use.
The Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) Act 2023 introduced domestic regulation of nicotine inhaling products including:
• A minimum age of sale of 18
• Further advertising restrictions in cinemas, on public transport and near schools
• Prohibition on the sale of nicotine inhaling products by self-service, at events aimed at children, and from temporary or moveable premises.
A significant provision in the Act was the licensing system for the retail sale of tobacco products and nicotine inhaling products, which became operational for all retailers on 2 August 2026. Previously, there was a once-off registration system for tobacco retailers, and no register for retailers of nicotine inhaling products.
Those who wish to sell these products must now apply for a licence, pay the required fee and renew that licence annually. The licensing system will give the HSE's National Environmental Health Service robust oversight of who is selling nicotine inhaling products. The legislation allows for increased penalties for offences such as selling to minors, including revocation of a licence. In addition, licences will not be granted to temporary or moveable premises such as those at festivals, and the sale of these products at events aimed at children is also prohibited.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish election observers to be deployed to Serbia for the upcoming OSCE/ODIHR election observation mission; the number who have previous election observation experience; and if she will consider increasing the size of the Irish contingent and the proportion of experienced observers.
reply:
The Government is committed to supporting democratisation, human rights, and the rule of law, as a key element of our foreign policy. Support to election observation is central to this commitment and Ireland has contributed observers to international election observation missions since the 1990s.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade maintains and administers a roster enabling Ireland to respond to calls to participate in election observation missions coordinated by the OSCE and the EU. The current five-year Roster commenced on 1 January 2024 and has 169 members.

reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the reason the allocation to the National Treatment Purchase Fund in the Estimates for Public Services has been reduced from €230 million in 2025 to €200 million in 2026 and to €150.4 million in 2027; the number of patients treated through NTPF-funded activity in 2025 and to date in 2026; the number expected in 2027; and whether the minimum waiting time for eligibility for NTPF-funded treatment will remain at nine months in 2027.

The Government is focused on having a public health service in which everyone has timely access to high-quality scheduled care, where and when they need it.
The only sustainable solution to addressing waiting times in acute hospitals is by increasing core activity within the public health service through improved productivity and efficiencies and through ongoing reform and leveraging enabling supports.
Measures to do this are underway, such as continuing the implementation of POCC contract, 5/7 working and implementation of Seven Day Services; Increasing the level and volume of services that will be available earlier in the day, in the evening and at weekends in acute hospitals.

Other productivity measures such as OPD optimisation through the OPD toolkit is increasing activity levels where it is operational and through the theatre utilisation programme, which aims to increase theatre effectiveness and patient throughput to help reduce surgical waiting lists.
Funding for the National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) is to supplement this increased activity and provide targeted measures to address specific areas of concern.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Health the reason lung transplant patients are not reimbursed for vaccinations they must have before undergoing transplant surgery (details supplied); and if consideration will be given to extending reimbursement to this cohort given the significant cost of the vaccinations required.
reply:
Prior to solid organ transplantation, including lung transplantation, it is important that patients remain up to date with their vaccinations. This can be done through their local medical practitioner or local hospital service.
While some vaccinations may be required in advance of transplantation, others may be recommended.
I have been informed by the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital that Shingles, RSV, and HPV vaccines are recommended but not mandatory prior to lung transplantation. The Hospital has advised that not having these vaccines does not preclude a patient from being listed or transplanted.
Where a patient has queries about vaccinations in advance of transplantation, these should be discussed with their transplant team, who can provide specific advice.
Regarding reimbursement, I am advised that the HSE Primary Care Reimbursement Service does not supply vaccines or provide reimbursement support for vaccines through community pharmacies under the Statutory Drug Schemes.
When the public health imperative to support particular vaccines to defined cohorts becomes national policy, vaccines are directly procured by the HSE and supplied through the national vaccine distribution arrangements to GPs and pharmacies for eligible cohorts.
The Shingles, RSV or the HPV vaccines are not reimbursed under Community Drug Schemes including both the General Medical Services and Drugs Payment Scheme.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health the supports she plans to put in place for pregnant women who go to accident and emergency departments and face long wait times.
reply:
The Government is committed to ensuring that pregnant women who require urgent or emergency care receive safe, timely and appropriate assessment. All patients presenting to an emergency department are triaged and seen according to clinical urgency. Any woman whose condition requires immediate attention will therefore be prioritised accordingly.
Where clinically appropriate and local arrangements allow, pregnant women are directed to dedicated maternity emergency and assessment services, including Emergency and Assessment Units or maternity emergency rooms within maternity networks.
The HSE continues to work with hospital groups and maternity services to support clear referral pathways, appropriate escalation and coordination between emergency departments and specialist obstetric teams. These arrangements are intended to ensure that pregnant women are assessed in the most appropriate clinical setting and that any deterioration or additional risk is identified and managed promptly.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health her plans to reduce accident and emergency wait times.
reply:
I recognise that long waits in emergency departments can place additional burden on patients and their families. Patients attending the ED are prioritised according to clinical need so that those requiring the most urgent treatment are seen first. Reducing waiting times and ensuring that patients receive safe and timely care remains a priority for me and for this Government.
The HSE’s 2026 Urgent and Emergency Care Operational Plan provides the framework for improving performance across the full patient pathway. It focuses on strengthening operational management, enabling people to avail of appropriate care and supports outside of acute hospital settings, improving emergency department and in-hospital processes, and supporting timely discharge. The Department continues to work closely with the HSE to support delivery of the Plan and ongoing improvements in urgent and emergency care.
A central element of the Plan is to provide more appropriate alternatives to emergency department attendance. This includes expanding and promoting Injury Units, strengthening GP out-of-hours services, increasing access to community diagnostics and specialist ambulatory pathways, and using virtual wards and enhanced community care to treat suitable patients closer to home.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health for an update on the new National Maternity Hospital, the scheduled opening date, the expenditure to date and the projected expenditure.
reply:
Government is committed to the development of the new National Maternity Hospital (NMH) at the St Vincent’s University Hospital (SVUH), Elm Park.
It is a major infrastructural investment by the State for women’s health, providing much needed facilities for women and babies for generations to come. The extra capacity to be provided at the new NMH will help safeguard national neonatal, maternity and gynaecology service provision.
The procurement and tender process for the main works contract concluded in 2025, and the outcomes were incorporated into a Final Business Case. This Final Business Case has been submitted for review to officials in the Department of Health and is being finalised in line with the requirements of the Infrastructure Guidelines.
Concurrently, the successful tenderers entered a non-binding pre-construction services agreement (PCSA) with the HSE. This PCSA process brings contractors and suppliers together to agree detailed delivery programmes, de?risk sequencing, and mobilise supply chains.

The PCSA process has now concluded and, together with the final business case, will inform a Memorandum for Government, which I hope to bring to Government in the coming weeks, seeking approval for the HSE to proceed to sign main works contracts and commence full construction.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Health for an update on the National Children's Hospital, the scheduled opening date, the expenditure to date and the projected expenditure.
reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a Government priority. Everything possible is being done to ensure this world-class hospital will open as quickly as possible, on behalf of children, young people, and their families.
I have been clear that the responsibility for committing to, resourcing, and delivering this project sits squarely with the project’s main contractor, BAM Ireland. The State will not reduce the pressure or dilute that accountability.
Ultimately, realising substantial completion is dependent on BAM’s execution and delivery of its own programme. BAM has shifted its Substantial Completion date 20 times over the last 6 years. On 13 July, BAM issued an updated programme to the Employer’s Representative (ER- independent third party responsible for administering the contract). The ER subsequently wrote to BAM for further detail to inform that review. That updated programme is still awaited from BAM.
In June, Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) gained early access to Level 1 where the critical care beds are, and this is welcome. However, access to Level 2, remains outstanding due to BAM’s repeated failure to deliver as committed. Achieving substantial completion is essentially a ‘volume exercise,’ to complete over 5,728 rooms. There has been a continued reduction in resources on site and while 5,079 of the 5,728 (88%) rooms have been delivered to the contractual standard, this is still falling behind BAM’s own completion targets.

question: Deputy Johnny Guirke asked the Minister for Transport the measures he is taking to ensure that the shortage and availability challenges in rural Ireland at peak times for small public service vehicles is dealt with.
reply:
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry, including the local area hackney licence, is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
The local area hackney (LAH) licence is a special, limited hackney licence that supports rural community transport through a locally operated hackney service. As of 31 August 2026, there are 23 licensed LAH drivers and 28 licensed vehicles.
In April 2026, the NTA introduced a series of enhancements to the local area hackney (LAH) licence intended to increase uptake. Under the new approach, where a local community gives support to an LAH licence applicant, the applicant will receive a licence offer from the NTA. question: Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Health if guidance will be issued (details supplied) to pharmacies to allow patients who depend on essential prescribed medicines, including pregabalin, to obtain a limited emergency supply for use during prolonged power outages, evacuations or other disruptions.
reply:
Provision is made under Regulation 8 of the Medicinal Products (Prescription and Control of Supply) Regulations 2003 (as amended) to permit pharmacists, in emergency circumstances, to supply certain prescription only medicines without a prescription. Emergency supply can be carried out at the request of a patient or at the request of a prescriber. Pregabalin is not currently classified as a controlled drug under Ireland's Misuse of Drugs legislation and therefore may be dispensed under these ‘emergency supply’ provisions, as appropriate. Additionally, registered pharmacists must, at all times, act in accordance with a statutory Code of Conduct.
The Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland – the pharmacy regulator has issued advice on its website on emergency supply provisions and on its statutory Code of Conduct for pharmacists, which are accessible at www.psi.ie.
My Department does not currently intend to issue any supplementary guidance on this matter.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Health the steps she has taken to ensure that eligible patients will have access to a medication (details supplied) since its approval for reimbursement without avoidable capacity delays; whether regional services will be developed to assist in access and ongoing care; if she will outline the way in which patients will be identified and assessed; the way prescriptions will be issued; the way in which monitoring will be organised; and the way in which the medicine will be supplied through community pharmacies.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys®.
In relation to the operational matters raised, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Health the average distance travelled by patients attending specialist menopause clinics; and whether consideration is being given to establishing additional regional services.
reply:
The delivery of menopause care is primarily based in the community and most women can access appropriate assessment, advice and treatment through their GP.
For women who require complex specialist menopause care that cannot be suitably managed within primary care, there are six specialist menopause clinics in operation nationally, one in each maternity network.
I am not aware of data being collected on the average distance travelled by patients attending specialist menopause clinics. However, these services are organised on a maternity network basis, with clinics located in the National Maternity Hospital, the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, Nenagh Hospital, Galway University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital.
These clinics accept referrals from GPs within their respective catchment areas.
At present, there are no plans to establish additional regional specialist menopause clinics, though funding was provided to expand the existing service last year. The current model is designed to provide specialist menopause care, where needed, through the six maternity networks. The majority of menopause care is delivered as close to home as possible through primary care services, ensuring minimal travel to services.

question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Health the arrangements in place for the follow-up care, monitoring and management of patients who undergo surgical procedures abroad under the cross-border directive; the supports available to patients who subsequently develop complications following their return to Ireland; the person or body responsible for co-ordinating their ongoing care; whether data is collected on complications and adverse outcomes arising from procedures undertaken under the directive.
reply:
Under the terms of the EU Cross Border Directive (CBD), where a patient has received healthcare abroad, in another EU/EEA country under the provisions of the CBD, and medical follow-up proves necessary the home country (in this case Ireland) is obliged to provide the patient with the same follow-up treatment it would have provided had the treatment taken place on its territory.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Health the measures in place to ensure that claims to private health insurers in respect of private patients treated in public hospitals are completed and submitted within the required period; whether recovery of this money is monitored as part of hospital performance management; and the steps being taken to recover claims reported as unpaid over the past three years.
reply:
The billing and collection of private health insurance income is an operational matter for the HSE.
The Department expects that all valid income due to the public health service is identified, billed and collected promptly. The Department has raised this matter directly with the HSE and monitors progress through its ongoing financial oversight and engagement arrangements.
The latest information provided by the HSE indicates a material improvement in the position, with outstanding private health insurer debt reducing by approximately €40 million, or 20%, from €200 million to €160 million. Claims awaiting action and sign-off by consultants also reduced by approximately €13 million, or 23%, from €55 million to €42 million. It is important to distinguish between outstanding debt and debt written off. Outstanding debt includes claims at various stages of processing and collection, whereas the HSE reported that €3.4 million was written off in 2025 due to claims not being submitted within the relevant time limits.
As the matters raised by the Deputy regarding the processes in place for the submission of claims, the monitoring of income recovery as part of hospital performance management, and the recovery of unpaid claims are operational matters for the HSE, I have asked the HSE to respond directly to the Deputy with the most up-to-date information available.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport whether he will reconsider the current arrangements whereby a person returning to Ireland, whose Irish driving licence has expired for more than ten years but who has continued to hold a valid driving licence and driving entitlement in another jurisdiction, may be required to recommence the driver licensing process; and if he will consider permitting such persons to renew their previous Irish driving entitlement subject to appropriate verification and road-safety safeguards.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 68, 69 and 70 together.
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all member states must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. Therefore, EU/EEA licences are recognised in all member states.
Under section 38 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended, it is an offence to drive a vehicle in a public place without a valid driving licence. Irish driving licences may be renewed at any point up to ten years after expiry. This gives the holder twenty years from the award of the licence to ensure it is renewed.
After ten years without a valid licence, the holder is no longer considered a qualified driver and may not renew that licence. This provision is set out in Regulation SI 537/2006 - the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006, made under the 1961 Act.
Where a driver, who is resident in Ireland, holds a valid exchangeable licence, such as an EU/EEA licence obtained by passing a test in the EU/EEA or a licence for which Ireland has an exchange agreement, it may be exchanged for an Irish licence on application to the National Driver Licence Service.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport if his Department has examined the driver licensing arrangements in other EU member states, including the Netherlands, regarding the renewal of driving licences that have been expired for an extended period; if he has considered introducing a comparable mechanism in Ireland for returning emigrants who can demonstrate continued driving experience abroad; and the outcome of any such examination.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 68, 69 and 70 together.
Irish driver licensing operates within a framework of EU law, which sets out the driver licensing legislation with which all member states must comply. Licence formats, vehicle categories and driving test standards are all set at EU level. Therefore, EU/EEA licences are recognised in all member states.
Under section 38 of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended, it is an offence to drive a vehicle in a public place without a valid driving licence. Irish driving licences may be renewed at any point up to ten years after expiry. This gives the holder twenty years from the award of the licence to ensure it is renewed.
After ten years without a valid licence, the holder is no longer considered a qualified driver and may not renew that licence. This provision is set out in Regulation SI 537/2006 - the Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations 2006, made under the 1961 Act.
Where a driver, who is resident in Ireland, holds a valid exchangeable licence, such as an EU/EEA licence obtained by passing a test in the EU/EEA or a licence for which Ireland has an exchange agreement, it may be exchanged for an Irish licence on application to the National Driver Licence Service.
Where an Irish resident's licence is not exchangeable, such as a non-EU/EEA licence where there is no licence exchange agreement with Ireland or an EU/EEA licence that was received in exchange for such a licence, the holder may obtain an Irish licence in th

question: Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health if her attention has been drawn to concerns regarding access to a treatment (details supplied); the engagements she has had with the HSE and clinicians about this; and the steps she is taking to ensure timely access to treatment.
reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013 the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical devices.
Following extensive engagement between the HSE and Biogen, the HSE’s Senior Management Team (SMT) approved the reimbursement of Skyclarys for patients over 16 years of age with Friedreich’s Ataxia.
From the 1st October 2026, omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is approved to be added to the list of reimbursable items under the High-Tech Drug Arrangements for the treatment of Friedreich’s ataxia in adults and adolescents aged 16 years and older. Prescribing of omaveloxolone (Skyclarys®) is through the High-Tech Hub and will be restricted to designated approved consultants.
The National Ataxia Clinic at Tallaght University Hospital has put in place additional clinics to assess suitability for treatment with Skyclarys.
For the small number of patients who attend other hospitals, assessment will be managed locally by the responsible clinical teams and treating physicians.
A number of patients attending Tallaght University Hospital, Cork University Hospital, and University Hospital Galway have received approved prescriptions for Skyclarys®.
In relation to the operational matters raised, I have asked the Health Service Executive to respond to the Deputy directly.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh den Aire Leanaí, Míchumais agus Comhionannais if consideration has been given by her Department to screening for dyslexia as part of the AON process.
reply:
Under the Disability Act 2005, an Assessment of Need is a specific assessment process carried out by the HSE to determine whether a child or young person has a disability as defined within the Act, and if they do, to identify the health and education needs (if any) arising from that disability.
A person can apply for an Assessment of Need if they think they or their child has a disability, as defined by the Disability Act. The definition of disability is very specific in the Act. It means a substantial restriction in the person’s capacity i.e. that a person has a significant difficulty with communication, learning, mobility or significantly disordered cognitive processes. In addition, this restriction should be permanent or likely to be permanent and require the continued provision of services to meet the person’s needs.
If a determination of disability is made, the applicant’s health and/or education needs are identified as well as the health services required to meet those needs. Although the Assessment of Need process can include the identification of a child’s education needs, the identification of the education services that they may require is not part of the process.
The Assessment of Need process is not designed to screen for particular conditions. Any clinical assessment undertaken as part of an assessment of need is focused on identifying the person's needs arising from their disability and informing the identification of supports. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will publish a multi-year residential disability care strategy with annual delivery targets and a capital plan; the timeline for same.
reply:
This Government, together with the HSE, acknowledges that demand for residential services is very high and is committed to the ongoing development of residential services for those who need them. A key focus of this Government and the HSE, is an increased emphasis on longer term planning for residential placements and a number of actions are underway this year and into next year to expand the provision of residential services.
The Department of Health’s 2021 Disability Capacity Review projected a need of an additional 1,900 residential places by 2032 and an extra 3,900 places to return to levels of provision prior to the beginning of the 2008 recession. In the shorter term, The Action Plan for Disability Services 2024-2026 represents a national strategy for capacity increases and service and policy reform in disability services. It was informed primarily by findings from the Disability Capacity Review. The Action Plan seeks to meet extra need over the 2024-2026 period in residential services through around 900 additional residential care places to tackle unmet needs and ensure supply keeps pace with demographic change and 500 new community-based residential care places to replace disability care in large institutional and campus-based settings, with a view to ending that form of provision by 2030.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport the way in which he has allocated the €2 billion allocated to his Department under the ICNF; the amount that has been spent to date; the amount that has been allocated to date; and the amount that has yet to be allocated, in tabular form.
reply:
As the Deputy may be aware, the Government has committed over €10 billion in funding to support the delivery of major public transport infrastructure projects over the period 2026 to 2030 in the National Development Plan (NDP) Review 2025, published in July last year, with an additional €2 billion committed from the Infrastructure, Nature and Climate and Fund (ICNF) to support MetroLink.
MetroLink is the only project under the remit of my Department which has been designated funding from the ICNF. This allocation will assist in moving MetroLink into construction. For 2026, MetroLink has been funded solely from Vote 31 and none of the €2 billion allocation has yet been drawn down from the ICNF.
Government consented to "Approval Gate 2" for MetroLink on 16th September, marking a significant milestone. With Government's approval, MetroLink will now be able to proceed to the detailed procurement phase, with the main tender packs expected to issue to market in the first half of 2027 and heavy construction works anticipated to commence in 2028.
I also warmly welcome the additional €6 billion earmarked for the construction of MetroLink to 2030, as provided for under "Budget 2027".

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality in the context of the review of the Right to Request Flexible Working provisions as outlined in her previous reply, if the review will examine the increasing level of congestion facing commuters and the knock on impact on their wellbeing.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 666, 667, 668 and 669 together.
Under the Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023, there is a provision for a review of the Right to Request Flexible Working provisions. As noted in my previous response this review is currently being scoped and is due to be undertaken in the coming months.
It is important to note that the review is a Statutory review and is to be focused on how the provisions for requesting flexible working operate, with an additional element to review as to whether the right should be extended to all workers rather than just carers and parents as is currently legislated for.
As part of the National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030 and its associated first Action Plan, the review will also focus on what additional flexibilities may be introduced to workplaces to support parents and carers.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality to provide details of the funding being made available in 2027 for the assessment of need targeted waiting list initiative, commonly referred to as Cara’s Fund; the total allocation in 2027 and how this compares with the allocation in 2026; the number of children whose assessments are expected to be completed through the initiative in 2027; the criteria that will apply in identifying and prioritising children for assessment; whether private providers will continue to be commissioned to provide assessments under the initiative; and the number of children awaiting an AON nationally.
reply:
The Department and the HSE are working intensively to address delays in the provision of Assessments of Need to children and young people and their families.
It is important to emphasise that the provision of an Assessment of Need and the delivery of services are separate issues. Children do not need an Assessment of Need report to access health or education supports, and having an Assessment of Need does not speed up access to services. Support continues to be provided through HSE Primary Care, Children’s Disability Services Teams, and CAMHs. Families can access and apply for services directly through the HSE.
Nevertheless, the Disability Act 2005 makes provision for a statutory assessment of need where a person thinks they or their child may have a disability. The Assessment of Need process determines whether an applicant has a disability as defined under the Disability Act, and if so, identifies the health and education needs resulting from this disability (if any), as well as the health services and supports required to meet those needs. Assessment of Need applications are processed in the date order in which they are received within the relevant area. There is no prioritisation of applications.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the timeline for the publication of the national childcare scheme review; the reason the publication of the review has been delayed from the original scheduled time of Q3 2026.
reply:
The independent evaluation of the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) commenced in March 2026 following a procurement tendering process which launched in late 2025. It is expected that the evaluation run for approximately 18 months with a final report expected to be published in Q3 2027. This evaluation aims to assess the performance of the NCS to date and its operation within the wider early learning and childcare funding and policy environment.
The evaluation will examine whether the NCS, as part of the wider funding model, is making high-quality early learning and childcare more accessible and affordable, particularly for families in the lowest income groups and the most disadvantaged households. It will also identify any improvements that could be made to enhance accessibility and affordability and to ensure that the NCS is working for as many families as possible.
The evaluation will include consultation and engagement with parents, educators, practitioners, providers and representative organisations. Any changes to the NCS will be carefully considered in light of the findings of this evaluation.

The full business cases are being developed for these projects in preparation for final approval, including the project the Deputy mentions.
Projects are developed into full business cases following the approval of a preliminary business case, in line with the framework set out in the Infrastructure Guidelines.
The nature of the development work required to prepare the full business case varies by project but can include independent property valuation, building surveying, due diligence checks on the property, conveyancing, procurement and appointment of technical advisors, detailed design work and associated cost planning, and operator selection. The projects included in the announcement on 30 September are expected to come on stream during 2027.

question: Deputy Aengus Ó Snodaigh asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality when she expects to publish the findings of her Departments review of the mother and baby institutions payment scheme.
reply:
The Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme opened for applications in March 2024.
The underpinning legislation for the Scheme provides for a number of reports and reviews to be produced. Section 48 of the Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme Act provides for two reviews of the operation of the Scheme, the first of which is to take place around the Scheme's mid-point.
The scope of the review is prescribed in the Act. It is focused on administrative and operational aspects of the Scheme. It will consider issues such as the level of uptake of the Scheme, the experience of applicants, the extent to which payments have been made and if the Scheme is achieving its purpose as set out by the Oireachtas. The Act does not provide for a revisiting of Scheme scope or eligibility criteria, matters already decided on by the Oireachtas during the legislative process.
Department officials have been undertaking preparatory work for the review over the last number of months and I approved the overall approach and authorised the review to commence on 16th of September. The review will include statistical assessment, business processes analysis and a survey of applicant experience, overseen by a Steering Group and independently quality assured.
I do not wish to estimate timeframes at this juncture but I will ensure the review report will be laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas when completed.

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the recourse an adopted person has when their adoption file reveals serious concerns about the circumstances in which their adoption took place.
reply:
The Adoption Act 2010, which came into effect on 1 November 2010, was introduced to ensure high standards in both domestic and intercountry adoption.
An adopted person who has concerns about the circumstances of their adoption has a number of options available to them.
If their concern relates to the Child and Family Agency, Tusla, an adopted person can make a complaint to that body through the complaints process set out on the Tusla website. If the concern relates to the Adoption Authority of Ireland, they can make a complaint in accordance with the complaints procedure set out on the Authority’s website. Complaints concerning registered social workers can be made to CORU, the health and social care regulator, under its Fitness to Practice process.
In addition, an adopted person has the right to complain to the Office of the Ombudsman or the Ombudsman for Children. An adopted person may also wish to seek independent legal advice and, depending on the circumstances, may wish to pursue a personal injuries claim through the Injuries Resolution Board, bring judicial review proceedings or seek other appropriate reliefs through the courts.

question: Deputy Aisling Dempsey asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her plans to increase the statutory two week paternity leave.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years. The Government is committed to supporting workers, including by extending paid leave for parents to allow them to spend more time with their child during their earliest years.
The Paternity Leave and Benefit Act 2016 provides the relevant parent (other than the mother of the child) with 2 weeks paid Paternity Leave. Ireland's statutory Paternity Leave arrangements are fully aligned with the requirements of the EU Work-Life Balance Directive, which introduced a minimum standard for Paternity Leave across EU Member States.
Under the Parent’s Leave and Benefit Act 2019, working parents are also entitled to nine weeks of paid Parent's Leave for each relevant parent, to be taken in the first two years after the birth or adoptive placement of a child. Parent's Leave is an individual separate entitlement and is non-transferable between parents.
Under the Parental Leave (Amendment) Act 2019, an employee who is a relevant parent in respect of a child under the age 12 is entitled to 26 weeks’ unpaid Parental Leave for each child. Where a child has a disability or long-term illness, the entitlement can continue until the child is 16. A relevant parent is a parent, an adoptive parent, or a person acting in ‘loco parentis’. Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to Parental Leave.

question: Deputy Maeve O'Connell asked the Minister for Defence if her Department has adopted or is developing initiatives to encourage former members of the Defence Forces to re-join.
reply:
Encouraging talented former personnel to re join the Defence Forces continues to be a priority for me as part of the overall recruitment and retention initiatives within the Defence Forces.
There are two methods by which a person can ‘re-join’ the Permanent Defence Force (PDF) – re-enlistment and re-commissioning.
In April 2020, a scheme was launched to re-enlist former PDF enlisted personnel. The focus of the scheme is on those former PDF personnel with particular skillsets identified by the Chief of Staff which are not available within the Defence Forces. Applicants can initially re-enlist for a minimum term of six months to a maximum term of three years. There was an amendment made to the Defence Act in 2024 to allow members to apply for further terms.
The Re-Commissioning of Former Officers of the Permanent Defence Forces Scheme facilitates the re-entry of former officers, where vacancies exist, and where there are particular skillsets that are not available in the PDF at the time of the application, to be re-commissioned.
Recommissioned officers are offered a short service commission for a period of three years. Subject to vacancies, the recommissioned officers may be offered a substantive appointment after three years if the requirement for the particular skill set still exists.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the actions she is taking to engage with a childcare centre (details supplied) in relation to their withdrawal from the core funding model; and the actions she will take to support parents with the knock-on price increase.
reply:
I am aware that The Magic Roundabout Crèche and Montessori, registered as Beautiful Minds Crèche and Montessori Ltd, has not participated in the Core Funding scheme since the 2023/2024 programme year.
Core Funding is a supply-side grant to early learning and childcare providers towards their operating costs. It is designed to promote affordability for parents and sustainability for providers through increased funding to the sector, paid on a consistent and equitable basis.
As Core Funding is an optional scheme, service providers have the autonomy and business freedom to withdraw from or choose not to participate in Core Funding, even though this will result in the loss of the significant financial support it offers them and the substantial benefits and certainty it brings to families.
If a Partner Services wishes to withdraw from the Core Funding Programme, they must provide 3 months’ notice to the Scheme Administrator. This must be done by submitting a Service Request on the Early Years Early Years Hive outlining the withdrawal date and the reason for the withdrawal.
However, if an existing Partner Service decides not to enter a contract for the new programme year starting on 1 September, they, as private businesses, would no longer be subject to the provisions of the Core Funding Agreement and, by extension, the required minimum notice period to parents. They are also not required to provide a reason for choosing not to reapply for Core Funding to the Scheme Administrator.

The Programme for Government 2025 - Securing Ireland's Future commits to introducing paid surrogacy leave and department officials are examining how best to implement this commitment. They are also engaging with officials from the Department of Social Protection as the Minister for Social Protection has responsibility for the payment of any associated benefits.
The Minister for Health leads on the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024, which includes provisions in relation to surrogacy which have implications for the introduction of surrogacy leave, while policy on parentage is a matter for the Minister for Justice. It is not possible to finalise provisions in relation to surrogacy leave in advance of the commencement of that Act as it will determine who is to be recognised as a parent when a child is born through a surrogacy arrangement.
Decisions on the date of commencement of the 2024 Act are matters for the Minister for Health. I can assure the Deputy that this Department will work closely with relevant Departments, once the 2024 Act has commenced, to progress proposals for surrogacy leave.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the rationale for increasing State funding to the greyhound racing industry in Budget 2027.
reply:
Rásaíocht Con Éireann (RCÉ) is a commercial state body established under the Greyhound Industry Act 1958 chiefly to control greyhound racing and to improve and develop the greyhound industry. RCÉ is a body corporate and a separate legal entity to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.
The horse and greyhound racing industries, via Horse Racing Ireland (HRI) and RCÉ, receive financial support from the State through the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund. The Programme for Government commits that the Government will continue to support the Horse and Greyhound Fund, considering the vital economic and social contribution generated by these sectors in rural areas.
In Budget 2027, €102m has been allocated to the Fund of which €81.6m will be allocated to HRI and €20.4m to RCÉ. The allocation is subject to Oireachtas approval and is split 80/20 between HRI and RCÉ respectively in line with the relevant legislation.
The proposed increase in the Fund will be linked to the implementation of the recommendations contained in the Indecon Review, in respect of equine and greyhound welfare and integrity. This will form part of my Department’s overall animal welfare package and is in line with the Programme for Government commitments on equine and greyhound welfare and with the strategic plans of both RCÉ and HRI.

Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the total allocation for the bovine TB eradication programme in 2027 compared with 2026, given that the Budget 2026 expenditure report provided over €157 million and the Budget 2027 expenditure report lists €142.4 million; the cost of increasing reactor compensation ceilings by €500.
reply:
Budget 2026 provided an increased budget for the bTB programme with €157 million allocated for 2026. This was to allow the bTB programme to focus on driving down disease through the implementation of the measures laid out in the bTB Action Plan which I launched in September 2025.
The primary driver of the cost of the bTB programme is disease levels and there has been encouraging progress in recent months in reducing bTB levels. The latest statistics for 2026 indicate 5,372 herds have suffered a bTB breakdown in the last 12 months which is down 10.9% compared to this time last year with a herd incidence now of 5.42% compared to 6.03% this time last year. This is due to the combined efforts of all stakeholders in engaging with farmers to reduce the risk bTB poses to Irish herds and rural communities.
I am confident that the changes I have introduced in the bTB Action Plan will help drive down disease levels further. To continue this progress I have secured a further allocation of €142.4 million for bTB measures in 2027.
The On Farm Market Valuation Scheme (OFMV) is the principal compensation measure available to Herdowners whose herds are affected by a bovine TB breakdown in their herd. The Scheme aims to compensate farmers up to the open market value of an animal as if they were not affected by disease, subject to ceilings. question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether Budget 2027 includes a dedicated support for farmers facing fodder deficits following the 2026 drought, including a fodder transport support scheme, further to the Tánaiste's indication on 24 September 2026 that Budget 2027 would include fodder support; and the amount allocated.
reply:

Minister Browne and I granted a one-week extension to the slurry spreading period extending it to the 7 October 2026. question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the timeline for the publication of the new Animal Welfare Strategy, the consultation for which closed in January 2026; the reason it has not been published.
reply:
The term of Ireland’s first ever Animal Welfare Strategy 2021-2025 - Working Together for Animal Welfare reached a conclusion at the end of 2025.
In 2025, a process was initiated to develop a new animal welfare strategy, which will act as a framework for engagement and collaboration to direct future activities with the aim of benefiting both animals and Irish society.
Development of the strategy is now approaching completion following a broad stakeholder engagement including a non-statutory public consultation that was launched on November 19th and ran to January 2nd. In excess of 1750 individual submissions were received as part of that process.
The new strategy will continue to adopt a ‘One Health, One Welfare’ approach, acknowledging and valuing the inter-dependencies between human, animal and environmental health, and taking an evidence-led approach to policy making, target-setting, monitoring and evaluation.
I anticipate that the new strategy will be published in the near term.

question: Deputy Denise Mitchell asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine further to Parliamentary Question No. 64947/26, the plans in place in the event of a significant disruption of trade flows affecting the approximately 4.5 million tonnes of animal feed which the State imports annually.
reply:
Whilst 80% of animal feed in Ireland is derived from grazed grass/preserved forage, about 6.5 million tonnes (2025) of compound feed is manufactured in Ireland. Approximately 2.2 million tonnes of home-grown cereals are produced – barley, wheat and oats (includes human consumption) and some 5.1 million tonnes (2025), imported.
In the case of pigs and poultry, virtually all their nutrition is derived from compound feeds. The main commodities imported are maize and maize by-products, soyabean meal and hulls, rapeseed meal, vegetable oils and fats, minerals and vitamins. Imports from the EU make up approximately 25% of imported feed, with the balance sourced from third countries, mainly Argentina, USA, Canada and Brazil.
The issue of feed supply is linked to the overall principles of European food security. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), in supporting farm incomes and sustainable food production, plays a fundamental role in ensuring European food security. At the Informal meeting of EU Agriculture Ministers which I hosted in Dublin and Kildare in September, discussions focused on the European Commission’s new Livestock Strategy and Protein Action Plan, including the need to strengthen European protein production.
With regards to Irish feed importers, these companies have well established commercial relationships and have significant knowledge and experience in dealing with trade and climate disruptions as well as logistical difficulties.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if the criteria for health testing are different when only contract rearing for one farmer than that of multiple contract rearing for multiple farmers.
reply:
The Bovine TB Action Plan, Addressing Bovine TB (bTB) in Ireland outlines changes to bTB testing requirements for contract rearing as follows
• All animals returning from a contract rearer will require a 30-day pre-movement test.
• If a contract rearer is rearing animals from more than one herd, then all animals over 42 days will require a 30-day pre-movement test before they can enter the contract rearing herd.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the action his Department is taking in view of the fact that tropilaelaps, a parasite mite originating from Asia, is now present in Europe and spreading west; if they are monitoring the progression of this pest, in view of the fact that this pest is a severe threat to the Irish Honey Bee, and once established, eradication is not achievable and permanent costly control measures are required.
reply:
My Department is very aware of the increasing threat posed to the Irish beekeeping sector by Tropilaelaps spp., and the Animal Health Risk Assessment Unit in my Department is currently carrying out an assessment of the risks posed to bees from these pests.
My Department operates the Sentinel Apiary Programme (SAP) the aim of which is to ensure the early detection of two exotic pests, Tropilaelaps spp. and the Small Hive Beetle. The 2026 programme is ongoing with 12 volunteer beekeepers participating. For anyone who might be interested in participating in the programme for 2027 they can contact [Beekeeping@agriculture.gov.ie] for further information.
Furthermore, my Department engages with the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs in Northern Ireland on issues such as Tropilaelaps spp. including a bee health contingency test exercise held in February 2024.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons granted international protection status, that is, refugee status, subsidiary protection or permission to remain, in each of the past ten years, who were nationals of countries designated as safe countries of origin at the time of their application; the countries concerned; and the number granted status from each such country in each year, in tabular form.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, International Protection applications from the previous ten years involve two separate pieces of legislation, namely the International Protection Act 2015, which applies to applications made before 12 June 2026, and the International Protection Act 2026, which applies to applications made on or after that date.
Under Section 215 of the International Protection Act 2026, the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration is empowered to make an order designating a country as a safe country of origin. A country may only be designated as a safe country of origin only if I am satisfied that, on the basis of the legal situation, the application of the law within a democratic system and the general political circumstances, it can be shown that there is no persecution and no real risk of serious harm. These provisions are similar to those in the previous applicable legislation, section 72 of the International Protection Act 2015.
If an applicant for international protection is from a country designated as a safe country of origin, their application will still receive a full consideration on its merits. However, if you are from a designated safe country, you will be dealt with through an accelerated process or the border procedure.
My Department does not publish statistics on the number of people who were granted international protection status, by nationality.
