question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the amount collected to date for the gambling social impact fund; the amount disbursed; the organisations funded; and the amount allocated specifically to addiction treatment and recovery services.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 576, 579, 580 and 582 together.
The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the ‘2024 Act’) establishes a comprehensive framework for the licensing and regulation of betting, gaming, and certain lotteries, including activities provided online to persons in the State. It also establishes a new, independent statutory body, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). Last year, I signed orders to commence the first provisions of the 2024 Act and establish the GRAI from 5 March 2025.
The provisions of the 2024 Act and the powers of the GRAI are being rolled out on a phased basis and, in that context, I signed an order on 3 February 2026 to commence those parts of the Act that allowed the GRAI to begin accepting applications for the issuing of betting licences. The existing remote betting licensees, then operating under a licence issued by the Office of the Revenue Commissioners up until 30 June 2026, could apply for a licence from the Authority to commence on 1 July 2026. Similarly, in-person betting licensees (on track and on the high street) whose Revenue-issued licences expire on 30 November 2026 can apply to the Authority for a licence from 1 December 2026. As the GRAI builds up its resources, commencement of the licensing of the gaming and lotteries sector will take place. In that context, it is expected that licensing for gaming (remote and in-person) will commence in early 2027 and licensing for lotteries will commence in due course.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of applications for international protection awaiting a first-instance decision at the international protection office as of the latest date for which figures are available; the number of these pending for more than 12 months, more than 24 months and more than 36 months, respectively; the current median processing time; and if a statement will be made on the matter.
reply:

This investment has already demonstrated results.
In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first instance decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. This year, as of 1 October 2026, IPAT had already closed 6,902 appeals, exceeding the total number of appeals completed during the whole of 2025.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of protected disclosures within An Garda Síochána that remained at initial assessment stage at the end of each of the years 2023, 2024 and 2025; and the longest period any such disclosure has remained at that stage.
reply:
In An Garda Síochána, a Garda member or a staff member has a number of options if he or she wishes to make a protected disclosure. They can report concerns directly to the Protected Disclosure Unit within An Garda Síochána; they can go directly to Fiosrú; they can go directly to the Office of Protected Disclosures Commissioner, or they can report their disclosure to a Minister.
The legislation places reporting obligations on all public bodies concerning the number of disclosures made in each year. These reports are published by my Department, An Garda Síochána and Fiosrú - the Office of the Police Ombudsman.
Details of the disclosures for the relevant years are available in the relevant Garda Annual Report under Section 22 of the Protected Disclosures Act 2014 (as amended). These are available at: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/annual%20reports/an-garda-siochana-annual-reports/
I am advised that all disclosures received are given due attention.
An Garda Síochána has recently published an updated Protected Disclosures Policy, which is available at: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/policy-documents/protected-disclosures-policy-and-procedure.pdf
As outlined in the Policy, under Section 9.6, either the Protected Disclosures Unit within An Garda Síochána or the reporting person can request a review at the conclusion of either the assessment stage or the examination/investigation stage. Section 9.7 also outlines the file closure process for disclosures.

question: Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to join family applications, the reason decisions are issued in such uneven bursts; and whether a daily, steady processing target for join family can be introduced.
reply:
Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland for employment, study and family reasons, as well as for visitors travelling for business or tourism. These are important screening processes designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system, and each visa application is assessed on its own merits, taking all relevant information into consideration at that time.
I am acutely aware that Join Family applications are of significant importance to the individuals and families concerned. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland. While every effort is made to process applications as quickly as possible, applications can vary considerably in complexity and in the level of examination required. Consequently, decisions are issued once an application has been fully assessed, rather than according to a fixed daily processing pattern.
My Department continually reviews processing arrangements with a view to improving efficiency and reducing waiting times for applicants. However, it is important that each application receives appropriate consideration on its own merits and in accordance with immigration policy and legislative requirements.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the report of the Garda Vetting Review Group, established in April 2021; the changes proposed; and the implementation of those changes.
reply:
The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust.
The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary.
Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers.
In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the visas for Gazan students who were due to study in Ireland; and the interventions his Department has taken to help them obtain their visas.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 518, 528, 539 and 552 together.
I am conscious of the exceptionally difficult circumstances facing people in Gaza and the wider region and my officials from my Department continue to engage closely with colleagues across Government in responding to those challenges.
As judicial review proceedings are currently before the Courts in relation to Palestinian study visa applicants, it would not be appropriate for me to comment on those matters in detail.
I can advise the Deputy that there has been no change in policy in relation to visa applications from Palestinian nationals. Applications from Palestinian students are assessed against the same criteria that apply to all visa-required nationals seeking to study in Ireland. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to the individual circumstances of the applicant and the information provided in support of the application.
It is important to recognise that visa decisions are based on the facts of each individual case. Refusal decisions may arise for a variety of reasons, including where applicants are unable to satisfy established immigration requirements relating to identity and documentation, financial resources, English language requirements, or other matters relevant to the assessment of the application. question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the contract for emergency accommodation to house Ukrainian refugees (details supplied) will conclude.
reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether an international protection applicant residing in IPAS accommodation who receives a custodial sentence retains their allocated accommodation for the duration of their imprisonment; whether their daily expenses allowance continues during imprisonment; whether the accommodation is available to them automatically on release; and if not, the criteria that determine whether accommodation and the allowance are restored.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 541 and 542 together.
Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, International Protection Applicants are provided with material reception conditions, including housing, food, clothing and a Daily Expenses Allowance (DEA).
When people seeking international protection take up an offer of accommodation at an IPAS accommodation centre, they are provided with the ‘IPAS House Rules’ which explains the rules and procedures that are designed to make reception and accommodation centres safe and effective. This document which includes information on absence policy is issued to all residents on arrival.
In line with Section 76 of the International Protection Act 2026, accommodation is offered to applicants on the understanding that they will be living in their allocated accommodation centre on a daily basis. It is the responsibility of IPAS to ensure that accommodation is available to all international protection applicants without sufficient means and that all allocated beds are used on a continuous basis. Attendance in centres is monitored by centre managers and by IPAS.
If an applicant is in custody and therefore not living in allocated accommodation on a daily basis, this accommodation is withdrawn by IPAS and the applicant may reapply for accommodation upon their release. They are not eligible for the Daily Expense Allowance during the time spent outside of IPAS accommodation.

reply:

Character and conduct checks are also carried out before applicants can be granted any permission to remain in the State. An Garda Síochána notifies my Department of any matters that may be relevant to its considerations.
Where a person has applied for citizenship, further checks are carried out as part of the good character assessment. An Garda Síochána is requested to make enquiries into the applicant’s background; the detail and extent of which is a matter for An Garda Síochána. For sound security and operational reasons, it is not the practice to comment on the enquiries that may be conducted.

reply:
My Department continuously evaluates and adapts its strategies to deal with the evolving cyber security threat landscape. Frontier AI models are creating unprecedented opportunities for cyber security; conversely however, they have the capabilities to create novel and heightened security risks. The National Cyber Risk Assessment, which I published in December 2025, highlighted how AI drives systemic risk by increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of cyberattacks.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), is an operational arm of my Department and holds the lead role in the management of major cyber security incidents across government. The NCSC also specifically monitors developments in AI-enabled cyber capabilities on a continuous basis and collaborates with our international partners in the EU and more broadly on this issue. The Deputy will appreciate that the National Cyber Security Centre does not comment on arrangements for the sharing of cyber security intelligence.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the rationale for setting the minimum annual income requirement under the temporary protection transition scheme at €29,432; if he will consider providing flexibility or individual assessment for applicants who fall below the threshold due to variable working hours, caring responsibilities, disability or other circumstances, but who have a sustained record of employment and PRSI contributions in the State; and if a review of the operation of the income threshold is planned following the commencement of the scheme.
reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme opened for applications on 30 September 2026.
An applicant must demonstrate that they have been in employment or self-employment for at least six months immediately prior to the opening date of the Scheme, with average gross earnings of €29,432, and must continue to be in employment both at the date of application and at the date a decision is made on their application. This rate is set to reflect full-time minimum wage employment.
It is important to note that the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an additional pathway for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland on an independent basis. Persons who do not satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to benefit from Temporary Protection and its associated rights and entitlements while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. Temporary Protection is currently in place across the EU until March 2028. People in Ireland will continue to have access to the associated rights of the Directive for the duration of Temporary Protection to include the right to reside in Ireland and the right to access to social welfare, education, and employment.

reply:
The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department.
This application is based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency.
Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family.
Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link:

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current processing time for applications to the National Garda Vetting Bureau.
reply:

The Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) is responsible for the Garda Vetting system under the general superintendence of the Garda Commissioner, under the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Acts. As Minister, I have no role in the Garda Vetting system, nor in individual applications.
I am advised by the Garda authorities that vetting applications are processed on a first-come, first served basis in chronological order from the date of receipt. The current average turnaround time for vetting applications is approximately seven business days from the date the application is received at the GNVB, for 85% of applications received.
Detailed statistics related to the work of the GNVB are updated monthly and are available at:
https://www.garda.ie/en/about-us/organised-serious-crime/garda-national-vetting-bureau-gnvb-/garda-vetting-statistics.html

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the amount being spent on free bus travel for Ukrainian people; and the number of Ukrainians who have free public transport.
reply:
The Free Travel Scheme is available to everyone who is 66 or over, and to certain people who are under 66 in receipt of qualifying payments or who meet the medical conditions for Blind Pension and legally living permanently in the State.
The total expenditure to date of the Free Travel scheme was €83.7 million provided to a total of 1,184,036 people in September 2026. Expenditure on the Free Travel Scheme is recorded at overall scheme level and cannot be broken down by recipient category. The monetary breakdown by beneficiaries of Temporary Protection from Ukraine is not available.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection his views on whether existing State financial supports for people with a disability are sufficient in the context of Article 28 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that guarantees the right to an adequate standard of living and social protection without discrimination; and if this is being considered in relation discussions around the Cost of Disability payment as set out by the Disability Federation of Ireland.
reply:
The Government recognises the additional costs that disabled people can face in their daily lives and is committed improving outcomes for disabled people by introducing permanent measures. That is why the Programme for Government includes a commitment to introduce a permanent annual cost of disability payment.
Last year, the Government published the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People 2025-2030. The strategy was developed with significant input from disability groups and advocates. It is a whole-of-Government framework for the implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
The strategy, includes a commitment to a Strategic Focus Network Summit on the Cost of Disability, emphasising the cross-government nature of the issue. In advance of the Summit, I launched an extensive consultation process on the cost of disability including bilateral meetings with disability representative groups and DPOs, and a public consultation which received more than 1,100 submissions. I hosted the Strategic Focus Network Summit on May 13th attended by over 300 people, in person or online.
The submissions to the consultation process, the output of the Strategic Focus Network and the engagements I attended such as the Pre-Budget Forum and the National Economic Dialogue have all informed the approach that we, across Government, have taken in Budget 2027 towards addressing the cost of disability.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the way in which an inheritance received by a recipient of disability allowance is assessed under the means test; the amount of capital that may be held before any reduction in payment applies; the amount at which the payment ceases entirely; if consideration has been given to disregarding, in whole or in part, an inheritance received from a parent by a person with a lifelong disability.
reply:
Disability Allowance (DA) is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. DA is a weekly payment for people aged 16 to 66 with a disability expected to last at least one year. Eligibility is subject to medical assessment, means test and habitual residence conditions. Applicants must demonstrate that they are substantially restricted in undertaking work that would otherwise be suitable given their age, experience, and qualifications, as a result of their condition.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially equitable allocation of scarce resources.
Inheritance is treated as capital and is thus assessable under Social Welfare legislation.
DA has one of the highest capital disregards operated by my Department. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This is compared to a €20,000 disregard for most social welfare payments. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of disability allowance claims reduced or closed in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026 due to capital arising from an inheritance; the number of those recipients who subsequently lost entitlement to the free travel pass as a result; if his Department collects this data; if not, the reason.
reply:
The Department does not collect or maintain detailed data on individual sources of assets and so it is not possible to provide a breakdown of the number of recipients whose payment was reduced or ceased due to inherited capital nor those who lost entitlement to the free travel pass in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, as requested by the Deputy.
Although the specific data requested is not available, I would like to highlight that as part of the “Make Work Pay” initiative, persons who move directly from certain long term Social Protection schemes such as Disability Allowance to employment are entitled to retain their Free Travel entitlement for a further period of 5 years, where they previously had the entitlement to free travel on the scheme.
Any changes to means testing could only be considered in the context of the budgetary process.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will clarify the eligibility criteria for the household benefits package and fuel allowance in the case of an Irish citizen (details supplied), who is in receipt of a disablement pension but resides in Northern Ireland; if residence outside the State automatically disqualifies a person from the household benefits package; and if the same residency requirement applies to the fuel allowance.
reply:
The Household Benefits Package comprises of an electricity or gas allowance, and a Free Television Licence. Only one Household Benefits Package is payable per household. The Household Benefit Package is generally available to applicants aged 66 years or over, who are in receipt of a social welfare type payment, or who satisfy a means test. The package is also available to applicants under age 66 who are in receipt of certain social welfare payments. For applicants aged 70 or over, there is no requirement to be in receipt of a qualifying payment or to satisfy a means test.
Fuel Allowance is a means-tested payment to assist pensioners and other long-term social welfare dependent householders with their winter heating costs. The payment is made over the winter season - from September to April or, if preferred, by way of two lump sum instalments - one at the start of the Fuel Allowance season (usually late September) and one in January. Only one Fuel Allowance is payable per household. For those aged 66 years or over, the applicant must satisfy a means test and be living alone or only with other qualified people. For those aged under 66 years, the applicant must be in receipt of certain social welfare payments and be living alone or only with other qualified people.
Both Household Benefits Package and Fuel Allowance are assistance-based payments and, as such, to qualify for either of these payments, the applicant must be legally resident in the State.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Social Protection to give consideration to points raised in correspondence (details supplied) and allow for a full rate of carer's allowance in such situations.
reply:
The Government recognises the invaluable contribution made by family carers often over many years and into pension age, as outlined in the case raised by the Deputy.
Generally, under the single payment per person rule, people who qualify for multiple social welfare payments typically receive only the higher of the available options.
However, in recognition of the important contribution made by carers, an exception applies where a person who is receiving a primary social welfare payment and who is also providing full-time care and attention may receive a half-rate Carer's Allowance in addition to their main payment. This arrangement applies to almost all weekly social welfare payments, including the State pension.
There are currently more than 112,000 people in receipt of Carer’s Allowance at an estimated cost of more than €1.4 billion in 2026. Of that total, 52,377 are receiving their full primary social welfare payment together with a half-rate Carer's Allowance payment.
Currently, eligible Carer’s Allowance recipients who qualify for the full State Pension (Contributory) may see their weekly payment increase from €270 to €453.30 at age 66, an increase of up to €183.30 depending on their circumstances. Following Budget 2027, from next January the weekly payment in this case will increase from €453.30 to €468.30, an increase of €15.00.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection the timeline for a decision to be made on a carer's allowance (details supplied) review.
reply:
Carer's allowance, CA, is a means-tested social assistance payment made to a person who is habitually resident in the State and who is providing full-time care and attention to a child or an adult who has such a disability that, as a result, they require that level of care.
An application for CA was received from the person concerned on 14 May 2026.
It is a condition for receipt of CA that every claimant shall furnish such certificates, documents, information, and evidence as may be required for the purposes of deciding their claim. A request to provide additional information issued to the person concerned on 26 June 2026. As the person concerned failed to supply all of the information requested, the claim was disallowed on 18 July 2026.
The person concerned was notified of their right to have the decision reviewed (where further information is available) or to appeal the decision to the Social Welfare Appeals Office (SWAO).
A subsequent review was initiated on foot of further documents received on 05 October 2026 and, following this review, CA was awarded from 14 May 2026.
The first payment will issue to the nominated bank account of the person concerned on 15 October 2026. Any arrears due will issue shortly.
The person concerned was notified of this decision in writing on 08 October 2026.
I hope this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Defence if the Air Corps is finding it increasingly difficult to fulfil its Service Level Agreement with the HSE for air ambulance services due to the lack of technicians and maintenance issues.
reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Social Protection the estimated real-terms change in the value of core weekly social welfare rates in 2027, following the €10 increase announced in Budget 2027, given HICP inflation of 3.2 per cent in 2026 and forecast inflation of 3.0 per cent in 2027 as set out in the Budget 2027 expenditure report.
reply:
Budget 2027 provides for €30 billion in social protection expenditure, a €2billion increase on 2026. Social welfare payment rates will increase by €10, at a cost of some €755 million.
The €10 rate increase to pension payments is a 3.3% increase on 2026 rates. The increase will come into effect in January 2027. This increase is greater than the forecasted inflation for 2027 and means that, for the first time, the State Pension (Contributory) will exceed €300 per week, increasing to €309.30. The €10 rate increase to working age schemes represent a 3.9% increase on 2026 rates.
The across the board rate increase announced in Budget 2027 will assist in mitigating the prices increase for both pension and working age recipients.
In determining Budget rates, consideration is given not only to the headline rates but also targeted secondary supports. That is why, as part of Budget 2027, I also announced an increase to the Living Alone Allowance of €3 per week, the Child Support Payment of €6 and an increase of €5 to the weekly rate for Fuel Allowance. An initial Cost of Disability payment of €500 for recipients of long-term disability payments will also be paid in the first quarter of 2027.
Changes to social welfare rates, are based on a wide range of inputs used by my Department, most notably CSO data including the survey of income and living conditions, SILC, the labour force survey, the monthly CPI and HICP releases and the CSO earnings and hours in employment surveys. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of international protection applicants who, while in receipt of a social welfare payment or dependent-related payment, entered prison in each of the past five years; what happened to each payment during imprisonment; the number transferred to a spouse, partner or other dependent; and the total annual cost involved.
reply:
My department administers the Daily Expenses Allowance which is paid to International Protection Applicants who reside in, or are waiting for, accommodation provided by the International Protection Accommodation Services. The current weekly rates of payment are €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. In addition there is an increased rate of €113.80 per week for an adult applies where a person is unaccommodated and is on a waiting list for International Protection Accommodation Service.
Where an International Protection Applicant enters prison, their Daily Expenses Allowance claim is closed, as they no longer satisfy the conditions for payment
Daily Expense Allowance is paid on an individual basis, meaning that each eligible adult has their own payment and couples are not paid together. Where there are children in the family, the other parent can apply to have the children added to their Daily Expense Allowance payment.
The Department does not compile statistics on recipients of Daily Expenses Allowance who enter prison, nor does it maintain records of the number of child payments transferred to the other parent. Consequently, the statistical information requested is not available.
I trust this clarifies the issue for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons who became Irish citizens in each of the past five years who subsequently received social welfare payments and were subsequently imprisoned; what payments they were receiving immediately prior to imprisonment; whether those payments ceased, were suspended or continued for dependants; and the total value of payments made to their dependants during their imprisonment.
reply: The Department of Social Protection does not collect or maintain data on persons becoming Irish citizens, or on customers' legal status. Statistics on welfare payments to and legal status of naturalised citizens are not available.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons whose social welfare payment was suspended or terminated following imprisonment in each of the past five years; the number whose qualified adult or child increases continued to be paid to another person; the number of such cases involving non-Irish nationals; and the number involving persons who had previously acquired Irish citizenship.
reply:
Statistics on suspension or termination of welfare payments due to imprisonment are not available. My Department operates over 90 schemes and services, operated across a number of different operational systems, and claim closure reasons are not always populated; in other cases multiple reasons for a closure could apply but only one reason is recorded.
The Department of Social Protection does not collect or maintain data on persons becoming Irish citizens, or on customers' legal status. Statistics on welfare payments to and legal status of naturalised citizens are not available.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if consideration is being given to providing additional pension protections for parents who have provided lifelong care to a son or daughter with a disability and who may have reduced pay related social insurance contribution records as a consequence of their caring responsibilities.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 488, 489, 490, 491, 492 and 493 together.
My Department provides State Pension payments through the State Pension (Contributory), which is a contributory payment based on a person's social insurance record, and the State Pension (Non-Contributory) which is a means-tested social assistance payment.
The State Pension (Contributory) (SPC) is funded from the Social Insurance Fund through the contributions paid by workers and employers. The rate of payment reflects the number of social insurance contributions paid over a working life. Eligibility for the SPC is based on a number of criteria:
• Being aged 66 or over.
• Having entered the Social Insurance system 10 years before drawdown of the SPC.
• Having a minimum of 520 paid social insurance contributions (i.e., 10 years reckonable PRSI contributions).
This Government acknowledges the important role that carers play and is fully committed to supporting them in that role. Accordingly, carers are not excluded from access to the SPC. Once a person has met the minimum requirement of 520 paid contributions, the State Pension system gives significant recognition to those whose work history includes extended periods outside of paid employment, often to raise families or in a full-time caring role including:
• PRSI credits (which include Credits for Carer's Benefit and Carer's Allowance), and
• Homemaking Disregards and HomeCaring Periods to recognise caring periods of up to 20 years outside of paid empl

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Social Protection if he has considered extending the age limit for domiciliary care allowance from sixteen to eighteen-years-of-age.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 486 and 487 together.
Domiciliary Care Allowance is a non-means tested payment to a parent or guardian in respect of a child under 16 who has a severe disability and requires substantially more care and attention than would normally be needed by a child of the same age.
From January 2026, the monthly rate of Domiciliary Care Allowance increased from €360 to €380. More than 65,950 families currently receive the payment in respect of approximately 75,496 children, with estimated expenditure of almost €359 million in 2026.
Domiciliary Care Allowance stops being paid when a child turns 16 years of age. If the young person has a disability that significantly impacts their daily living activities, they can then apply for a Disability Allowance payment in their own name of €254 per week. Where full-time care is required after a child turns 16 years of age, carers may continue to qualify for supports such as Carer's Allowance or Carer's Benefit, subject to the relevant eligibility conditions.

If the young person has a disability that significantly impacts their daily living activities, they can then apply for a Disability Allowance payment in their own name of €254 per week. Disability Allowance is a weekly means-tested income support payment for people aged 16 or over whose illness or disability means that they are substantially restricted from doing work that would be suitable for a person of their age, experience and qualifications.
Where full-time care is required after a child turns 16 years of age, carers may continue to qualify for supports such as Carer's Allowance or Carer's Benefit, subject to the relevant eligibility conditions.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Social Protection the length of time it is currently taking for reviews of disability allowance applications to be undertaken.
reply:
Disability Allowance is a weekly allowance paid to people with a specified disability who are aged 16 or over and under the age of 66. This disability must be expected to last for at least one year and the allowance is subject to a medical assessment, means test and Habitual Residency conditions.
Processing times for new applications vary across schemes, depending on the differing qualification criteria. Schemes that require a high level of documentary evidence from the customer, particularly in the case of illness-related schemes, can take longer to process.
Currently the average number of weeks to award a Disability Allowance claim in September 2025 is 5 weeks. The average processing time for an appeal on Disability Allowance, from date of appeal to the last decision on the appeal, was 12.7 weeks.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will consider an increase in the secondary dinner rate with a drink in the school meals programme to €3,20 from €2.50 to equalise it with the hot schools meal and backdate it to the beginning of this school year, as providers are finding it difficult to maintain services with the costs incurred.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 478 and 483 together.
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week. The budget for 2026 is €286 million.
The Hot School Meals Scheme introduced in 2019 was specifically developed for Primary Schools. Recognising that the vast majority of primary schools do not have catering facilities the funding model is calibrated to allow for off-site preparation and delivery to the schools. In contrast, the dinner option available under the School Meals Programme for DEIS Secondary schools was developed and tendered on the basis that meals would be prepared on-site, utilising the canteen facilities available in those schools.
Secondary schools issued requests for tenders based on the payment rates available, rates that were well known among interested food business operators within the food services industry.
The rate for the dinner model was increased in 2023 when there was an increase for all options under the School Meals Programme. There are no plans for a further increase at this time.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Frankie Feighan asked the Minister for Social Protection if the mechanism to pay suppliers under the current school meals programme has been modified; and if the Minister is satisfied that all suppliers will be paid within 30 days of invoices having been submitted.
reply:
Under the School Meals Programme, the primary relationship is between the school and supplier. My department provides the funding for the meals directly to the school and it is the responsibility of each school board to administer the Programme in their school including managing the procurement process. All schools are responsible for choosing their school meals supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules. These rules clearly define the successful tenderer's responsibilities and obligations, including adherence to the nutritional standards.
The payment mechanism for the School Meals Programme has not been modified. Funding is awarded on receipt of a fully completed and signed application form which includes all supporting documentation. These include a signed service level agreement with the Department, a menu compliant with the Programmes Nutrition Standards, details of income and expenditure including banks statements and invoices.
Schools as independent public bodies are responsible for paying suppliers invoices.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will give consideration to removing the mandatory certificate of benefit comparison requirement for straightforward defined contribution-to-PRSA transfers, where there is an identifiable fund value; in situations where the consumer is receiving appropriate regulated financial advice, including the material benefits being surrendered and the reasons the transfer is considered suitable, given this would remove an unnecessary cost and administrative barrier for ordinary defined contribution pension savers seeking to consolidate their pensions.
reply:
Under section 113 of the Pensions Act 1990, as amended, when assets are transferred from an occupational pension scheme to a PRSA, the PRSA provider is required to furnish the individual with a Certificate of Benefit Comparison (CBC), which compares the possible benefits of the scheme with the possible benefits from the PRSA.
The report of the Inter-Departmental Pensions Reform and Taxation Group in November 2020 recommended that the Pensions Authority reconsider the requirements in relation to the provision of CBCs, in particular in relation to transfers to PRSAs from defined contribution pension arrangements and make recommendations to my Department for legislative change where necessary.
My Department has worked in conjunction with the Pensions Authority to examine the requirements for CBCs and has developed policy and draft legislative proposals to simplify the requirements in the case of transfers from defined contribution schemes to PRSAs.
It is anticipated that these proposals will be submitted to Government in the near future for approval and referral to the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel of the Government for drafting.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Defence if she will examine the possibility of extending access to the swimming pool at the Curragh Camp to residents of the Curragh, Newbridge and surrounding areas; if any assessment has been carried out regarding wider community use of the facility; and the measures that would be required to facilitate public access.
reply:

Permission for the use of the pool is subject at all times to Defence Forces requirements and signed conditions, which includes the requirement for the schools and organisations to have appropriate insurance.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of applications for fuel allowance refused to date in 2026.
reply:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans for funding to be made available to local authorities through the Housing Activation Office for projects to unlock housing.
reply:
The Housing Activation Office (HAO) is responsible for managing the €1 billion Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund (HIIF), which was launched by Government in January 2026 to support the delivery of housing-enabling infrastructure.
Under the first funding call opened in January 2026, I invited applications from local authorities and the Land Development Agency. Following assessment of the applications received, 82 infrastructure projects were accepted onto the HIIF programme in June 2026.
These projects relate to sites where infrastructure deficits have been identified as barriers to housing delivery. The approved projects span transport, water, wastewater, electricity and other housing-enabling infrastructure and will support the activation of housing sites at both a local level and a number of strategically important locations.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Defence further to Parliamentary Question Nos. 121 and 123 of 7 May 2026, if the Strategic Workforce Plan referred to, has been submitted; if so, the timeframe for its finalisation; if the plan contains recommendations on lateral entry, lateral mobility or the establishment of a formal pathway for suitably qualified from other military forces; the status of work being undertaken by her Department or the Defence Forces on such a policy; and if she plans to progress a formal lateral transfer pathway in the event that this is not specifically recommended in the plan.
reply:

Last year saw 790 inductions to the Permanent Defence Force (PDF)- the highest figure in twenty years- while the total number of applications for careers in the PDF exceeded 16,500.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the actual and projected number of residential dwellings and population for each local authority for 2020, 2025 and 2030 under the assumptions used for national and regional planning; and the resulting number of dwellings per 100 persons in each local authority for each of those years, in tabular form.
reply:
The Revised National Planning Framework (NPF) was finalised and approved by Government and the Oireachtas in April 2025. The Revised NPF strategy sets out the need to plan for a projected population of at least 6.1m people in Ireland by 2040. Taking into account ‘pent-up’ demand, the strategy sets out a need to plan for the delivery of approximately 50,000 additional housing units per annum nationally, to 2040.
As part of the revision process, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) were engaged to update their previous projections relating to population growth to 2040, based on demographic and econometric modelling and having regard to the results of Census 2022 and other factors with potential to influence fertility, mortality and migration trends.
The ESRI projections published in July 2024 estimated that the population of Ireland will increase by around one million people or by 20% over 2022 levels, to around 5.7m by 2030 and approximately 6.1 million people by 2040, with higher figures of 5.9m and 6.3m people respectively in a ‘high-migration’ scenario.
To ensure that local authority development plans reflect the requirements of the NPF in respect of housing as soon as possible, I issued the NPF Implementation: Housing Growth Requirements Guidelines under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 in July 2025. question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if targets have been established for the number of vacant residential properties to be returned to use for each year from 2026 to 2030; if so, to provide those targets, by local authority, in tabular form; and, if not, the reason progress in reducing residential vacancy is to be measured and assessed.
reply:
Work to address vacancy and dereliction is being advanced and monitored through a range of measures supported by Government, including the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, which has been expanded and extended to 2030, the Vacant Above the Shop Grant, and the Expert Advice Grant.
My Department also provides annual funding to local authorities to strengthen their capacity to tackle vacancy and dereliction. This includes funding for Vacant Homes Officers and the Compulsory Purchase Order Activation Programme, which assists local authorities identify and bring vacant and derelict properties back into use.
While the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant aims to support the delivery of 20,000 homes, annual targets are not set for the return of residential properties to use.
The management and maintenance of local authority social homes is the responsibility of respective local authorities under s.58 of the Housing Act 1966. Local authorities must ensure, in line with these responsibilities, that all tenanted properties comply with the Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) Regulations 2019 and that they make adequate budgetary provision for repairs and cyclical maintenance, drawing on housing rental income as part of their annual budget process.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he will consider introducing a moratorium on the approval of new solar farm developments pending the publication of updated national solar farm planning guidelines; and whether such moratoriums or prohibitions are legally possible.
reply:
My Department has no plans to place a moratorium on planning applications for solar energy developments pending the finalisation of the intended National Planning Statement. In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement for solar energy development.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether motions passed and agreed by elected members of local authorities who opposed wind farm or solar farm developments and seeking moratoriums on future developments can be taken into account by planning authorities and by An Coimisiún Pleanála when determining planning applications.
reply:
Public participation is a crucial element of all substantive decision-making processes under the Planning and Development Act 2000, and the Planning and Development Act 2024. It is likely that both of the proposed draft National Planning Statements on Wind Energy and Solar Energy development will be subject to Strategic Environmental Assessment and that a public consultation will be held as part of this process, whereby individuals and stakeholders – including the local authorities and their elected members – will have the opportunity to make observations on the draft National Planning Statements.
In addition, it is open to any member of the public to make an observation or submission on a planning application, including in relation to solar energy developments, and the planning authority is statutorily obliged to consider such submissions before making a decision on the application. Persons who make submissions are also entitled to be notified of any significant further information provided to the planning authority by the applicant and to be notified of the authority’s decision on the application.
Furthermore, any person who made a submission on a planning application may appeal the planning authority’s decision on the application to An Coimisiun Pleanála or may make a submission to the Board in relation to an appeal of that decision.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the review of HAP rates; and if changes will be made to the rates or levels of discretion in 2026.
reply:
The HAP scheme plays a vital role in housing eligible families and individuals. At the end of Q1 2026, over 133,100 HAP tenancies had been set up since the scheme commenced, of which there were 48,355 households actively in receipt of HAP support nationally.
Maximum rent limits for HAP were set for each housing authority area in 2016 in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection. Since 11 July 2022, each local authority has statutory discretion to agree to a HAP payment up to 35% above the prescribed maximum rent limit. Discretion can be increased up to 50% above the prescribed maximum rent limits for Homeless HAP tenancies in Dublin. Local authorities also have additional flexibility to apply a couple HAP rate to single-person households.
I gave my approval for a review of the current HAP rent limits to be undertaken to ensure there is sufficient support under the HAP scheme to assist eligible households in accessing accommodation in the private rental sector.
As part of this review, the Housing Agency carried out an analysis of the rental market and submitted its report to my Department on 16 July. This helped inform my Department’s review of the HAP rent limits, which has now concluded. I am currently considering its findings before setting out the next steps.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the child homelessness strategy; when it will be published; and the additional funding for homeless prevention that will be allocated for 2027.
reply:
Supporting individuals and families experiencing or at risk of experiencing homelessness is a priority for my Department and Government. Our housing plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The Plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own.
Increased supply is key to addressing homelessness. Government is focused on making sure that everyone has access to good quality, affordable and secure homes that suit their needs.
Our Plan recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that we face and introduces a number of key measures to address homelessness.
Addressing family homelessness is a key priority for Government. Our housing plan commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. This has brought together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. It is intended it that the plan will be published shortly.
Prevention of homelessness in the first instance is an absolute priority. There are many prevention initiatives already underway in my own Department and across G

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to PQ PQ69374/26, to outline the engagements he has had with DCEE on this matter; to provide the dates on which his officials met with officials from DCEE on this matter since taking office; and the dates on which he himself met the Minister for Climate, the Environment and Energy since taking office, in tabular form.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider a review of the commercial rates for an industry (details supplied).
reply:
Tailte Éireann is an independent Government agency and provides a property registration system, property valuation service, and national mapping and surveying infrastructure for the State. Tailte Éireann is independent in the exercise of its valuation functions under the Valuation Act 2001, as amended (the Act). Tailte Éireann has overall responsibility under the Act, for the maintenance of all Valuation Lists used by Local Authorities in the calculation of rates liability.
Schedule 3 of the Act paragraphs 1(a) and (b), provides that all buildings and lands used or developed for any purpose, are rateable. The starting premise under the Act is that all interests (including buildings) and all developed land are rateable unless expressly exempted under Schedule 4. There is a very specific range of exemptions that can be applied, and Tailte Éireann has no discretionary latitude to grant exemptions not covered by Schedule 4.
Paragraph 5 of Schedule 4 provides that ‘farm buildings’ are an exempt category of property. question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the development of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Bill 2024; when the Bill will come before the Houses of the Oireachtas; and if the remediation scheme will cover balcony defects.
reply:
Drafting of the Apartment and Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme Bill is at an advanced stage and it is listed for publication this session. The statutory scheme will be in place as soon as possible following its passage through the Dáil.
The Scheme will provide supports for the remediation of relevant fire safety, structural safety and water ingress defects in purpose-built apartment buildings, including duplexes, constructed between 1991 and 2013. It is envisaged that 100% of eligible remediation costs will be funded. The content of the final Bill will be a matter for the Government to agree in due course.
It is expected that applicants to the current Interim Remediation Scheme will transfer seamlessly over to the new statutory scheme, which will be managed by the Housing Agency. My Department and the Housing Agency will work to ensure that applications under the statutory scheme are progressed as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of households on social housing waiting lists in November 2025 that had entered the State within the previous ten years; and if he will provide a breakdown by immigration category.
reply:
My Department does not collect data on households qualified for social housing support by date of entry to the State. Accordingly, the information requested is not available.
Details on the number of households qualified for social housing support in each local authority administrative area is provided in the annual statutory Summary of Social Housing Assessments (SSHA).
The most recently published summary for all counties, conducted in November 2025, is available on my Department's website, along with all summaries since 2011 at www.gov.ie/en/collection/62486-summary-of-social-housing-assessments/.
Details of the citizenship of the main applicant qualified for social housing support for each local authority are included in tables 2.9 and A1.9 in the report.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if persons granted refugee status, subsidiary protection status or permission to remain are subject to the same social housing waiting list rules and prioritisation criteria as Irish citizens; and if he will provide details of the exemptions that apply.
reply:
Social housing support is intended to address a household’s long-term housing need. Therefore, households applying for such support have a long-term permission to reside in the State. It is the responsibility of the local authority to make a decision in each individual case with regard to qualification for social housing support, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended, and associated Housing Circulars.
Persons granted refugee status, subsidiary protection status or permission to remain are eligible to be considered for social housing support, from the date of granting of such status, on the same basis as an Irish citizen. The residency requirements governing access to social housing support arise from the State's constitutional, European Union and international legal obligations. These requirements seek to ensure that social housing supports are available to persons who have a lawful and sufficient right to reside in the State, while complying with Ireland's obligations under domestic law, EU law and international protection frameworks

question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of people who have applied for the enhanced defective concrete blocks grant scheme in Limerick; the estimated total number of applicants in Limerick in the future; the reason the cost of demolition and the removal of asbestos is not allowed under the scheme; and his views on whether it is unfair that an individual may have to pay significantly more than the grant awarded to rebuild their house.
reply:
The total number of applications received by Limerick City and County Council under the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme, as at 31 August 2026, is 100. In February 2026, the County and City Management Association (CCMA) produced a revised estimate of the number of affected dwellings for private and social homes. The estimated number of private dwellings for Limerick City and County Council was 550 affected homes.
I understand that the costs associated with demolition where asbestos removal is required are considered by the particular designated local authority to be eligible costs and may be covered within the overall grant amount approved under the scheme, subject to the terms and conditions of the grant.
It should be noted that homeowners eligible for works under the DCB grant scheme may also apply for energy upgrade grants administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) similar to other homeowners.
Following updated cost reports from the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland (SCSI) and advice from the Expert Group established to consider the matter, increases in the grant scheme remediation rates were provided for over and above the original amounts contained upon commencement of the current grant scheme in 2023. The overall Scheme Cap also increased by 10% from €420,000 to €462,000.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the total amount of Local Property Tax collected nationally in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026; the total amount allocated to local authorities; the total amount redistributed through equalisation; and the total amount of additional revenue generated through local adjustment factors.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 430, 431, 432, 434, 437, 438 and 440 together.
The Revenue Commissioners are responsible for the collection and administration of Local Property Tax (LPT), with the proceeds subsequently transferred to the Local Government Fund (LGF) for distribution to local authorities in accordance with Government policy. LPT allocations are determined annually, in advance of collection, and are based on estimates (from data provided by the Revenue Commissioners) of the LPT yield expected in each local authority area for the relevant liability year.
Apart from the yield, there are three other factors that ultimately determine the annual LPT allocation for an individual local authority’s own use; namely, the local authority’s LPT baseline (minimum funding requirement), the amount of any surplus above an authority’s LPT baseline used to self-fund certain local housing or roads services, and, finally, the local adjustment factor.
From the outset it is important to note that the LPT allocation model was revised in 2023 to provide for 100% of the estimated LPT yield generated within each local authority area to be retained within that area. As a result, all equalisation funding is now provided directly by Central Government and there is no redistribution of LPT receipts between local authorities.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage further to the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, which states that €5.6 billion in capital expenditure is being provided to Programme A – Housing in 2027, the reason the Estimates for Public Services 2027 set out in the same report provide capital of €5,201 million for Programme A, compared with €5,218 million in 2026; and a reconciliation of the two figures.
reply:
The difference between the figures published in the Estimates for Public Services 2027 and those set out in the Vote Chapter arises for technical reasons. Certain capital subheads previously managed within the Department's Planning Division are now under the remit of the Housing Activation Office within the Department's Housing Division, and are included in the NDP Sectoral Plan for Housing. This transfer is not yet reflected in the subhead structure used for the Estimates for Public Services 2027.
The updated subhead structure will be reflected in the Revised Estimates Volume (REV) to be published later this year. Under the revised structure, Programme A capital will amount to €5.6 billion and Programme D capital will reduce to €45 million (both net of apportioned administrative costs), as indicated in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report. This is a presentational change only and does not affect the overall level of funding provided.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the reason the number of housing assistance payment and rental accommodation scheme tenancies provided for falls from some 61,000 in the Budget 2026 Expenditure Report to approximately 56,000 in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, notwithstanding provision for over 8,000 new tenancies in each year.
reply:
The figures in the Budget Expenditure Reports reflect estimates of the number of Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) and Rental Accommodation Scheme (RAS) tenancies requiring continued support in the relevant year.
The lower combined estimate for 2027 reflects the net reduction in active HAP tenancies during 2026, whilst active RAS tenancies have increased slightly. It should be noted that both schemes are demand led.
My Department is satisfied that funding provided for 2027 is sufficient to support the number of existing and new tenancies under both schemes. Demand and expenditure will continue to be monitored throughout the year.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the status of the strategic review of the approved housing body sector, the analysis of cost rental schemes including the cost rental equity loan scheme, and the financial analysis of the capital advance lease facility funding model, each of which the Budget 2026 Expenditure Report stated was due for completion in 2026; whether each has been completed; and when each will be published.
reply:

The Report represents the most comprehensive examination ever undertaken by the State of the AHB sector and sets out an ambitious transformative vision for the sector's evolution over the decade ahead, underpinned by a detailed roadmap of eight interlinked and mutually reinforcing policy development reforms.
The report of the AHBSF is available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/publications/report-of-the-approved-housing-body-ahb-strategic-forum/

I propose to take Questions Nos. 430, 431, 432, 434, 437, 438 and 440 together.
The Revenue Commissioners are responsible for the collection and administration of Local Property Tax (LPT), with the proceeds subsequently transferred to the Local Government Fund (LGF) for distribution to local authorities in accordance with Government policy. LPT allocations are determined annually, in advance of collection, and are based on estimates (from data provided by the Revenue Commissioners) of the LPT yield expected in each local authority area for the relevant liability year.
Apart from the yield, there are three other factors that ultimately determine the annual LPT allocation for an individual local authority’s own use; namely, the local authority’s LPT baseline (minimum funding requirement), the amount of any surplus above an authority’s LPT baseline used to self-fund certain local housing or roads services, and, finally, the local adjustment factor.
From the outset it is important to note that the LPT allocation model was revised in 2023 to provide for 100% of the estimated LPT yield generated within each local authority area to be retained within that area. As a result, all equalisation funding is now provided directly by Central Government and there is no redistribution of LPT receipts between local authorities.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 69365/26, (details supplied) if he is aware of concerns that data centres are putting the delivery of housing at risk; the measures he is taking to ensure that he delivers housing targets in light of these concerns.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 43 together.
Section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 (as amended) sets out the responsibilities of the CRU with regard to electricity security of supply, which includes ensuring that supply and demand growth remain in balance. CRU have a dedicated email for queries via oireachtas@cru.ie.
EirGrid complement this role in their function as Transmission System Operator (TSO) through developing, managing and operating the transmission grid in Ireland. They balance supply and demand on an on-going basis, while also planning for Ireland’s long-term electricity needs. As part of its role in planning the electricity system, EirGrid publishes an annual All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment (AIRAA) which provides a forecast for supply and demand on the all-island electricity grid over the next ten years. Ireland’s electricity security of supply is improving year on year. Overall, the AIRAA 2026-35 shows marked progress on the outlook for security of supply over the last five years.
The Government continues to work with electricity system operators to assess the various expected future demands on the system including from economic and population growth, housing, electric vehicle and heat pump targets in addition to data centre growth as part of their network development plans to ensure medium and long term future demands on our electricity system continue to be supported.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the national guidance issued to local authorities regarding the retention, termination and reallocation of social housing where the tenant is imprisoned.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 426 and 427 together.
The management and administration of local authority housing tenancies is, in the first instance, a matter for each local authority in the exercise of its statutory functions under the Housing Acts 1966 - 2026.
My Department does not issue specific guidance or policy to housing authorities dealing with tenancy arrangements or the termination of tenancies solely on the basis that a tenant has received a custodial sentence. Any decision regarding the continuation, management or termination of a tenancy is a matter for the local authority concerned, having regard to the relevant legislative provisions, the terms and conditions of the tenancy agreement, the circumstances of the individual case, and the local authority's own policies and procedures.
Local authorities act in accordance with the provisions of the Housing Acts 1966 - 2026, fair procedures and their broader responsibilities in relation to tenancy and estate management. Accordingly, responsibility for decisions affecting individual tenancies rests with the relevant local authority.

reply:
The Local Authority Home Loan, is a Government-backed first-time buyer mortgage for creditworthy applicants who cannot get sufficient funding from commercial lenders to purchase or build a home. The loan has been available nationwide from local authorities since 4 January 2022. The loan is available to first time buyers or persons who become eligible to be treated as first time buyers under the Fresh Start principle.
The Fresh Start principle means that the persons who have previously owned a property but have been divested of their interest in their former property as a result of a relationship termination or insolvency are eligible to be treated as first time buyers for the purpose of these schemes. The following categories of persons who have previously owned a property are eligible to apply for these schemes:

• Applicant(s) that previously purchased or built a residential dwelling/dwellings, but has been divested of this through insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings, are eligible to apply. question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether his Department is considering applying a rent pressure zone to older persons' accommodation.
reply:
The Residential Tenancies Acts 2004 to 2026 (RTA) regulate the landlord-tenant relationship in the residential rental sector and set out the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants.
On 1 March 2026, the Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into operation. The Act provides for a national rent control and significantly strengthens security of tenure for tenants, while also encouraging more private investment in the rental market. The new national rent control limits rent increases to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), up to a maximum of 2%. For new build apartments and student-specific accommodation, however, rent increases are capped at the level of inflation (CPI) only.
In order to stimulate investment and keep existing landlords in the market, the resetting of rents to market value is now allowed, as part of the reform of rent controls for new tenancies created on or after 1 March 2026, with certain exceptions. The linking of rent control to a property, rather than a tenancy, under the previous Rent Pressure Zone (RPZ) system of rent control made investment in rental accommodation less attractive in Ireland. By allowing rent resetting for new tenancies from 1 March 2026, existing and new landlords, who are vital for the sector, can ensure that their investment remains viable.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of cost rental homes in Balbriggan, Skerries, Rush and Lusk which have received funding approval, approval in principle or other approval from his Department; the number of homes involved in each project; and the current stage of each project.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 421 and 422 together.
The Government's housing action plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities, reinforces and expands the range of existing measures to tackle the issues of supply and affordability, under a new Starter Homes Programme. This programme will deliver an average of 15,000 starter home supports annually, to 2030, underpinned by an unprecedented level of investment by Government.
This expanded delivery, under the new housing plan, will build upon the significant progress already made under the previous plan Housing for All, published in 2021, with over 24,000 affordable housing supports having been delivered from 2021 to end Q1 2026.
Key priorities under the programme include scaling up the delivery of starter homes for purchase, particularly for fist time buyers and fresh start applicants, through the local authorities and the Land Development Agency.

To date, 16 schemes have received funding approval under the AHF to support the delivery of over 1,350 Starter Homes for purchase and rent in Fingal. Local authority Starter Home projects which have received AHF support include Aster Park in Rush, Priory Fields in Skerries, Balleally Rise in Lusk and Hampton Garde

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the efforts being made to decrease waiting times for those waiting for the warmer home scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 31 and 42 together.
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.
