question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether a school may satisfy a parent's exercise of the right under section 30(2)(e) of the Education Act 1998 by requiring a child to remain physically present in the classroom while the instruction to which the parent has objected is delivered; if not, the national guidance that has been issued to schools regarding the physical removal or alternative supervision of a child during such instruction.
reply:
Under the provisions of the Education Act 1998, where schools provide religious instruction, parents or in the case of a student who has reached the age of 18 years, the student, can request that the student attend the school without attending religious instruction in the school. It is expected that this right will be upheld by schools on foot of a parental request.
The manner in which a school ensures that this right is upheld is a matter for the school concerned. Each school must determine the particular arrangements which are most appropriate in its individual circumstances having regard to local issues such as available space, supervision requirements and how the school concerned organises classes etc.
Guidance for good practice is available to schools in the follow-up paper to the Report of the Forum on Patronage and Pluralism in the Primary Sector which was published in 2014. The paper provides an overview of different types of arrangements that schools can put in place to facilitate parents who do not wish for their children to attend religious instruction. The paper encourages school authorities to consider their policies and practices and to review whether they are taking the steps necessary to welcome all pupils and make them feel included.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of special needs assistants in post at the end of 2025 and at the latest date in 2026; and the way that the budget 2027 provision of 2,339 additional SNAs, bringing the total to 28,000, reconciles with the budget 2026 figure of almost 24,900.
reply:
Budget 2026 provided an additional 1,717 SNA posts bringing the total to 24, 900 SNAs available to our schools to support the care needs of their pupils. During 2026, as the Deputy may recall, funding was provided for additional SNA posts bringing the total to 25,890.
I am delighted to have secured an additional 2,339 special needs assistants in Budget 2027 to support children across mainstream and specialist settings.
This will bring the total SNA allocations to over 28,000 to support pupils with care needs in our schools.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the actions he has taken pursuant to his obligations under section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 to satisfy himself that data centre will not pose a risk to the continuity, security and quality of supplies of electricity.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 43 together.
Section 9 of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 (as amended) sets out the responsibilities of the CRU with regard to electricity security of supply, which includes ensuring that supply and demand growth remain in balance. CRU have a dedicated email for queries via oireachtas@cru.ie.
EirGrid complement this role in their function as Transmission System Operator (TSO) through developing, managing and operating the transmission grid in Ireland. They balance supply and demand on an on-going basis, while also planning for Ireland’s long-term electricity needs. As part of its role in planning the electricity system, EirGrid publishes an annual All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment (AIRAA) which provides a forecast for supply and demand on the all-island electricity grid over the next ten years. Ireland’s electricity security of supply is improving year on year. Overall, the AIRAA 2026-35 shows marked progress on the outlook for security of supply over the last five years.
The Government continues to work with electricity system operators to assess the various expected future demands on the system including from economic and population growth, housing, electric vehicle and heat pump targets in addition to data centre growth as part of their network development plans to ensure medium and long term future demands on our electricity system continue to be supported.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she considers a book (details supplied) for third year junior cycle SPHE, to be appropriate and age-appropriate for students; and if her Department or the NCCA has reviewed its content for suitability for use in schools.
reply:
The Curriculum specification and prescribed material for any subject are determined by the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) – https://ncca.ie/en/.
To support teachers in teaching the curriculum, NCCA publishes online toolkits. The SPHE Toolkits have been developed to assist teachers in teaching Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE). The resources presented on the toolkit aim to provide a range of relevant materials to support teaching and learning in SPHE. The toolkit states that each resource should be considered with respect to the needs and interests of children, their parents, the wider school community, and a school’s SPHE and RSE policies. The resources listed are not intended as exhaustive or prescriptive as each school will decide what resources are best suited to their needs and their context.
Apart from a small number of prescribed texts at post-primary level, determined by the NCCA, the decisions on which textbooks, programmes and resources, if any, to use in primary and post-primary schools are taken at school level. Any concerns regarding material published in textbooks should be raised with the publisher themselves.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth what constitutes “regularly” for the purposes of her Department's requirement that exclusive school uniform supply arrangements should be tendered regularly under Circular 0032/2017; the way in which her Department verifies that schools comply with this provision; and the number of schools that have been found not to comply since the circular was issued.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 326 and 327 together.
Under the Education Act 1998, all recognised schools are managed by school Boards of Management. Individual school authorities are responsible for the drawing up of a school policy in relation to the wearing of uniforms. My department does not engage in procurement on behalf of schools, nor does it supervise school procurement activities. Responsibility for school uniform procurement rests with individual schools and their Boards of Management. Schools are advised to consult with parents and students when drafting a policy on uniforms.
Circular 0032/2017 sets out best practice guidelines and schools should create their uniform policies, and all policies, in consultation with their whole school community. As the Deputy is aware, Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms.
The provision and use of digital devices in post-primary schools is a matter for the board of management, having regard to their unique circumstances, educational programmes and the needs of their students. Schools are best placed to determine how technology can support teaching and learning in their settings, including decisions relating to device usage.

question: Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an updated timeframe on when the works on a new school build (details supplied) will recommence.
reply:
The new build for Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire is a large scale capital project for the construction of a sixteen classroom primary school in Dublin 1.
The building project to complete the new build for Gaelscoil Coláiste Mhuire, Dominick Street is at Stage 3 of the Architectural Planning Process – Tender Action and Award.
The Department can confirm that following a confidential conciliation process concerning all matters in dispute between the Department and the original contractor, the conciliator issued a formal recommendation for the resolution of those disputes, and that recommendation was accepted by both parties.

question: Deputy Niall Collins asked the Minister for Education and Youth the status of an application (details supplied).
reply:
Under the Assistive Technology Scheme, as set out in my Department’s Circular 0010/2013, funding is provided to schools towards the cost of computers and specialist equipment which are required for educational purposes.
All equipment provided under this scheme supports children with more complex disabilities who, in order to access the school curriculum, require essential specialist equipment. It must be clear that the existing IT equipment in the school is insufficient to meet the child's needs. Where necessary, schools may also purchase new or additional equipment or software for students from normal school resources or funds.
In the case referred to by the Deputy, department officials have confirmed that a decision letter in relation to the Assistive Technology application was issued to the school on the 8th of October 2026.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Education and Youth if there are funding schemes, grants or other avenues of support available for a school (details supplied) in County Laois.
reply:
Supporting special educational needs (SEN) provision in schools is a priority for my department. The furniture and equipment needs of children with special educational needs is highly sensitive and individualised and as a result applications for funding are generally dealt with on a case-by-case basis as opposed to a general level of grant funding.
A school that has an existing or approved SEN classroom can make an application for a sensory room start up grant funding to my department. In order to be considered eligible for this grant the school must meet the following criteria:
The school must have an existing SEN classroom or be in the process of opening one;
The designated sensory room must be separate from the SEN classroom or any other room with its own entry/exit door and accessible from the main corridor, and should not require any major refurbishment. Part of classrooms, sensory spaces, and sensory pods do not qualify for the grant.
It should be noted the school in question received a grant of €7,000 in March 2022 for the provision of a Sensory room. Only one sensory room grant is funded by my department per school.

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the arrangements in place for Leaving Certificate students who, due to disability, medical needs or school avoidance, cannot regularly attend school to complete required coursework or additional assessment components; whether alternative arrangements are available to allow these students to complete the assessments; and the way in which she will ensure they are not prevented from taking any specific subject as a result.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 320 and 376 together.
The State Examinations Commission (SEC) has statutory responsibility for administering the State examinations and for setting authentication requirements for any coursework components in line with overall examinations and assessment policy.
Prior to the implementation of revised subject specifications and assessment arrangements under the Senior Cycle Redevelopment (SCR) programme, 28 existing Leaving Certificate subjects already included assessment components beyond written examinations, including oral examinations, practical performance tests, and coursework. This variety of formats is being maintained as the SCR programme is implemented.

To protect examination integrity and ensure inter-candidate equity, the SEC advises that it requires all coursework to be authenticated. question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department has assessed the likely impact of the proposed EU own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment, including its potential effect on collection, reuse, repair and recycling, and its interaction with the forthcoming revision of the EU Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment framework.
reply:
Negotiations on the proposed EU own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) are being led by the Department of Finance as part of the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) package. The proposal has both environment and fiscal implications.
The EU framework governing the collection and environmentally sound management of WEEE is also under review, with a legislative proposal expected to be published later this year as part of the EU Circular Economy Act.
I understand that this review will seek to address, inter alia, the need to further incentivise and improve WEEE collection, while also refining the methodology used to calculate collection rates. It is particularly important that the methodology reflects developments such as longer product lifespans and policies promoting reuse and repair. Any assessment of the eventual impact of the proposed own resource, from an environment and circular economy perspective, will need to take account of these developments.
The expected focus on the calculation rate methodology will likely prove significant in underpinning the metric on which the own resource is based. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the mechanisms in place to ensure that children with dyslexia and other reading challenges are identified at as early an age as possible.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 317, 318 and 319 together.
The Department of Education and Youth has invested considerably in ensuring that all recognised mainstream schools have been allocated additional special education teaching resources to support children with special educational needs, including students with literacy difficulties.
There are 15,200 special education teachers allocated to primary and post-primary schools to enable them to support children with special educational needs, including those with literacy difficulties.
It is important to note that the majority of students with literacy difficulties currently receive additional teaching support from a special education teacher in a mainstream class.
This is provided on the basis of the individual student’s learning needs, identified in schools, as opposed to being based on a requirement for a child to have a diagnosis, or an assessment, of a particular disability.
Furthermore, there are four schools dedicated to supporting students with specific learning disability (SLD). There are also fourteen SLD classes in eleven mainstream primary schools located across the country, in counties Dublin, Clare, Louth, Galway, Kerry and Wexford.
However, I recognise that more needs to be done. I am happy to advise that my officials in conjunction with the NCSE are currently at an advanced stage in developing a pilot programme to test best practice and support policy formulation going forward.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the reason Bus Éireann reserves payments and then in many cases to refuse access to school bus transport and issue a refund (details supplied); her views on after offering/providing a place/service; and if this practice has been assessed and deemed financially sound.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth. The application and payment process is managed by Bus Éireann via their online family portal.
Bus Éireann are preparing a response on the matter for the Deputy and will respond directly in this regard.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm an appeal regarding teacher allocation has been received from a school (details supplied); if the points outlined in the appeal will be comprehensively considered, taking into account the school's previous enrollment; and the unique experience of the school.
reply:
The key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level is the staffing schedule for the relevant school year and pupil enrolments on the previous 30 September.
The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school referred to by the Deputy has been allocated a post on this basis.
The staffing process also contains an appeals mechanism for schools to submit a staffing appeal to an independent Primary Staffing Appeals Board. One of the appeals criteria is aimed at schools that receive a projected enrolment post but do not meet the required enrolment on 30 September. Such schools may submit an appeal to the October meeting of the Primary Staffing Appeals Board. Information and application forms are available in Circular 0025/2026.

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Education and Youth the processes and supports in place to protect a child's right to education in the event that a school does not have enough SNAs to open at regular hours.
reply:
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is the statutory body responsible for the provision of special education and allocating supports for students with special educational needs.
Special needs assistants (SNA)s play a central role in the successful inclusion of students with additional and significant care needs in schools. They help ensure that these students can access an education to enable them to achieve their best outcomes and reach their full potential.
SNA posts are allocated to schools as a school-based resource. Principals/board of managements deploy SNAs within schools to meet the care support requirements of the students enrolled whom SNA support has been allocated.?This provides schools flexibility in how the SNA support is utilised.?
If a school has a concern with either their SNA allocation for the 2026/27 school year or the outcome of a SNA review/appeal, they should discuss the matter with their NCSE Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO).
My department and the NCSE are committed to ensuring that sufficient special education placements remain available for students with special educational needs and will continue to review and monitor the situation as to where new specialist provision is required.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that families attending a school (details supplied) are currently privately funding school transport at significant cost due to the absence of a Bus Éireann school transport service; if her Department has assessed the transport needs of pupils attending the school; whether consideration will be given to establishing a dedicated school transport route or extending an existing route to serve the school.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The purpose of my Department's School Transport Scheme is, having regard to available resources, to support the transport to and from school of children who reside remote from their nearest school.
Under the terms of the School Transport Schemes, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kms from and are attending their nearest national school. At post primary level, they are eligible where they reside not less than 4.8 kms from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre. Distance is determined by the Department/Bus Éireann and rules have regard to ethos and language.
Children who are not eligible but who apply for school transport are considered for spare seats that may exist after eligible children have been facilitated; such seats are referred to as concessionary seats.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment or retention of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
Bus Éireann has advised that 13 applications have been received from this school for the 26/27 school year, 4 of which are deemed eligible and 9 are not eligible.
At present, this does not warrant the establishment of a new service from the

question: Deputy Daniel Ennis asked the Minister for Education and Youth to confirm what supports are in place to assist special schools that are understaffed due to leave.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
DEY Circular 0054/2019 provides that each employer shall develop and maintain a policy on teacher/special needs assistant (SNA) absences, including non-statutory schemes e.g. Job Sharing, Career Breaks, Unpaid Leave, specific to the needs of the school authority. In drawing up this policy, the welfare and educational needs of the pupils must take precedence over all other considerations and must be in accordance with the rules of the relevant circulars. This policy shall have due regard to the capacity of the school to meet its obligations to its pupils and may therefore apply a limit to the number of teaching and SNA staff that may avail of non-statutory leave schemes at any one time. Employers must consider applications in the context of other statutory and non-statutory leave and must also take into account the availability of an appropriately qualified replacement teacher or SNA.
My department actively engages with the representative bodies for special schools, in order to help to address some of these additional challenges these schools face over their mainstream counterparts.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Education and Youth the current status of the Education (Medical Emergencies in Schools) Bill 2026, introduced by Deputy Eoghan Kenny, including whether the Government intends to support the progression of the Bill through the Houses of the Oireachtas and the anticipated timeframe for its consideration at Committee Stage.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 307, 308, 309 and 310 together.
The Board of Management of each school is responsible for the care and safety of all pupils.
Where the school is aware of potential difficulties that may arise as a consequence of a medical condition suffered by one or more pupils, it may be possible for the management authorities, working in conjunction with parents, teachers and children to put preventative measures in place to lessen the possibility of any difficulties arising or to ensure that, if a pupil suffers from an illness requiring, for example, the administration of medication, that appropriate treatment is available.
The administration of medicines in primary schools is the subject of an agreement between the Irish National Teachers Organisation and the organisation representing school management at primary level.
While this agreement specifies that no teacher can be required to administer medicine or drugs to pupils, it also sets out procedures that must be followed where a teacher or teachers agree to do so. The position is that either the parents of the child should make themselves available to administer medication as required, or where they wish the staff in the school to administer it, they should indemnify the school.
My Department cannot direct any member of the Board of Management or the teaching staff of the school to administer medical treatment to pupils, action and procedures which are normally carried out by medical professionals such

question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to report on the criteria used by the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes; and if this includes whether the occupant is suffering from a disability or long-term illness.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 31 and 42 together.
The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the review of the formal recognition of QQI level 6 qualification for special needs assistants relative to their pay scale and conditions.
reply:
As you are aware my department published the first ever SNA Workforce Development Plan (the Plan), in June of this year. Built around five strategic pillars, the Plan recognises the vital contribution SNAs make to supporting children and young people with special educational needs and enabling their full participation in school life. It sets out a clear framework to strengthen and support SNAs through enhanced professional development, greater role clarity, workforce sustainability measures and stronger collaboration across school communities.
The Plan was developed following extensive engagement and consultation with stakeholders across the education sector and sets out high level objectives and policy developments under five key pillars including in the area of learning and development for SNAs.
Currently, the minimum educational requirement for appointment to the post of SNA is set out in Circular 0051/2019 ‘Recruitment and Appointment Procedures for Special Needs Assistants (SNAs). The current requirement is a level 3 qualification on the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) or a minimum of three grade Ds in the Junior Certificate or equivalent.
In the research phase of the Plan my department conducted the first national survey of special needs assistants (SNAs). The purpose of the survey which was accessed by more than 13,000 SNAs was to gather information about SNAs and their work to inform the Plan. Findings from the survey on the highest level of education attai

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth to provide an update on the engagement between her Department and trade unions representing school secretaries and caretakers.
reply:
School secretaries and caretakers are at the heart of the school and are the key interface between students, parents, school leaders, and other staff. Without them, our schools would be unsustainable. In supporting these vital school staff members, we also support the school community as a whole.
Following intensive and constructive engagement between the Department of Education and Youth and Fórsa trade union at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on the 1st of September 2026, a set of proposals aimed at resolving three elements of the dispute was issued by the WRC. Both parties recommended the WRC’s proposal for acceptance.
The WRC-recommended proposal includes enhanced terms and conditions for secretaries and caretakers including a pay framework for caretakers, bereavement leave and sick leave/acute illness leave for both secretaries and caretakers.
The Department notes the positive outcome of the secretaries’ and caretakers’ vote on the WRC proposal and is committed to working constructively with Fórsa trade union to implement the agreed proposals on a phased basis, as set out in the WRC proposal.
With regards to the claim for a comparable pension entitlement, following hearings in the Labour Court a recommendation was issued by the Court to the parties on 15 July 2026. The Department notes the outcome of the Fórsa ballot on this matter, and it is closely considering the recommendation of the Court and engaging with colleagues in Government as appropriate.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Education and Youth If her Department will review the current conditions pertaining to illness leave for school secretaries employed through her Department.
reply:
My Department is providing a payroll service for school secretaries which are covered under the terms of Department Circular 36/2022. The provision of a payroll service is part of a package agreed with FÓRSA, the trade union representing school secretaries, following a series of engagements at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). The agreement includes revised terms and conditions related to salary and leave entitlements.
The revised leave arrangements which have been included in the agreement are set with reference to statutory leave entitlements.
My Department has recently engaged with Fórsa under the auspices of the WRC in relation to the introduction of an acute illness provision for school secretaries covered under the terms of Department Circular 36/2022 and that process is ongoing.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to detail the level of oversight her Department has over patron bodies; and the actions her Department can take if a school is not compliant with the Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300 and 303 together.
The Education Act, 1998 sets out the key roles and functions that are discharged by patrons and boards of management in the running of schools. Each primary school has a patron which is charged with carrying out the functions and exercising the powers conferred upon a patron under the Act. It is the duty of the patron, for the purposes of ensuring that a recognised school is managed in a spirt of partnership to appoint a board of management. The composition of the board is agreed nationally between patrons of schools, national associations of parents, recognised school management organisations, recognised trade unions and staff associations representing teachers, and the Minister.
The agreed procedures for the appointment of boards of management of primary schools and the rules under which these boards operate are set out in the department’s publication ‘Governance Manual for Primary Schools 2023-2027’. The term of office of the current boards of the circa 3,300 primary schools will expire on 30 November 2027 with new boards being appointed from the 1 December 2027. It is intended that this publication will be reviewed and updated as appropriate by my department in advance of that date in consultation with the relevant education partners at primary level including the National Parents Council. The National Parents Council is the representative organisation for parents of children attending primary school.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment further to Parliamentary Question No. 69365/26, given that the "Responsibility for policy relating to data centres is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment"; if he is aware of this decision by the regulator to cap data centre power demand (details supplied); the way in which this will impact the Large Energy User Action Plan; the measures he is taking to ensure that his plans for data centre expansion do not place our energy grid at further risk of blackout.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 24 and 30 together.
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) published their decision on Grid Code Modification MPID 345 and the associated Compliance and Derogation Framework on 22 September 2026. The Decision is to enhance system stability and reliability, safeguarding security of supply. The CRU is an independent regulator and accountable to a Committee of the Oireachtas. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the reason "high degree of caution" travel advice was issued in relation to Brazil on 2 October 2026; if this was influenced by the decision of the US administration to suspend consular services in Brazil; and if she is concerned that the decision by the US was an attempt to influence the election campaign underway.
reply:
As I’m sure the Deputy is aware, my Department provides travel advice to assist our citizens in respect of more than 200 countries and territories worldwide. This advice provides an objective assessment of the risks our citizens could face while travelling, working, or living overseas, with a view to helping them to make informed decisions linked to their personal security.
The advice also includes a security rating, which represents my Department’s estimation of the relative safety and security of a country at a specific point in time, and is a useful tool in highlighting to a citizen how safe or unsafe a country or territory is to visit.
There are four levels of security status. Currently Brazil is assessed to be at level two, where citizens are advised to exercise a ‘High Degree of Caution’. Countries or territories in this category might have additional risks such as serious crime and/or terrorism, specific targeting of foreigners, disease or extreme weather events. Citizens travelling to this country can expect more or higher risks than they would find in Ireland.
This current security status for Brazil has been in place since November 2021. Travel advice for Brazil is formulated based on consultation with our Embassy in Brasilia, Consulate General in São Paulo, relevant local authorities, and other partners as appropriate.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on a school capital project (details supplied).
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter my department's pipeline of projects under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme. The project will provide nine mainstream classrooms (seven prefab replacements), five Special Education Tuition (SET) rooms, one Graphics room, one Music room, one Textiles room, and a two class Special Education Needs (SEN) base. The project is devolved to Catholic Education - An Irish Schools Trust (CEIST) to deliver.
The Stage 2a developed design report has been submitted to my Department and is currently under review. All school building projects, including this one, will undergo the necessary due diligence as outlined in the Public Infrastructure Guidelines. Managing timing, scope, and cost is crucial to ensuring that the overall school building programme remains with the funding parameters.
My department will continue to engage directly with CEIST, as appropriate, throughout this review if further information is required.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will consider the timing and percentage of capitation grants issued to schools to best to meet the need of the cost of schools when re-opening in September.
reply:
The Government is committed to increasing funding to support schools and the Programme for Government commits to increasing capitation funding to schools of all types to ensure that schools can meet the elevated day-to-day running costs.
This commitment builds on the progress made in recent years. The Department of Education and Youth has secured €53 million in Budget 2027 towards increased capitation grant funding for primary, post-primary and special schools to provide additional financial support towards their running costs. This will see an increase in the mainstream capitation grant rates paid to schools of €68 per pupil for primary schools from €274 to €342 and of €40 per student for post-primary schools from €406 to €446. These increases will take effect from September 2027 and this additional funding will benefit schools around the country in managing their day-to-day running costs.
The increases announced in Budget 2027 are in addition to the increases as part of Budget 2026. The last four budgets have resulted in an increase in the level of mainstream capitation grant rates of almost 87% (€159) paid to primary schools and 41% (€130) paid to post-primary schools.
The department is committed to providing funding to recognised primary and post-primary schools in the Free Education Scheme by way of per capita grants. question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth the position regarding the 72 hours provisions listed in Circular 0071/2011; and the engagement she has had on this matter with trade unions representing special needs assistants.
reply:
As part of the agreement between my department, the relevant unions and school management boards on a standard employment contract for SNA's in 2005, all SNAs are required to be available for a number of days at the start and finish of each school term, not exceeding 12 days in total.
Under the Croke Park Agreement it was agreed to introduce greater flexibility to the use of these 12 days. Accordingly, DEY Circular 71/2011 was issued on 15 December 2011 which outlined that these 12 days now equate to 72 hours (pro-rata for part-time SNAs) to be used by schools as an additional bank of hours to be utilised and delivered outside of normal school opening hours and/or the normal school year.
This time outside of classroom hours (up to a maximum of 72 hours per school year) is used to complete training and upskilling as well as partaking in planning, reviewing and collaboration with colleagues. It allows SNAs to complete these important tasks without taking away from the time spent supporting students during the school day.
As you are aware my department published the first ever SNA Workforce Development Plan (the Plan), in June of this year. The Plan recognises the vital contribution SNAs make to supporting children and young people with special educational needs in our schools.

reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
The department has long held the position that children should be educated in the most inclusive environment possible. For the vast majority of children, this means being educated alongside their peers in mainstream schools and classes. To support those who attend mainstream classes, but who may have some additional needs, the department has allocated approximately 15,000 special education teachers to schools to assist them in meeting those needs. There are, however, some children whose needs are at a level of complexity that they cannot have those needs met in a mainstream environment.
Current Department of Education policy is based on a continuum of provision for children and young people with special educational needs, ranging from fulltime placement in mainstream settings to specialist provision, including special schools and classes.
Since 2017, and the introduction of a needs-based approach the Department allocates additional teaching supports directly to schools through the special education teaching (SET) model. This aims to ensure that those with the highest level of need have access to the greatest level of support in a timely and flexible manner, without the requirement for a diagnosis of disability.

reply:
While there is not a standalone module on ‘disability awareness’, disability, inclusion, equality and respect for diversity are embedded across both the primary and post-primary curriculum.
Primary
The redeveloped Primary Curriculum places a strong emphasis on inclusion and ensuring that every child experiences a sense of belonging and participation in school life. The new Wellbeing specification (including SPHE) includes learning about:
• valuing and respecting all people
• developing empathy and positive relationships
• understanding diversity and inclusion
• promoting a sense of belonging for everyone in the school community.
Post-primary
At junior and senior cycle, subjects which foster students' awareness and promote understanding and empathy towards people experiencing various forms of discrimination include CSPE, SPHE, Religious Education, History and Politics and Society. Students learn about:
• equality and human rights
• diversity and inclusion
• respect for all members of society
• challenging prejudice, discrimination and exclusion

question: Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which disability inclusion and awareness is taught to trainee teachers; the number of hours per year of their course that is dedicated to disability training.
reply:
Under Section 38 of the Teaching Council Act, all initial teacher education programmes must be accredited by the Teaching Council for registration purposes. The Council reviewed its policy on standards for programmes of initial teacher education (ITE) and published updated standards in Céim Standards for Initial Teacher Education in October 2020.
The Céim standards require programmes to include foundation studies, professional studies and school placement and are underpinned by seven core elements that underpin all aspects of programme design. Inclusive Education is one of the seven core elements which underpin all aspects of programme design and delivery in accredited ITE programmes.
Céim describes inclusive education as one that ‘includes the fostering of appropriate learning environments, including digital ones, that support the development of student teachers’ ability to provide for the learning needs of all pupils by utilising, for example, a universal design for learning framework’.
The term inclusive education is any aspect of teachers’ learning aimed at:
• Improving their capacity to address and respond to the diversity of learners’ needs,
• Removing barriers to education through the accommodation and provision of appropriate structures and arrangements; and
• Enabling each learner to achieve the maximum benefit from his/her attendance at school.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware that up to 70 children in the Ballinasloe area are currently without school transport following the withdrawal of private operators from the system; the action her Department will take to ensure all affected children have access to school transport.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
Under the current terms of the mainstream scheme, children are eligible for transport at primary level where they reside not less than 3.2 kilometres from and are attending their nearest national school, and at post primary level where they reside not less than 4.8 kilometres from and are attending their nearest post primary school/education centre as determined by the department/Bus Éireann, having regard to ethos and language.
A minimum number of 10 eligible children residing in a distinct locality, as determined by Bus Éireann, are required before consideration may be given to the establishment of school transport services, provided this can be done within reasonable cost limits.
The scheme is a demand led scheme based on the number of eligible children who apply. It is operated using a mix of Bus Éireann owned vehicles and directly recruited drivers, and private contractors who recruit their own drivers to operate on the scheme. Private operators who are not contracted under the scheme are outside the remit of the Department.
Bus Éireann has advised that there are no operational issues with services operating as part of the school transport scheme in the area referred to by the Deputy. 348 mainstream and 105 SEN pupils have been allocated on school transport services into schools in the area in question for the 2026/27 school year.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the operation of section 32 of the Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022, including the number of local authorities who have availed of its provision and put CCTV into operation.
reply:
Since 15 February 2024, when the relevant provisions of the Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022 were commenced, all local authorities have been able to put in place the necessary procedures to facilitate the GDPR-compliant use of CCTV and other mobile recording technologies to combat littering and illegal dumping.
The use of these technologies is an operational matter for each local authority, which must determine the most appropriate enforcement response based on local circumstances and priorities. Accordingly, my Department does not maintain a central record of the number of local authorities that have introduced CCTV schemes under these provisions.
I am aware, however, that Carlow County Council recently secured the first conviction for illegal dumping arising from the GDPR-compliant use of CCTV under the new legislative framework. This represents a significant milestone and demonstrates the effectiveness of these powers in supporting environmental enforcement. Funding for these cameras was secured through the Department’s Anti-Dumping Initiative which has made available some €26 million to local authorities, community groups and other stakeholders since its establishment in 2017.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if Government employment or job-creation projections and targets for 2026 to 2030 have been disaggregated by region; to provide by region and year; and to provide the equivalent regional projections or targets underpinning the national planning framework for comparison, in tabular form.
reply:

Separately, my Department has undertaken a statistical analysis to examine how projected national employment growth is likely to be distributed regionally. The analysis is anchored to the central scenario in the Department of Finance’s Future Forty framework and extends to 2040. It provides a baseline projection of how regional employment might develop if historical relationships between national and regional employment continue. However, these projections are not Government employment or job-creation targets.
The analysis indicates that employment would grow across all regions, with some concentration in Dublin and the wider eastern region, reflecting the existing scale of these labour markets as well as their projected growth rates. At the same time, most regions exhibit broadly similar growth rates over the projection horizon, and are projected to grow at rates broadly in line with the national average. Differences in the number of additional people employed largely reflect the existing distribution of employment across the regions.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether he is considering measures to ban a product associated with ineradicable and significant occupational safety risks (details supplied) with regard to his responsibility for workplace safety legislation and in line with a proposal under consideration in California.
reply:
The safety, health and welfare of workers is a priority for my department. There are existing legal obligations under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and associated regulations requiring employers to identify, assess and control risks arising from exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust.
In particular, work involving exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust generated by a work process is classified as carcinogenic under the Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances (CMRS) Regulations. These Regulations require employers to reduce the use of carcinogenic substances in the workplace, in particular by replacing them, insofar as is technically possible, with a substance, mixture or process which, under its conditions of use, is not dangerous or is less dangerous to employees’ health or safety. Employers are also required to ensure that the level of exposure of employees is reduced to a level as low as technically possible, representing a high duty of care.
The existing framework therefore places significant obligations on employers to prevent or minimise exposure to respirable crystalline silica dust. These include conducting risk assessments, implementing appropriate engineering controls and safe systems of work, using dust suppression techniques such as wet cutting, providing suitable respiratory protective equipment and undertaking health surveillance where appropriate.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment for an update on matters raised in correspondence (details supplied).
reply:
The Companies Registration Office (CRO) has advised that it has no statutory power under the Registration of Business Names Act 1963 to remove a person from the register of business names, nor does it have a power to remove or suppress a residential address that has been properly registered under that Act.
Unlike the Companies Act 2014, which contains provisions allowing for the non-disclosure of a company officer's residential address in certain exceptional circumstances, no equivalent provision exists in the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.
Accordingly, there is currently no statutory mechanism available to the Registrar to remove, redact or suppress a residential address from the business names register, including in circumstances where personal safety concerns have been raised. Similarly, the fact that a person who has made a registration of a business name, and who subsequently determines that that registration was not required, does not provide a legal basis for the removal of the registration or the associated address from the register.
My Department is currently developing legislation to repeal and replace the Registration of Business Names Act 1963.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on whether the right-to-request model is sufficient in the context where an employee's request to work remotely is refused but the WRC cannot examine whether the refusal itself was reasonable.
reply:
Under Part 3 of the Work Life Balance Act 2023, employees are able to refer a dispute to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) where an employer fails to fulfil their obligations under the Act. The WRC and the Labour Court can direct employers to comply with the requirements of the Act however, neither the WRC nor the Labour Courts are empowered to assess the merits of the employer’s decision, nor are they empowered to overturn a refusal of remote working. The obligation on the employer is to comply with the procedures set out in the Act.
It is not the Government’s role, nor the role of the Workplace Relations Commission, to effectively assess and direct when employees can or cannot work remotely. Providing a right to request strikes the right balance between flexibility and the need for businesses to remain competitive, profitable and viable.
The Department completed a statutory review of the right to request remote working provisions of the Work Life Balance Act 2023 in March 2024. The report is available on the Department’s website and has been laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. The review found that, when used, the legislation is operating effectively in practice with the majority of requests to work remotely being either fully or partially approved. While the number of requests made under the legislation is currently low, when employees do avail of their right, the legislation works well. On this basis, amendments to the primary Act are not proposed at this tim

The Warmer Homes Scheme (WHS) aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax revenues and the European Regional Development Fund.
The scheme targets support to those on the lowest incomes who are living in the least efficient homes so that the resources available can have the greatest impact in addressing energy poverty. Over 8,100 homes were upgraded last year, 109% of the annual target.
Applications to the scheme are assessed on the basis of when they first apply to the SEAI. Homes with the worst Building Energy Ratings also known as BER (E, F or G) are then prioritised for works. No other prioritisation takes place under the scheme.
Under the WHS, a pre-works BER is an obligation mandated for EU funding via the ERDF. The BER rating enables the SEAI to prioritise the worst performing homes and it is also key in determining the increase in energy efficiency as a result of the works upon completion.
Over 8,060 upgrades were completed under the scheme to end September 2026, an increase of 34.5% on the same period last year. At the same time, 11,823 applications have been received to the WHS to end September compared to 7,905 in the same time window last year, an increase of 49.6%.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he is examining whether consumers should have a statutory right to speak with a human customer service representative, rather than being required to deal exclusively with artificial intelligence or automated systems, when engaging with telecommunications, utility and other essential service providers.
reply:
With the exception of financial products or services, there is currently no general provision in Irish consumer protection law requiring traders to provide consumers with access to a human customer service representative or preventing the use of artificial intelligence, chatbots or other automated systems for customer interactions. The way a trader provides customer service is a commercial decision for the trader.
However, under Part 5 of the Consumer Rights Act 2022, there is certain information which traders must provide to consumers before they enter a contract. This includes information which will allow consumers to contact traders and direct complaints, such as the geographical address at which the trader is established, the trader’s telephone number and the trader’s email address. Where applicable, traders must also provide consumers with information as to their complaint handling policy.
Where a consumer is seeking to exercise their rights under consumer protection law, such as seeking a remedy for a non-conformity with a good or service, they must be able to contact the trader in order to do so. Where a trader fails to facilitate consumers in exercising their statutory rights, this may give rise to issues under consumer protection legislation, depending on the circumstances.

reply:

The current guidance was published in November 2023 following enactment of the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 2022.

question: Deputy Eoin Hayes asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the way in which his Department accounts for the difference in the figures in the Expenditure Report released for Budget 2027 between the detailed selected measures totalling just over €1 billion and the allocation for new initiatives totalling over €1.8 billion.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection was allocated €31 billion in Budget 2027, an increase of over €2 billion or 7% on the REV 2026 allocation.
As set out in Table 5 on page 162 of the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, when account is taken of the net effect of various timing and other adjustments, €1.8 billion is being provided to fund both new and existing policies, including policy adjustments and the expansion of services.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the specific savings and efficiency measures each Department will implement in 2027 to meet the expenditure levy totalling €446 million set out in the Budget 2027 Expenditure Report, in tabular form, by Department; and the reason the Department of Education and Youth is not subject to the levy.
reply:
The achievement of value for money in public expenditure is a Government priority, with an agenda for reform and efficiencies established over the past year. Public expenditure must be managed to maximise value for money for the taxpayer and support the delivery of Government priorities within the voted allocation, as outlined in Circular 18/2025 (Value for Money Obligations).
Earlier this year, the Government agreed that additional funding of €646 million would be provided to the Department of Education and Youth in 2026. To accommodate this reprioritisation and deliver on the 2027 ceiling agreed under the Medium Term Fiscal Plan, an Expenditure Levy of €446 million has been reflected in all Budget 2027 funding allocations, with the exception the Department of Education and Youth.
In April, my Department wrote to all other Departments highlighting the Government decision to apply an Expenditure Levy for 2027 and emphasising the need to achieve savings. Given that the levy was applied to offset a permanent increase in the funding allocation for the Department of Education and Youth, no levy was applied to that Department.
In September 2026, I wrote to all Ministers, asking them to identify efficiencies and reforms in the context of the Estimates process for Budget 2027. Reforms and efficiencies were published and are set out in tabular form for each Vote or Vote Group in Part II of the 2027 Expenditure Report, which can be accessed at the following link: assets.gov.ie/static/

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation if guidance exists for his Department, and public bodies under the aegis of his Department, on responding to parliamentary questions where the information sought is held on individual case files rather than in a centrally collated format; and whether the existence of information on individual files is considered sufficient grounds for not providing the information requested.
reply: I wish to advise the Deputy that my Department processes Parliamentary Questions in line with the Standing Orders of Dáil Éireann. Responses to individual Parliamentary Questions are considered on a case-by-case basis, having regard to the nature of the information sought, the information available and the requirements of the relevant Standing Orders. The Deputy will also be aware of the provisions of Circular 25/2016: Protocol for the Provision of Information to Members of the Oireachtas by State Bodies under the aegis of Government Departments/Offices, which sets out a protocol for the provision of information to members of the Oireachtas by State bodies.

reply:
The Infrastructure Guidelines and the Capital Works Management Framework (CWMF) set down the procedures that public bodies who are charged with the delivery of public infrastructure and building projects must follow.
Securing value for money is an ongoing priority for this Government and is at the heart of all decision making, at every stage of a policy or programme lifecycle. Delivering value for money is about securing the efficient and effective use of public resources in the pursuit of better public services, living standards and infrastructure for the people of Ireland. It is not solely concerned with costs and price levels – it also involves the consideration of quality, specialist expertise, and social and environmental impacts.

The design of LPT was considered by an interdepartmental group chaired by Dr. Don Thornhill in 2012. In 2019, the tax was subject to a review by an interdepartmental group chaired by the Department of Finance. This model was used to compare the impact that different reform scenarios for LPT would have on household incomes relative to a benchmark position where the property value increases but there is no change in the structure of LPT. The results indicate that all scenarios were progressive rather than regressive to varying degrees.

reply:
Finance Act 2021 introduced Part 22A Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) into the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997. RZLT is an annual tax, calculated at a rate of 3% of the market value of the land within its scope. The tax is due and payable from 2025 onwards in respect of land which satisfied the relevant criteria on 1 January 2022, or in the course of 2022, as where land satisfies the relevant criteria after 1 January 2022, RZLT will be first due in the third year after the year in which it satisfies the relevant criteria. RZLT first arose on 1 February 2025 and the 2026 liability was payable by 23 May 2026, subject to certain exceptions.
The legislation underpinning RZLT provides for a number of exemptions, deferrals and abatements subject to the relevant criteria being met. The legislation does not provide for a specific exemption for local authorities. Local authorities that own land meeting the criteria for RZLT are subject to the tax. It is important to note that, to come within the scope of RZLT, land must be both zoned by the local authority for residential use and serviced. The intention of RZLT is to activate development of this residentially zoned and serviced land to meet critical housing needs.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the increase in rent a room relief is universal or solely for multi-room lets; and the assessment or analysis carried out on the likely impact this will have on rents charged.
reply:
Rent a Room relief was introduced in 2001 as an incentive to encourage individuals to let rooms in their sole or main residence as residential accommodation in order to bring about an increase in the availability of rental accommodation.
To qualify for the exemption, it is necessary for the residential premises to be situated in the State and occupied by the individual as his or her sole or main residence during the tax year. The relief only applies to individuals. It does not apply to companies or partnerships. Nor does it apply to income from the carrying on of a trade, such as the trade of operating a B&B.
Currently, the scheme provides an exemption from Income Tax, PRSI and USC on rent received where a person rents out a room or rooms in his or her principal private residence and the rent received does not exceed €14,000 per year. This figure includes payments for utilities (such as gas and electricity) and any other charges.
The Rent a Room rental income ceiling was last increased in Budget 2017 from €12,000 to €14,000.
Budget 2027 announced an increase in the maximum rental income which can qualify for the relief from €14,000 to €16,000. This revised ceiling will apply to the 2027 year of assessment and subsequent years.
The increased rental income ceiling of €16,000 will apply to all claimants regardless of the number of rooms let or the number of tenants accommodated.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if the estimated cost of the CGT changes outlined in budget 2027 of 46.5million first year and 186 million full year are based on CGT for individuals and some corporates in respect of gains on development land solely or if it also includes chargeable gains for corporates; in the case of the former provide a full estimated cost including all chargeable gains for corporates.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that, in general, capital gains tax (CGT) is chargeable on a gain arising on the disposal of an asset, at the rate of 31% for disposals made on or after 7 October 2026. The chargeable gain is generally the difference between the cost of acquisition of the asset and sales proceeds realised on the disposal of the asset.
Chargeable gains may arise to individuals, non-corporate persons and companies. With the exception of chargeable gains arising on the disposal of development land, companies pay corporation tax on chargeable gains, rather than CGT. As the rates of corporation tax and CGT are different, a chargeable gain which arises to a company is adjusted, such that when the relevant corporation tax rate is applied to the adjusted amount, the result is the same as if the chargeable gain was subject to the relevant CGT rate.
I am further advised by Revenue that the €186 million full year cost outlined in Budget 2027 includes the chargeable gains for corporates. As outlined above, this is payable as corporation tax but is included in the overall estimated CGT costing.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline all legal advice his Department received, either internally, from the Attorney General or from the European Commission, regarding the impact on Ireland’s derogation from the ETS 2 system of a reduction in the rate of carbon tax for certain fuels; to confirm if there is a rate of carbon tax, or an overall quantum of carbon tax revenue, that the State cannot fall below, or it risks losing the derogation.
reply:
As part of the Fit for 55 package, the European Commission published a proposal to revise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive. The revised proposal was agreed in May 2023 when the EU adopted Directive 2023/959. This Directive strengthened rules in relation to the existing EU ETS and made provision for the introduction of a separate but adjacent system for the Buildings, Road Transport and Additional Sectors (ETS2).
Directive 2023/959 provides for Member States who operate a national carbon tax in buildings, road transport and additional sectors to apply for a derogation from obligations under the EU ETS2 once certain criteria are met. The derogation allows a Member State with a national carbon tax rate equivalent or higher than the average ETS2 auction price, in a given reference year, to exempt regulated entities from the obligation to surrender ETS2 allowances between 2027 and 2030.
In December 2023, Ireland requested a derogation under Article 30 (e)(3) of the ETS Directive. Following engagement with the Commission, amendments were made to carbon tax legislation in Finance Act 2025 to align the scope of Ireland's Carbon Tax with the ETS2 Directive.
Subsequently, Ireland secured a derogation which is subject to ongoing review. In order to retain this derogation, Ireland is required to ensure its carbon tax rate is higher than the average auction clearing price in the ETS2 system for each reference year. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to outline the level of funds currently held in the Climate and Nature Fund.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund (ICNF) was established in 2024 alongside the Future Ireland Fund (FIF), following the commencement of the Future Ireland Fund and Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund Act, 2024.
The Act sets out that annual contributions of €2bn occur each year between 2025 and 2030, subject to the results of an annual fiscal and economic assessment process carried out by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and my Department.
Given these annual contributions, and an initial transfer of €2bn from the National Reserve Fund (NRF) in 2024, the Act provides for resourcing of the ICNF of up to €14bn.
Management and investment of the ICNF rests with the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA), who invest according to the long-term investment strategy. The financial accounts of the ICNF are published in the NTMA’s annual report each year, which are available on the NTMA’s website. A detailed schedule of investments held by the ICNF as at 31 December 2025, is published in the NTMA’s 2025 Annual Report
The NTMA has informed me that the ICNF was valued at approximately €4.1 billion as of 31 December 2025. So far this year an additional €1.5bn has been transferred to the ICNF, with a further €500m to transfer before year end.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of businesses currently authorised under section 56 of the Value-Added Tax Consolidation Act 2010; the estimated annual value of VAT zero-rated under the scheme; the estimated cash-flow and Exchequer impact arising from the operation of the scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 203, 204, 205 and 206 together.
The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is required to comply. VAT is a tax on consumption of goods and services within the EU, and each Member State is obliged to operate its own VAT system in accordance with a common framework of principles and rules that are designed to support coherent application of the tax across the EU, protection of the tax base, and facilitation of trade.
The EU VAT Directive provides that VAT is not charged on goods exported from the Union. The Directive also provides that VAT does not apply on the supply of goods cross-border within the EU between VAT-registered businesses; in those cases, it is the business who receives the goods who is obliged to account for VAT on them in its own Member States, and not the supplier. The Directive further provides that a Member State may, subject to certain procedures and limitations, relieve from VAT the inputs of a business that is exporting or making intra-Community supplies.
In accordance with the Directive Ireland applies its zero rate of VAT to exports outside the EU and to intra-Community supplies of goods. This means that businesses predominantly engaged in making such supplies outside the State would be in a permanent repayment position for VAT. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated number of existing investors who will remain subject to deemed disposal following the introduction of the personal investment account announced in Budget 2027; the number facing a deemed disposal charge in 2027; the estimated cost to the Exchequer of extending equivalent treatment to these existing investors.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. Nor do they specify the number of investors or policyholders to whom the Investment Undertaking Tax (IUT) or Life Assurance Exit Tax (LAET) paid by the investment fund or life company relates.
Similarly, as respects investments in certain Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds in respect of which investors are required to self-assess tax due, taxpayers are not required to separately report data for each category of chargeable event when filing their tax return.

question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the timeline for the application of the derelict property tax; and when the digitally accessible online register will be activated.
reply:
The introduction of a new Derelict Property Tax (DPT) forms part of the ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030’ housing plan. The tax will be collected by the Revenue Commissioners and will be based on registers of derelict properties that are compiled and maintained by local authorities.
In its first year of operation, the tax will apply to towns and cities which were recorded as having populations of 4,000 or greater in Census 2022. In the second year of operation, the tax will expand to towns with populations of 2,000 or greater.
DPT will be legislated for as part of Finance (No. 2) Bill 2026. Local authorities will conduct visual surveys of the designated towns and cities under the tax and place derelict properties that they identify on a derelict property register. They key timelines for the first liability year for DPT are as follows:
• 1 January to 31 August 2027: Local authorities inspect the relevant towns and identify derelict properties.
• 1 September 2027: Preliminary registers of derelict properties are published.
• 1 September 2027 to 30 November 2027: Property owners can seek review of inclusion on register.
• 1 September 2027 to 29 February 2028: Local authorities decide on reviews.
• 28 February 2028: Final registers of derelict properties published and Revenue pay and file window opens.
• 23 June 2028: First pay and file deadline.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he is aware of concerns among medically vulnerable electricity customers regarding solar panel supports where their electricity supplier is not participating; whether customers must change supplier to qualify; how those in fixed-term contracts will be accommodated; why customers can no longer apply directly; the timeframe for contacting eligible households; whether installing solar panels independently could affect future eligibility for the medically vulnerable scheme; and if he will review the arrangements to ensure households are not disadvantaged due to their electricity supplier.
reply:
The Solar PV for the Medically Vulnerable Scheme is a targeted scheme for the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels for customers/households who are registered on the life support category of the Priority Services Register. These homes have a dependence on electrically powered equipment, including medical equipment, life protecting devices and assistive technologies such as dialysis machines and respirators. As such, these households may have a higher energy demand than the average user and this scheme is designed to go some way towards helping to reduce those energy costs.
The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) in conjunction with energy suppliers and is open to all suppliers who wish to participate, with each energy supplier contacting their own eligible customers directly, in line with the work plans for their solar PV installers.
The scheme is energy supplier-led, meaning each energy supplier is responsible for contacting their own eligible customers directly. Government, through the SEAI, funds each energy supplier for the installations they provide to their eligible customers.
It is important to note that suppliers, who manage the administrative aspects of the scheme under the SEAI, issue offers to eligible homeowners. Each participating supplier received an allocated amount of funding under their Memorandum of Understanding with the SEAI and contacts eligible households in batches, based on operational capacity.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if there are planned changes to the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme in 2027, following the publication of Budget 2027.
reply:
My Department and I share concerns that the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme or DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. The Government has now agreed to commence from early 2027 the Department of Transport’s Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). The VAS will provide direct financial assistance to all individuals with qualifying vehicle adaptation needs to meet the costs of those adaptations. The VAS will improve individuals’ functional mobility that in turn can contribute to better social and economic opportunities.
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) remains with the Department of Finance and will be kept under review. Learning from the commencement and initial operation of the VAS will further inform reform options for the DDS.
As the Deputy will be aware, when this government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families.
Budget 2027 delivers significant progress for disabled children and adults, bringing the budget to over €4 billion for the first time.
This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People. The commitment to develop a new scheme by the Department of Transport, and in this context review the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme, are strong commitments in this strategy.

reply:

European and Irish legislation requires the regulation of financial services firms providing investment services in relation to investment products. The law lists the various types of regulated investment services and investment. Regulated firms may also sell investment products which are not specifically mentioned in the law (i.e. unregulated products). Where they do so, certain investor protections, which apply to regulated activities do not apply.
The Central Bank recently reviewed the Consumer Protection Code (CPC) and this included a review of the rules around the sale of unregulated products by regulated entities. As part of the review, the Central Bank held a public consultation, and changes came into effect in March 2026.
Under the Code’s Standards for Business, firms are required to ensure that all information they provide to customers is presented in a way that seeks to effectively inform the customer.
