question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the introduction of an electric vehicle salary sacrifice scheme, similar to that operating in the United Kingdom; the findings of any such assessment, including the implications for benefit-in-kind taxation and the Exchequer; whether he plans to introduce such a scheme.
reply:
Section 121 of the Taxes Consolidation Act (TCA) 1997 provides that where a car is made available for the private use of an employee then the employee is chargeable to BIK. Where such a benefit is provided for an employee by his or her employer, the employer is required to include that notional payment as part of the employee’s emoluments and to deduct tax via the PAYE system accordingly.
A CO2-based BIK regime for employer provided vehicles became effective from 1 January 2023. From that date the taxable BIK amount is based on the car’s original market value (OMV) and the annual business kilometres driven, with new CO2 emissions-based bands determining whether a standard, discounted, or surcharged rate applies. The number of mileage bands was also reduced from five to four.
Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and plug in hybrids benefit from a preferential rate of BIK, while fossil-fuel vehicles are subject to higher BIK rates. This new structure with CO2-based discounts and surcharges is designed to incentivise employers to provide employees with low-emission cars. This brought the taxation of employer provided cars into step with other CO2-based motor taxes as well as with the long-established CO2-based vehicle BIK regimes in other EU Member States.
Furthermore, there is a BIK exemption on the installation of an EV charging facility by an employer at the home of a director or employee, subject to certain conditions.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether his Department has assessed the combined impact of income tax, USC, PRSI and the withdrawal of income-related supports on the financial benefit to working households of additional earnings; whether measures to address abrupt eligibility thresholds are being considered with the relevant Departments.
reply:
As part of the Budgetary process, officials in my Department conduct a distributional analysis of all the changes made to the welfare and tax system. This analysis is carried out using the ESRI’s SWITCH model, which accounts for the interaction between policy changes, and the impact that these have on households. The results of this assessment are published each year in the Beyond GDP document.
The Department of Finance also works closely with other Departments to ensure that budgetary measures do not create unintended interactions that discourage individuals from taking on additional work. For example, the Tax Policy Changes Book, produced by Department officials, examines how changes to selected Department of Social Protection payments affect the effective marginal tax rates faced by workers across different income levels.
These considerations are also reflected in policy. Budget 2027, for instance, raised the 2 per cent threshold for USC to account for the increase in the minimum wage. This was done to ensure that part-time workers on minimum wage continue to face a low marginal tax rate on any additional hours worked. Similarly, the Working Family Payment thresholds were also increased, allowing low-income families to work additional hours while continuing to receive income support from the state.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will ensure that online retailers within the European Union apply the appropriate VAT rate when selling products to Irish consumers, including the 0% VAT rate that applies to certain items such as children’s clothes.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that the VAT rating of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they are exempt from VAT or fall within the categories of goods and services listed in Annex III of the EU VAT Directive, to which Member States are permitted to apply lower VAT rates subject to certain rules.
The EU VAT Directive allows that a Member State may be permitted to maintain a historic VAT treatment, subject to strict conditions, including that the scope of its historic treatment is not expanded. On this basis, Ireland retains its long-standing application of the zero VAT rate to the supply of certain children's clothing not exceeding the size “appropriate to children of average build of 10 years of age”.
I understand from Revenue that, in the practical administration of the measure, the zero rate applies to clothing, specifically designed for children, in sizes up to and including 32-inch chest, 26-inch waist and 152cm height. Clothing for persons above 10 years, and clothing in excess of these sizes is liable to VAT at the standard rate currently 23%. Also, in accordance with the legislation, if clothing is not described, labelled, marked or marketed on the basis of age or size then the standard rate of VAT applies.

The deferred tax remains as a charge on the property and must be paid before a sale or transfer can be completed. Interest is charged at 3% per annum on the deferred amount.

reply:

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Transport his views on concerns regarding roaming deer on road safety issues; and the steps he will take to address the matter.
reply:
The safety of all road users is a priority for me and my Department. I am aware of concerns regarding the risk posed by stray deer, particularly on rural roads and during periods when deer are more active, however management measures in relation to deer do not come under the remit of my Department or agencies.
The Irish Deer Management Strategy Group (IDMSG) was set up in 2023 with representatives from the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM), National Parks & Wildlife Service (NPWS) and Coillte.
The role of the IDMSG was to develop initiatives to ensure sustainable deer numbers while achieving the objectives of landowners ranging from biodiversity, forestry, agriculture, animal health and road safety.
I would encourage the Deputy to contact these bodies directly for further information.
In relation to road safety, appropriate road signage including hazard warning signs regarding deer or other wild animals is the responsibility of the local authorities.
The Road Safety Authority (RSA) advises motorists to stay alert and reduce speed when driving in areas with known deer populations and particularly where deer warning signs are in place. I have referred the Deputy's question to the RSA and requested that they advise if there is any further relevant information they can provide in relation to this matter.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport whether National Transport Authority contracts or public bus service licences contain requirements concerning unnecessary engine idling and vehicle emissions; the way in which any such requirements are monitored; and whether consistent engine-off guidance will be introduced for extended layovers at bus stops and termini.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing the provision of public passenger transport services nationally.
PSO services support a wide range of Government policy objectives, including climate action, sustainable mobility, regional development, social inclusion, compact growth, economic competitiveness, as well as the accommodation of population growth.
Under Bus Connects we are transitioning to a Zero Emissions Bus Fleet, which will see the procurement of zero emission electric buses. There are now over 100 electric buses in operation in Dublin and circa 30 in Limerick, with more to come.
In light of the NTA’s responsibility in this area, I have forwarded the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport the statutory provisions, governing prolonged stationary engine idling by buses and coaches on public roads and at bus stops; the authorities responsible for enforcement and the sanctions available; whether these provisions address vehicles left running unattended; and whether he will consider specific measures to restrict unnecessary idling, subject to defined safety and operational exceptions.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I am aware of the impact that vehicular emissions arising from engine idling can have on air quality and public health. Engine idling can contribute to both carbon emissions and local air pollution, particularly in built-up areas and public spaces such as outside schools. From a regulatory perspective, under current traffic legislation, notably S.I. No. 190/1963, Road Traffic (Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles) Regulations 1963, Article 87(1)(a)), it is already an offence to leave a vehicle unattended while its engine is running. This provision is intended to address vehicle safety and security concerns primarily.
To address and mitigate transport-related air pollution more broadly, a broad range of national measures are currently in place. These include multi-stakeholder working groups such as UTRAP - the Urban Transport-Related Air Pollution (UTRAP) Working Group which is co-chaired by the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications and the Department of Transport, and consists of representation from a range of key government departments, agencies and local authorities. The group was established among other things to address rising concerns about the level of transport-generated ambient air pollution in certain areas.
Other initiatives include funding instruments and supports for the uptake of low-emission electric vehicles, a NOx component of the Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT) to discourage the purchase of higher-emitting

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No. 261 of 29 September 2026, if he is aware that the Road Safety Authority already has a Road Safety Advocate Programme (details supplied); the difference between his proposed new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme and the RSA's Road Safety Advocate Programme which already exists and has carried out numerous activities; and the cost of his proposed new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme.
reply: As the Deputy is aware, the Government approved proposals on 29 July to further reform the Road Safety Authority (RSA) while maintaining the one organisation. One of the key reform proposals is the introduction of a new Road Safety Ambassadors Programme this year which will see the appointment of road safety advocates to work with the RSA to target different audiences with road safety messaging. This new programme will enhance and expand existing road safety advocacy programmes. My Department is engaging with the RSA on the implementation of the reform proposals including the Road Safety Ambassadors programme. The RSA is largely self-funded and income from customer services, such as driver testing, driver licencing and the NCT service, is used to fund public interest work. As part of Budget 2027, the RSA has been directed to ringfence €20m for investment in road safety public awareness and promotional campaigns. This is an increase of €2m on the 2025 and 2026 investment in this important area.

Embedding Universal Design in all new infrastructure and fleet,
Addressing legacy accessibility deficits, particularly in older, Victorian-era train stations, and
Providing supports that enable independent travel wherever possible.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport the amount of fare revenue that his Department expects to generate from PSO supported services in 2027.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. However, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport.
As the statutory body responsible for regulating fares across services operated under PSO contracts, the National Transport Authority (NTA), is central to shaping a public transport system that is fair, efficient, and accessible. Through its management of fare strategies, they help to ensure that pricing structures support social inclusion and modal shift, while also underpinning the financial viability and resilience of the PSO network.
Fare revenue currently covers approximately 38% of the cost of operating the PSO services nationally. Any overall increase in revenue generated from the NTA’s recent fare determination announcement will be reinvested directly into public transport services, delivering better connectivity, capacity and reliability for passengers and commuters across the network. This is vital in ensuring that fare revenue continues to make a sustainable contribution alongside significant levels of subsidy, while maintaining the affordability and accessibility of public transport.
In light of the NTA's responsibility in this area, I have forwarded the Deputy's question to the NTA for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a response within ten working days.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport the position regarding the ICE2EV scrappage scheme; and if it is proposed to be extended beyond the initial pilot.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scrappage Scheme was designed and launched as a capped pilot initiative, supported by €17 million in funding from the Climate Action Fund, comprising of €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the EV purchase grant.
The strong level of interest in the scheme is encouraging and highlights increasing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This positive response aligns with Ireland’s broader Climate Action objectives, including the ambition to increase the uptake of electric vehicles to 30% of the national car fleet by 2030.
The policy purpose of the capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, validation and payment processing remains ongoing. A post-completion evaluation of the scheme will be undertaken to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions in this area. The evaluation will consider a range of factors, including the drawdown of available funding, participation across different geographic areas, the characteristics of vehicles being scrapped, and the types of electric vehicles supported under the scheme.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Transport if the planned review of the TaxSaver scheme announced in Budget 2027 will include consideration of extension to the scheme to include shared mobility services.
reply:
In line with the announcement made as part of Budget 2027 by the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance, Simon Harris. T.D., my Department will initiate a comprehensive review of the TaxSaver Scheme over the coming year, in close cooperation with the Department of Finance.
The TaxSaver Scheme is an important element of the Government's wider approach to supporting sustainable travel. The forthcoming Review will provide an opportunity to build on the success of the existing Scheme and to consider how it can continue to best support commuters into the future.
Commuting habits have evolved significantly in recent years, especially in light of an increase in hybrid working as well as more flexible and multimodal travel patterns. It is important that our supports keep pace with these changes and continue to enable people to make sustainable transport choices for their daily journeys.
While the scope of the Review has not yet been finalised, I am keen that it considers all opportunities to support greater sustainable transport choice. The contribution that shared mobility can make in expanding transport options will be an important consideration, subject to the agreed terms of reference for the Review.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position Ireland has taken in discussions on the European Commission’s proposed new own resource based on non-collected waste electrical and electronic equipment; and the way in which this proposal fits with Ireland’s wider priorities for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework.
reply:
Pursuing agreement on the next EU long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is an overarching priority for the Irish Presidency. At the European Council in June, the President of the European Council, Antonio Costa, tasked the Irish Presidency with advancing work on new Own Resources.
On 10 October, the Presidency published our revised compromise proposal, or Negotiating Box. This is an important milestone in MFF negotiations and includes carefully considered adjustments on a range of issues, including on the Commission’s proposal for new Own Resources.
The Presidency’s Negotiating Box is based on strong evidence gathered through an extensive programme of engagement including bilateral meetings with all Member States, and several discussions at EU negotiating fora. In assessing proposals for new Own Resources, the Presidency has been guided by the principle that a significant package of new Own Resources will be essential, while also needing to be capable of generating sufficient new revenue, securing agreement by all Member States, and being implementable by 2028.
The Negotiating Box therefore sets out a package of new Own Resources, which includes a proposed new Own Resource on e-Waste.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide the rationale for the €26 million cut within Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety section of his Department's budget when compared to 2026; and the initiatives or schemes which had funding cut or removed as part of this budget decrease.
reply:
In his capacity as Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, my colleague Seán Canney T.D, has responsibility for the Irish Coast Guard and the SAR Aviation Contract.
It should be noted that Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety encompasses a range of services and bodies, including the Irish Coast Guard, the Commissioners of Irish Lights and related departmental administration costs. Consequently, changes in the overall Programme E allocation cannot be attributed solely to Coast Guard expenditure or to any single programme within the Vote.
The reduction in the 2027 allocation for Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety, from €162.5 million in 2026 to €136.6 million in 2027, is primarily attributable to the non-recurring nature of certain expenditure incurred in 2026 and the impact of expenditure control measures applied across Government.
A significant element of the 2026 provision related to one-off costs associated with the transition to the new Irish Coast Guard Search and Rescue (SAR) Aviation Service contract. In addition, the 2027 provision reflects the application of the Government's expenditure levy and associated expenditure management measures.
The Irish Coast Guard will continue to provide its statutory maritime search and rescue, maritime safety and emergency response functions.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide a breakdown of funding that will be provided to road safety initiatives in 2027.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has responsibility for the promotion of public awareness of road safety and of measures, including the advancement of education, relating to the safe use of roads.
The RSA is largely self-funded and income from customer services, such as driver testing, driver licencing and the NCT service, is used to fund public interest work.
As part of Budget 2027, the RSA has been directed to ringfence €20m for investment in road safety public awareness and promotional campaigns. There will be a focus on broadening and enhancing educational programmes to make our roads safer for all road users. This is an increase of €2m on the 2025 and 2026 investment in this important area and ensuring that one-off expenditure increases in 2023 and 2024 are now embedded in budgeting and business planning.
The Deputy may also wish to note that €718 million was initially allocated for 2026 under the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme for the improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads, with approximately 90% of this funding allocated to road maintenance and renewal.
Under this programme, my Department provides supplemental funding to local authorities under several different grant categories. Approximately €14 million was provided for low-cost safety improvements in 2026, which funded over 300 projects. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport to provide an update on the progress to establish a PSO flight service between Dublin and Derry.
reply:
This Government is fully committed to establishing a new Public Service Obligation (PSO) air service between Dublin Airport and City of Derry Airport. This will deliver the Programme for Government commitment to establish air connectivity between the two cities.
As City of Derry Airport is outside of the European Union, the PSO air service will operate outside of Regulation (EC) 1008/2008, which provides for the common rules for the operation of air services in the Community. My Department has had extensive engagement with the Chief State Solicitors Office (CSSO) and the Office of the Attorney General in recent months, in relation to the appropriate legal framework to underpin the procurement. Detailed work is being undertaken to ensure that the Request for Tenders (RfT) is compliant with the appropriate Regulations as well as EU State aid rules.
My Department anticipates being in a position to publish the RfT very shortly, with a view to a contract being awarded this year and services commencing on the route as soon as operationally feasible by the successful operator.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport following the publication of Budget 2027, to provide an update on his Department's planned vehicle adaptation scheme; when applications will open; and the criteria that will be imposed as part of the scheme.
reply:
As Minister of State for International and Road Transport, Logistics, Rail and Ports, I can confirm that in recent months my officials have made significant progress in the development of the Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). Guided by the proposals set out by the Transport Working Group of the National Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Senior Officials Group on Disability, as well as further engagement and consultation, the Department has established the key principles and parameters underpinning the Scheme. This has facilitated the development of a high-level framework for its operation, further details of which are available on Gov.ie (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-transport/press-releases/minister-canney-announces-framework-for-new-vehicle-adaptation-scheme/).
In line with the social model of disability, the VAS will be based on an individual's needs, not characteristics. Accordingly, eligibility will extend to drivers and passengers who require assistance to enter, exit, or operate a vehicle, rather than being linked to any particular medical condition or disability. The Scheme will be simple to access, use, and receive payments through. It will not be means tested and applicants needing adaptations will not be required to pay upfront themselves.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Transport whether the road transporters support scheme will operate in 2027, following the publication of Budget 2027.
reply:
My Department received over 4,400 applications in respect of approximately 31,500 vehicles during the original application window. As of 06 October, all applications have been assessed and approved for payment.
The Scheme was introduced to provide support to eligible road transporter operators with rising fuel costs. The Scheme provided payments for the months of March, April and May as the average cost of a litre of diesel exceeded €1.90 as measured by the CSO. An allocation of €120 million was provided for this initial period.
The RTSS will receive an additional €73 million in 2026, enabling payments to be made for a further two months to assist haulage and passenger operators with the high price of diesel.
Since the beginning of the fuel crisis, both I and officials from the Department of Transport have engaged with representative bodies from the road transport sector. The Scheme’s additional allocation reflects both the immediate need for financial support and the ongoing commitment of Government to work with the sector to support Ireland’s essential trade and strategic supply chains.
This Government will continue to engage with representatives from the road transport sector and monitor the situation.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her plans to open a new Irish Consulate General Office in Doha Qatar in 2027.
reply:

Ireland enjoys strong bilateral relations with Qatar. I had the opportunity to travel to Doha in July this year, where I had a positive meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs. We already have strong trade, investment and people-to-people links, and we are committed to deepening these.
Our Embassy team in Abu Dhabi regularly visits Qatar in support of our broad policy objectives, including the development of political and trade relations, and supporting the needs of Irish businesses and the wider Irish community.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Transport the reason the allocation for maritime transport and safety is reduced from €162.5 million in 2026 to €136.6 million in 2027; whether this reflects the completion of the transition of the Irish coast guard search and rescue aviation service to the new operator; and to confirm that coast guard service levels will be maintained in 2027.
reply:
In his capacity as Minister of State for International & Road Transport, Logistics, Rail & Ports, my colleague Seán Canney T.D, has responsibility for the Irish Coast Guard and the SAR Aviation Contract.
It should be noted that Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety encompasses a range of services and bodies, including the Irish Coast Guard, the Commissioners of Irish Lights and related departmental administration costs. Consequently, changes in the overall Programme E allocation cannot be attributed solely to Coast Guard expenditure or to any single programme within the Vote.
The reduction in the 2027 allocation for Programme E: Maritime Transport and Safety, from €162.5 million in 2026 to €136.6 million in 2027, is primarily attributable to the non-recurring nature of certain expenditure incurred in 2026 and the impact of expenditure control measures applied across Government.
A significant element of the 2026 provision related to one-off costs associated with the transition to the new Irish Coast Guard Search and Rescue (SAR) Aviation Service contract. In addition, the 2027 provision reflects the application of the Government's expenditure levy and associated expenditure management measures.
The Irish Coast Guard will continue to provide its statutory maritime search and rescue, maritime safety and emergency response functions.

In advance of the Railway Order for these works, expected to be lodged in 2027, planning permission has been granted by Cork City Council for the first of the new stations at Blackpool, while an application for the second station, at Dunkettle, is under consideration.

question: Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Transport his plans to repeat the scrappage scheme for older cars, which has operated very successfully earlier in the year and enabled owners of older cars to purchase e-cars.
reply:
The ICE2EV Pilot Scrappage Scheme was designed and launched as a capped pilot initiative, supported by €17 million in funding from the Climate Action Fund, comprising of €10 million for the scrappage grant and €7 million for the EV purchase grant.
The strong level of interest in the scheme is encouraging and highlights increasing consumer engagement with the transition to electric vehicles. This positive response aligns with Ireland’s broader Climate Action objectives, including the ambition to increase the uptake of electric vehicles to 30% of the national car fleet by 2030.
The policy purpose of the capped initiative was to test the effectiveness of scrappage as a tool to stimulate EV uptake among those who may not otherwise transition in the near term, with the ultimate goal of delivering additional emissions reductions necessary for our climate targets.
While the pilot scheme has closed for new applications, validation and payment processing remains ongoing. A post-completion evaluation of the scheme will be undertaken to assess its effectiveness, emissions impact and overall value for money, and to inform future policy decisions in this area. The evaluation will consider a range of factors, including the drawdown of available funding, participation across different geographic areas, the characteristics of vehicles being scrapped, and the types of electric vehicles supported under the scheme.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Transport the regulations that apply to rickshaws; the authority or department responsible for checking safety; and if this will be reviewed in the lifetime of this Government.
reply:
For the Deputy's information, if a rickshaw is fitted with a small engine or electric motor of any kind, it is considered to be a mechanically propelled vehicle (MPV). Under road traffic law, if an MPV is used in a public place it is subject to all of the regulatory controls that apply to other vehicles i.e., it must be roadworthy, registered, taxed and comply with the following regulations:
• SI 190 of 1963 – Road Traffic Construction, Equipment and Use of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 189 of 1963 – Road Traffic Lighting of Vehicles Regulations 1963.
• SI 5 of 2003 – Road Traffic Construction and Use of Vehicles Regulations 2003.
The drivers of all vehicles on public roads, including motorised rickshaws, are required to comply with road traffic legislation and to behave in a safe manner paying due care to other road users. The enforcement of such road traffic legislation is a matter for An Garda Síochána.
A provision was contained in section 31 of the Road Traffic Act 2016, which was aimed at amending section 20 of the Taxi Regulation Act 2013, to allow the National Transport Authority (NTA) to make regulations for “non-motorised passenger transport” in towns and cities which includes rickshaws propelled by pedal cycle. It is important to note that the section 31 provision does not allow for the regulation of rickshaws with an electric motor, only non-motorised rickshaws. Section 31 was subsequently found not to be legally permissible and could not be commenced.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to clarify whether ODA funding as outlined in Budget 2027 is more or less than the funding provided for ODA in 2026.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to annual increases in Official Development Assistance (ODA), working towards the UN target of providing 0.7% of Gross National Income.
I am very pleased that Budget 2027 has provided an increased allocation of €855 million for the international development programme, Irish Aid, managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. This is a €14 million increase on the Budget 2026 allocation.
At a time of great uncertainty internationally, when some other countries are cutting their international development budgets, this is an important demonstration of the Government's commitment to Ireland's work on long term development and life-saving humanitarian assistance, with a focus on reaching the furthest behind first. The Government has increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme every year since 2020.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the progress of payments under the fuel income support scheme.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
Applications under the scheme closed on June 2nd and payments commenced on July 22nd. To date 31,025 applicants have received payments totalling €26.52 million. It is expected that the total final payments under this scheme will be approximately €27 million.
Incomplete payments are due to a number of issues. For certain cases my Department is waiting on further information from applicants to allow them to be set-up on payment systems or a request has been made for further evidence, for example fuel receipts. As information is supplied cases are being cleared and payments will continue to be made on a weekly basis.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will outline the framework set out under the National Bioeconomy Strategy 2026–2030.
reply:
At the outset, I wish to highlight that the new National Bioeconomy Strategy 2026-2030 has not yet been published. This will occur on the occasion of the Global Bioeconomy Summit which the Government, in conjunction with the International Advisory Council for the Global Bioeconomy, will host here in Dublin on October 20th and 21st. The Taoiseach, Minister O'Brien and I look forward to presenting the Strategy to the national and international audience that will gather for that important Summit.
Notwithstanding this, I can refer the Deputy to the framework of the Strategy that was set out in the draft that was issued for public consultation in July. The Strategy’s Vision is that by 2030, Ireland’s bioeconomy is a core driver of economic prosperity, climate action, and rural regeneration. It is characterised by the sustainable and circular use of biological resources, innovative high-value industries, and thriving local communities.
The Strategy focuses on five strategic objectives and contains targeted actions for each of these. They are:
• Scaling Infrastructure, Technology and Investment.
• Strengthening Market Demand and Development.
• Leveraging Innovation, Knowledge and Skills.
• Bioeconomy as a tool for Climate Action and Circularity.
• Improving Governance, Cooperation and Partnerships.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider adding a cap on the number of breeding females permitted within a dog breeding establishment to the legislation proposed in this area.
reply:
In order to bring a coherent approach to dog control, policy and legislative responsibility under both the Control of Dogs Act 1986 and the Dog Breeding Establishments Act 2010 transferred to my Department last year. In both cases, local authorities retain responsibility for all operational and enforcement matters.
On 19th May 2026, my Department published draft legislation, the Dog Breeding Establishments Bill 2026 to update the existing regulatory framework for dog breeding establishments in Ireland across three key areas - welfare and breeding, sales and record keeping, and administration and enforcement.
The Bill was approved for priority drafting and is currently undergoing pre-legislative scrutiny with the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Agriculture.
The Bill has seventeen Heads and addresses three broad areas: welfare and breeding standards, sales and record-keeping, and administration and enforcement.
It seeks to address concerns about excessive numbers through a mandatory staffing ratio of 1:20 which creates an indirect but real constraint on establishment size. The strengthened improvement notice regime will explicitly empower authorised persons to require a reduction in the number of dogs on premises where welfare concerns arise.
Local authorities also retain the ability to set conditions on the number of breeding females as part of the registration process, and this avenue remains open to them, particularly in respect of new applications.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine when the updated Land Use Strategy will be published; and to provide an update on same.
reply:
The Land Use Review Phase 2 titled “A Living Land” was published in July of this year. It provides an evidence base to inform and support landholders and policymakers in their future decisions for land-use, in the context of achieving Ireland’s agricultural, socio-economic, climate and environmental objectives.
The report is not an articulation of government policy or a strategy in relation to land use, given that there are many economic, environmental, and social elements to be balanced in considering land use. Rather, this report will help to inform and support future considerations in this complex area. For example, the role of State-owned lands in leading the way to achieve integrated land use objectives.
To consider fully the recommendations of the Phase 2 of the Land Use Review, my Department has committed to co-chair with DCEE, a Land Use Taskforce, with members to include DHLGH and other relevant Departments and bodies.
Establishment of a Land Use Taskforce is the next step to examine how the State can encourage optimal use of land to meet a variety of societal needs including socio-economic, restoring nature, improving water quality, enhancing climate adaptation and mitigation.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number and value of TAMS solar applications approved and not approved to date in 2026; if he will approve additional funding to meet the demand.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme with a defined budgetary allocation. The budgetary allocation for TAMS 3 is spread across all eleven sub schemes therefore it is not possible to allocate a budget to each of the eleven schemes individually.
TAMS 3 has been hugely successful to date, with over €195 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024. Over the first eight tranches of the scheme, all valid applications received were approved.
However, to ensure the available budget for TAMS 3 is distributed fairly over the remainder of the current CAP programming period, it was necessary to limit the number of approved applications per tranche from Tranche 9 onwards by applying ranking and selection criteria to manage the budget to the end of 2027.
Specifically in respect of the Solar Capital Investment Scheme (SCIS) the number of applications and the level of funding provided to date has also well exceeded expectations, to the extent that more than 20% of the TAMS budget is being spent on SCIS.
A total of 7,331 applications have been received under the SCIS with approvals of 3,787 issuing to farmers allowing them to proceed with their investments. The average payment under SCIS is €18,777 per application with an estimated value of the overall approved applications in excess of €71m. Payments amounting to €39.5m have issued to 2,107 farmers since payments commenced in June 2024.

question: Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the urgent measures he and his Department is taking to address the backlog in aquaculture licence renewals, reviews and new applications in County Mayo; whether additional resources or personnel will be allocated to the Aquaculture and Foreshore Management Division to tackle the significant backlog, in view of the fact that some licences have expired and some applications submitted remain undetermined due to delays.
reply:
Applications for aquaculture and foreshore licences are considered by my Department in accordance with the provisions of the Fisheries (Amendment) Act 1997, the Foreshore Act 1933 (as amended) and applicable national and EU legislation. The licensing process is complex and involves consultation with a wide range of scientific and technical advisors, in addition to various Statutory Consultees. The legislation also provides for a period of public consultation.
The length of time taken to process an aquaculture licence application varies depending on a number of factors including location, species, scale and intensity of production, statutory status of sites and potential visual impact. My Department also takes full account of all scientific and technical advice, in addition to all issues identified during the public and statutory consultation phases.
Further factors that can impact the time taken to process an application can include; the requirement for an Appropriate Assessment and whether the application is required to be accompanied by an Environmental Impact Assessment Report; the need for additional underwater or archaeological assessments, etc. Decisions in respect of aquaculture licence applications are only taken following the fullest consideration of all consultations and public interest elements of each application, including environmental considerations.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking to enable farmers to participate directly in Ireland's renewable energy transition; and the opportunity he foresees for renewable energy to provide an income stream for farms.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware overall national energy policy formation is the direct responsibility of my colleague the Minister for Climate Energy and the Environment. My Department works closely with the Department of Climate Energy and the Environment on energy related matters from an agricultural perspective, as well as with a wide range of industry and other stakeholder groups.
Solar and Biomethane are renewable energy options available to farmers which can improve their financial resilience through the diversification of their income stream. Both Solar and Biomethane have received significant support from my Department.

This was Ireland’s first major policy statement on Biomethane. A key outcome of the Strategy was the Biomethane Capital Grant Scheme, which was run by my Department. The scheme recently concluded with funding of approximately €19 million issued to 7 projects. Not only will these projects contribute to the achievement of Ireland’s Biomethane target set out in the Climate Action Plan, but they also represent an opportunity for farmers to provide feedstock for biomethane generation, thus providing a new income stream for farmers. question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will support a ban on surgical artificial insemination of greyhounds.
reply:
The Veterinary Council of Ireland (VCI) in April 2024 updated its Code of Professional Conduct for Veterinary Practitioners to prohibit veterinarians from carrying out surgical artificial insemination in dogs due to ethical and welfare considerations. However, this new prohibition does not apply to greyhounds, as the practice is provided for in legislation under the Artificial Insemination of Greyhound Regulations 2005.
The report of the Working Group on Control of Dogs, which was approved by Government in March 2023, and has been published online at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/0d6d7-working-group-on-control-of-dogs/#report-of-the-working-group-on-the-control-of-dogs, includes a recommendation that surgical artificial insemination in canines be prohibited, where the word canine encompasses all breeds of dogs.
In 2024, my Department held a public consultation on whether the practice of carrying out surgical artificial insemination in greyhounds should be banned or not and the results of the public consultation are now available on: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/animal-welfare/#surgical-artificial-insemination-in-greyhounds.
In compliance of section 5 of the Greyhound Racing Act, S.I. question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the supports his Department is providing to Irish farmers to deal with rising input costs in the agriculture sector.
reply:
The agri-food sector has demonstrated its ongoing adaptability and resilience despite numerous uncertainties and economic pressure in recent years. The Government continues to provide strong support to farmers via Ireland’s €10.3 billion CAP Strategic Plan, as well as other national sectoral schemes. This results in payments to support farmers of over €2 billion annually.
I am conscious of the exceptional cost pressures family farms are facing at present. I introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support, alongside the fuel excise and levy reductions and delay of Carbon Tax increases introduced by Government. To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.
I acknowledge that the impact of prolonged dry weather this year has increased the challenges family farmers face this year. The dry conditions resulted in significant supplementary feeding on affected farms and the use of silage and other fodder conserved for winter feeding. This has increased costs while also reducing the quantity of fodder available for the coming winter. Responding to the ongoing challenges, I have also availed of the flexibility to increase the rate of advance payments under the BISS, CRISS and Eco-scheme from 70% to 75%, helping to put more money in farmers pockets as early as possible in the year.
Flexibilities have also been provided on requirements associated with certain actions under the A

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures his Department has taken to introduce additional resources for enforcement of animal welfare legislation.
reply:
My Department has lead policy responsibility within government for animal welfare, which is protected by legislation. I am committed to ensuring that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner. All reports of alleged animal neglect or cruelty received by my Department are investigated and appropriate action is taken.
My Department and authorised officers appointed under the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, including An Garda Síochána, Customs agents, local authorities and the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (NSPCA), undertake appropriate enforcement action, where breaches or shortcomings are identified. Since the Act came into operation in March 2014, 230 cases have been successfully prosecuted by my Department and the NSPCA.
My Department has policy and legislative responsibility for the Control of Horses Act 1996. However, Local Authorities are responsible for operation of the Act, and they may take a range of actions in relation to equines, including prohibiting horses in certain areas, issuing licences and seizing horses. These powers can be used in respect of straying horses, including horses put on land without owner’s permission, including public land. Local authorities may also prosecute offenders.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the position regarding work ongoing to address animal cruelty concerns related to the export of live animals; and if he has engaged with animal welfare organisations in this regard.
reply:
The intra community trade and export of live animals to third countries is a private commercial activity which is regulated by my Department in accordance with EU and National Regulations. Relevant Regulations for this sector include Council Regulation (EC) No. 1/2005 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations which is given effect at national level by S.I. No. 675/2006 European Communities (Animal Transport and Control Post) Regulations 2006. S.I. No. 580/2007 - Diseases of Animals (Animal Transport) (Roll-on Roll-off Vessels) Order 2007 and S.I. No. 356/2016 - Carriage of Livestock by Sea Regulations 2016.
My Department demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. My Department has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and temperature control.
Ireland is a major livestock trading country. Based on data collected by my Department, from 1 January to 20 September 2026, some 278,000 bovines were the subject of intra-community trade, or exports to third countries, from Ireland; 203,000 of these bovines were un-weaned calves. question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of bluetongue cases notified to his Department; if he is satisfied that the measures being put in place are adequate to control the disease.
reply:
As of 2nd October 2026, there have been 21 cases of bluetongue serotype three (BTV-3) across the country notified to my Department since mid-July 2026. Recent detections of bluetongue highlight the importance of submitting carcases of livestock suffering from unexplained mortalities and samples from animals with suspected clinical signs for veterinary investigation
Vaccination is the best tool we have to mitigate the losses which can be caused by BTV-3. To that end, I included bluetongue vaccination as an option in the 2026 beef and sheep welfare schemes. With the recent detections in both cattle and sheep herds of BTV-3, the majority with clinical signs, farmers that have not vaccinated their stock yet should talk to their private veterinary practitioner as to whether vaccination is appropriate for their flock or herd.
My Department undertakes extensive surveillance in relation to bluetongue to inform on farm decision making around vaccination. I encourage farmers who carried out vaccination in 2026 to consult their veterinary practitioner in relation to the need for a booster vaccination in 2027.
Additional information on BTV-3, including the latest figures on cases detected, can be found on the Government Website at: www.gov.ie/bluetongue.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the issues discussed at the recent meeting of Agriculture Ministers held in Ireland. .
reply:
I had the pleasure of hosting the Informal Meeting of EU Agriculture Ministers in Dublin and Kildare from 6 to 8 September, as part of Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU. The plenary session was held at Dublin Castle on 8 September.
Plenary discussions centred on the Commission’s Livestock Strategy and Protein Action Plan, and particularly on how research and innovation can strengthen the competitiveness, sustainability and resilience of European livestock farming.
Ministers considered how to support farmers, particularly smaller farms, in adopting new technologies and practices through investment, advice and knowledge transfer. Key considerations included food security, farm incomes, support for rural communities, the need to strengthen European protein production, and the need to accommodate diverse farming systems, including Ireland’s grass-based model.
The discussion included contributions from representatives of European farmers, co-operatives and young farmers, and the European Parliament. The European Economic and Social Committee also presented its opinion on the Livestock Strategy. In addition, Commissioner Hansen provided an update on drought conditions affecting European farmers, which have created significant pressures on fodder production, water availability and livestock management.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether he intends to introduce a dedicated farm succession or retirement scheme to support generational renewal in agriculture; and the measures being considered to address barriers faced by young farmers in accessing land and taking over family farms.
reply:

There are currently a range of supports in place. Ireland’s CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 provides substantial resources focused on generational renewal. There are also strong national taxation measures to facilitate succession and assist land mobility. Teagasc education and knowledge activities focus on equipping young farmers with necessary education, training and advice to build long and successful careers in farming. As stated in the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming Report, the total financial support to generational renewal in Ireland was some €428.6m in 2024.
However, farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions. That is why the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established, to consider whether the existing supports are having the desired effect, and how supports might best be configured for the future. question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps his Department is taking to amend the policy to allow farm vehicles registered in the UK, brought in through Northern Ireland and purchased by Irish farmers without a phytosanitary certificate to be registered with Customs in Ireland.
reply:
Under EU plant health law second hand agricultural vehicles and machinery originating from a third country are regulated and subject to import controls. This is to prevent the spread of plant pest and diseases associated with soil and plant debris contamination attached to such machines. This means a phytosanitary certificate is required on entry into the EU for all second hand agricultural vehicles and machinery. Ireland is therefore required to comply with these EU wide requirements.
Under the Windsor Framework the movement of second hand agricultural machinery from Great Britain (GB) to Northern Ireland (NI) can happen without a phytosanitary certificate only if it is going to a person and entity in NI and such machines must stay in NI. In these cases it must travel with a UK/NI plant passport and such imports must be notified to NI authorities. For agricultural machines purchased in GB by an Irish importer and imported through NI such imports must be pre notified to the NI plant health authorities in DAERA and the importer is required to present the consignment and the necessary phytosanitary certification on import.
Where the custom procedure has not been complied with and a second hand agricultural vehicle has come through Northern Ireland without the necessary phytosanitary certification, my Department will refer importers to contact NI authorities on their situation. question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the actions he will take to support farmers with the rising cost of fuel.
reply:
The Government recognises the exceptional pressure that rising fuel costs are placing on our farmers and agricultural contractors.
A substantial support package for agricultural or green diesel (MGO) has been put in place, with the full removal of all non-carbon excise on green diesel of 7.4c/l, and a further payment worth up to 20c/l through the Fuel Income Support Scheme.
The Fuel Income Support Scheme was introduced as a targeted income support, alongside the excise and levy reduction. The payment of 20c/l covered the months of March up to the end of July 2026, which coincides with peak fuel usage on farms. These supports, totalling 27.5c/l, exceed by almost 6c/l the entirety of excise (carbon and non-carbon) charged on green or agricultural diesel prior to the conflict in the Middle East.
To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.

The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the progress of the Bovine TB Action Plan.
reply:
In recent years there has been a significant increase in bovine TB levels nationally. I am very aware of the emotional and financial challenge for Irish farmers, their families and rural communities of a bovine TB breakdown.
To address these high disease levels, I have undertaken extensive engagement with stakeholders and farming organisations to agree measures to tackle disease levels. I launched the ‘Bovine TB Action Plan:Addressing Bovine TB in Ireland’ in September 2025 it includes 5 measures and 30 actions underpinned by scientific research, evidence and veterinary expertise. The aim of the Action Plan is to reset the TB programme by putting in place measures necessary to tackle the current disease situation.

• 30-day pre-movement testing for contract reared heifers.
• The introduction of mandatory Gamma Interferon Test (GIF) testing in large breakdowns of breeding herds (this will apply to herds in a bTB restriction on or after 13 April 2026).

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the status of negotiations with the British government to reinstate access for Irish fishermen to their traditional fishing grounds at Rockall; and if he will seek international mediation or arbitration to resolve this long running injustice, that has cost our fleet millions of euro each year.
reply:
Rockall is a small, uninhabitable rock located approximately 160 nautical miles west of the Scottish islands of St. Kilda, and 230 nautical miles to the north-west of Donegal.
As the Deputy is aware, Ireland has not sought to claim sovereignty over Rockall. The UK claimed sovereignty over Rockall in 1955 and sought to formally annex it as part of Scotland under its 1972 Island of Rockall Act. The consistent position of successive Irish Governments is that Ireland does not recognise Britain’s claim of sovereignty over Rockall.
Accordingly, Ireland does not accept that a 12 nautical mile (22km) territorial sea exists around Rockall. Ireland’s long-held view is that a rock incapable of sustaining human habitation does not allow for the creation of a territorial sea. Therefore, the agreement under the TCA relating to access to the UK 12-200 mile zone should apply inside the 12nm zone around Rockall.
We understand that the UK takes a different view.
Irish vessels have traditionally fished for haddock, which is subject to a quota limit, and squid, which is not subject to a quota limit, in the waters around Rockall. Haddock may be caught both within and outside 12 nautical miles of Rockall, but squid is caught within 6 nautical miles of Rockall. Other stocks caught in the waters around Rockall, both within the 12 miles area and outside, are monkfish and megrim.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline his views on the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021.
reply:
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage.
Following legal advice from the Office of the Attorney General in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department procured independent scientific evidence and in October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).
The research work concluded, and the research report was subsequently evaluated by an external expert. Following the completion of the evaluation, the research service provider was afforded the opportunity to respond to the evaluator’s comments and these comments were received in September 2025. My Department is currently finalising the overall response to the report and I will publish same in due course.

question: Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the status of the work of the interdepartmental working group established to examine the racing of horse-drawn vehicles on public roads; the progress made to address the serious animal welfare concerns associated with the practice; whether the group is examining the measures required to prohibit racing of all horse drawn vehicles on public roads; and when recommendations are expected.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government.
The welfare of equines is protected by legislation and there is a commitment in the Programme for Government to build on existing inspectorate supports across the country, ensuring a consistent approach to dealing with horse welfare. However, it must be emphasised that primary responsibility for the health and welfare of equines lies with the owner or keeper.
The use of horse-drawn vehicles, as with all vehicles on public roads, is governed by the relevant provisions of the Roads and Road Traffic Acts, which is under the remit of the Minister for Transport. The drivers of such vehicles are required to comply with road traffic legislation, with the enforcement of this legislation falling under the remits of my colleagues the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and the Minister for Transport.
I have written to both Ministers, expressing my concern about the subject of horse-drawn vehicles on public roads from the perspective of road safety and animal welfare and asked them to nominate senior officials to meet with counterparts from my Department to scope out the issues involved and how they might be addressed. An initial meeting of this group has taken place, and I understand that further meetings are planned in order to progress this complex issue.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline the funding available for TAMS under budget 2027.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme, that has been hugely successful to date, with payments of over €195 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024.
The TAMS on-farm capital investment scheme continues to be one of my key priorities over the lifetime of this Government. In Budget 2027 I have secured an increase in the 2027 TAMS allocation to €93.35 million, the largest ever annual budget allocation in on-farm investment scheme by my Department.
This underlines the Government's renewed commitment to supporting competitiveness on Irish farms, generational renewal, and crucially, will fund farmers to invest in additional slurry storage, a critical component in supporting Ireland’s Nitrates Derogation.

reply:

reply:

2. Participating in the green transition.

reply:

reply:

question: Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether his Department has undertaken an assessment of risks to Ireland's food security arising from climate change related risks, such as drought, flooding, biodiversity loss and disruption to global food supply chains; and whether he will consider establishing a cross-departmental review of Ireland's food security resilience in view of growing climate-related risks.
reply:
Ireland is one of the most food secure countries in the world, ranking second of 113 countries assessed for food security in the Global Food Security Index. Furthermore, the most recent Teagasc Sustainability Report finds that Irish dairy, cattle, tillage and sheep farms produce protein sufficient to meet the requirements of over 36 million people (or 30 million people on a net basis).
Nonetheless, recent extreme weather events challenge established assumptions on food security. My Department's Climate Change Sectoral Adaptation Plan (2025 to 2030) provides the strategic framework for strengthening resilience across the agriculture, forestry and seafood sectors. The current plan represents the most comprehensive climate adaptation assessment undertaken to date of climate risks affecting the sectors under the Department's remit and reflects the findings of Ireland's National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA). question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking at EU level to secure increased fishing opportunities and quota allocations for the Irish fishing fleet.
reply:
The share allocation of stocks between Member States was established as a principle of the first Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) in 1983 and was based on the average catch of each Member State over a period of reference years (track record).
Any change to the existing system of quota allocations would require a majority of Member States to agree under the qualified majority voting system. This would require other Member States to give up existing quota shares, and therefore poses particular challenges in a qualified majority voting context.
Notwithstanding these challenges, I have frequently raised the matter of Ireland's fishing opportunities at the AgriFish Council, and will continue to seek additional opportunities for Ireland at every available opportunity.
Ireland has consistently called for the European Commission to fully analyse and report on the impacts of Brexit on the CFP, and in particular, the impact on the EU and Member States’ fishing opportunities as a result of quota transfers under the EU-UK Trade & Cooperation Agreement (TCA). I have emphasised to the Commissioner of Fisheries and Oceans, Costas Kadis, the need to address the impacts of Brexit on our fishing sector when Ireland carried a disproportionate burden of the quota transfers to the UK under the TCA.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if his attention has been drawn to the findings of a recent survey which show that a third of farmers intend to leave the sector within the next five years.
reply:

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the implementation of the recommendations of the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming; the specific measures being progressed to encourage earlier and more effective succession of family farms to the next generation; and the timeframe for their delivery.
reply:
Supporting young farmers and facilitating generational renewal is a priority of mine and critical to ensure a bright future for the agri-food sector. The challenge of generational renewal in farming is widely recognised at both national and EU level. It is important that we have skilled, innovative young farmers coming into the sector to secure a viable and sustainable future for Irish farming. We recognised the need to consider whether existing supports are having the desired effect, and how supports might best be configured for the future. Farm succession is a complex issue and there are many factors that impact farmers’ decisions and that is why the Commission on Generational Renewal in Farming was established.
The Commission adopted an objective, evidence-based approach to examining all the factors involved and engaged closely with stakeholders. They have produced a thorough analysis and have made 31 recommendations across a wide range of areas including CAP Supports; Pensions; Taxation; Access to Finance; Access to Land; Collaborative Arrangements; Advisory Services; Education and Training; Gender Balance; and the Overall Attractiveness of the Sector.
An implementation group in my Department has considered the recommendations and progress is being monitored on an ongoing basis. Some of the recommendations may be commenced in the short term, but some will be more medium term:
• The current CAP is fully programmed. Recommendations around CAP supports will have to be consid

question: Deputy Joe Neville asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of animal welfare cases which his Department has begun since the beginning of 2026.
reply:
Animal welfare is a key priority for me as Minister and for the Government.
My Department has lead policy responsibility within Government for animal welfare and takes this matter most seriously.
I am committed to the policy that animal welfare standards are vigorously applied in a fair and even-handed manner and remain committed to the continued robust enforcement of the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, which provides a modern framework for regulating and applying standards in the area of animal health and welfare. My Department keeps the Act under review in light of key developments in the areas of animal welfare, the law and having regard to the practical lessons learnt from operating the Act.
Since the introduction of the Act, approximately 1,000 staff within my Department have been designated as authorised officers. A large number of these authorised officers are based in my Department’s network of Regional Veterinary Offices throughout the country, providing nationwide coverage. Their responsibilities include carrying out welfare inspections in every county and providing advice and support to the keepers of animals, however primary responsibility for protecting the welfare of animals rests with the owner or keeper.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the action his Department is taking to ensure that the IT issue affecting non-productive investment applications received under the ACRES and ACRES-CP scheme for 2025 from applicants who transferred to a registered farm partnership during the scheme and who cannot submit a claim for their 2025 application.
reply:
The Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme, or ACRES, is the current agri-climate environment measure provided under the 2023-2027 CAP Strategic Plan (CSP). There are two approaches within ACRES namely ACRES General and ACRES Co-Operation.
Non-Productive Investments (NPIs) are actions that are available to participants in the Co-operation approach of ACRES to directly address environmental issues on the farm, thereby increasing the farmer's capacity to improve field scores through appropriate management, as well as to contribute to wider environmental objectives.
There are a number of steps in the processing of NPI payments. Initially applications for NPIs are made on behalf of a participant by their advisor in an NPI-Annual Works Plan (AWP). All applications are screened by the local Co-Operation Team and decision letters will follow to advise if the actions within the AWP have received approval or not.
Approved actions may then be implemented by the participants, and the details can then be submitted to the NPI claims system.
It is important to note that there is no obligation on a participant to carry out an approved action, and the claim serves as confirmation from the participant that the action has been implemented. Once a claim is submitted, NPI payment may then issue.
To date almost €9.7 million has issued in NPI payments to farmers with almost 98% of 2023 AWP claims and nearly 93% of 2024 AWP claims paid.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the steps he is taking, including during Ireland’s EU Presidency, to secure an adequately funded, ring-fenced CAP budget post-2027; and the steps he is taking to oppose the proposed reduction in CAP funding.
reply:
Since the European Commission published its proposals for the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) in July 2025, I have engaged directly with my EU counterparts on the issue through bilateral meetings, and at meetings of the Agriculture and Fisheries (AGRIFISH) Council of Ministers.
Since Ireland assumed the Presidency of the Council of the European Union in July 2026, I have continued this engagement, with a particular focus on progressing the negotiations and building consensus among Member States. In September, Ireland hosted an informal meeting of EU Agriculture Ministers, which provided Ministers with an opportunity to have a broader discussion on the future CAP and on the issues arising in the negotiations.
At the AGRIFISH Council meeting on 28 September, Ministers took stock of the progress made and provided further political guidance on the outstanding issues. Ministers welcomed the progress achieved to date, and broadly supported the Irish Presidency’s approach to advancing the negotiations. The Presidency is now working with Member States and the European Commission to resolve the remaining issues, with the objective of reaching a Partial General Approach on the CAP Regulation at the AGRIFISH Council meeting on 26–27 October 2026.

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will consider the provision of additional financial supports to farmers in the upcoming Budget to address concerns over significant winter fodder deficits arising from the extreme dry weather conditions experienced in recent months.
reply:
I am very aware of the pressures that farmers are experiencing due to the prolonged dry spell of weather this summer. In mid-August, I met with Teagasc and the main farm organisations to discuss the impact of the prolonged dry weather on farming at that time.
I requested the Chairperson of the National Fodder and Food Security Committee to reconvene the Committee. The Committee brings together farm organisations, advisers, industry and Government to assess the fodder position and coordinate the response. The Committee has met twice, most recently on 7th September and is responsible in ensuring co-ordinated messaging across all stakeholders to farmers.
A fodder survey carried out by Teagasc in mid-August showed variation in winter fodder supplies between farms and regions, with the South-East the region of greatest concern. However, following regular rainfall since the end of August, grass growth has recovered significantly.
Teagasc are reminding farmers to reassess their fodder stock situation, complete updated fodder budgets, and address any likely shortfall early. Teagasc will conduct another advisor led fodder survey in October following the maize harvest.
The Committee highlighted that the primary focus should be for farmers to maximise production of feed at individual farm level for the remainder of the autumn by making the most of the current recovery in grass growth, including nutrient application before statutory deadlines.
