Work is close to finalisation on the drafting of the National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose the NIS2 Directive and establish Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) on a statutory basis, and will be published shortly. This legislation is a priority for myself and this Government and I hope to be in a position to notify transposition of the NIS2 Directive by the end of 2026.
The NCSC is engaging with its constituents and stakeholders to ensure the requirements of the Bill are communicated ahead of time and has produced resources and guidance for entities that fall within the scope of NIS2. The NCSC has also prepared a media campaign for launch when the bill is enacted.
Some of the resources and guidance currently available to entities on the NCSC website includes:
• Draft Risk Management Measures and the Cyber Fundamentals (CyFun) framework, both designed to help organisations comply with NIS2 requirements.
• Guidance on Cyber Governance for Management Board Members in NIS2 Entities. This new resource is specifically designed to support Management Board members fulfil their leadership responsibilities and protect the continuity of essential services with confidence.

question: Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if the home support policy with the eligibility and prioritisation criteria promised in the Action Plan for Disability Services 2024–2026 has been published; and if age-based exclusions are consistent with the policy.
reply:
A key programme of reform is ongoing in the home support sector, encompassing disability, older persons and mental health services. The programme has a vision at its centre of an equitable, person-centred, and enabling home support service that enhances service user and staff experience. The reform programme is being led by the Department of Health and the HSE, in conjunction with the Department of Children, Disability and Equality.
A crucial element of the home support reform programme is the development of a regulatory framework for home support providers. This work is being led by the Department of Health, and the Department of Children, Disability and Equality has been engaging with them on all elements of the framework that impact disability services.
The home support regulatory framework comprises:
- primary legislation providing for the licensing and regulation of public and private home support providers;
- secondary legislation (regulations) establishing the minimum requirements with which home support providers must comply; and
- National Standards currently under development by the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) to support progressive quality improvements in home support service provision across the sectors.

question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether, further to the provisions of the Children Act 2001, he will consider introducing legislation providing criminal liability for a parent or guardian where it can be established that a wilful or reckless failure to exercise reasonable care or control has contributed to antisocial or criminal behaviour by a child under 18 years.
reply:
The Government recognises the critical role that strong family relationships and effective parental supervision play in preventing youth offending.
The role of parental supervision orders, which are already provided for under the Children Act 2021 and other parental measures, will be further considered in the development of a new Youth Justice Strategy over the coming year.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention, and the budget allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at €43 million for 2026.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so that the cycle of offending by young people is broken.
The Departments of Health and Children, Disability and Equality play important roles and deliver a number of parental and child interventions and supports. For example, the HSE has responsibility for delivering Parenting Capacity Assessments, and Tusla has responsibility for child interventions and related parental supports.
It is important to recognise that our existing Youth Justice Strategy has been successful in diverting children who have engaged in criminal or anti-social behaviour away from the Criminal Justice system and towards more positive pro-social behaviour and life choices.

question: Deputy Aindrias Moynihan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline his engagements with the distillery industry in the establishment of a clear farm to bottle providence model for Irish Whiskey, ensuring a clear link between Irish land, Irish farmers and Irish grain.
reply:
The public consultation on the Irish Whiskey Technical File has only recently closed and over the course of the consultation, approximately 200 submissions were received. I was pleased to see the broad level of public engagement from across the spirit drink industry and beyond.
In relation to a farm to bottle providence model, there are several distilleries operating this model in Ireland. This option is open to all distilleries and there are obvious benefits that they can highlight as part of their marketing.
I have made it clear that I am committed to promoting the use of Irish grain in the distilling industry. I have stressed this in my meetings with the Drinks industry and have asked my Department to explore options as part of a wider review. I continue to support new market development and market access efforts for our quality, sustainable food and drink products including Irish whiskey.
My Department is now in the process of reviewing the submissions received from the public consultation.
Over the coming weeks and months my Department will engage with key stakeholders and experts on the proposals. Once the proposed amendments have been reviewed and assessed, then the process of updating the product specification including any required European Commission approval will begin.
I will ask my officials to closely examine any request that strengthens the promotion of Irish Grain and how those asks can fit within the rules that govern the spirit GI regulations.

question: Deputy Pearse Doherty asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the reason a compliance notice issued requiring a consignment to be re-dispatched to a third country after a container was inspected at Dublin Port, released and delivered to its owner home in County Donegal, when a phytosanitary certificate e16 was submitted to Revenue as part of a Transfer of Residence application.
reply:
My Department carries out Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) checks on certain goods and machinery imported into the EU from third countries at designated Border Control Posts (BCPs). Used machinery must be accompanied by a valid phytosanitary certificate where required. In this case, there were concerns regarding the validity of the phytosanitary certificate presented at documentary inspection. This is being investigated further.
Following the issuing of a compliance notice, the consignment was released from Customs control in error.
My Department undertook a review of the case and concluded that local engagement with the importer was the appropriate course of action while the matter is investigated. In this context, my Department has since withdrawn the compliance notice while this process is ongoing.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional funding he will provide under the farm safety scheme for farmers in Cork to upgrade livestock handling facilities and farmyards; and the way in which he will ensure smaller family farms can access these supports.
reply:
The Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS 3) provides grants to farmers to build and/or improve a specified range of farm buildings and equipment on their holdings. Overall, the scheme has proved very popular, with an unprecedented level of applications received.
The Farm Safety Capital Investment Scheme is a measure in TAMS 3, which provides an incentive to farmers to avail of investments to improve their own safety and that of their farm. This scheme includes a number of investment items such handling equipment, tank covers, pens and bale slicers, all of which make the day to day running of a small family farm safer and more efficient.
I have ensured that 100% of valid applications submitted under the FSCIS continue to be approved including those from Cork farmers, supporting farmers in improving their own safety and that of their farm.
In addition, the current TAMS 3 ranking and selection criteria ensure that farmers with smaller holdings, regardless of their location, are treated more favourably than those with larger farm holdings. For example, a maximum of 20 marks is allocated to farmers with five hectares declared on their Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS) application, with the marks decreasing as the size of the holding increases, thus ensuring that smaller farms can be ranked higher than large enterprises, and are therefore more likely to be selected.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the measures he is taking to protect the viability of dairy, beef and sheep farms in Cork in light of high production costs; and the additional supports he plans to introduce for family farms as part of Budget 2027.
reply:
The agri-food sector has demonstrated its ongoing adaptability and resilience despite numerous uncertainties and economic pressure in recent years. The Government continues to provide strong support to farmers via Ireland’s €10.3 billion CAP Strategic Plan, as well as other national sectoral schemes. In 2025, €244 million worth of CAP funding was provided to farmers in Cork.
I am conscious of the exceptional cost pressures family farms are facing at present. I introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support, alongside the fuel excise and levy reductions and delay of Carbon Tax increases introduced by Government. To date total payments of €26.52m have been made under the Fuel Income Support Scheme, with over 31,000 farmers and contractors paid.
Regarding any extension of excise reductions, taxation policy is the responsibility of my colleague the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance. In advance of the budget, I work closely with him on taxation issues relating to the agri-food sector, considering a range of proposals. I also work closely with the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation on expenditure proposals. Working across Government, we will continue to keep developments in global energy markets under close review and remain ready to respond as circumstances evolve.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine whether or not the native Irish honey bee is under threat; and if he will make a statement on the matter:.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 219 to 221, inclusive, together.
The movement of bees within the European Union is governed by Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (the Animal Health Law) which is supplemented by Commission Implementing and Delegated Regulations (Regulation (EU) 2020/688 and 2021/403). These EU regulations contain specific provisions to safeguard the health of bees located in the territory of the Union.
The Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, a Private Members Bill, which seeks to ban the importation of non-native honey bees is currently before Dáil Éireann, Second Stage. Progression of the Bill through Dáil Éireann is subject to the procedures of the Oireachtas.
Following legal advice in relation to the Protection of the Native Irish Honey Bee Bill 2021, my Department sought tenders for research services to provide independent scientific evidence in the form of a comprehensive assessment of the threat to the Native Irish honey bee Apis mellifera mellifera and the impact upon biodiversity and the ecosystem from the introgression/crossing/cross-breeding of the native Irish Honey Bee with non-native species based on the most reliable scientific data available. In October 2023, a contract was signed with the National University of Ireland, Galway for the provision of research services on the native Irish honey bee (Apis mellifera mellifera).

question: Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if adequate funding will be put in place in order that farmers can invest in rooftop solar, since the ranking and selection outcomes impacted solar applications under the targeted agricultural modernisation scheme (TAMS) in late 2025, the approval rate announced for eligible solar applications has fallen to just 10%.
reply:
The Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Scheme (TAMS) is a demand-led scheme with a defined budgetary allocation. The budgetary allocation for TAMS 3 is spread across all eleven sub schemes therefore it is not possible to allocate a budget to each of the eleven schemes individually.
TAMS 3 has been hugely successful to date, with over €195 million issuing to farmers since payments commenced in June 2024. Over the first eight tranches of the scheme, all valid applications received were approved.
However, to ensure the available budget for TAMS 3 is distributed fairly over the remainder of the current CAP programming period, it was necessary to limit the number of approved applications per tranche from Tranche 9 onwards by applying ranking and selection criteria to manage the budget to the end of 2027.
Specifically in respect of the Solar Capital Investment Scheme (SCIS) the number of applications and the level of funding provided to date has also well exceeded expectations, to the extent that more than 20% of the TAMS budget is being spent on SCIS. To date, a total of 3,793 SCIS applications have received approval to proceed with their investment while payments amounting to €39.5 million have issued to 2,107 farmers.
Given the need to manage the remaining budget available for TAMS 3, in recent tranches I have prioritised approvals for core on-farm investments related to farm safety and nutrient storage on the basis of the importance of continued investment in these measures. As

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he has made a submission to the Minister for Finance or the Government seeking the retention of the Agricultural Diesel Rebate at its current rate of 12 cent per litre beyond 1 October 2026.
reply:
The Diesel Rebate Scheme is for road transport operators and is primarily a matter for my colleague the Minister for Transport.
In relation to the agrifood sector, significant support has been provided by way of reductions in excise on Marked Gas Oil (or agricultural/green diesel), the subsequent extension of those reductions, delay of Carbon Tax increases and the Fuel Income Support Scheme.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.
I have also secured agreement on a package of €46.1 million for a scheme to support farmers impacted by higher fertiliser and energy costs as a result of the Middle East Crisis. €30.8 million in Exchequer funding will be provided for this scheme as a top-up to the €15.38 million in exceptional aid allocated by the EU. The development of the scheme is at an advanced stage by my Department and I will announce the details shortly.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of applicants approved under the fuel income support scheme; the total amount paid to date under the scheme; the amount of the original allocation that remains unspent.
reply:
My Department has introduced the Fuel Income Support Scheme as a targeted income support to assist farmers and agricultural/forestry contractors facing unprecedented increases in fuel costs.
Separate schemes have been put in place to support fishers and specialist horticultural growers.
Applications under the scheme closed on June 2nd and payments commenced on July 22nd. To date 31,025 applicants have received payments totalling €26.52 million. It is expected that the total final payments under this scheme will be approximately €27 million.
Incomplete payments are due to a number of issues. For certain cases my Department is waiting on further information from applicants to allow them to be set-up on payment systems or a request has been made for further evidence, for example fuel receipts. As information is supplied cases are being cleared and payments will continue to be made on a weekly basis.
As announced in the Budget, I am pleased to have secured agreement on the extension to the end of this year of the important fuel supports schemes provided for farmers and agricultural contractors, fishermen and women and horticulture producers impacted by higher fuel prices. The allocation of €31.2 million to cover the five months August to December 2026 for these supports will be rapidly implemented by my Department.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration If he will review a case of two students from Gaza (details supplied); the reason their visa was refused; and if, following review, his Department will reverse the decision and allow them to come here to study, as they have a host ready to provide accommodation.
reply:

It is important to note that visa applications form part of a screening process designed to establish that a person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel, and all such applications undergo this process. There are no special arrangements in place for Palestinian nationals, nor are there any plans to introduce any. Each application is considered on its own merits, having regard to all of the information and documentation submitted, the circumstances of the applicant, the purpose of the proposed travel, previous immigration history, where relevant, and the requirements of Ireland's immigration policy and legislation.
In relation to the visa applications referred to by the Deputy, I can advise that, following full consideration by a Visa Officer, the applications referred to were refused. The reasons for those decisions were set out in the refusal letters issued to the applicants. One of the applicants has since submitted an appeal of that decision.
It is important to recognise that visa decisions are based on the facts and circumstances of each individual case. The reasons for refusal are communicated directly to applicants and may vary from case to case depending on the particular circumstances presented.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procedures in place to ensure that the safety, welfare and best interests of children affected by the deportation of a person convicted of a serious criminal offence are considered throughout the deportation process (details supplied); and whether guardians or other relevant family members are notified of deportation arrangements where safety or welfare concerns arise.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules-based. The enforcement aspects of our immigration laws, including deportation orders, are essential to ensuring the system operates effectively and that there is confidence in the application of the legislation in this area.
A deportation order is a legal requirement to leave the State and is made following a full assessment of a person's individual circumstances. A decision to make a deportation order will only be taken after a fair and comprehensive examination of all the facts and circumstances of the individual case has been conducted. Any such decision will be made in accordance with immigration legislation and will include consideration of any relevant constitutional rights and rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).
When considering the immigration status of an individual convicted of a serious criminal offence in the State throughout the deportation process, including when making a decision to issue a deportation order due to the absence of a valid immigration permission and the individual's criminality, it is of paramount importance to me and my officials that, where dependent minors are identified as being affected at any stage of the process, their best interests are prioritised. Each case is considered on its own merits and on the basis of the information available throughout the process. No decision is made without due regard to, and extensive consideration

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has conducted a cost-benefit analysis of his proposals to make it harder for people to attain citizenship.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The proposed changes do not seek to restrict integration or exclude migrants from Irish society. Rather, they are intended to ensure that citizenship reflects a genuine and lasting connection to Ireland, an understanding of the State and its institutions, and an ongoing commitment to Irish society.
The residence period requirements in other EU Member States were considered in determining the revision to residency period requirements contained in the Bill.
As with all significant legislative proposals, a Regulatory Impact Assessment will be undertaken as the legislation is developed. Regulatory Impact Assessments are an important part of the legislative process and provide an opportunity to assess the potential impacts of proposed measures.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of non-Irish nationals released from prison in 2025, who were the subject of a deportation order at the time of release; the number of those persons who were removed from the State; the number who were not removed and the reasons.
reply:

Effective enforcement of our immigration laws, including the implementation of deportation orders, is essential to maintaining confidence in the integrity of the system and ensuring that our legislation is applied consistently.

The process of arranging enforced deportations and removals is often complex and can take time to complete. It frequently involves legal challenges, difficulties in obtaining travel documents, and the arrangement of flights and the necessary permissions for accompanying escorts.
In 2025, 29 individuals who were subject to valid deportation orders were released from custody at the end of their custodial sentences.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he is aware that Cork City Council are struggling to afford the Coroner's Service, the funding he has provided for the service in the last 12 months; and whether he will consider directly funding the service.
reply:
The Coroner Service comprises a network of coroners located in districts throughout the country. Responsibility, including financial support, for the Coroner Service has been a matter for local authorities since the introduction of the modern coroner system.
Legislative change is required to remove the responsibility of funding the Coroner Service outside of Dublin from local authorities.
In October 2024, Government approval was given to draft a general scheme of a Bill to significantly reform the Coroner Service. As part of this work, my Department is examining ways to increase efficiencies and minimise the impact of the death investigation process on bereaved people. Department officials are currently working on drafting the Heads of Bill in this regard, with the aim of bringing them before Government in the coming months.
The proposed legislation to reform the Coroner Service will provide for a national coronial service to be centrally funded, thereby removing the responsibility for coronial services outside of the Dublin area from the local authorities. It will also provide for the establishment of an independent Office of the Chief Coroner, the appointment of full-time salaried coroners, and the discontinuation of the existing fee-based system.
A restructured and modernised Coroner Service will drive consistency and assist coroners to better meet the needs of bereaved people, through the provision of enhanced ICT, administrative, and family liaison supports.

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether transitional arrangements will be considered for EU citizens and Stamp 4 EUFAM holders in respect of the proposed changes to residence requirements and other eligibility criteria for Irish citizenship.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The proposed changes do not seek to restrict integration or exclude migrants from Irish society. Rather, they are intended to ensure that citizenship reflects a genuine and lasting connection to Ireland, an understanding of the State and its institutions, and an ongoing commitment to Irish society.
While the proposals may affect the timeframe within which some individuals become eligible to apply for citizenship, they do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or establish a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will clarify how the income requirement under the temporary protection transition scheme will be assessed for recent graduates who have moved into full-time employment on a salary above €29,432 after a period of full-time study; whether the "average gross earnings" test is calculated over the six months before 30 September 2026 or annualised.
reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition Scheme opened for applications on 30 September 2026.
Applicants must meet a number of eligibility criteria under the published policy, including having resided in Ireland as a Beneficiary of Temporary Protection for at least one year prior to 30 September 2026 and being resident in independent accommodation at the time of application.
An applicant must demonstrate that they have been in employment or self-employment for at least six months immediately prior to the opening date of the Scheme, with average gross earnings of €29,432, and must continue to be in employment both at the date of application and at the date a decision is made on their application.
If a person cannot demonstrate a full year of income, they must be able to demonstrate that their income would reach this threshold were they to earn at that rate for a full year.
For the most up to date information to include the Temporary Protection Transition Scheme policy and FAQ please see Ukraine Updates (EN).https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of the Civil Reform Bill 2025; and the expected publication date of the draft Bill.
reply:

The Joint Committee on Justice, Home Affairs and Migration issued its report on pre-legislative scrutiny of the General Scheme of the Civil Reform Bill on 23 June 2026. Amongst a range of improvements to civil law procedures, the Bill will codify the existing law on judicial review, placing it on a statutory basis. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions.
Given the significant challenges currently facing our State in terms of housing shortages, energy deficits, inadequate water supplies and climate changes, all of which are exacerbated by the demands of a rising population, we can no longer delay on reform of the judicial review system. I am confident that the Civil Reform Bill will remove weaknesses in the current Judicial Review regime, eliminate impediments to progress and deliver reform for the public benefit. question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 66442/26, regarding a school (details supplied), the further practical assistance can be provided where the school has been unable to secure a suitable School Meals provider despite contacting local and national providers; and whether an alternative arrangement can be facilitated where the local meals on wheels provider has already confirmed it cannot provide the service.
reply:
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week.
All schools as independent contracting authorities are responsible for choosing their school meals supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules.
In the case of the school referred to by the Deputy, my Department is aware of the difficulties experienced in securing a provider. Departmental officials have been in contact with the school and have engaged with local meals on wheels to support them source a supplier.
Officials have also explored the possibility of a collaborative procurement arrangement with neighbouring schools and will continue to work with the school to identify any viable options. My Department remains available to support the school in its efforts to secure a provider and will continue to engage with the school and relevant stakeholders on this matter.
I want to assure the Deputy that my Department will continue to work with the school concerned to explore all available options with a view to facilitating participation in the School Meals Programme as soon as possible.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Social Protection to provide an update on the disability allowance appeal of a person (details supplied).
reply:
Disability Allowance (DA) is a weekly means-tested payment available to people aged 16 years and over and under 66 years of age who have a specified disability that is expected to last for at least one year. Entitlement to DA is subject to the person satisfying the medical qualifying conditions, a means test, and the habitual residence condition.
The Department periodically reviews claims in payment to ensure that recipients continue to satisfy the qualifying conditions of the scheme.
The Department initiated a review of the medical eligibility of the person concerned on 22 June 2026. The person was issued with a self-assessment Medical Review form (MR99) for completion and return. The completed form was received by the Department on 03 July 2026.
Following a review of this form, another Medical Review form, a MR33 was issued to the person concerned for completion by their doctor. The completed form was received on the 26 August 2026 and the person concerned has been found to continue to meet the medical eligibility required.
A letter informing the person concerned has been issued on 02 October 2026.
I trust this clarifies the position for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Social Protection the estimated cost in 2027 if the income disregard for carer's allowance increased to €1,300 for a single person and €2,600 for a couple.
reply:
The Programme for Government contains the commitment to continue to significantly increase the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance across a series of Budgets with a view to phasing out the means test over the lifetime of the Government.
Budget 2026 has increased the earnings disregard for Carer’s Allowance by €375 to €1,000 per week for a single person and by €750 to €2,000 per week for a couple. These are the largest ever increases in the Carer's Allowance income disregards and are evidence of the Government's determination to deliver on its commitment to Carers. This change came into effect from July this year.
Budget 2027 further increases the Carer’s Allowance weekly income disregard, to €1,150 for a single person and €2,300 for a couple. Within the Government’s first two Budgets, the Carer’s Allowance disregard has increased by 84%. A couple earning €126,000 will now be able to get a full payment without being in any way affected by the means test.
The estimated full-year cost to increase the earnings disregard from €1,000 to €1,300 for a single person and from €2,000 to €2,600 for a couple is estimated at €7.8 million.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection the measures planned in Budget 2027 to extend help with home heating costs to low paid working households who do not qualify for the fuel allowance.
reply:
The criteria for Fuel Allowance are framed in order to direct the limited resources available to the Department in as targeted a manner as possible. To qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment, a person must satisfy all the qualifying criteria, this ensures that the Fuel Allowance payment is targeted at those who are more vulnerable to fuel poverty, including those reliant on social protection payments for longer periods and who are unlikely to have additional resources of their own. There have been significant improvements made in recent years to the Fuel Allowance scheme especially in relation to those of pension age. These improvements have resulted in many more households qualifying for the payment and have resulted in the Budget for the scheme increasing significantly.
Fuel Allowance eligibility encompasses 22 qualifying schemes, demonstrating the comprehensive nature of the support available to eligible households. In addition to these qualifying schemes, people over 66 do not need to be in receipt of a payment from this Department to qualify for Fuel Allowance, subject to satisfying the means test. According to the latest CSO data, there are just over 1.8 million households in Ireland. Of these, 463,910 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide.
The following measures have been provided in Budget 2027 in relation to fuel allowance eligibility:
• The Fuel Allowance will increase by €5 to €43 per week

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether a successor compensation scheme will be set up for successful applicants to the cessation of turf cutting compensation scheme and whose payments have now ceased (details supplied); to provide an update on the measures his Department is considering to succeed the cessation of turf cutting compensation scheme; if a replacement support is being considered; if so, the details of such support or supports.
reply:
The Cessation of Turf Cutting Compensation Scheme (CTCCS) was established following engagement with stakeholders in 2011 for active domestic turf cutters arising from the restrictions on turf cutting on 53 raised bog special areas of conservation (SAC) and was extended in 2014 to include 36 raised bog natural heritage areas (NHA).
This scheme has compensated those impacted by restrictions on turf-cutting on protected sites, and over its 15-year term has helped to ensure the conservation of important peatland sites of unique ecological value.
Several supports and incentives exist to aid the conservation of these sites:
• The Protected Raised Bog Restoration Incentive Scheme, which is a once off, area based financial incentive and voluntary land purchase scheme which enables the conservation of protected peatlands.
• The Peatlands and Natura Community Engagement Scheme aims to encourage local communities, organisations, educational institutions, and other stakeholders to actively contribute to the conservation and restoration of Natura 2000 sites and peatland areas and funds a diverse range of initiatives with community benefit.
• Other supports, such as those operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority Ireland and the Department of Social Protection, are available to those with older homes, inefficient heating systems and those most at risk of fuel poverty.

question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the work of Cuan in County Louth.
reply:
Cuan, the statutory agency responsible for leading and coordinating the response to domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, continues to support the development of services and accommodation for victims and survivors in County Louth.
There are currently 17 domestic violence refuge units available in County Louth.
I was very pleased to be present earlier this year as we broke ground on the new €6.5m refuge in Dundalk, which will be operated by Women’s Aid. This project received Capital Assistance Scheme Stage 4 approval in January and forms part of the Government's wider programme to increase refuge accommodation and supports for victims and survivors of domestic violence.
When completed, it will complement the existing refuge units already available in Louth and significantly improve local capacity for victim-survivors and their children. The centre will enable Women’s Aid Dundalk to deliver a comprehensive range of wraparound services, including counselling and ongoing support for women and families.
I am advised that Cuan is collaborating with a range of stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and local authorities, to facilitate local action and support the development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he is aware that local authorities are no longer continuing roles funded on pilot basis due to funding uncertainty.
reply:
Under Section 159 of the Local Government Act 2001, each Chief Executive is responsible for the staffing and organisational arrangements necessary for carrying out the functions of the local authority for which he or she is responsible. It is a matter for each local authority as an entirely independent corporate entity, having full responsibility under law for the performance of their functions and the discharge of their governance and other responsibilities, to determine its own spending priorities, having regard to both locally identified needs and available resources. They receive income from a variety of sources including grants from Central Government, Local Property Tax proceeds, commercial rates and other locally-raised charges.
Where a local authority is implementing a programme or project that is funded by another Government Department, State agency or other external funding body, certain associated delivery costs are ordinarily expected to be met from that funding source. Each public body that seeks to have services delivered through local government should engage directly with the sector to agree service delivery and funding arrangements.
My Department does not fund posts in local authorities unless they relate to programmes specifically under my Department's remit such as housing, planning, etc. The Exchequer provides support for the additional costs associated with public service pay agreements, but not pay support for loca government staff generally.

reply:
The Housing First approach to addressing homelessness places direct access to housing first and foremost for vulnerable individuals using homeless services consistently or intermittently over long periods of time, and those unable or resistant to accessing homeless services and who may then become habitual rough sleepers. These individuals often have complex high support needs such as mental or physical health problems, addiction issues or dual diagnosis (the presence of mental ill health and a substance addiction).
Housing for All committed to the further expansion of Housing First. A new National Implementation Plan, which provides for a further 1,319 tenancies covering the period 2022-2026, was published in December 2021. These targets are based on an analysis of need, which involved all key stakeholders and was supported by The Housing Agency. The implementation of the Plan is a joint initiative of my Department, the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the criminal justice sector (the Probation Service and the Irish Prison Service) and Local Authorities, in conjunction with NGO partners. A key initiative under Delivering Homes, Building Communities is the further expansion of the Housing First programme to create 2,000 tenancies to help eliminate long term homelessness.

question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether a households (details supplied) income after incapacitated tax credit is applied, is considered assessable income for social housing under the Housing Means Policy 2026.
reply:
Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.
The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy. Under the Household Means Policy, the determination of whether a household meets the applicable income limits is based on its net income. Net income is defined as gross income less Income Tax, Universal Social Charge (USC), PRSI and, where applicable, the Additional Superannuation Contribution (ASC).
Accordingly, where a household benefits from an incapacitated tax credit, the effect of that credit is reflected in the calculation of the household's net income through the reduction in income tax liability. The resulting net income is assessed for social housing eligibility purposes under the Household Means Policy.
My Department has been examining the existing income limits in the context of current market and household income conditions, including the suitability or otherwise of the current framework having regard to the significantly changed landscape since the standardised income limits were introduced. reply:

This includes the reservation of land for use and cultivation as allotments and prescribed community gardens and the regulation, promotion, facilitation or control of the provision of land for that use. All development plans that are currently in place were made under the Planning and Development Act 2000 and planning authorities will, in due course, commence the preparation of new 10 year development plans under the Act of 2024.

reply:
The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) of my Department is currently undertaking a review of its MOUs as part of a broader assessment of commitments and resource allocation across the organisation and it is expected that this review will be completed by the end of the year.

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to review correspondence from a person (details supplied).
reply:

The Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) was established as a quasi-judicial, independent statutory body under the RTA to operate a national tenancy registration system and to facilitate the resolution of disputes between landlords and tenants.
The Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into effect on 1 March 2026, introducing a new national rent control for tenancies, which limits rent increases to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) up to a maximum of 2% per annum pro rata.
Under the RTA, rent reviews for private tenancies may take place every 12 months, or earlier in limited circumstances, with any rent increase restricted. question: Deputy Joanna Byrne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport his views on a recent media report which suggested a Department of Culture, Communications and Sport proposal on telecoms broadband infrastructure for new homes could add almost €400 million to the cost of building these new homes over the next five years; if he has concerns about the risk of these additional costs impacting the affordability of new homes; if he has engaged with the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport on this proposal; and the measures he has undertaken to ensure that these costs do not materialise.
reply:

The matter referred to by the Deputy relates to the implementation of Article 10 of the EU Gigabit Infrastructure Act (GIA), which requires Member States to establish technical specifications for telecommunications in-building physical infrastructure, fibre wiring in new buildings and buildings undergoing major renovation. The objective of these provisions is to ensure that homes and businesses are "fibre-ready" and capable of accessing high-quality digital connectivity services in the future. This is a requirement arising from directly applicable EU legislation and forms part of wider efforts to reduce the overall cost and complexity of deploying gigabit-capable broadband networks.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if he will consider steps to lessen the burden on independent radio due to recent increases in regulatory charges for radio compared to other media and will he make provision for this in Budget 2027.
reply:
There is a long-standing principle that costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves. Therefore, the Broadcasting Act provides for the imposition by Coimisiún na Meán of levies to meet the costs of its full range of statutory functions and duties. Furthermore, the Act vests authority and responsibility for such a levy in Coimisiún na Meán.
As Minister, I do not have a role in approving the proposed income or expenditure of Coimisiún na Meán, or importantly in the setting of the annual levy for any category of regulated entities, including that of sound broadcasting.
I have, however, met Coimisiún na Meán in order to seek clarity regarding their approach to implementing their statutory responsibilities with regard to the levy. It was also an opportunity for me to impress upon them the need to take the opportunity to more clearly communicate such matters to their stakeholders and the wider public, and also consider how the levy can in future be formulated to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on the sector.
I do not intend to replace An Coimisiún’s existing levy income with direct Exchequer funding as I believe that this would run contrary to the long-standing principle that the costs of regulation are met by regulated sectors themselves.

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons diverted by An Garda Síochána to health services under the health diversion scheme since its commencement; the number of Garda members who received specific training on the operation of the scheme prior to its commencement and to date; and the number of occasions on which a person eligible for diversion was not referred.
reply:
The Health Referral Scheme is a health-led response for people who are found in possession of drugs for personal use for the first time. The scheme provides eligible adults with an opportunity to engage with health services at an early stage, receive advice and support and, where appropriate, be referred to further services.
The scheme is now live nationally and is supported by investment in HSE services across all health regions.
The scheme does not legalise drug use but has been introduced as a health-led pathway for eligible first-time personal possession cases, with a focus on early intervention, reducing harm and supporting people to access appropriate services.
All first-time drug offenders must be assessed for suitability for the scheme by the investigating Garda member, in consultation with their Superintendent or an Inspector acting in that capacity. Where a decision is made not to offer a health referral, the rationale for that decision must be clearly recorded and communicated to the person concerned.
It should be noted that the scheme is voluntary. If the person is eligible and consents to partake in the scheme they are referred to the HSE for support. Those referred will receive information and advice on reducing harm and if additional support is needed, the person may be referred to addiction or other health services.
As the scheme has only recently been implemented, the specific data on the numbers referred or partaking in the scheme are not available.

reply:

The Night-Time Advisors are employed by the local authority in the selected locations (Dublin City, Cork City, Limerick City, Galway City, Kilkenny, Sligo, Drogheda, Longford Town and Buncrana). The pilot projects remain a key element in my Department's support for the Night-Time Economy nationwide.
In 2025, the Department commissioned Communiqué International to undertake an independent review of the nine Night-Time Economy pilots, to look critically at the structures involved in supporting the Advisors, the visibility and impact of each in their respective areas, the future roll-out and/or expansion of the pilots and whether a further roll-out is warranted and what needs to be put in place to make this model effective. I have reviewed the recommendations in the Report and recently approved an extension of the pilot until June 2027.
Discussions have now commenced between officials in my Department and local government in relation to the outcomes of the review, and the potential future expansion of the project, with all partners working towards mapping out a pathway forward for a more permanent structure for this valuable initiative.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the expected timeline to sign off and roll out the new Code of Behaviour guidelines for special schools.
reply:
Under section 23 of the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, the Board of Management of each school must prepare and make available a code of behaviour for its students. A code of behaviour specifies the standards of behaviour that shall be observed by each student. The current guidelines to schools on developing a code of behaviour issued from the National Educational Welfare Board in 2008.
The review and updating of the 2008 ‘Developing a code of behaviour guidelines for schools’ is an action in Cineáltas: Action Plan on Bullying. Tusla Education Support Service (TESS) are leading to update the code and to reflect current Department of Education and Youth policies and procedures for schools.
A steering group chaired by TESS was formed and its membership comprised of representatives from the management bodies, unions (teaching and student), parents’ representative body along with officials from my department. A structured systematic consultation processes took place which included children and young people. The updated Code of Behaviour guidelines are nearing finalisation. The rollout of the new Guidelines will be led by TESS and will include supports for schools to assist them in updating their current codes.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline the work being undertaken to standardise all policies and procedures across all special schools.

Special schools are designated as primary schools and are governed by the same policies as these schools. Policies are updated and schools are kept informed of changes by means of circular letter. These circulars are circulated and published on my department's website and are available on gov.ie.
A number of initiatives specifically designed to support special schools have been developed such as those outlined in Circular 0028/2024 which appointed Administrative Deputy Principals and post-primary teachers in special schools. In addition, there are a number of pilots running in a number of special schools nationwide.
The Department endeavours to ensure that policies, resources and supports for schools are underpinned by extensive reviews of research and evidence. Further, the policy-making process is informed by the outcomes of consultations with relevant stakeholders and professionals, including cross sectoral engagements.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth to outline the work she is doing to provide full time behavioural therapists for a school (details supplied); and if work is being undertaken to provide multi-disciplinary teams, comprised of an occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and psychologist for these schools.
reply:
My department is committed to strengthening access to therapy supports for children and young people with special educational needs through the Education Therapy Service (ETS), delivered by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The service provides access to Speech and Language Therapy (SLT) and Occupational Therapy (OT) within school settings, supporting students' communication, participation, independence and learning while also building the capacity of school staff to meet students' needs effectively.
My department recognises that access to therapeutic supports has been a longstanding challenge. Historically, therapy services were provided through the HSE and schools had limited direct access to dedicated educational therapy supports. Following the allocation of funding to establish the ETS, my department has begun building a new model of service delivery from the ground up, representing a significant development in the provision of supports for children with additional needs.
The ETS is currently focused on delivering SLT and OT directly within schools. The service will work closely with school communities, parents and children to maximise participation and engagement in learning and school activities.
Therapists will focus on educationally relevant goals in line with a child’s student support plan while engaging with health services to ensure the best possible outcomes for children and young people. The service complements existing health and disability serv

question: Deputy Jennifer Whitmore asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports available to young people aged 16 and over seeking a post primary school place, given that the educational welfare service does not support those aged 16 and over.
reply:
Under the Education (Welfare) Act, 2000 Educational Welfare Officers (EWOs) of the Child and Family Agency work with young people and their families who are experiencing difficulty with school attendance. The role of an EWO is to work with parents, children/young people and schools to support attendance at school.
The Education (Welfare) Act, 2000, covers a child who has reached the age of 6 years and who;
has not reached the age of 16 years, or
has not completed 3 years of post-primary education, whichever occurs later.
The Educational Welfare Service (EWS) is a statutory service covering approximately 4,000 schools nationally, both DEIS and non-DEIS, and both primary and post-primary.
The EWS will provide advice to the parents of a child over the age of 16 years who are seeking a post-primary school place. If a parent requires advice at any time, they can contact the local EWS regional office for their area. Contact details are available at the following link: www.tusla.ie/get-in-touch/education-and-welfare/.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether, in light of the Department's promotion of physical activity through the Active School Flag and ‘Run Around the EU’ Challenge, she will commit to instructing schools to discontinue formal school uniforms and adopt comfortable, practical and cost-effective alternatives, including tracksuits or suitable leisurewear, which facilitate physical activity and reduce costs for families.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, Circular 0032/2017 is currently being reviewed. In addition to a focus on reducing costs for parents, the review is looking at the comfort and sustainability of school uniforms. My officials will continue to engage with the education partners, including the National Parents Council, as we progress this important work.
Ultimately, decisions on school uniforms are a matter for individual schools and Boards of Management. The decision whether to have a uniform in a school is entirely the prerogative of the individual school and my department has no input in this regard.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth if consideration has been given to the development of a HIQA type section of the inspectorate in her Department.
reply:
Consideration has not been given to the development of a HIQA-type section in the Inspectorate of my Department. The Inspectorate operates predominantly as an educational evaluation and improvement service, working across Early Learning and Care settings, schools and other centres for education. It provides for quality assurance of the Irish education system experienced by children and young people from birth to eighteen years; and it fulfils an accountability remit and regulatory and compliance functions, as set out in the Education Act 1998 and in the published Inspection Policy (DEY, 2025).
HIQA functions as an independent regulator concerned with safety, statutory compliance and risk in health and social care services. The operational contexts of the two organisations are quite different, and they deliver on their statutory functions differently.
A key driver of quality and standards within the Inspectorate and across schools, settings and centres, is the Inspectorate’s Evaluation Support and Research Unit (ESRU). It designs and publishes the research procedures, standards, survey tools and quality criteria that underpin the Inspectorate’s evaluative and advisory work. This work is research-informed and evidence-based. ESRU draws on the expertise of inspectors in policy support roles to ensure that inspection procedures are based soundly on expert research and latest curriculum developments. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Education and Youth if consideration could be given to the special circumstances surrounding a school transport issue (details supplied).
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
The National Council for Special Education acts in an advisory role to the Department on the suitability of placements for children with special educational needs. Under the terms of the School Transport Scheme for Children with Special Educational Needs, the Department will consider the report of the Special Education Needs Organiser (SENO). School transport is provided to children with special educational needs who are attending the nearest school to their place of residence that is or can be resourced to meet their educational needs, as identified by the SENO.
The Department and Bus Éireann are very conscious of the specialised nature of transport provision for children with special educational needs. This is reflected in the standard of dedicated service provided and the fact that these services are generally planned and timetabled to operate on a door-to-door basis. In certain cases, the Department also provides funding to schools for the employment of escorts to accompany children whose care and safety needs require this level of support while they travel to and from school.

reply:

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Education and Youth the intervention that is required where a student remains on a reduced timetable while awaiting a recommended special class placement; the way compliance with reduced school day guidelines is monitored; and the ways her Department ensures that a shortage of suitable placements does not result in prolonged loss of teaching time.
reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government, my Department and the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported in mainstream schools, while special classes and special schools provide additional supports for students with more complex needs. This approach is guided by the principle of inclusion and supporting students to receive an education in the most appropriate setting for their needs.
The Department's position is that all students should attend school for the full school day wherever possible. Reduced School Days should only be used in exceptional, limited and time-bound circumstances and must not be used as a substitute for an appropriate placement or the supports required to meet a student's needs.
Where a student remains on a Reduced School Day while awaiting a special class placement, schools are encouraged to engage with the NCSE, the National Educational Psychology Service (NEPS) and the Tusla Educational Support Service (TESS) to identify supports that may facilitate full-time attendance. Through data-sharing arrangements between TESS and the NCSE, SENOs are notified when a student with special educational needs commences a Reduced School Day and can work with schools to identify additional supports and interventions.

reply:
Enabling students with special educational needs to receive an education that meets their needs is a priority for this Government. It is also a key priority for me, my department and for the National Council for Special Education (NCSE).
The vast majority of students with special educational needs are supported to attend mainstream classes with their peers. Where students with more complex needs require additional supports, special class and special school places are provided. This is in keeping with policy on an inclusive education, which promotes that students will be supported to receive an education in the most inclusive setting possible.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she can provide an update on the allocation of the €4 million capital allocation for Youth Affairs for her Department for 2026; if she can provide a timeline for the process including when the calls were issued and deadlines for applying; the number of applications made; and if the full allocation will be used.
reply:
The Department of Education and Youth is committed to supporting the delivery of high-quality youth work and non-formal developmental opportunities to young people.
In this regard, there has been a significant increase in dedicated capital funding for the youth sector which will be aligned with the National Development Plan (NDP) framework. Youth capital funding of €4 million will be available annually to support the youth sector from 2026 to 2030. This annual capital allocation represents a significant increase of €3.5 million on the 2025 allocation and an enhancement on the annual youth capital allocations of recent years.
The 2026 youth capital funding scheme was launched in July and notified to eligible youth organisations and youth services with clear guidance documentation on the operation of the scheme and application process provided. The application deadlines were in August and September, depending on the relevant funding stream.
The €4 million funding available in 2026 will be utilised to support the purchase of essential equipment, upgrades to youth facilities and digital infrastructure for youth organisations and youth services.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth the way in which her Department intends to ensure that the NDP allocation for Youth Affairs to 2030 is rolled out in a way that ensures that youth spaces and places are provided, upgraded or expanded; and if she is confident that the funding scheme will be delivered in a way that is accessible to youth organisations in terms of the application process and deadlines to apply and spend the funds.
reply:
The department places a high value on both formal and non-formal education, recognising that youth work provides unique developmental, social and participative opportunities for young people that complement and enhance outcomes achieved through the formal education system.
Youth capital investment of €20 million over the period 2026 to 2030 will support development and sustainability and this funding represents a significant increase on the annual youth capital allocations of recent years.
The NDP Sectoral Investment Plan funding of €20 million for the youth sector was informed by the level and type of demand for capital expenditure within the sector over recent years and with a view to providing more capacity to continue targeted investment in essential upgrades to youth facilities, equipment, and digital infrastructure in a modern youth work environment.
The overarching vision is to ensure that young people have access to safe, inclusive, fit-for-purpose spaces that support meaningful engagement, development, and participation. This framework marks the first time that the youth sector has had clear visibility and certainty regarding capital funding over a multi year period.
Importantly, establishing a defined capital envelope under the NDP provides a predictable basis for planning, allowing the youth sector to prepare projects in a structured and strategic way. It also supports value for money and a coherent long term development of youth facilities nationally.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth the ways that the ETS and CDNT services are designed to work alongside one another in a complimentary fashion.
reply:
As you are aware, in line with the 2025 programme for Government, there is a commitment to introduce a national therapy service in education settings. The Education Plan 2025, which was announced on the 19th of June 2025, confirmed Government approval for the establishment of the Education Therapy Service (ETS).
The ETS is an additional support for children with special education need and has been established as a critical and important support for children and young people in their school environment. It is to supplement and not replace family centred supports provided by existing children’s health and disability services.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) ETS and Health services therapists have distinct but complementary roles and will work together, where appropriate, to provide coordinated support for children and young people.
NCSE ETS therapists focus on educationally relevant needs within the school context, while HSE and HSE-funded services continue to provide support within their established scopes of service, including the child and family context. A child or young person may receive support from both services where needs arise across different contexts.
Since the establishment of the ETS work has been ongoing with existing services to ensure alignment and integration with these services. A Health and Education Oversight Group has been established for the ETS. This group provides strategic leadership across both sectors.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update in relation to progress on a new school building (details supplied).
reply:
The brief for the project referred to by the Deputy is to provide a new 16 classroom Special school including the demolition of some existing buildings. It also includes the retention of an extension completed in 2012.
The major building project for the school is currently at an advanced stage of architectural planning – Stage 2(b) Detailed Design, where the Design Team have secured all statutory approvals and are preparing the suite of tender documents.
My Department remains committed to progressing this matter and will make contact in the coming days to arrange a meeting with the School Principal and relevant stakeholders.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Education and Youth her plans to address the teacher shortage in a school (details supplied).
reply:
This Government is committed to ensuring that every child has a positive school experience, with access to qualified and engaged teachers who are dedicated to supporting their learning.

The staffing arrangements include a provision whereby schools experiencing rapid increases in enrolment can apply for additional permanent mainstream posts, using projected enrolment. The school has been allocated a post on this basis and will retain the post, pending confirmation of enrolment of 141 pupils on 30 September. Information and application forms are available in Circular 0025/2026.
Teaching is an attractive profession, and there are a significant number of newly qualified teachers graduating annually. Over 1,800 newly qualified primary teachers registered with the Teaching Council in 2025 and CAO data for 2026 shows a consistent demand for undergraduate ITE programmes. Salaries are competitive, starting at €45,833 and rising to €84,412 under the current pay deal. Few teachers resign, with less than 3% of the teaching workforce resigning or retiring annually from contracted teaching posts.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Education and Youth for an update on the progress of a schools additional special classroom accommodation (details supplied).
reply:
The school referred to by the Deputy was approved to enter the Department’s pipeline of school buildings under the Additional School Accommodation Scheme for a project providing a three-classroom special educational needs base. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery.
The project is currently at Stage 2b, Detailed Design. During this stage, statutory approvals are obtained and the project design is further progressed to reflect any conditions of planning.
The project remains at Stage 2b. In order for the Department to assess the project's readiness to progress to tender, an updated cost plan is required reflecting any cost implications arising from the planning process and associated planning conditions.
Until this information has been submitted and reviewed by the Department, it is not possible to determine whether the project is ready to progress to tender and, consequently, it is not possible to provide a definitive timeline for the project's advancement. Any progression to the next phase will be subject to the satisfactory review of the required documentation and the project being considered in the context of the prioritisation framework under the National Development Plan.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Education and Youth further to Parliamentary Question No. 66822/26, if she will provide a timeline for the establishment of the Workforce Advisory Group; and the timeline that exists for the Strategy to be developed.
reply:
Action 7 in Opportunities for Youth: National Strategy for Youth Work and Related Services 2024-2028 is to produce a Workforce Development Strategy in respect of the youth work sector. This strategy will include consideration of training needs and the requirement for high-quality, accessible and inclusive youth work services and opportunities. Support for youth workers emerged as a strong theme in the consultation with the youth work sector as part of the development for Opportunities for Youth.
In advance of the development of the strategy a consultation with the youth work sector was undertaken and included a survey of the workforce and an employer questionnaire which were followed by 11 in-person and online sector consultations.
It is proposed that the development of the Workforce Development Strategy, will be supported by a workforce advisory group. The exact makeup of this oversight structure is currently being advanced. Engagement with the National Youth Council of Ireland regarding the establishment of the workforce advisory group, including its membership, is underway.
It is proposed that this group, which will include representatives from across the sector, will work with the department to prepare the Workforce Development Strategy and support the implementation of the strategy over the coming years. It is intended that this group will be established and meet this year, at which point a timeline for development of the strategy will be agreed.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department will conduct an audit of community special schools in light of the recent reports of substandard facilities and service.

It also emphasises the critical requirement to maximise the use of existing school accommodation.
The optimisation of existing school capacity is a key aspect of the department’s infrastructure strategy. This supports an inclusive approach, addresses climate objectives and ensures value for money, recognising the many competing demands across the programme. Modular projects are targeted in contexts where existing capacity is not sufficient to deliver on school place requirements. This approach has been taken in undertaking repurposing works in a number of community special schools, as well as in existing school buildings that facilitated the establishment of new community special schools in recent years.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to address the minimum working hours for retail workers (details supplied).
reply:
While the facility to change the existing hours of work of employees is a matter which can be agreed between the employer and the employee, Ireland’s Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 and the Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 provide important provisions to improve job security and working conditions for part-time workers and for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles.
The Protection of Employees (Part-Time Work) Act 2001 is accompanied by a Workplace Relations Commission Code of Practice on Access to Part-Time Work which states that, as far as possible, employers should give consideration to requests by employees to transfer from full-time to part-time work; and requests by employees to transfer from part-time to full-time work-or to increase their working time should the opportunity arise.
The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 is a significant piece of Irish legislation aimed at improving job security and working conditions, particularly for employees in precarious or variable-hour roles. The 2018 Act inserted banded hours provisions into the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997. Under the legislation, employees whose actual hours differ from their contract can request to be placed in a band of weekly hours that reflects their average over the previous 12 months. Employers must respond within 4 weeks and can only refuse under specific conditions.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider a review of legislation to ensure there is a statutory right to a minimum bereavement leave.
reply:
There is currently no form of statutory bereavement leave in Ireland. Bereavement leave is normally addressed through employment contracts and can be negotiated between employers and employees when entering into contracts of employment. Employers may also grant bereavement leave at their discretion if their employees suffer the bereavement of close family members.
The introduction of any new form of broad-based employment rights or leave entitlements require careful consideration to ensure that the needs of employees are adequately met and to assess impacts for employers. There is currently no commitment in the Programme for Government to introduce bereavement leave for the loss of a family member.
