question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the estimated annual cost to the Exchequer of reducing the VAT rate on agricultural diesel from 13.5% to 9%.
reply:
The VAT treatment of goods and services is subject to EU VAT law, with which Irish VAT law is obliged to comply. In general, the EU VAT Directive provides that all goods and services are liable to VAT at the standard rate, unless they fall within the categories of goods and services specified in Annex III of the VAT Directive, in respect of which Member States may apply a lower rate of VAT.
Motor fuels are not included in the categories of goods and services for which the EU Directive allows a lower rate of VAT, and so they are generally liable to VAT at the Member State’s standard rate, which in Ireland is currently 23%.
However, the Directive also allows that a Member State may retain a historic VAT treatment that it had in place, subject to certain strict conditions, and on this basis, Ireland continues to apply its reduced VAT rate, currently 13.5%, to the supply of marked gas oil (commonly known as ‘agricultural diesel’ or ‘green diesel’). Under the conditions imposed by the Directive, the rate is ‘parked’, which means that it cannot be reduced below 12%. If a good or service is removed from the parked rate arrangement, it can only be subject to VAT at the standard rate.
Therefore, Ireland does not have scope under EU law to apply its second reduced VAT rate of 9% to agricultural diesel, as proposed by the Deputy. Furthermore, the Directive limits a Member State to having no more than the two reduced rates we already operate, so it would not be possible for Ireland to ap

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if it is proposed to expedite the signing of a double taxation agreement between the Government of Ireland and the Government of Barbados.
reply:
Ireland's long-standing policy has been to expand, maintain, and enhance Ireland's tax treaty network to remove barriers and facilitate trade. Ireland has signed 78 comprehensive tax treaties, of which 75 are currently in effect. Ireland remains open to assess all options to develop its tax treaty network further in that context.
Ireland published a Tax Treaty Policy Statement (https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/irelands-tax-treaty-policy-statement.pdf) in 2022 and the statement formalises the policy of maintaining and enhancing the network of double tax agreements to provide for continued economic prosperity. The statement also provides the criteria for the creation of a priority list of potential partners.
Priority A jurisdictions for Ireland are the members of the G20. Priority B is to have tax treaties in place with all current OECD member countries and accession countries, as well as EU accession countries. Priority C is to modernise Ireland’s older tax treaties which may not be fully in line with recent treaties and current international norms.
These criteria assist in identifying and prioritising future tax treaty negotiations generally. It is Irish policy that the status of any current or future double tax treaty negotiations remain strictly confidential. Therefore, I am unfortunately unable to update you on the specific status of any current negotiation, or the possible timeframe of any future negotiation.

reply:
The Central Credit Register (CCR) is a database operated by the Central Bank of Ireland under the Credit Reporting Act 2013.
It stores personal and credit information on loans of €500 or more and produces credit reports on request to lenders and borrowers.
Lenders are obliged to report information that is accurate, complete and up to date and the consent of the borrower is not required for this.
Credit information submitted by lenders in respect of loan agreements is held on the CCR for a period of a maximum of five years at any given time.
Where all of the liabilities under a loan agreement have been repaid, written off or discharged, credit information continues to be held on the CCR for a period of five years.
If a borrower defaults or ceases to make repayments and the loan has not been repaid, written off or discharged, then information in respect of that loan agreement may continue to be reported to the CCR.
However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a range of measures were implemented to support borrowers experiencing payment difficulties.
Borrowers were offered flexible loan repayment arrangements, including payment breaks of up to six months on mortgages and other loans for personal borrowers impacted by COVID-19.
The Central Bank has advised that it worked to ensure that COVID-19-related payment breaks operated in borrowers' best interests and in line with regulatory requirements.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance whether he intends to review the current Capital Acquisitions Tax rules, which provide for differing tax-free thresholds depending on the relationship between a beneficiary and the disponer; the policy rationale for retaining these distinctions; the estimated Exchequer cost of equalising the applicable thresholds; and whether options for reform are being examined as part of preparations for budget 2027.
reply:
Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) is a tax which applies to both gifts and inheritances and is charged at a rate of 33%. For CAT purposes, the relationship between the person giving a gift or inheritance and the person who receives it determines the maximum amount, known as the “Group threshold”, below which CAT does not arise. The group thresholds were most recently increased in Budget 2027.
The Group A threshold increased to €420,000 from €400,000. This threshold applies where the beneficiary is a child of the disponer. This includes adopted children, stepchildren and some foster children. Parents may also fall within this threshold where they take an inheritance from a child.
The Group B threshold increased to €44,000 from €44,000. This threshold applies where the beneficiary is a brother, sister, niece, nephew, or lineal ancestor or lineal descendant of the disponer. Following recent changes made to Capital Acquisitions Tax legislation, the Group B threshold also applies to persons who receive gifts and inheritances from the wider family of their foster parents, for example, from their foster siblings, uncles, aunts and grandparents.
The Group C threshold increased to €22,000 from €20,000 with this threshold applying to all other cases.
My Department produced a Tax Strategy Paper that sets out the policy rationale for retaining these distinctions and the estimated cost to of equalising the applicable threshold which is linked here:
https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/01a7

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport whether students resident in the State who attend recognised third-level institutions in Northern Ireland are eligible for a student or young adult TFI Leap card; if not, the rationale for excluding such students, given that students resident in Northern Ireland attending third-level institutions in the State may avail of the scheme; and whether he considers this approach equitable.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. The National Transport Authority has responsibility for the regulation of fares charged to passengers in respect of public transport services provided under public service obligation (PSO) contracts.
Third level students travelling from the South to third level institutions in Northern Ireland can avail of the 50% student/YAC reduction on the proportion of the journey carried out in the South. This means, for example, if 90% of the journey is through the South and the remaining 10% is through Northern Ireland, then the 50% discount will just apply to the 90% of the journey that is carried out within the State. The discount does not apply to the element of the journey that is carried out outside of the State.
The Young Adult Card initiative is an opt-in Scheme, meaning that while the discount is available on all PSO services, it is only available on those commercial bus operators that have decided to participate in the Scheme.
It is also important to note the National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for the regulation and approval of fares on public transport services operated under Public Service Obligation (PSO) contracts, within Ireland only. This includes determining fare structures and available ticket products for eligible passengers, such as those using Student Leap Cards and Young Adult (YAC) Leap Cards, across PSO-funded services.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport if the European Union’s clean corporate vehicle proposal to set binding national targets for the number of electric vehicles in corporate fleets from 2030 is achievable; and if he believes that Ireland will be in the position to achieve the target set out in the European Union’s clean corporate vehicle proposal.
reply:
The proposal on Clean Corporate Vehicles forms part of the European Commission’s Automotive Package, published on 16 December 2025. It is designed to accelerate the transition to zero and low emission corporate fleets, reduce fossil fuel expenditure in road transport and accelerate the availability of zero emission vehicles on the second-hand market.
Ireland supports the objectives of the Clean Corporate Vehicles proposal, recognising the significant role that corporate vehicles play in accelerating the uptake of zero emission vehicles and in driving wider market transformation.
Many Member States, including Ireland, are relying heavily on a rapid transition to deliver on their decarbonisation plans. Ireland’s Climate Action Plan target is to have 30% of the national vehicle fleet be electric by 2030. This is Ireland’s single biggest transport mitigation action up to 2030.
The current Commission proposal includes a 58% minimum 2030 target for the share of zero-emission vehicles among large undertakings, while allowing Member States flexibility regarding the implementation pathway. It is important to note that the measure remains at proposal stage, with negotiations underway at EU level. The Regulation will not be finalised until agreement is reached between the Council and the European Parliament, a process that has not yet concluded.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the position of the Government on the European Commission's Savings and Investments Union Strategy and associated proposals, including the Commission's recommendation on savings and investment accounts; whether Ireland has sought or secured an opt out from any element of those proposals.
reply:
Consideration of the proposed Investment Account is taking place in the context of the EU Savings and Investments Union project (SIU). The Savings and Investments Union (SIU) is a flagship project within EU financial services policy. It aims to deepen and further integrate Europe’s capital markets, support growth, and enhance the resilience of the financial system. SIU is the umbrella term for the Capital Market Union and the Banking Union, and it is initiative a key priority for this Commission’s legislative term.
The main aim of SIU is to help European citizens to invest more to ensure that they have better financial outcomes and are better provided for in the future. Furthermore, the project also seeks to deepen the pools of capital that can be made available for investment purposes to ultimately grow the European economy. In March 2025, the European Commission launched the SIU Strategy, which included discrete measures to advance the SIU project. From the outset, Ireland has been a strong supporter of the SIU and its objectives.
Since the publication of the SIU Strategy in March 2025, the European Commission has been active in bringing forward a number of legislative and non-legislative reforms that were announced in the Strategy, including reviews of the Securitisation Framework and the Supplementary Pensions Framework as well as the Market Integration and Supervision Package.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if consideration has been given to the policy of introducing a personal tax credit for people with a disability in employment.
reply:
The Government recognises the significant financial pressures experienced by households with disabilities, particularly amid the heightened cost?of?living conditions of recent years. In response, we have implemented targeted budget measures designed to support those most vulnerable.
When this Government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families, in line with our Programme for Government commitments.
There are currently a number of tax measures within the tax system that support people with disabilities and carers, this includes Tax Relief for Health Expenses which provides relief to individuals who have incurred costs in respect of qualifying health expenses and the Blind Person’s Tax Credit, which is available to a blind person or a person who has impaired vision.
There are more than 346,000 people with disabilities in Ireland who are already in work. They are contributing to our economy, supporting their families and communities, and making an enormous contribution to our country.
Recognising there is a significant gap in participation, over the course of the next year, the Government is committed to examining what further measures can be taken to recognise the contribution of those who are already working while doing more to remove the barriers faced by those who want to enter or remain in employment.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of individual taxpayers who have paid tax as a result of the so-called "deemed disposal" rule in relation to exchange traded funds in each year since it was introduced; and the total tax revenue generated in each year.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. Similarly, as respects investments in certain Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds in respect of which investors are required to self-assess tax due, taxpayers are not required to separately report data for each category of chargeable event when filing their tax return.
On the basis of the information available to Revenue work undertaken in the context of Budget 2026, and based on tax paid over the last eight years at the time it was examined, if it was assumed that 100% of tax paid by funds in respect of unit holders, tax paid by life companies in respect of policy holders, and income tax accounted for by individuals in respect of their investments in Irish domiciled funds, offshore funds and life products

reply:

• No minimum contribution requirement.
• Maximum annual contribution limit.
• One account per person.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport If his attention has been drawn to the actions of the French government which has introduced a specific penalty of €100 per tonne for non-compliance with CORSIA offsetting obligations together with the possibility of an operating ban; whether the Government will introduce an equivalent national penalty for non-compliance with CORSIA that is consistent with the excess emissions penalty applicable under the EU ETS, in order to ensure that Irish airlines operate on a level playing field with competitors in other Member States and to support the integrity of multilateral climate action.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 93 together.
The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) was adopted by ICAO in 2016 as a global market-based measure to address CO? emissions from international aviation. The scheme requires airlines to offset emissions above an agreed baseline and is being implemented in three phases: a Pilot Phase (2021-2023), Phase I (2024-2026) and Phase II (2027-2035). Participation is voluntary during the first two phases, while from 2027 the scheme will apply more broadly, subject to certain exemptions, including for Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States and Landlocked Developing Countries. Ireland, together with all EU Member States, has participated in CORSIA since its commencement. Participation has continued to expand, with 130 States participating in the scheme from 1 January 2026.
CORSIA enters Phase II from 1 January 2027 during which participation will be determined based on 2018 Revenue Tonne Kilometres (RTK) data. As a result, participation is anticipated to expand further to 134 States as Brazil, China, India and the Russian Federation will come into scope for participation.
Within the EU, both CORSIA and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are implemented through Directive 2003/87/EC. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the measures in place to ensure quicker recognition of driving licences of bus and truck drivers from outside the European economic area.
reply:
The exchange of non-EU driving licences is managed through the National Driver Licence Service, the provision of which is delegated under national legislation to the Road Safety Authority. The requirements of the licensing process, including licence exchange, are available on www.ndls.ie.
There are various factors which can affect the time it takes to process licence exchange applications. For example, the applicant may need to submit outstanding information, such as a medical or eyesight report, or the physical driving licence itself in the case of an online application.
The most common reason for delays is in verification of the driving licence by the other licensing authority. However, it is vital, to protect the safety of Irish road users and the integrity of the Irish licensing system, that the validity of a driving licence presented for exchange can be verified.
Neither I nor my officials have any role in the exchange application process. Therefore, I have therefore referred your query regarding the exchange of bus and truck licences to the Authority for direct reply. Please contact my office if a response is not provided within 10 working days.

question: D'fhiafraigh Deputy Conor Sheehan den Aire Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail, agus Gaeltachta an bhfuil sé i gceist ag a Roinn tacú leis an togra le haghaidh Gaelchampas don Earnáil Phoiblí i gCarna; cad iad na céimeanna coincréiteacha atá á dtógáil ag an Roinn chun scrúdú a dhéanamh ar an dréachtmholadh siollabais agus ar an gcostáil atá curtha chun cinn ag an nGrúpa Oibre; agus an ndéanfaidh sé ráiteas ina thaobh.
reply:

Tá critéir incháilithe agus coinníollacha bainteach leis an chlár agus tá eolas faoin gclár sin le fáil ar shuíomh mo Roinne. Tá an clár seo oscailte d'iarratais don bhliain ar fad agus níl aon spriocdháta faoi leith ann chun iarratas a dhéanamh.

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the amount of ORIS funding that has been allocated to Tipperary County Council for each of the years 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
The Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS) provides funding under several measures for the development of new outdoor recreational infrastructure and for the necessary repair, enhancement or promotion of existing outdoor recreation infrastructure in countryside areas across Ireland. This includes walking trails, cycleways, mountain access routes and facilities at rivers, lakes and beaches.
My department continues to provide substantial investment in outdoor recreation across Ireland, including in County Tipperary. Since 2022, over €3 million has been allocated to Tipperary County Council to support the delivery of 30 projects.
Applications are now open for the 2026/2027 Outdoor Recreation & Infrastructure Scheme under measures 2 and 3, which refer to projects with funding of up to €200,000 and €500,000 respectively. The deadline for applications for smaller projects under measure 1 and the project development measure has now passed and my officials are reviewing these applications.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if the impact of these transport challenges on student participation, retention and educational opportunity has been assessed; the measures being considered to support affected students.
reply:
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026–2035, published in March of this year, recognises the relationship between accommodation availability and student commuting patterns.
The Strategy highlights the need to address long and unsustainable student commutes through greater integration of accommodation, transport planning and sustainable mobility initiatives. It recognises that excessive commuting can create barriers to accessing and participating in higher education and sets out measures to better understand and address these challenges through improved data collection, coordinated planning and cross-sectoral collaboration.
In particular, the Strategy includes commitments to support higher education institutions (HEIs) in developing sustainable commuting policies, improving understanding of student travel behaviours and strengthening engagement with relevant transport stakeholders. HEIs are encouraged to use data-driven insights to assess student mobility needs and support more efficient and sustainable commuting, while participating in sustainable transport initiatives and promoting active travel and public transport options.
The Strategy also provides for a pilot programme aimed at strengthening collaboration between HEIs, the National Transport Authority (NTA), local authorities and transport operators. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the progress that has been made in acquiring lands for a third level institution in Swords County Dublin; if a site has been identified and purchased; and the exact location.
reply:
Dublin and Dún Laoghaire ETB (DDLETB) are currently being supported by SOLAS in developing their Preliminary Business Case for their proposal under the FET College Major Capital Programme.
The site preference for this new college is Swords due to its population base and future growth projections. A site option was previously identified but unfortunately despite the best efforts of DDLETB, they were not able to complete the legal and site due diligence on the site due to a number of issues remaining outstanding including access and site boundaries.
I understand that DDLETB are currently working closely with the Local Authority towards the identification of other sites in the Swords area, suitable for this FET College. A meeting is being arranged this week between my officials, the Local Authority and DDLETB to progress this.
SOLAS and my department will endeavour to continue to support DDLETB in progressing this major capital project which will deliver key FET infrastructure to meet the needs of learners in Fingal and surrounding areas.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide funding for public owned college student accommodation in Tralee, County Kerry, given that currently all student beds in Tralee are privately owned.
reply:
The Government recognises the importance of ensuring an adequate supply of affordable and sustainable student accommodation across all regions, including Tralee, County Kerry.
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026–2035, published in March 2026, provides the framework for increasing student accommodation capacity, improving affordability and supporting the long-term delivery of student accommodation nationwide. The Strategy notes that lessons were learned following a Short-Term Activation Programme, which provided Government funding to assist in the delivery of around 1,000 new PBSA beds., namely that the cost per bed under the programme indicated a funding level that would be untenable for the State, given the projected requirement of 42,000 addition student beds by 2035.
A key initiative under the Student Accommodation Strategy is the Higher Education Institution Student Accommodation Programme (HSAP), which is being advanced by my Department in partnership with the Higher Education Authority and the National Development Finance Agency. The programme will assist HEIs in securing additional Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA) capacity, through private development, delivering accommodation on or near campus via nomination agreements, licensed sites, and site servicing arrangements.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to the ongoing delays in registration of students at Technological University Dublin following on from issues with result delays earlier this year; and the action that has been taken to resolve this issue.
reply:
Thank you, Deputy, for your question.
I am aware of issues raised earlier this academic year regarding the publication of some examination results and the associated timing of registration for certain students at Technological University Dublin (TU Dublin). However, at this point in time I understand that those issues have been resolved.
As the Deputy will no doubt be aware, TU Dublin is an autonomous higher education institution under the Technological Universities Act 2018 and, as such, is responsible for the management of its academic and administrative affairs, including student registration and the administration of examinations.
Nevertheless, my officials have engaged with the HEA to seek updates from TU Dublin in relation to these matters.
As of 18th September, TU Dublin confirmed 93% of the overall student cohort had been issued an invitation to register (ITR). The University also clarified that students who have not yet received an ITR continue to have full access to the University’s facilities and resources while awaiting the completion of the relevant results and registration processes. Arrangements were also in place to facilitate access to learning materials for students awaiting registration.

reply:

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to increase the support for dyslexic students in third level education.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 728, 729 and 730 together.
Under the National Access Plan (NAP) 2022-2028 inclusion and diversity in the student body in Higher Education is a key priority.
The Plan has identified a number of priority-groups who continue to be underrepresented in higher education including students with disabilities.
The Programme for Access to Higher Education (PATH) is the main funding stream that supports the implementation of the NAP. PATH is delivered through five strands that work together to widen participation and support student success, with PATH 4 targeting those with disabilities.
Targets in the NAP for new entrant students with a disability are set at 16% by 2028, and we have reached this at the midterm point of the plan with current figures at 16.3%.
The main source of funding for Students with disabilities is the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) which allocates funding to HEIs for the provision of services and supports to full- and part-time students with disabilities. The FSD provides supports for students with dyslexia, autism and mild general learning difficulties among a wide range of disabilities which are supported by the fund.
The FSD aims to ensure that students with disabilities have the necessary supports and equipment to enable them to access, fully participate in and successfully complete their chosen course of study. In Budget 2026 I increased funding by €1m bringing the total annual fund in higher education to over €10.5m

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health whether the free HRT scheme will be extended to cover hormone replacement therapy for patients with congenital or permanent endocrine conditions, including testosterone replacement for Klinefelter syndrome.
reply:
The HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. This arises from the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted marketing authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA). Pharmaceutical companies must apply to the HSE for reimbursement.
Under the Free Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) arrangement, which came into effect on 1 June 2025, where a woman has been prescribed a HRT product on the reimbursement list by her healthcare provider for the purpose of alleviating the symptoms associated with all stages of menopause, the cost of the HRT medications or products, and the dispensing fees will be met by the State.
This measure is intended to support the management of the symptoms of menopause and, therefore, relates to the provision of treatment for a specific medical condition/life stage i.e. menopause. HRT is the most commonly used treatment for managing symptoms of menopause and has shown to be the most effective intervention.
Menopause has been highlighted as a key priority area by the Women’s Health Taskforce. It is a key action in the Women’s Health Action Plans. A number of measures have been implemented in recent years to improve the experience of menopause for women in Ireland, including this HRT arrangement.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health the action the HSE and HPRA are taking on the current supply shortage of budesonide orodispersible tablets in the State.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), as the competent authority in Ireland for coordinating the management of medicine shortages, has advised that it has received no notifications indicating a current supply interruption affecting Jorveza (budesonide orodispersible tablets).
Ireland has a multi-stakeholder Medicines Shortages Framework, operated by the HPRA, through which the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the HPRA and other stakeholders work together to help prevent and mitigate medicine shortages and minimise any impact on patients.
Marketing authorisation holders are required to report actual and anticipated medicine shortages to the HPRA. Where a shortage is reported, details are assessed by the HPRA and published on its publicly available medicines shortages database.
Patients who are experiencing difficulty obtaining their medication should consult their healthcare professional, such as their GP or pharmacist.

reply:
Opening the National Children’s Hospital Ireland (NCHI) is a top priority. Whilst waiting for construction to conclude, there is a significant ongoing programme of work to prepare for the opening of the hospital, involving preparation for operational commissioning, implementation of the EHR, and the integration of current service and staffing in advance of transition.
The National Oversight Group (NOG), chaired by the Secretary General with membership including the HSE CEO, oversees and monitors the progress of the NCHI Project and Programme. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the steps being taken to protect and expand midwife led continuity of care services, including the Domino scheme and home birth service at Cork University Maternity Hospital, in line with the National Maternity Strategy.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. The DOMINO Scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital remains operational and available both to women currently using the service and to new patients who meet the eligibility criteria. Their decisions are underpinned by detailed analysis of existing services, including operational metrics, performance trends, and customer feedback, and also take account of competing funding pressures, affordability considerations, and broader public transport priorities to ensure resources are targeted where they deliver the greatest benefit.

question: Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to reduce waiting times for endometriosis assessment and specialist treatment in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 686, 687 and 688 together.
On 18 October 2025, I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. The Framework sets out for the first time in Ireland a defined clinical pathway for women with endometriosis, which spans primary to secondary care to specialist complex care in tertiary settings.
Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain. The Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Health if her Department is considering measures aimed at reducing the financial burden on coeliac sufferers who must abide by a gluten free diet.
reply:
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical items, in accordance with the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
In line with the 2013 Act and the national framework agreed with industry, a company must submit an application to the HSE to have a new medicine added to the formal Reimbursement list. In making a relevant reimbursement decision, the HSE is required under the Act to have regard to a number of criteria including efficacy, the health needs of the public, cost effectiveness and potential or actual budget impact.
Gluten-free products were removed from the list of reimbursable items under the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme, with several other products, in September 2012. The marketplace has evolved whereby such products are widely available in supermarkets at a more reasonable price than was historically costed to the State when they were available in pharmacies through the statutory schemes, and without incurring the further extra costs of a dispensing fee. There are currently no plans to reinstate these products on the list of reimbursable items under the GMS and other community drug schemes.
Patients can claim tax relief for certain food products if they have specific dietary requirements due to a medical condition. This applies to persons with coeliac disease where they require gluten free foods specifically manufactured to be gluten free.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Health the advice that she can provide to a person (details supplied) resident in Monaghan who has contacted every GP in the county and has been unable to register with a GP for them and their child.
reply:
GPs are private practitioners, most of whom hold a GMS contract with the HSE for the provision of GP services without charge to medical card and GP visit card holders. Eligibility for a medical card, or a GP visit card for those aged between 8 and 69 years of age, is primarily based on means testing. All children under 8 years of age and all those aged 70 years and over are eligible for a GP visit card.
Where a person that holds a medical card or GP visit card, or a person eligible for either card, experiences difficulty in finding a GP to accept them as a patient, the person concerned having unsuccessfully applied to at least three GPs in the area (or fewer if there are fewer GPs in the area) can apply to the HSE Eligibility Unit which has the power to assign a GMS patient to a GP's GMS patient list, in accordance with the GMS contract. Likewise, a parent on behalf of an eligible child who experiences difficulty in finding a GP that will accept their child as a patient can apply to the HSE Eligibility Unit also.
People who do not hold a medical card or GP visit card access GP services on a private basis and can make enquiries directly to any GP practice they wish to register with. As private practitioners, it is a matter for each individual GP to decide whether to accept additional private patients.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health the total capital expenditure incurred by the HSE and her Department on the development of day-surgery centres and elective hospitals in each year from 2020 to date, by site; the estimated final project cost for each completed, active and planned facility; and the expected opening date of each facility.
reply:
Since its approval by Government in December 2021, the Elective Ambulatory Care Programme has been evolving to ensure that medium term demand and capacity for elective day-case care can be met through the delivery of a national network of nine Surgical Hubs in the first instance, while also planning for future elective care capacity requirements through a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (ETCs), also known as Elective Hospitals, in Cork, Galway and Dublin.
Four Surgical Hubs are now operational in Tallaght (the Reeves Centre), South Dublin (Mt Carmel), North Dublin (Swords) and Cork, with Hubs at Waterford, Limerick and Galway due to open in the coming months. Plans are also advancing for Surgical Hubs in Sligo and Letterkenny. Together these nine Hubs will provide significant additional elective care capacity across the country, including 30 day-case theatres, 16 minor operations theatres, and 38 outpatient diagnostic/treatment rooms, and will help drive down waiting times for elective day-case care.
The Elective Treatment Centres, also known as Elective Hospitals, are being developed to meet the longer term elective care needs of the country. Locations identified are in Cork (at St Stephen’s Hospital, Glanmire), Galway (Merlin Park) and Dublin (emerging preferred sites previously identified at Connolly Hospital in Blanchardstown and at Crumlin-Children’s Health Ireland). The HSE is continuing to progress the detailed design works for the ETCs in Cork and Galwa

The strategy marks a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland, representing the development of a unified approach to the delivery of diabetes care.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport if he is satisfied that the regulatory framework governing the SPSV sector is being determined by the National Transport Authority in the public interest rather than being shaped by the corporate structures and business models of large international platform operators.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 64 and 65 together.
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV) industry is a matter for the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
The principal function of the NTA is the development, operation and maintenance of a regulatory framework for the licensing and regulation of the standards to be applied to SPSVs, their drivers, and dispatch operators. This is done in accordance with the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016 and all associated regulations and orders.
As part of its role, the NTA continues to review and modernise the regulatory framework for SPSVs and regularly involves relevant stakeholders and the public in this process through public consultations. For example, the structure of the taxi and hackney market has undoubtedly changed since liberalisation of the market in 2002, and more notably in recent years, in relation to the role of dispatch operators. In response to this, the NTA held a Call for Inputs consultation on the dispatch operator licensing framework earlier this year. The results of this Call for Inputs exercise will be presented to the NTA’s Board later this year and a public consultation will be held soon afterwards on legislative developments arising from this Call for Inputs exercise.

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Health if the MCAP review has commenced; if stakeholders have been appointed to the review group; and the length of time the review is expected to take once it begins.
reply:

The Group will:
- Review the current operation of the Medical Cannabis Access Programme and the availability of Schedule 2 Cannabis products.
- Examine the appropriateness to expand the range of conditions covered by the programme, where sufficient evidence exists that cannabis may prove beneficial.
- Review the current access to Schedule 1 Cannabis products and the current operation of the ministerial licence.
- Develop a national policy on access to, and the administration of cannabis products that are subject to ministerial licence.
The Review Group is comprised of a wide range of medical specialists and experts including patient representatives.
The timeline for completing the “Review of Access to Cannabis for Medical Use” which also evaluates the Medical Cannabis Access Programme (MCAP) is anticipated to be in the region of 12 months from the date of the group's initial meeting which took place on 27th May 2026.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the way in which the suspension of the DOMINO scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital is consistent with the supported care pathway under the National Maternity Strategy 2016–2026; and whether the successor to that strategy will commit to protecting and expanding midwife-led continuity of care schemes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. The DOMINO Scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital remains operational and available both to women currently using the service and to new patients who meet the eligibility criteria. It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health for an update on the proposed prohibition on the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16 years of age.
reply:
Stimulant drinks, commonly known as energy drinks, are often marketed as products that improve energy, focus and performance. However, many contain high levels of caffeine and sugar and may have negative effects on health, particularly for children and young people.
In September 2026, Safefood published its report, A survey of energy drinks on the island of Ireland 2026. The report found high levels of energy drink consumption among young people, with more than half of 15 to 24-year-olds reporting that they consume energy drinks at least once a week. The report also found strong public support for restrictions on the sale of energy drinks to children, with more than three-quarters of adults supporting the introduction of a legal age restriction.
The Government recognises the public health concerns associated with the consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks by children and young people. The Department of Health is considering the findings of the Safefood report and other available evidence in relation to possible measures to reduce children's access to these products. question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health the current status of the Rotunda Maternity Hospital capital project; and the timeline for progressing this project.
reply:

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on plans to make the shingles vaccine free for people aged over 65.

HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health if the recruitment freeze in Galway University hospital will be lifted in order to fill the 23 vacant midwifery posts; and the way in which she plans to retain recently qualified midwives in Ireland while a recruitment ban is in place.
reply:
There is no recruitment embargo in place in the HSE. However, due to ongoing budgetary issues, several Regional Health Authorities (RHA) have been placed in a strengthened financial control framework. One of these is the West & North-West RHA, which includes Galway University Hospital.
In the period from 1 January 2026 to 31 August 2026, the West & North-West RHA incurred pay costs of €1,286 million against a budget of €1,254 million, equating to a deficit of €32 million (2.6%). To manage these costs, the HSE placed the West & North-West RHA in a strengthened financial control framework, one of whose measures is a requirement for HSE CEO approval of any proposed recruitment. A further requirement for Departmental sanction of any recruitment proposals was announced in recent weeks.
These controls are about ensuring that new recruitment is properly prioritised, affordable, evidenced and clearly linked to patient need. The HSE must show that the need and any patient-safety risk have been assessed, that alternatives such as redeployment, roster changes, skill-mix changes, staff banks, agency conversion, cross-site working or the use of vacancies have been considered, and that funding or a genuine recurring offset is available.
Any requests to recruit additional midwives to Galway University Hospital maternity services will be considered in this context.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health her plans to increase education about HPV, and the vaccine in schools.
reply:
Increasing vaccination uptake rates in the routine HPV vaccination programme is vital in order for Ireland to achieve elimination of cervical cancer by its target date of 2040. The World Health Organisation has set a target for all countries to ensure that 90% of girls are vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by the age of 15 years.
The ages at which vaccines are recommended in the immunisation schedule are recommended by the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC), in order to give each child the best possible protection against vaccine preventable diseases. As the HPV vaccine is a preventative measure, it is intended to be administered, if possible, before a person becomes exposed to HPV infection. Therefore, the gender-neutral HPV vaccination programme targets all girls and boys in first year of secondary school.
The Laura Brennan HPV Catch-up Vaccination Programme offered HPV vaccination to 5th and 6th year students in secondary school for the 2025/2026 academic year, as a once off opportunity, for those who previously missed the HPV vaccine while in first year of secondary school.
The second phase of the programme launched on 3 September with HSE vaccination teams visiting post-primary schools across the country to offer the HPV vaccine to eligible students.
The programme is open to:
• All eligible boys and girls in 2nd to 5th year of post-primary (secondary) school.
• Home-educated young people born between 1 September 2008 and 31 August 2013.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 544 and 594 together.
The Cross Border Directive allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the cross-border directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.

It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Transport if his attention has been drawn to the rising increase in driving test wait times as reported today (details supplied), particularly in Dún Laoghaire where wait times have risen again to 19 weeks this month and the impact this is having on those waiting for tests for employment/education and other reasons; if he will outline the immediate steps he is taking to bring down waiting times permanently; and if emergency slots have been considered for those who can provide supporting evidence of the necessity of an early test.
reply:
Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for all aspects of the National Driver Testing Service.
The latest information provided to me by the RSA indicates that, as of 19 September, the average waiting time for an invitation to book a driving test at the Dún Laoghaire/Deansgrange test centre was 18 weeks. I am assured by the RSA that work is continuing to reduce waiting times in line with the target 10-week service level agreement.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she is familiar with the remit of the UK Office of Public Guardian; and which Irish statutory body performs the same or similar functions by investigating allegations of mistreatment of elderly people at the hands of family members who may have powers of attorney over their affairs.
reply:
In Ireland, under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 (2015 Act), the DSS has statutory responsibility for the review, registration and supervision of Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPA), including the investigation of complaints in relation to the execution of a person’s responsibilities as an attorney under the Act. Safeguarding of adults with decision-making difficulties is central to the EPA application and registration process under the 2015 Act.
As part of the registration process for an EPA, the DSS must review it with regard to the suitability of the attorney and its compliance with the 2015 Act. There are also notice periods set out in the 2015 Act which enable notice parties to object to the registration of the EPA on number of grounds, including, inter alia, that the donor did not have capacity, that fraud, coercion or undue influence was used to induce the donor to execute the instrument creating the EPA, or that the attorney is not a suitable person to carry out that role.
If non-compliance issues are identified but not addressed and/or objections are deemed to be well-founded, then the DSS will decline to register the EPA, a decision that may be appealed to the Circuit Court. These measures help to ensure that the attorney is suited to the role and will act in line with the person’s will and preferences.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the reason private supervised-access providers, including an organisation (details supplied), can continue to be used under court orders where a State agency has raised safeguarding concerns and ceased using the provider; the regulation and oversight that applies to such providers; whether courts are notified of safeguarding or vetting concerns; the reason no State supervised-access service exists; and whether the use of Garda branding by private providers is authorised.
reply:
In relation to the supervised access provider referred to by the Deputy, Tusla has advised that it has not used its services since 2024 and has blocked its use as a provider to Tusla.
In a small number of cases, Tusla uses external providers, such as supervision and access centres, often at the direction of the courts. These services are typically used when a child is in the care of Tusla.
With regard to the commissioning of these services, a process exists, as it does for all external third-party providers, to register with Tusla. This involves a governance process, including confirmation of qualifications, Garda vetting, mandatory training and membership of relevant professional bodies, among other checks.
Any reports prepared by such providers form only part of the overall evidence presented to the courts. Where commissioned by Tusla, reports are considered in the context of individual case management and are ultimately subject to scrutiny by the courts, where they may be challenged by contradictory evidence, for example from social workers, guardians ad litem, psychologists, foster carers and parents.
It is important to acknowledge the independence of the courts in family law proceedings. Tusla is only one of a number of parties that may contract or arrange supervised access services on the basis of court orders.
In many family law cases, Tusla may have no involvement at all, the case may be entirely between the parents.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the individualised or person-managed funding arrangements are currently available to disabled people who require substantial personal assistance; can an existing HSE-funded care allocation be transferred into an individualised or person-managed arrangement; and if not, the current pathway for someone in these circumstances to obtain such an arrangement.
reply:
A personalised budget is a payment made in lieu of specialised disability support services that would otherwise be arranged or provided on the individual's behalf. Personalised budgets enable individuals to organise and manage their own support arrangements in a manner that best reflects their needs, preferences and goals.
To test the delivery of personalised budgets in an Irish context, a Personalised Budgets Demonstrator Pilot was launched in 2019 with a view to identifying the best approach for the wider roll-out of the model following the initial demonstration phase.
The Pilot was established on a cost-neutral basis and expressions of interest for participation were sought from disabled adults in receipt of HSE funded specialist disability services.
In 2023, responsibility for specialist disability services transferred from the Department of Health to the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth (now the Department of Children, Disability and Equality), and with it, responsibility for the Personalised Budget Demonstrator Pilot.
The Pilot concluded in May 2025 and subsequently entered its evaluation phase, led by the National Disability Authority (NDA). The NDA has produced an evaluation report that is now nearing finalisation. The report sets out key findings from the Pilot, drawing on the experiences of participants, families and other stakeholders.

question: Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she will ensure that social care workers working with children and young people in State care, in the community and voluntary social care sector Section 56 organisations funded by Tusla can access the public service pension, and that this is not restricted as planned to specific entities and residential roles outlined in the decades old Section 66 of the Child Care Act 1991, at a time when retention of these professionals is challenging and to avoid two-tier pension access for these critical professionals.
reply:
Pay is one of a number of challenges impacting the early learning and care and school-age childcare workforce. The level of pay for early years educators and school-age childcare practitioners does not reflect the value of their work for children, families, society and the economy.
Although the Government is the primary funder of the sector, it is not the employer and cannot directly set wages or conditions for any staff in the sector.
The Joint Labour Committee is the formal mechanism established by which employer and employee representatives can negotiate minimum pay rates for different roles across the sector, which are set down in Employment Regulation Orders, and is independent in its functions.
Pay and conditions are improving. Through the work of the JLC and successive ERO’s, minimum pay rates have now risen three times in four years, delivering an average 15% increase in minimum rates of pay. This marks significant progress in professionalising the workforce. The latest ERO came into effect in October 2025 which saw an increase in minimum pay rates of, on average, 10% and is estimated to have increased pay for over 67% of staff in the sector.
Outcomes from the Joint Labour Committee process are supported by Government through Core Funding. question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will review HSE guidance and training for adult disability services on the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, particularly how staff should assess and manage foreseeable safety risks when a person wishes to leave a service unaccompanied; how families’ views should be considered, consistent with the person’s rights; and whether she will issue clarification to providers.
reply:
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act (2015 Act), which commenced in 2023, marked a landmark reform of Ireland’s capacity laws, bringing the state into much closer alignment with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The commencement of the 2015 Act represented an important shift away from a ‘best interests’ approach to a rights-based approach, privileging a person’s will, preferences and autonomy.
The 2015 Act brought an end to wardship in the State for adults by repealing the outdated Lunacy Regulation (Ireland) Act 1871 and replacing it with a rights-based model of tiered decision support arrangements. This new suite of tiered decision support arrangements is designed to enable those with diminished decision-making capacity to retain as much control over their own lives as possible, and over the decisions that affect them.
The HSE has developed a range of training and resources for staff across the HSE and HSE-funded services, including disability services, to support the implementation of the 2015 Act in practice. This includes e-learning programmes on supporting decision-making in health and social care, as well as guidance for healthcare workers on applying the legislation in practice.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question 62049/26, if the statutory public consultation process has concluded; if the amendments to the CIÉ pension schemes have been agreed; and when retirees of CIÉ will finally receive their long awaited pension increase.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.
Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department is progressing the agreement of bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including review of the relevant draft Statutory Instruments, and the matter of increases to pension payments.
Under the Transport Act, 1950, a Statutory Consultation process is required regarding amendments to CIÉ Pension Schemes, which took place over the early summer 2026, and representations from interested parties are currently under review.
Every effort is being made to progress this matter at the earliest, keeping in line with the appropriate procedures, compliance with all applicable requirements, and necessary approvals as part of the formal process, which is now well underway and imminent.

question: Deputy David Cullinane asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the waiting lists for an assessment of need at end September in each of the years 2022 to 2026, nationally, by region and integrated healthcare area; the number of applications at each stage of the process; the number of assessment reports overdue for completion; the number of applications overdue by more than six, nine and 12 months; the number of service statements overdue and issued within and outside the one-month timeframe; the number of applications involving privately procured assessment; and the number of applicants referred to or supported by another service, in tabular form.
reply:
The delivery of an effective, efficient Assessment of Need system is a priority for the Government.
While an assessment of need report is not required to access to children’s services, including Primary Care, Children’s Disability Services Teams, CAMHs, or education supports, demand for Assessments of Need has increased significantly in recent years, reflecting both the increase in population and the number of families exploring all options to access services for their child. The number of applications for assessments of need have almost tripled since 2020, with over 13,100 applications received in 2025. The most recent HSE data for Q2 2026 shows that 7,100 applications were received in the first six months of this year. The level of demand has exceeded the capacity of the system to meet it and has contributed to there being over 23,282 assessments overdue for completion by end-June.
These delays are unacceptable, and the delivery of an effective, efficient Assessment of Need system is a priority for the Government. There has been intensive work by the Department and the HSE to address delays in the provision of assessments of need to children and their families. This is evident in the continued improvement in the number of completed assessment of need reports with 5,939 reports completed nationally in 2025 - a 43% increase compared to the number completed in 2024. This improvement is reflected in the 3,043 reports completed in the first half of this year and must continue.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the circumstances in which sustainability funding may be provided to an early learning and childcare service required to relocate as a consequence of defective concrete; the categories of expenditure which may be supported under such funding; and whether the funding can contribute towards temporary relocation, long-term relocation or replacement accommodation.
reply:
The sustainability fund for service providers is a support mechanism introduced to ensure the stability and viability of early learning and childcare services for those participating in the Core Funding model. The fund is accessed through a collaborative process involving the service, their local City/County Childcare Committee (CCC), and Pobal, who assess financial eligibility and need.
A childcare service required to relocate due to defective concrete may be eligible for Sustainability Funding under the Emergency Relocation Supports strand. This strand provides community not-for-profit services facing financial difficulty with once-off funding to assist with rental and relocation costs while alternative long-term accommodation is secured.
Once a service engages with their local City/County Childcare Committee, they will be able to avail of supports through the case management process.
Contact details for all City and County Childcare Committees are available on the gov.ie website.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the policy measures in place to ensure that childcare capacity is maintained within communities where an existing early learning and childcare facility is affected by defective concrete; and the supports available to prevent the permanent loss of childcare places in such areas.
reply:
The defective concrete blocks issue is an ongoing wider government issue. Responsibility for defective concrete blocks remediation and capital reconstruction rests primarily with other government Departments and local authorities. The Department of Children, Disability and Equality does not have direct responsibility for structural remediation or compensation for defective concrete affected buildings.
However, the Department of Children, Disability and Equality works with Pobal and local Childcare Committees to offer Case Management Supports to services in difficulty. Through this, services may also access Sustainability Funding following an assessment of need. There are examples of sustainability funding for services who needed to relocate due to defective concrete.
Any service which is affected by defective concrete blocks should contact their local City/County Childcare Committee in the first instance.
The City/County Childcare Committee will assist the service in finding a suitable alternative location and will engage with Pobal and the Department regarding sustainability funding to facilitate the relocation of the service.
The local City/County Childcare Committees will also source suitable alternative places for children in attendance of these services to ensure minimal disruption to their learning and care should the service be unable to relocate.
Contact details for the CCCs can be found at City and County Childcare Committees.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional measures that can be introduced to prevent the illegal hunting of livestock by lurcher hounds in the Loop Head peninsula.
reply:

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will designate Greencastle Harbour, County Donegal as a pelagic landing port for catches over ten tonnes, considering the safety concerns for those vessels that currently have to land at the next nearest designated harbour in Killybegs.
reply:
I am advised that a key component of Ireland's Control Plan, operated by the Sea Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA), currently in force for pelagic landings is that of pre-transport, control-supervised weighing undertaken on publicly-owned weighbridges - which Greencastle port does not have at present.
In light of this, there are no current plans to designate Greencastle port in the manner suggested by the Deputy.
However, I would also like to assure the Deputy that the designation of ports for landings does not preclude vessels from coming into ports for force majeure reasons such as safe harbour.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to detail the methodology which will be used to calculate grants and premiums rates for the next forestry program.
reply:

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to list the number of engagements between his Department and the European Commission in relation to the next forestry programme.
reply:
The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) contains a general prohibition on the use of State aid to prevent distorting the internal market. However, the TFEU also provides for a number of specific policy objectives that may be supported through the use of State aid by a Member State.
Ireland’s next Forestry Programme will therefore require State Aid approval from the European Commission to implement. This requires submission of a formal application under the Guidelines for State aid in the agricultural and forestry sectors and in rural areas. All efforts are directed towards building on the potential contained in our current Forestry Programme 2023-2027 for the post 2027 period, so that we can continue to deliver lasting benefits for climate change, biodiversity, wood production, economic development alongside quality of life.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine given the importance of afforestation towards climate change mitigation, if his Department will conduct annual reviews when targets are constantly missed in order to address shortcomings, if changes are advised.
reply:
The 2024 Climate Action Plan recognises that afforestation is one of the largest land-based, long-term climate change mitigation measures available to Ireland and sets out the Government’s target of 8,000 hectares of new forestry per year.
The Forestry Programme 2023–2027 provides the implementation mechanism through financial incentives and a range of different forest types available to landowners for afforestation. The 8,000 hectare target is an ambitious one, as forestry remains demand led and is a complex land use choice which is not solely based on incentives. Progress towards this target is closely monitored and my Department are continually developing opportunities to increase the rate of planting.
Last year, my Department prepared a Forestry Opportunities Map which incorporates environmental considerations and associated mapping layers relevant to the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. The Forestry Opportunities Map fed into the Land Use Review (Phase 1 and 2) which forms part of the Programme for Government. The map identifies areas most suitable for planting, primarily based on environmental considerations and soil productivity.
Further, in March this year my Department published the results of a Mid-Term Review of the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. This included a comprehensive package of financial and administrative measures which provided for increases in grants and premia in key areas including forest roads, fencing and agroforestry. question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine in the context of negotiations on revising the EU Animal Transport Regulation, increasingly frequent extreme heat events, the position Ireland is taking on proposed temperature requirements; and if Ireland supports species/category-specific temperature ranges based on EFSA evidence (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 484, 486 and 488 together.
In December 2023, the EU Commission published a legislative proposal for new rules on the protection of animals during transport, to replace the current EU Regulation (EC) No 1 of 2005 protection of animals during transport and related matters in the context of the EU’s Farm to Fork Strategy. Ireland is strongly committed to improving animal welfare standards during transport and supports the revision of the EU Regulation for this sector.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the projected allocation to Ireland under the Common Agricultural Policy in the European Commission's proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028 to 2034, compared with the allocation for 2021 to 2027, in tabular form; if CAP funding will remain ring fenced under the proposed single national and regional partnership plans.
reply:
In July 2025, the European Commission published its proposals for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as part of its wider proposals for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for the period 2028–2034. These proposals represent a significant structural change to the current model of CAP delivery, as it is proposed that the CAP will form part of a broader National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP), which consolidates several EU funding streams under a single framework.
It is important to note that the funding for the CAP forms part of the broader EU budget negotiations, which is negotiated by Finance Ministers, and is ultimately agreed by Heads of State and Government.
Under the proposals, Ireland’s indicative ring-fenced CAP allocation is €8.162 billion, within a total NRPP allocation of €11.4 billion.
Over the current programming period of the Multiannual Financial Framework (2021-2027), Ireland receives approximately €10.7 billion in EU funding for the CAP.
Comparing the proposed allocation for Ireland’s CAP for the 2028-2034 period with the current CAP period is not a like-for-like comparison. Different interventions or schemes are included in the €8.162 billion ringfenced amount, compared to the €10.7 billion figure for 2021-2027.
In addition, the proposed framework is intended to allow Member States the possibility to supplement CAP interventions from the wider NRPP allocation, thereby offering flexibility to address national priorities.

question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of the 40 new dog warden roles promised that have now been allocated; and if a breakdown of such allocations will be given by Council areas.
reply:
In July 2024, Government funding of €2 million was announced for local authorities to support the resourcing of additional dog warden services in 2025. The funding was intended as a contributory allocation towards the hiring of additional dog wardens. The funding was not intended to provide for the full cost of employment, rather to act to defray the overall cost of same. This funding recognises the increased demands in the area of dog control. Funds were provided to 30 local authorities to support the resourcing of additional dog warden positions in 2025.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 468, 469, 470 and 474 together.
All IPAS accommodation centres are inspected each year, either by HIQA, by Department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the Department. The inspection regime, along with a range of other key quality and compliance actions, has been stepped up significantly over the last 18-24 months, as the Department works to improve standards and value for money across the IPAS system. In 2026 to date, 332 inspections have been completed, covering 261 separate properties. These inspections are fully transparent and available online on gov.ie.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if Garda vetting is required for staff working in designated accommodation centres for beneficiaries of temporary protection; the complaints process in place in these centres; and the safeguarding measures in place in these centres.
reply:
Garda vetting of employees is a matter for employers to manage in Designated Accommodation Centres, as my Department does not directly employ staff working in accommodation settings for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection from Ukraine.
